films.x: Follow one enrolment from a tap on a phone to a decision, through Databricks and dbt.
c: You just enrolled in your first university class.
One tap. It feels like nothing happened.
But that tap was written straight into the student system, the system of record: a snapshot of that moment.
Now it's about to travel through a platform most people never see.
Let's follow it.
Every system at the university keeps its own records: students, learning, people and finance.
Think of each one as its own colour of light.
Some changes travel as events, the moment they happen.
An integration platform routes them, retries them and keeps them secure,
and Zerobus Ingest lands them in the lakehouse within seconds.
Other data arrives in bulk, as files, like the nightly file of new offers.
Auto Loader reads each new file exactly once, and remembers where it stopped.
Everything lands in bronze, exactly as it arrived.
Only what matters right now travels hot. The rest can wait for the next delivery.
Before any of this can make sense, we need a sketch of the world we're trying to understand.
What is a student? A class? An enrolment? And how do they connect?
That's the conceptual model: agreed with the business, and written down once.
Get the sketch wrong, and the pieces never fit.
Every picture built on top of it is wrong too, no matter how clean the data is.
Get it right, and every piece has its place.
Now the refining starts. dbt holds the recipes: models, tests and documentation, all in version control.
Databricks runs them, on a SQL warehouse.
Look closer at bronze, and the pieces are rough:
glitches, duplicates, errors, different formats, different clocks.
First, dbt declares each source, and checks that it's fresh.
Staging models clean each source: clear names, one format, one clock, no duplicates.
Tests run at every step. A missing value stops here.
Intermediate models join the sources, exactly as the sketch says.
An enrolment with no matching class stops here.
What comes out is silver: one clean, consistent picture of the university.
And every step is recorded, so any piece can be traced back to the tap that started it.
Then the light is split again, this time into business domains: teaching, students, research and finance.
Each domain holds many data products. Think of them as paintings.
The subject is the domain. The style is what the audience needs.
Analysts get every detail.
Executives get the essence, in a few bold shapes.
Government reports get a painting made by strict rules, like counting students on census date.
Live operations get a quick impression of right now.
In dbt, each painting is a mart with a contract and an owner: a data product.
And its label is an exposure, recording where the painting is shown, and to whom.
That's gold.
Step back, and the whole system comes into view.
Application domains flow in on one side.
Bronze keeps what arrived. Silver makes it consistent. Gold makes it useful.
Business domains flow out on the other, into dashboards, apps and Genie.
dbt governs every step, from source to exposure, and its lineage maps every connection.
And the Databricks lakehouse runs and stores it all, governed by Unity Catalog.
But pictures without meaning are just noise.
The platform is the bricks. Meaning is the shared language.
In the dbt Catalog, anyone can read what each picture shows, where it came from, and who owns it.
Words are defined once: an enrolled student is one still enrolled on census date.
Unity Catalog marks trusted data as certified, decides who can see what, and masks personal details.
And a university's knowledge lives everywhere: intranet pages, policy libraries, the handbook, process maps.
Through MCP, a standard plug that lets AI connect to other systems,
the platform reads those sources where they live, with your permissions.
Together with the sketch, they become one map of meaning: Genie Ontology.
Some questions need one answer, right now: is there still a seat in Tuesday's 9 am class?
Others need every record, over years: which classes fill up first?
Different jobs, different engines.
Lakebase, a Postgres database built into the platform, gives apps a fast desk copy of what they need,
kept in sync automatically, with changes flowing back.
Now the pictures go out, four ways.
Events: when something changes, the integration platform rings a bell, and each system comes back for exactly what it needs.
SQL endpoints: a reading room where tools can scan millions of records for big questions.
Copies: for older systems that can't read the originals, the integration platform delivers copies.
Useful, but every copy has to be kept up to date.
And the fourth way changes everything.
A projector shows the original somewhere else, without making a copy.
OpenSharing projects live research data to a partner university.
Mirroring lets Microsoft Fabric see the same pictures in place.
Federation turns the projector around, so we can see other systems where they live.
One original. No copies to keep in sync.
People meet the data in two ways.
Apps: a Databricks App shows an officer a student's record,
she fixes a wrong degree code, and the correction flows straight back into the platform.
And conversation: Genie.
Ask: which first-year classes need more seats next semester?
A Genie Agent answers with certified numbers and shows its sources, guided by Genie Ontology.
And it only shows you what you're allowed to see.
One tap became a snapshot, then a clear picture, and finally a decision:
a new class opens, and 140 more students get a seat.
Move less. Mean more.

films.x: Two trusted numbers disagree. When does a simple model need more precision, and how do you use a reference model without copying it?
c: In The Inner Life of Data, we drew a sketch of the university: a student, a class, an enrolment, a term and a course.
It was an oversimplification. Good enough to start, not good enough to count.
That's normal. Every model starts simple, and gets sharper when a real question needs it.
The day after census date, the Head of School asks Genie a simple question.
How many students were enrolled in Data Science 101 on census date?
Genie says 131. The certified census report says 118.
Both come from clean data. Every test passed.
The difference isn't in the data. It's in the meaning.
So before we change anything, we ask a wider question: how does this kind of business generally work?
In many industries, someone has already modelled it, and their model makes a good first template.
Often there's more than one to choose from, so which one you pick, and why, matters too.
TCSI could be one of the choices: it's public, and it describes the data Australian universities report to government.
Many universities actually use MortarCAPS, the sector's own data standard. Here, we'll check our sketch against TCSI.
It's a reference to check against, not a model to copy. We'll see where it fits our business, and where it doesn't.
First question: what is a class?
Lay the reference over our sketch, and it has no class at all. It has units of study, and enrolments in them.
Our one box was hiding three things.
The unit: Data Science 101, the subject itself.
The offering: that unit, in one teaching period, at one campus. This is what students enrol in.
And the class: the Tuesday 9 am tutorial, a place in the timetable.
Genie counted places in tutorials, and some students sit in two.
So say exactly what one row stands for. That's called the grain.
Next: where does the census date live?
Our sketch put it on the term: one date for everyone.
The reference records it with each unit enrolment, because each unit of study has its own census date.
A summer intensive of Data Science 101 has a census date weeks away from the semester's.
Put each detail on the thing it truly describes. Here, we adopt the reference.
Now, two students appear twice in the count.
Each is studying a double degree: data science, and business.
Our sketch said a student belongs to one course. That's not how the university works.
The reference already has the answer: a course admission. One student, in one course, from one start date.
Each unit enrolment counts towards one course admission, so each student is counted once.
When two things connect many to many, the link often deserves its own box.
Last question: enrolled when?
Genie counted today. The census report counted on census date.
Enrolments change. A student is waitlisted, then enrolled, and later withdraws.
The reference keeps each enrolment's current status. We need its history, so we extend the model.
Each change is kept with its date, and the census count becomes a snapshot of one day.
The sketch is sharper now. But it's still a sketch.
This is the conceptual model: the things that matter, and how they connect, agreed with the business.
Zoom in, and it becomes the logical model: what identifies each thing, its details, and how many of each.
Zoom in again, and it becomes the physical model: the actual tables in the platform.
Same meaning, three levels of detail. The business owns the first, engineers own the last, and all three must agree.
How to build those tables is a story for another film.
Lift the reference away, and you can see the whole fit.
Check: before you invent something, look for it in a reference model.
Adopt: where it fits the business, use its ideas and its words.
Extend: where the business needs more, add it, in the same style.
Record: write down every difference and why, so the next person knows what is standard and what is ours.
A reference is a starting point, not a cage. Where the business is truly different, the business wins.
The Head of School asks again.
This time, Genie asks back: enrolled on census date, in the Semester 1 offering?
Then it answers: 118, and shows how it counted.
The sketch has a new version, and a note that says why it changed.
It won't be the last. Models evolve: not often, but always.
Check the reference. Fit it to the business.

films.x: Language and meaning. Four offices give four answers to one question: how many credentials did we award? To see why, the film goes back before writing, and before words.
c: It's graduation week, and the Deputy Vice-Chancellor wants one number for the speech: how many credentials did we award this year?
Four offices answer, with four numbers.
The registrar says 7,420. Short courses says 10,600. Careers says 14,650. The learning platform says 26,900.
Nobody is wrong. Each office is counting a different idea, under the same word.
To see why, we have to go back. Before computers, before writing, before words.
In the 1960s, researchers showed pigeons hundreds of photos. The birds learned to peck at the ones with people in them, even photos they had never seen.
Honeybees can learn the idea of same and different, and use it on colours and patterns they've never met.
No words at all. Yet each of them sorts the world into kinds.
Concepts come first. Words come later, to point at them.
Vervet monkeys give different alarm calls for different hunters.
A leopard call sends the group up into the trees.
An eagle call makes them look up, and dive into the bushes.
A snake call has them stand tall and search the grass.
Each call stands for a kind of thing, and everyone who hears it knows what to do.
Some animals go further. Dolphins, elephants and marmosets use calls that work like names, for one individual.
A kind of thing, and one particular thing: categories, and identifiers. Every data model needs both.
A baby points before it can talk, to share what it's looking at with you.
That shared attention is the root of every word: this one, here, that.
Human words go further than any call. They combine without limit, and they reach things that aren't here: yesterday, a promise, a rule.
Even what someone knows. You can't see it. So people have always needed words, and later records, to show it.
When did speech begin? Nobody knows exactly. Words leave no fossils.
Inside the human brain, researchers have found single cells that respond to one person: to photos of them, a drawing of them, even their written name.
Many forms, one idea.
Think of it as a triangle. A word points to an idea in someone's mind, and the idea points to things in the world.
The word never touches the thing directly. That gap is where misunderstandings live.
A philosopher imagined a stranger pointing at a running rabbit, and saying: gavagai!
Does it mean the rabbit? Its ears? This moment of running?
Children solve this every day. They guess the whole thing first.
But every word hides a choice: what counts as one. Data modellers call it the grain.
Credentials have a grain, too. Mei has a degree and two microcredentials. Count graduates, and she's one. Count credentials, and she's three.
Ask people to picture a bird, and most will think of a robin or a sparrow. Hardly anyone thinks of a penguin.
Categories have typical members in the middle, and fuzzy edges.
We agree about the middle. We argue at the edges.
Is a degree a credential? Of course. A microcredential? Probably. A badge for turning up to a workshop? That's where the four offices part ways.
Words move, too. Nice once meant foolish.
Credential comes from the Latin for belief. Enrol meant writing a name on a roll. A diploma was a sheet of paper, folded in two.
Ambassadors still present their credentials: letters asking their host to trust the person who carries them.
Meaning moves slowly, and a word's history often explains its edges.
Back at the university, there's no system in sight. Just four offices, and a sheet of paper.
First, what is a credential? A trusted statement, that others can check, that someone has shown what they know or can do.
Awards and microcredentials are credentials. So are badges, when the learning was assessed. A badge for turning up isn't one.
The recipe is Aristotle's: name the kind of thing, then say what sets it apart.
Each word gets an owner and a date, and the sketch gains a box, in pencil. Version three, draft.
The answer for the speech is 11,890. And each of the four numbers now has a name.
Two of them counted things that aren't credentials: badges for turning up, and certificates of completion. Nobody lied. Until today, there was no agreed question.
None of this needed a computer. Contracts open with their definitions. Mergers stall on what counts as a customer. Funding depends on who is counted.
Agreeing on words is real work: people with different needs, trade-offs, and time. Disagreeing costs far more.
About five thousand years ago, people began pressing marks into clay, to keep records that outlast memory.
From minds, to marks, to systems. But before you can count anything, you have to agree what it is.

films.x: Models and systems. For more than a thousand years, credentials have had the same parts: someone trusted makes a claim about someone, in a way others can check. Today that idea lives in five systems, each with its own model of it, and the film shows how a conceptual and a logical model hold them together.
c: Almost four thousand years ago, student scribes in Mesopotamia practised on clay. Some of their school tablets hold a teacher's model, with the student's copy beside it.
In medieval Europe, a journeyman became a master by making a masterpiece: one piece of work, judged by the masters of the guild.
In China, imperial examinations tested candidates for thirteen centuries, and the rank they earned opened the way to office.
At medieval universities, a chancellor granted the licence to teach, under a wax seal. Then came the diploma, the transcript, the digital badge, and today, a credential signed with a digital key.
The materials changed every few centuries. The idea didn't.
Look closely, and every one of them has the same parts.
Someone trusted issues it: a guild, the examiners, a university.
It names a holder, and makes a claim about them: this person can do this.
It rests on evidence: a masterpiece, an examination, an assessment. And it has a date.
Someone else can check it: by the seal, by the signature, or today, by the digital key. Some expire. A few are revoked.
Today's standard for digital credentials uses almost the same words: issuer, holder, verifier, claims and evidence.
A conceptual model can outlast every material it was ever written on.
At the university, credentials now live in five systems.
The student system holds awards. The learning platform, completions. Careers, badges. A digital wallet, the signed copies.
And the new short-course platform, bought off the shelf, holds the microcredentials. It calls learners customers.
Buying a system means adopting its model, whether you look at it or not.
If you don't model your business, your vendors will do it for you.
Connect five systems in pairs, and you need up to ten translations. Each one is a place where meaning can slip.
In 1999, a spacecraft was lost at Mars. One team's software gave the thrusters' push in pound-force seconds. The navigation software expected newton-seconds.
Each program ran without an error. The meaning broke between them, and nobody held it to the spec.
So translate each system once, to a shared model. Five translations instead of ten, and one place where the meaning is written down.
Take one learner, Aisha. She has four IDs: a student number, a platform login, a customer number and a wallet address.
Her name comes from the student system, her email from IT, and her credentials from three different places.
Choosing which system is the source of each fact, and linking the records that are the same person, is master data management.
And shared lists of values, such as the kinds of credential, keep a word meaning the same thing in every system. That's reference data.
The sketch on paper says what matters. The logical model says it precisely.
What identifies a credential? Who issued it, to whom, for what, and when.
Its attributes, and the values each may take: the level, the volume of learning, the status.
How many of one relate to another: one learner holds many credentials, and one microcredential can count towards several awards.
And the rules: a revoked credential is never counted.
Still no technology. That's what makes it useful: it's the yardstick every system is held against, to choose a package, to map its fields, or to move to a new one.
Every part has an owner. The registrar owns the word award. The short-courses team owns microcredential.
Noor, the data architect, owns the logical model, and each team owns its own tables.
A change of meaning travels down, from the words to the systems. News of a change in a system travels up, before it ships.
Owners decide. Stewards keep it written down, and up to date.
The short-course platform still calls them customers. Nothing inside it changed.
But its customer now maps to learner, and its certificate to microcredential. The meaning is joined.
Systems come and go every decade or so. The ideas underneath them are centuries old.
Model them once, precisely, and hold every system up to that. Next: one model, many shapes.

films.t: Built to write, built to read
films.x: Shapes for data. On graduation day, thousands of awards are written one at a time; on planning day, ten years of them are read at once. Merchants in Venice kept the same facts in two books for the same reason, five hundred years ago.
c: In 1494, Luca Pacioli set down how Venetian merchants kept their books.
Every transaction was written into the journal, as it happened, one after another.
Then each entry was posted to the ledger, grouped by account, where it could be read, and balanced.
One set of facts, kept in two shapes: one for writing, and one for reading. And if the two sides didn't balance, something was wrong.
Five centuries later, the university has the same two jobs. On graduation day, thousands of awards are issued, each one complete and right. On planning day, someone reads ten years of them at once.
A shape built to write keeps each fact in one place. The learner's name is stored once, not on every award.
Every row has a key that identifies it, and rules the data must meet: every award belongs to a learner who exists.
And issuing an award touches three things at once: the award, the learner's record, and the transcript. All three change, or none of them do. Half an award is never saved.
This is normalisation, with keys, constraints and transactions.
Store the learner's name on every award instead, and it lives in three places.
She changes her name. Two copies are corrected. One is missed.
Her next certificate prints the old name.
And if the only place a course is described is on its awards, deleting the last award deletes the course.
These are called update and delete anomalies. Keeping each fact once is how a shape built to write avoids them.
Some systems write a whole thing at once, as one document: a digital credential, with its claim and its evidence inside, signed as a single piece.
Keep together what's written, and signed, together.
Document databases are built for this. They shine when a whole thing is written, and read, at once.
One document is easy to write and easy to check. Counting across a million of them is harder.
Planning day. How many awards, by faculty and by year, for the last ten years?
A shape built to read starts with the grain: one row per credential awarded.
The numbers to add up sit in the middle: the award itself, and its credit points.
Around them sits everything you'd filter or group by: the learner, the kind of credential, the faculty, the date.
A simple test: the facts are what you add up; the dimensions are the words after by, in the question.
It's called a star. Reading it takes two steps, not seven.
A learner moved faculty in the middle of the year. Do her awards count for the old faculty, or the new?
Keep both, each with the dates it was true. Awards before the move count for the old faculty, and after it, for the new.
An award that's revoked and reissued keeps its history too. Nothing is overwritten. Each change has a date.
Not every change needs history. Correcting a typo can simply overwrite. A move between faculties can't. Decide for each attribute, and write it down.
Engineers call this a slowly changing dimension.
Now ask both shapes the same question.
The shape built to write needs seven joins, and a puzzle about history.
The shape built to read answers in two.
Then correct a name. Easy where it's stored once. Awkward in a shape that repeats it on purpose.
Each shape is fast at its own job.
One sketch. Two shapes, both built from the same logical model.
And a common confusion, cleared up: bronze, silver and gold say how refined data is, not what shape it has.
Many platforms keep a normalised shape in silver, close to the sources, and stars in gold. That's a choice, not a rule.
Any layer can hold either shape. The next question is which shapes to use for reading. There are several.

films.x: Shapes for reading. Four engineers argue for four shapes, while credentials from a new source wait to be added. The film follows them through each job, integrating, presenting and serving, and puts each shape in its place on the platform.
c: For most of the twentieth century, a library's card catalogue filed each book three times: under its author, its title and its subject.
One book on the shelf. Three ways in.
Every card had to be kept in step with the book, or readers went to the wrong shelf.
Data for reading works the same way: copies arranged for the questions people ask.
Ask four data engineers how to shape data for reading, and you may get four answers: a normalised core, a data vault, a star, or one wide table.
The arguments have names: Inmon's integrated core, Kimball's stars, Linstedt's data vault, and one big table.
This week, there's a new source to add: credentials from the short-course platform.
There's no best shape. There's a best shape for each job.
The first job is to bring many sources together, under one meaning.
One way is a normalised core: a shape built to write, but for the whole university.
Another is a data vault. Hubs hold the business keys, the things that identify a learner or a credential. Links hold the relationships between them.
Satellites hold the descriptions, and every change to them, with the source and the time each change arrived.
A new source just adds new satellites. Nothing that exists has to change.
It's built for change, and for audit. It isn't built for people to query.
For people, there's the star: one for awards, one for enrolments, one for fees.
They share the same learner and the same calendar, so one question can cross them: awards and fees, for the same learners, in the same year.
These shared dimensions are called conformed. They make the stars agree with each other.
Engineers plan them on a grid called a bus matrix: the business processes down the side, the shared dimensions across the top.
Some questions are always about one thing: one learner.
So build one wide row per learner: their current course, their credit so far, every credential, and what's next.
It's easy for people, for machine learning and for AI assistants. Most questions become a single lookup.
Which learners are close to a graduate certificate? With a wide table, that's one filter, not five joins.
The cost: many columns to maintain, and the same measure defined twice, unless you're careful.
On the platform from The Inner Life of Data, each shape has its place.
Silver integrates, in a normalised core or a vault.
Gold presents stars for people, and serves wide tables to tools.
And a semantic layer can sit on top, so every tool asks for the same definitions.
Many sources that keep changing, and auditors who ask where each value came from: a vault.
Many processes that share the same context: conformed stars.
One entity, asked about in many ways, by people and by AI: wide tables.
And don't copy for its own sake. Every shape is another copy to keep in step, like the library's cards.
Choose per question, not per fashion. Most platforms use more than one.
The short-course credentials arrived this week. The vault took them without changing a thing.
The award star gained new rows, and each learner's wide row gained a column.
Next: what if the app and the analysts used the same database?

films.x: Hybrid databases. In 1879, a cash register added each sale to the day's total; within a few years, registers recorded each sale too. Today, hybrid databases write and read in one place, and remove the copy between them; they don't remove the model.
c: In 1879, a saloon keeper in Ohio patented a machine to keep track of every sale at his bar: the cash register.
Within a few years, registers rang up each sale as it happened, and kept a running total, ready to read at closing time.
Recording and counting in one place. It's an old wish.
At the university, writing and reading still live apart.
The app writes to its own database. Overnight, a copy travels to the lakehouse and gets refined, and the answer is ready tomorrow.
But some questions can't wait. An employer wants to check a credential now. A learner's wallet wants to show, now, how close she is to a graduate certificate.
That distance is why hybrid databases appeal.
A hybrid database writes and reads in one place.
Some keep two copies inside: rows for writing, and columns for reading, kept in step by the database itself.
Others put an operational database inside the lakehouse, with tables synced in both directions.
The idea has a name: HTAP, hybrid transactional and analytical processing.
Keeping two shapes in step means capturing each change as it happens, and applying it on the other side, in the same order.
That only works if every row has a stable key, so an update finds the row it changes, and a delete finds the row it removes.
Apply an award's revocation before its issue, and the award comes back to life. Order matters as much as content.
What goes? The nightly copy, the pipelines that move it, the wait, and a second set of permissions to keep in step.
Those are real gains.
Now count awards straight from the app's own tables.
Revoked awards are still in there, with a status. Last year's faculty has been overwritten. The count comes out wrong.
It's the same mistake as counting enrolments today, instead of on census date.
History, shared dimensions and definitions still need modelling. Hybrid removes the copy, not the model.
Data flows the other way now, too. Gold data is served back to the app: the next microcredential to suggest, or a learner who may need help.
Features for machine learning travel the same way: calculated in gold, served in milliseconds.
And AI agents need both shapes at once: they read what's known, and write down what they did.
So the modeller has new questions. For each idea, which shape is the source of truth?
Which way does each table sync, and who owns it?
How fresh must each answer be? Seconds for a wallet. A day for a plan.
Where do the definitions live, so the app and the report agree? In one place, not two.
And the data contracts from Silent change now run in both directions.
One logical model. A shape for writing, and a shape for reading, on one platform, with a shorter distance between them.
Hybrid removes the copy, not the model.
Next: making the meaning itself something a machine can read.

films.x: Meaning and AI. Asked which learners are one microcredential away from a graduate certificate, Genie finds the right tables and still guesses wrong: the stacking rules sit in a policy and an old web page that disagree. The film shows four ways to write meaning down, and how they stack.
c: In the 1750s, Linnaeus gave each species a two-part name, and a place in a hierarchy. Scientists still use his system.
Nearly a century earlier, John Wilkins designed a language to classify everything in the universe. It never took hold.
In 1860, Florence Nightingale asked hospitals to record the same things, in the same way, so that they could be compared.
An international list of causes of death followed in 1893. Today, it's the International Classification of Diseases.
Shared definitions let strangers compare. The ones that last are made for a purpose, not for everything.
At the university, the Head of School asks Genie: which learners are one microcredential away from a graduate certificate?
Genie finds the tables. It finds a column called is_micro, and another called stack_ok.
It reads the stacking rules too: in a policy document, and on an old web page. They don't agree, so Genie guesses, and it's wrong.
An assistant answers from what it reads. Meaning outside a managed glossary, with no owner and no version, can contradict itself, or be wrong.
There are four common ways to write meaning down, and they stack. A glossary: words and their definitions, for people.
A taxonomy: kinds of things in a hierarchy, like Linnaeus's.
An ontology: concepts, the relationships between them, and rules that a machine can check and reason with.
And a semantic layer: how each number is calculated, defined once.
They aren't rivals. Each one answers a different question.
In the ontology, the rules are written as statements. A microcredential is a kind of credential. A graduate certificate accepts up to four approved microcredentials towards its credit.
Connect the university's data to these statements, and it becomes a knowledge graph: learners, credentials and courses, linked by what they mean.
It's Aristotle's recipe made formal: the kind of thing, and what sets it apart, in a form a machine can use.
Where does all this meaning live? In Noor's architecture map, each data domain lists its entities: learners, credentials, certificates.
Each concept is written once: its definition, how it relates to the others, and the rules it follows.
The glossary shows the definitions, for people. The conceptual model shows how the concepts relate. The logical model adds how many, and the keys.
When a machine has to reason, the ontology is extracted from the same map, in OWL, the Web Ontology Language. Rules that check the data become tests.
They don't compete: they come from one map, so they agree. Change the map, and the views follow.
In the semantic layer, credentials awarded this year is defined once: what's counted, what's left out, which date, and at what grain.
Dashboards, spreadsheets and Genie all ask it, instead of each writing its own version.
Open formats for sharing these definitions between tools are starting to appear.
You don't have to start from a blank page. Finance, health, insurance and retail all publish shared models, and so does education.
Digital credentials have open standards too, with issuer, holder and evidence in them.
Even microcredential has official definitions: from Australia, from the European Union, and from UNESCO. They don't quite match.
So choose deliberately. Check, adopt, extend and record, as in A Sharper Sketch, at every layer.
This time, the meaning comes from one source of truth, the glossary. In Databricks, its definitions now sit on each table's page, next to the data.
The Head of School asks again. Genie reads the definitions, and asks back: approved for stacking, or all microcredentials?
Then it answers, and shows the definition it used.
Studies have found that grounding an assistant in explicit meaning makes its answers measurably more accurate. The difference is meaning it can read, and trust.
The triangle from the start of the series returns: the word, now in the glossary; the idea, now written in the ontology; and the data it points to.
Next: keeping all of it true, while everything changes.

films.x: Keeping meaning current. The meaning is written down end to end, from a word to a number. Then the world changes again, and an AI agent can watch, draft and check, while people decide.
c: In 1755, Samuel Johnson published his dictionary. He had hoped to fix the English language in place.
In its preface, he admitted that no dictionary can embalm a language. The Oxford English Dictionary is still being revised today.
In 2006, astronomers agreed a definition of planet. Nothing in the sky changed, and the count went from nine to eight.
In 2019, even the kilogram got a new definition.
Meaning moves. Every definition needs an owner, a date and a version.
At the university, three changes arrive in one month.
The government adds a new field to what universities report about microcredentials.
A credential was issued in error, and has to be revoked.
And a new measure, completion rate, appears in three dashboards, with three different definitions.
Models rarely break all at once. They drift.
A value nobody announced, as in Silent change. A column whose meaning slowly shifts. One measure, defined twice. A standard, updated for a new year.
Drift is the gap between what's written down and what's actually used.
This is where AI helps first. An agent can read the catalog, the lineage, the queries people run, and new data as it arrives.
It compares each definition in the glossary with the code that calculates it, and spots where the two have parted.
It flags each drift, with evidence: three definitions of completion rate, and the dashboards that use each one.
Noticing is tedious for people, and cheap for machines.
Then it drafts the change.
A new entry for the glossary. A new statement in the ontology. The logical model, the mapping to the government's field, the semantic layer, the contract, the tests, and a note saying why.
Drafting is cheap now. Judging the draft is still the job.
Mei, from the registrar's office, approves the meaning. Noor, the architect, approves the model. The teams approve the build.
The agent's draft goes through the same review as anyone's. The tests run on the proposed change, before anything ships.
The agent recommends. People approve. Everything is versioned.
A confident draft can invent a definition that nobody agreed.
A change can slip through that nobody reviewed. And an agent that learns from old reports can propose an old meaning back.
So the tests and the contracts check the agent's work too, just as they check ours.
Follow one change all the way through.
Completion rate gets one definition in the glossary, one statement in the ontology, one measure in the semantic layer, and one test.
The three dashboards agree. Genie gives the same number, and shows why.
Last year's report still reads with last year's definition, version two, unchanged. Each number keeps the meaning it had.
And the sketch's stamp finally reads: version three.
New ways to shape data keep arriving: data vaults, anchors, hooks, bridges, activity streams. More will come.
Look inside any of them, and you find the same four answers.
What a credential is. What makes it the same one everywhere. What one row holds. And when each thing was true.
What changes is the shape. Engines change, and an agent can draft a vault or a star from the model in minutes.
A search can find two credentials that look alike. Only the model can say whether they're the same one.
Learn the part that lasts: meaning, identity, grain and time. Every new shape is another way to write them down.
Back to the start of the series: a word, an idea, a thing, and a mark in clay.
A credential is a claim that others can check. So is every number in a report.
The tools have changed. The job hasn't: agree what things are, write it down, and keep it true.

films.t: Moving is easy, agreeing is the work
films.x: Moving data today. HR's contracts once reached Finance as a file each teaching period, and Rohan Desai's team spent two days working out what each column meant. Now a connector, a query in place and a mirror move them with little work. What's left is the contract Ingrid Holm and Noor Rahman agree.
c: June 1883, on the Murray River, the border between two British colonies: New South Wales and Victoria.
At Albury, a new bridge joins the railway from Sydney to the railway from Melbourne.
But each colony had built its railway to its own gauge: the distance between the two rails.
Victoria's rails were about a hand's length further apart, so no train could run on both.
At Albury, every passenger had to change trains, and every crate and bale of wool was lifted into another wagon.
It cost travellers time, and traders money, on every journey.
Each colony had its reasons: New South Wales changed its gauge with a new engineer, and Victoria kept the one both had first chosen.
For 79 years, everything stopped at Albury, and it would go on stopping until the rails agreed.
In 1962, Australia's government, with New South Wales and Victoria, opened a new line from Albury to Melbourne, built to one agreed gauge.
Freight ran straight through that January, and from April, passengers did too, with nobody changing trains.
Within a year, the freight it carried had grown by a third.
At the university, HR's contracts once reached Finance as a file each teaching period.
Rohan Desai's team spent two days working out what each column meant.
Moving the data was never the hard part. Agree what it means, once, and it passes straight through.
Modern data basics is about what the tools now make easier.
Moving data, running a platform, serving data to people and agents, and reading documents all used to take whole teams.
Databricks and dbt now do much of it.
Each film shows what got easier, what still needs people to agree, and where the official docs take you next.
We don't go deep, on purpose: courses and the official docs do that, and they stay up to date.
These films give the architectural advice: what matters, what to choose, and why.
Our story follows one contract. Linh Nguyen tutors HI101 this semester, on contract T-26188.
It was born in the HR system, which sends its data in two shapes, as The Inner Life of Data shows.
Events: each change as it's made. HR recorded Linh's contract on 14 July, and it reached the platform as one change.
And batches: on 20 July, the first day of the teaching period, the HR system sent its whole file again.
Events, messages and batches have had names since Hohpe and Woolf's Enterprise Integration Patterns, over twenty years ago.
What changed is how little it now takes to move them.
A managed connector brings a system's data in.
Sam Okafor, who runs the platform, picked the HR system and the tables to bring.
The connector reads only what changed, tries again when a read fails, and keeps its place.
Linh's contract lands in bronze, just as the HR system sent it.
A query in place reads another system without copying it in.
Finance's general ledger stays in the finance system, and the platform reads it there, without changing it.
For large volumes, or quick answers, the docs recommend a connector instead.
A mirror goes the other way: it shows the university's catalog in another team's tool, without copying it out.
Rohan works in Microsoft Fabric, and the platform's tables appear there, read where they live.
A share gives a partner the data where it lives, as Products in open formats and The marketplace showed.
And an API serves data on request: an app asks, and gets just what it needs.
Each does what teams once built and mended by hand. Moving is easy now.
So what's left for people? The contract at each interface: what the data means where two systems meet.
Ingrid Holm, in HR, owns the HR system's data.
Noor Rahman, the data architect, agrees its contract with her.
First, what each field means. pay_type has three values: CAS, FT and CON.
CON means continuing, not contract. Read it wrong, and Finance counts continuing staff as casual.
Second, who answers for it: Ingrid, by name.
Third, what a deletion means. When a contract is cancelled, HR deletes it.
So the contract says how that arrives: as a change, with its time, never as a row that's just missing from the next file.
The platform then closes that contract, and keeps its history.
Fourth, what's personal. Names, birth dates and emails come across, marked personal.
Bank details and rates of pay never leave HR.
They write it down in the Open Data Contract Standard, and Jun Park's tests check every row against it.
Silent change shows what happens when a new value arrives, and only one side knows what it means.
And A platform that watches itself shows a night when a field changes, and its contract doesn't.
At Albury, the trains always ran. What took 79 years was agreeing the gauge.
Now HR's contracts reach Rohan in Fabric the day they're made, meaning just what HR means, and nobody spends two days on them.
There are already standards for this.
Enterprise Integration Patterns for how data moves, and the Open Data Contract Standard for what it means.
Don't reinvent the wheel. Investigate, adapt, implement and iterate, starting from the official docs.
If these basics are still a struggle where you work, look first at your governance or your tooling: other modules here show both.
Let the tools move it; spend your time on the contract.

films.x: Data freshness. Until September, the university moved almost all its data once a night, and asked, everyone wanted theirs live. Contract changes came too late, and 23 tutors were paid two weeks late. Now Noor asks when someone acts on each kind of data, and it arrives in time for that.
c: April 1850. In Aachen, on Prussia's western border, Paul Julius Reuter sells the news of Europe's stock exchanges.
A telegraph line runs from Berlin to Aachen. Another runs from Paris to Brussels.
Between Aachen and Brussels, 122 kilometres with no wire.
Bankers and merchants buy and sell on the prices from other cities' exchanges, and they act the same day.
Across the gap, the prices went by train, and arrived hours after the day's trading had begun.
A price that comes after you've had to decide is no use to you: someone else, with fresher news, has made the deal.
Reuter's clients didn't need the prices at once. They needed them before they acted, so the news had to cross the gap faster.
So Reuter and Heinrich Geller, an innkeeper in Aachen who bred pigeons, flew the prices across the gap.
Each bird carried a thin slip of paper, from Brussels to Aachen, and the telegraph sent it on to Berlin.
The birds crossed in about two hours, six hours ahead of the train, so the prices arrived while there was still time to use them.
And it was only for a while: the pigeons filled the gap until the wire was joined.
Fresh enough means there in time for whoever acts on it.
Until September, the university moved almost all its data once a night. And asked, everyone wanted theirs live.
Some came too late: 23 tutors were paid two weeks late, and two people's pay went to a thief.
Now each kind of data arrives in time for the action it serves, and no sooner than it's needed.
In September, Noor, the data architect, asked one question of each kind of data: when does someone act on it?
Ask people if they'd like their data fresher, and they'll always say yes.
So Noor didn't take the answer from a question. She looked at real use: when people open the data, and what they do next.
Acted on days or weeks later: cold. A batch, once a night or once a week.
Acted on within minutes or hours: warm. Small batches, every few minutes or every hour.
Acted on within a second or less, usually by a machine: hot. Each event, the moment it happens.
The platform should offer all three. Which one each kind of data gets is the business's call, not the platform's.
Each answer goes into the data's contract: how fresh, and the action it's fresh for.
Each morning, Rohan, in Finance, and the faculties' managers look at what each faculty has spent this year against its budget.
Asked in August, Finance wanted it live, to the minute.
Noor looked at what happens next: spending is talked over once a month, and only then does money move between budgets.
Yesterday's figures are fresh enough. A view works them out each night at two, ready to read by seven.
It's a dbt model Jun wrote, with its schedule, tested like any other.
Most analysis is like this, and should stay cold: people decide over days and weeks, and a nightly run costs a small part of a stream.
Casual staff claim their hours in the claims app, and claims approved by noon on Monday are paid on Thursday.
The app checks each claim against the tutor's contract, which lives in another system: HR's.
Ingrid's team in HR often changes a contract on a Monday morning, while coordinators approve claims until noon.
Until September, the platform brought those changes across once a night, so the app saw them on Tuesday.
Too late for noon: that's how 23 tutors came to wait two more weeks for their pay.
Why through the platform at all? Ideally, contracts and claims would live in one system, and the new ERP will bring them together, in 2028.
Until then, the platform fills the gap, as the pigeons did.
Every organisation runs old systems beside new ones, so the ideal path is rare. Working around the gaps is part of the job.
Now the HR system pushes each change as it's made, through Zerobus Ingest.
Every five minutes, a pipeline brings the changes into a table of every contract as it stands.
This Monday, eleven contracts changed in the morning, and every claim against them was approved by noon.
Five minutes is fresh enough for a person who approves claims all morning, and it costs far less than a pipeline that never stops.
Hot is for when no person is waiting to decide, and the action must come at once, or it's useless.
In August, someone stole two staff members' passwords, and changed their bank accounts the night before pay day.
Their pay went to a stranger's account, and they waited three weeks to be paid again.
No report read the next morning could have stopped it: by then, the money had gone.
Now each bank account change is checked the moment it's made, against the sign-in behind it.
If it comes from a new device close to pay day, a rule holds that one pay within a second, and asks the person to confirm.
Since September, four changes were held. Three were the people themselves, confirmed within the hour; one was not.
But an event carries only what changed. The full record, and every correction, still comes in the nightly file.
So hot never comes alone: it needs the cold path beside it, and it costs the most, because it never stops.
Very few needs are like this. Keep hot for a machine that must act now.
In 1851, the wire closed the gap, and the pigeons were no longer needed.
Reuter took his news service to London, and from there to the world.
At the university, each kind of data now arrives in time for the people, or the machine, that act on it.
Spending, each night; contracts, every five minutes, until the ERP comes; a bank account change, within a second.
Today, 2,960 people are paid, 856 of them casual staff, Linh among them.
How fresh data must be is set by when someone acts on it, not by what the platform can do.
Where data is kept, and for how long, is another question, for a later film.
Start from the official docs, then investigate, adapt, implement, iterate.
Next: one copy of the claims, for the app and for Finance.

films.x: Two engines, one copy. At the university, tutors' claims went round by email, and payroll and Finance each kept a copy that never quite agreed. The new claims app writes each claim once, on Lakebase, and payroll, the claims job and Finance read that same row through Unity Catalog. No pipeline, no second platform.
c: Amsterdam, around 1600.
Ships from all over Europe trade there, and merchants pay each other in coin.
Between 800 and 1,000 kinds of coin change hands, many clipped, shaved at the edge for their silver, or worn thin.
Every payment means weighing coins, and nobody knows what a bag of them is really worth.
On average, coin there is worth about 9% less than good coin: a merchant owed a thousand guilders may get coin worth about nine hundred.
Payments are slow, disputed and risky. Amsterdam's trade needs money everyone can trust.
On the 31st of January 1609, the city opens an exchange bank, the Wisselbank, in its town hall.
Merchants bring their coin once. The bank weighs it, and writes its value in its ledger, on the merchant's own page.
From then on, a payment is a line moved from page to page, with no coin carried, and the ledger shows what each merchant holds.
Merchants pay about 5% more for a guilder in the ledger than for one in coin.
For over a century, bills from all over Europe are paid there.
Data has its bags of coin too: the same data copied into every system that needs it, each copy a little different.
At the university, tutors' claims went round by email, and payroll and Finance each kept a copy that never quite agreed.
Now each claim is written once, and payroll and Finance read that one copy.
Thursday, the 5th of November 2026: pay day at the university.
Linh Nguyen tutors HI101 on a casual contract, paid for the hours she claims.
Claims used to be spreadsheets sent by email and typed again by payroll.
The faculty kept its own tally, and Finance saw the hours only after pay day.
So when the university built an app for claims, the usual design was ready:
the app on its own database, a pipeline copying each change to an analytics platform, and reports on the copy.
Two platforms, a pipeline between them, two sets of permissions, and a copy always a little behind.
Noor, the data architect, chose one copy on one platform instead.
The claims app is built on Lakebase, the Postgres database in Databricks.
Linh writes each claim once, as a row, and her coordinator approves it in that same row.
Postgres serves the app. The platform keeps the same rows in a second form for analysis, so the lakehouse reads them without slowing it.
Payroll's list of claims still waiting and the job that builds the hours to pay both read that copy.
So does Finance's casual teaching cost, and all three read through Unity Catalog.
Each table has one writer. The app writes the claims.
The lakehouse writes the contracts from the HR system, and a copy goes to the app, which checks each claim against its contract.
As in Amsterdam's ledger, a claim is written once, and read where it's written.
What's gone: the pipeline, the second database, and the work of keeping two copies in step.
The integration services that ran between separate platforms come together on one.
One catalog governs who may read the claims for analysis, with the same permissions, lineage and audit as every other table.
What still moves? Payroll pays from a payroll system the university buys, which isn't on the platform.
So each pay run, the hours to pay leave the platform by noon on Tuesday, under a contract with payroll.
One thing moves, on purpose, instead of a copy of everything.
The night it fails comes later, in A platform that watches itself.
So, what should you choose?
Keep one copy where you can, and move data only when a reader truly needs it somewhere else.
Decide which system writes each table, and let the others read it.
Where a system you buy keeps its own copy, agree the contract at that interface, as Moving is easy, agreeing is the work showed.
Both at once showed one database that writes and reads. Here, one copy serves a whole platform.
There are already standards for this, so don't reinvent the wheel.
Investigate, adapt, implement and iterate, starting from the official docs.
In Amsterdam, a payment became a line moved in one ledger, and the same ledger showed what everyone held.
At the university, Linh's claim is one row: she writes it, her coordinator approves it, payroll pays it and Finance counts it.
Today, 856 casual staff are paid from rows like hers, and no team had to copy a claim to get there.
Keep one copy, governed once.

films.x: Where data is kept. Until September, the university kept all its data in the same storage, the costliest, whether it was read every day or once in seven years, and no old pay record was ever deleted. Now each kind is kept where it's read, and deleted when the law no longer asks for it.
c: February 2008. Deep in a frozen mountain on Svalbard, Norway's Arctic islands, a vault opens.
At minus eighteen degrees, it keeps copies of seeds from gene banks around the world.
Gene banks keep the seeds of crops and their wild relatives, so breeders can grow crops that stand drought and disease.
Near Aleppo, in Syria, a gene bank keeps 141,052 samples of wheat, barley, lentils and chickpeas, from the world's dry lands.
From 2008, it sends copies of most of them to the vault.
But a gene bank can be lost, to war, flood or a power cut, and a variety lost is lost for good.
In 2012, war came close to Aleppo. Most of the bank's keepers had to leave, and it could no longer send seeds out.
Breeders could no longer get the seeds they relied on, and every variety in the bank was at risk.
Unless the copies could come back, the collection would be lost for good.
In 2015, the keepers did what no one had done before: they asked the vault for their copies.
38,073 samples came out of the mountain, and that November they were sown in Lebanon and Morocco.
By 2020, nothing was left of the collection in Aleppo.
Yet no more than 1,657 of its samples were lost, and breeders can order its seeds again.
Seeds in use, kept close and ready; their copies, frozen far away, until the day they're needed.
Data can be kept the same way.
Until September, the university kept all its data in the same storage, whether it was read every day or once in seven years.
Years of old pay records filled the costliest storage, and none was ever deleted: a cost, and a risk to everyone in them.
Now where data is kept follows how often it's read.
In September, Noor asked each data owner a second question, after how fresh it must be: how often is it read?
Cloud storage comes in tiers, named hot, cool, cold and archive, after how often data is read.
The names sound like data's temperature, but they answer another question: not when someone acts on it, but how often anyone reads it.
Each tier down costs less to keep, and more to read. The archive tier takes hours to bring a file back.
So keep what's read often where reading is cheap, and what's rarely read where keeping is cheap.
How long it's kept at all is set by the law and the business, and it goes into the data's contract.
Every pay day, payroll sends the platform a record of each pay, with the hours each casual tutor worked.
Australian law asks employers to keep pay records for seven years, and after the first, they're rarely read.
Until September, every year's records sat in the hot tier, and none was ever deleted.
Now, a year after it's written, each file moves to the archive tier, the cheapest to keep.
Like the copies on Svalbard, they sleep until someone needs them.
The table is told, so queries for recent pay still run, and one that needs an archived year says which files to bring back.
Bringing them back takes hours, which is fine for an audit.
When a year's records turn seven, they're deleted, on a date set in advance, and their files removed for good.
In October, the oldest records, more than seven years old, were deleted.
How to delete well is for the films on data protection.
One record moves down as it ages.
Today, Linh's pay record is written. This year it's read often: for her payslip, a question, the year's end.
A year from now, its file moves to the archive tier, where keeping it costs a small part of what it did.
If an audit asks for it, it comes back in hours.
Seven years after her contract ends, it's deleted, and its files are removed for good.
At each step, where it lives follows how often it's read.
On Svalbard, the vault stays cold and still. In Lebanon and Morocco, the bank sends out its seeds again.
At the university, data is kept the same way: what's read often, where it's quick to read; old pay records, cheaply, until they're deleted.
Today, a pay day, 2,960 new pay records are written, Linh's among them.
How often data is read decides where it's kept; the law and the business decide for how long.
Storage has had tiers for years: there's no wheel to reinvent.
Start from the official docs, then investigate, adapt, implement, iterate.
Next: data as software, where scripts became software.

films.x: Data work as software. Every second Thursday, Rohan in Finance needs what casual staff are paid. For years a script on one person's laptop told him, until the claims moved in February and nobody could change it safely. Sam and Jun move it into the data project: tested, reviewed by someone else, released the same way.
c: Washington State, the 1st of July 1940.
A new bridge opens across the Tacoma Narrows, its road hung from two great cables: a suspension bridge.
Its deck, the road itself, is light and slender, built to the best theory of its day.
From the first day, the deck rises and falls in the wind, and people call it Galloping Gertie.
Nobody had tested how wind would move a deck like it.
On the 7th of November, a wind of about 40 miles an hour sets it twisting, until its middle tears away and falls into the water.
No one is killed, but the only road across the Narrows is gone for ten years. The next bridge had to be proven before it was built.
The engineers who looked into it said such bridges must first be tested as models in a wind tunnel, where a fan blows a steady wind.
At the University of Washington, Frederick Farquharson tests models for years.
The tests find a deck the wind can't twist: deeper, stiffer, and open to let the wind through.
The new bridge opens in 1950, tested before it was built, and it has carried traffic for 76 years.
Wind tunnels weren't new: wings had been tested in them since the Wright brothers. Bridges took up a practice from next door.
Data work did the same, and took up how software is made.
At the university, payroll's export to Finance ran for years as a script on one person's laptop.
Now it's software: tested before every change, reviewed by someone else, and released the same way every time.
Thursday, the 5th of November 2026: pay day at the university.
Every second Thursday, Rohan Desai in Finance needs to know what casual staff are paid that day, by faculty and unit.
For years, a script on one person's laptop told him.
Before six on each pay day, someone ran it by hand, and emailed its file to Finance.
Payroll's rule was inside it: a claim approved by noon on the Monday before is paid that Thursday; approved later, it waits two weeks.
It worked, and nobody is to blame. Its author moved to another team, and it kept running.
Then in February, the claims moved into the claims app, and the spreadsheets it read stopped coming.
One copy, no history of why, and no test to say if a change broke it: nobody could change it safely.
Sam Okafor, who runs the platform, and Jun Park moved it into the data project.
First into Git, beside the models, where every change is kept, with who made it and why.
Its sums became a model in dbt, and the rule is written once, on HR's calendar of pay days.
Ingrid Holm in HR confirmed the rule; a change to the pay days now starts with a ticket from HR.
Jun wrote the tests first, at the rule's edge: approved at 11:59 on the Monday, a claim is paid that Thursday; at 12:01, two weeks later.
In the weeds of data crafting shows how, in Declare it, then build it, Promises and proofs, and Built in layers.
Each change goes on a branch, and comes back as a pull request, with checks that build it and run every test.
Then someone else on the data team, not its author, reviews it.
Jun wrote the model, so Sam reviewed it; Sam wrote the job, so Jun reviewed that.
Nothing merges without that review, and every check green.
Finance and HR don't review the code: Rohan asked for the move in a ticket, linked to its branch and pull requests.
Change without surprises shows how a change reaches the people it touches.
And it holds when an agent writes the change: the agent proposes, and a person approves.
How it runs is a file too: a Declarative Automation Bundle lists the project's jobs, and where each one runs.
Payroll's export runs at six every Thursday, and builds and tests everything it reads.
Once a change is merged, the same files are deployed to test, and the job runs there first.
Rohan checks its figures in test against his own, and his ticket stays open until he says they're right.
Then the release waits for Noor, the data architect. When she approves, the same files go to production.
It runs as the platform's own account, never a person's: nobody deploys from a laptop.
The same files, the same steps, every time, so test and production can't drift apart.
This morning at six, it ran for the eighteenth time, and 856 casual staff are paid today.
None of this is new: software has been built this way for decades, and data work took it up, as bridges took up the wind tunnel.
So keep data work as software: in Git, tested, reviewed by someone else, and deployed the same way every time.
The next film, A platform that watches itself, follows a night when a job fails.
There are already standards for this, so don't reinvent the wheel.
Investigate, adapt, implement and iterate, starting from the official docs.
The bridge of 1950 was tested before it was built, and it still stands.
Payroll's export is tested before every change, and pay day is just another Thursday.
Data work is software.

films.x: Running the platform. On the night of Monday 2 November, the job that sends casual staff's hours to payroll fails: the claims app now sends 1:30 where it sent 1.50. By morning, the platform has traced the cause, said what it touches and proposed a fix. Sam reviews it, Noor approves it, and pay goes out on Thursday.
c: The twentieth of July, 1969.
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin are flying their lunar module down to the Moon, its computer steering.
Five minutes in, a light comes on, with a code: 1202.
The computer has more work than time.
The crew don't know the code, and ask Houston.
If the computer stopped, nothing would steer them; if Houston called an abort, they'd turn back without landing.
Someone had to decide, in seconds.
The computer's makers, at MIT, had built it to watch itself:
with too much to do, it starts again, keeps the steering and its most important work, and drops the rest.
And it raises the alarm, so people can decide.
In Houston, the guidance officer, Steve Bales, twenty-six, had just helped review its alarms:
1202 meant go on, unless it came too often or the descent went off course.
Half a minute after the alarm, the word goes up: go.
Four more alarms come; each time, go.
And Eagle lands.
The computer watched itself and said what was wrong, and people who knew decided.
This November, a job that pays the university's casual staff fails one night.
By morning, the platform has found why and proposed a fix, and a person decides.
At the university, casual staff, paid by the hour, claim the hours they teach in an app.
On the Monday before each pay day, at ten at night, the claims job builds the hours to pay, and sends them to the payroll system.
On Monday the second of November, at 3:02 in the afternoon, a new version of the app goes live.
Tutors can now type their hours as they say them: 1:30 for an hour and a half, where it sent 1.50.
Its contract still says decimal hours.
At 22:03, the job fails: it can't read 1:30 as a number.
Nothing wrong reaches payroll: the job stops, and the hours wait.
Payroll needs them by noon on Tuesday, to pay 856 casual staff on Thursday.
But the platform is watching.
Sam, who runs the platform, has Genie ZeroOps watching the pay run's jobs and tables:
an agent that works in the background, with nobody asking.
It finds the failure, at 22:03.
It traces the cause through lineage, to the claims app's table, where the hours changed form at 3:02.
It says what the failure touches: the hours for the payroll system, payroll's export, and casual teaching cost.
And it proposes a fix: read 1:30 as one and a half.
By morning, it's one insight in Sam's inbox, and nothing in production has changed.
It can trace only what the platform knows, so keep the lineage, and who owns what.
Tuesday, half past eight.
Sam checks the cause against the claims, and asks the agent to push its fix to a new branch.
It pushes only when a person asks, and confirms.
Sam opens a pull request, and its tests run, as they do for every change.
Then someone who didn't write it approves: Noor, at 9:05.
An agent never approves.
At 9:20, the job runs again, and payroll has the hours by ten.
On Thursday, 856 casual staff are paid, Linh Nguyen among them.
The platform proposes; a person approves.
The fix mended the night, not its cause.
The app's change was a good one, for tutors; what was missing was a step.
So Sam also opens a ticket for Ingrid Holm, in HR, who owns the claims' data: change the contract first, next time.
Then everyone who reads the hours knows, before the app changes.
On Apollo 11, the cause took a night to find:
a document between two systems had said too little, so a radar's electronics took about 13% of the computer's time.
For the next missions, the checklist changed, and the software learned to check.
Watching systems isn't new: site reliability engineers have done it for years, with alerts, people on call and blameless reviews.
What's new is that the platform does the first hours of the work, overnight.
Choose what it watches, keep the lineage and the owners it reads, and decide who reviews and who approves.
There are already standards, so don't reinvent the wheel:
investigate, adapt, implement, iterate, starting from the official docs.

films.x: Answers on demand. Rohan Desai, in Finance, needs what casual teaching has cost the Faculty of Health this semester. It used to take a report from the data team, and a week. Now he asks Genie One and gets A$1.84 million, with its query, and the questions asked every pay day get one dashboard.
c: London, 1936.
To know the exact time, people rang the telephone exchange, and asked the operator.
She read it from the clock on the exchange wall.
But it was never quite exact to the second.
And the exchange couldn't always answer just when a caller asked.
So a clock or a watch set by that answer could be out.
And the time is a question everyone asks, again and again.
The answer had to be there whenever anyone asked.
So the Post Office's own engineers built a machine to answer it: the speaking clock.
Jane Cain, one of the operators, recorded its words on glass discs.
A clock played them at the right moment.
And every hour, it was checked against Greenwich, where Britain's time was kept.
From 24 July 1936, anyone in London could dial TIM, for time.
They heard the time, right to a tenth of a second, at any hour of the day or night.
In less than a year, it answered more than 12 million calls.
The exact time, on demand, for anyone.
And that question no longer needed an operator.
At the university, the questions asked every pay day came in a 40-page report.
Any other question waited a week, for a report of its own.
Now any question is answered when it's asked.
And the questions that come back have a dashboard of their own.
Thursday, 5 November 2026: pay day at the university.
Rohan Desai, in Finance, is setting next year's budget for casual teaching in the Faculty of Health.
Casual teaching is done by staff paid for the hours they work, like Linh Nguyen, who tutors health informatics.
First he needs one number: what casual teaching has cost Health this semester, so far.
That used to take a report from the data team, and a week.
Today he asks Genie One, in his own words.
Like the time in 1936, the answer comes when he asks: A$1.84 million, so far.
With it, Genie says what it counted: the claims approved for casual teaching, plus on-costs.
On-costs are what the university pays on top of pay.
And it shows the query it ran, so anyone can check it.
His next question: and Semester 1?
A$2.21 million, with every claim in.
By lunch, Health's casual teaching budget is set, from this year's numbers.
Genie One answered from a Genie Agent, which Sam and Jun, in the data team, set up for this one subject.
Two earlier films show how one is built.
Here is what the team put in it.
Its data: one measure, casual teaching cost, by faculty, unit and teaching period.
Rohan defined it once, in September, as the next film shows.
Its rules, in their owners' words.
Rohan's: what cost means, and what this semester means.
Ingrid's, in HR: totals only, never one person's pay.
So it reads the measure, never anyone's claims.
Its examples: questions Finance asks, each with the query that answers it.
And its tests: questions with known answers, run after every change.
Each answer runs as the person asking, so they see only what they may read.
So the data team's work has moved.
Not a report for each question, but good models and their context, built once, for people and agents to explore.
They started small, and Rohan, who knows the subject best, was its first user.
Some questions come back every pay day, from the same people.
What did the pay run cost?
How many casual hours, in each faculty?
How many claims still wait for approval?
Like the time in 1936, they get a machine of their own: one dashboard, read at a glance.
It refreshes after each pay run, and goes to the people who act on it.
Today: A$9.6 million, paid to 2,960 people.
And 143 claims still waiting, for the next pay run.
For a question it doesn't show, its Ask Genie button opens the same Genie Agent.
It replaced a 40-page report, emailed every pay day.
The three figures people read were on its first page.
Now it's retired.
A rule of thumb: a question deserves a dashboard when it comes back on a schedule, and someone acts on what it shows.
Every other question is asked when it's needed.
In 1936, the question everyone asked got a machine of its own, and anyone could ask it, at any hour.
At the university, the questions that come back have one dashboard.
Every other question is answered when it's asked, from good models and their context, built once.
And Health's casual teaching budget was set from this year's numbers, in a morning, not a week.
None of these ideas is new; the tools now make them easier.
So don't reinvent the wheel: investigate, adapt, implement and iterate, starting from the official docs, linked on this page.
Ask for the answer; keep dashboards for the questions that come back.
Next: casual teaching cost, defined in the open, so every reader counts it the same way.

films.x: Each measure defined once. In August, three tools gave the Faculty of Health three numbers for casual teaching cost. They were three measures under one name, each its own domain's. Now Planning, HR and Finance each define theirs once, with an owner, as a metric view, and an open format carries it to any tool.
c: Near Paris, 1889. A small cylinder of platinum and iridium, kept in a vault, becomes the kilogram.
Forty copies go out to countries around the world, and each country checks its weights against its copy.
But only the cylinder in the vault is the kilogram, so about every forty years, the copies come back to be weighed against it.
By 1989, they have drifted apart, by up to about fifty millionths of a gram.
Nobody can tell which has moved, because by definition, the cylinder is always exactly one kilogram.
Every exact weighing in the world rests on one object, in one place, which could be scratched, or lost.
The kilogram had to rest on something no accident could touch.
In 2018, the world's conference on weights and measures voted to define the kilogram anew.
From May 2019, it's set by a constant of nature, the Planck constant: the same everywhere, and fixed exactly.
Any well-equipped lab can make a kilogram from it, for example with a Kibble balance, which weighs a mass against an electromagnetic force.
One definition, the same for everyone, and held by no single object or place.
In the United States, the standard of mass is now such a balance, in place of copy number 20.
At the university, a measure had the same problem.
In August, three tools gave the Faculty of Health three numbers for casual teaching cost, and nobody could tell which one was the answer.
Now each is defined once, under its own name, in a format any tool can read, and every tool gives the same numbers.
Casual teaching is the teaching done by tutors hired a semester at a time, who claim the hours they teach.
Planning next year, the Faculty of Health asked what it had cost in Semester 1.
The faculty's spreadsheet said 2.46 million dollars: the hours in the tutors' contracts.
Payroll's report said 1.88 million: the pay paid on the semester's pay days.
Finance's report said 2.21 million: the claims approved for the semester's teaching, plus on-costs, what the university pays on top of pay.
Each was right for its own question, but all three were called casual teaching cost.
Budget on payroll's number, and Health would be 330 thousand dollars short next year: about one tutorial in seven with no money for a tutor.
Each definition lived only inside its own tool, where no other tool could read it.
Like the kilogram, each number needed one definition that no single tool held.
In September, Finance, HR and Planning met with Jun Park, who builds the data project, and found not one measure, but three.
Each answers its own question, at its own moment: what the contracts allow, what is paid, and what the teaching costs.
Casual hours contracted is Planning's: Clara Jensen owns it, to plan next year's teaching.
Casual pay paid is HR's: Ingrid Holm owns it, counted by pay day, to check each pay run.
And casual teaching cost is Finance's: Rohan owns it, to set the budget, counted by the teaching period the teaching was done in.
Each owner decides what theirs means, in the glossary, before any code.
Whatever the tools, that is the minimum: every measure clearly catalogued, with its name, its owner and its meaning.
Now everyone can see why the three numbers differ, and which one answers their question.
Each measure's home is a metric view in Unity Catalog, beside the tables it's counted from.
A metric view holds a measure's definition once, and works out the right number however it's grouped: by faculty, unit or teaching period.
Unity Catalog governs it like a table: who may read it, and what reads it.
So every tool on the platform reads this one.
Jun writes it as a few lines of YAML in the data project, which builds it, as Meaning on the platform built awards conferred.
The data team reviews the code in a pull request, and Noor Rahman, the data architect, approves it for production.
Rohan, the measure's owner, is told what the change touches.
Its words go with it: a name to show, a description, synonyms for Genie, and its format, in Australian dollars.
None of this is new: for decades, BI tools have kept a layer of business definitions over the tables.
But each kept them in its own format, so no other tool could read them, and a new tool meant writing them all again.
dbt has a semantic layer too, MetricFlow, which reads measures defined in the project's YAML.
Planning counts learners near a graduate certificate with it, in the same project.
MetricFlow is open source, so other tools can build on it.
One tool for every measure is simplest, but that depends on the organisation: this university uses both.
So each measure gets one home, near most of its readers, and is never defined twice.
For tools to read each other's definitions, they need a common format: Apache Ossie.
It began as the Open Semantic Interchange, and more than fifty organisations now stand behind it, Databricks and dbt Labs among them.
Converters translate a definition between Ossie and each tool's own format: a metric view, MetricFlow, and many others.
dbt writes the project's measures in Ossie each time it reads the project, and it reads Ossie definitions too.
So casual teaching cost can go to any tool that reads Ossie, with its words and its rules, and nobody types it again.
Keep each rule inside the measure, so it travels with it.
And check what arrives: a converter says what it can't carry.
Ideally, the definition is written in Ossie first, in the data project, and the metric view is built from it.
Today, Thursday the fifth of November, is pay day.
Rohan asks Genie One what casual teaching has cost Health this semester so far: 1.84 million dollars.
The fortnightly dashboard's Ask Genie gives the same, from the same definition.
Last semester's is 2.21 million, and beside it, the other two measures, each under its own name and owner.
Rohan sets Health's budget for next year on the cost, with every tutorial's tutor in it.
Like the kilogram, each measure is one definition, written where anyone can read it, and held by no single tool.
The standards already exist, so don't reinvent them: investigate, adapt, implement, iterate, starting from the official docs.

films.x: Serving every reader. On pay day, Genie One tells Rohan Desai that casual teaching has cost the Faculty of Health A$1.84 million so far, but Finance's budget pack in Power BI says A$1.56 million under the same name. So every reader, people, reports, an app, an agent and a partner, reads one definition, each as itself.
c: Vienna, November 1968.
More people than ever drive from one country into the next.
At a United Nations conference, countries have spent a month on the rules of the road.
But their signs still differ. Many give their message in words, in the country's own language.
A driver from abroad can pass a warning of a sharp bend, and never know what it said.
And on the road, a missed warning can end in a crash.
Signs have to speak to every driver, whatever their language.
So, on the 8th of November, 31 countries sign a treaty: the Convention on Road Signs and Signals.
It defines each sign once: by its shape, its colour and its symbol.
A triangle edged in red warns. A circle edged in red forbids, or sets a limit. A blue circle says what you must do.
Today, 75 countries keep it, and a driver reads the same signs from one country to the next.
