And the signs have readers nobody planned for in 1968.
Since July 2024, every new car in the European Union must read the speed limit off the signs it passes.
Data has readers nobody planned for, too.
Casual teaching cost, defined once at the university, is read by people, Finance's reports, an app, an agent, and a partner outside.
A reader that can't reach the definition counts its own way. One that reads as someone else sees what it shouldn't.
Read where it's defined, each as itself, every reader gives the same number, and sees only what it may.
Today, at the university, it's pay day: Thursday, the 5th of November.
Rohan Desai, in Finance, owns casual teaching cost: what a semester's casual teaching costs.
In September, it was defined once, as a metric view in Unity Catalog.
Genie One reads it there when he asks: for the Faculty of Health, 1.84 million dollars so far this semester.
But in this morning's budget pack, a Power BI report said 1.56 million, under the same name.
Finance's analysts build their reports in Power BI, which reads the university's catalog through a mirror in Microsoft Fabric.
The mirror shows tables, and reads their data where it lives. But metric views don't appear in it.
So the report, built where the measure can't be seen, summed the pay paid, and called it casual teaching cost.
And through the mirror, every query runs as the one sign-in that set it up. The catalog's rights stay behind.
So the report now reads the measure from Databricks itself, through Power BI's connector, each analyst signed in as themselves.
It asks for the measure by name, and gets 1.84 million, as Genie One does.
Noor, the data architect, writes the rule down: mirror only what every reader there may see, and read a measure where it's defined.
In the Faculty of Health, Anil Kurian is planning next semester's tutors.
The faculties plan in an app the data team built with Databricks Apps.
It shows what casual teaching cost the faculty so far, beside the hours each unit will need.
Every faculty uses it, and each may see only its own.
An app can read in two ways: as itself, so everyone using it shares the app's rights, or as the person using it.
This one reads as the person, and may only run queries for them.
And the claims behind the measure carry a filter by faculty, set in Unity Catalog.
So Anil sees Health's numbers, and nothing in the app's code decides who sees what.
Let an app read as the person using it, and keep the rules where the data lives.
Every pay day, Rohan sends the deans each faculty's casual teaching cost so far.
Now Finance's pay-day agent drafts the note for him.
It asks Genie One through a tool server, as any agent can, and Genie One answers from the same definition.
Its instructions say sessional teaching cost, and Genie One knows the word: it's one of the synonyms Rohan gave the measure.
Like a car reading the signs it passes, an agent reads the words a measure is given: its name, its description, its synonyms.
The agent works alone, on a schedule, so it has a name of its own, under the same rules as people.
It may ask Genie One, and read the measure. It can't read the claims themselves: who worked which hours, and what they were paid.
It drafts. Rohan checks the note, and sends it.
Give every reader that works alone a name of its own, and only what its job reads.
Some readers are outside the university: a group of universities compares what teaching costs, faculty by faculty, each semester.
Sam shares it with them through OpenSharing: their own system reads it where it lives, so there's no copy to keep up to date.
Ingrid, who answers for HR's data, asks for one more rule: totals by faculty, never by unit.
A unit with one tutor would give away what that tutor was paid.
So the share holds one small table, made from the measure: casual teaching cost by faculty, for semesters that have ended.
The group reads the same definition's numbers, and nothing more.
Outside the platform, share the least a partner needs, and make it from the definition.
Back in Finance, pay day ends with one number.
1.84 million dollars for Health so far: in Genie One, in Power BI, in the app, and in the agent's draft.
And each reader sees only what it may.
Like the signs agreed in Vienna, the definition was made once, for people, and machines read it too.
But unlike a road sign, data isn't for anyone who passes: every reader shows who it is.
And every reader is written down in the data project, so a change to the measure names who it touches.
Read each measure where it's defined, through a door that carries it.
Let each reader read as the person it acts for, or as itself, with only what it needs.
And outside, share the least.
There are standards for all of this already, so don't reinvent the wheel.
Investigate, adapt, implement, iterate, starting from the official docs.
Even the road signs' convention keeps improving: a new text comes into force next week.
Next, the module's last film: files, read as data and as context.

films.t: Files as data and as context
films.x: Invoices, contracts and claims. In October, Finance received 3,860 supplier invoices, most of them PDF files, and typed each one in by hand; in September, one was paid twice. HR keeps every signed contract, and tutors claimed hours on spreadsheets. Each kind of document gets its own answer: read it, keep it, or write it as data.
c: Washington, 1842. A small office of the United States Navy kept its charts, and its ships' old logbooks.
A logbook is a ship's daily record: where it was, the wind, the weather, and the current, the sea's own flow.
Thousands of days at sea were written there, each ship in its own way, and nobody read them again.
So captains sailed the routes they knew, not the winds and currents that were really there.
Passages took weeks longer than they had to: more weeks at sea for the crews, with food and water running low, and cargo and letters late.
The answers were already in the logs. Someone had to read them.
So the office read its old logs into tables: the winds and currents of each patch of ocean, month by month.
From them, it drew wind and current charts, free to any captain who would keep a log in one set form, and send it back.
In 1853, at Brussels, ten nations, with the statistician Adolphe Quetelet in the chair, agreed one log for ships of every flag.
By the office's own count, ships sailing by the charts cut the average passage to California, round Cape Horn, from 183 days to 135.
And nations began to share their weather data, as they still do today.
Documents today are no different: written for people, each in its own way.
What's written for people can be read into data where it's worth it, and what we write can be written as data from the start.
Today, at the university, three kinds of documents show three answers: read them, keep them, or write them as data.
In October, Finance received 3,860 supplier invoices, most of them PDF files, each in its supplier's own layout.
Rohan Desai's team checks every one before it's paid: who sent it, its number, its date, its total, and each line.
For years, they typed them in by hand, and in September, one invoice, sent twice, was paid twice.
Now every file lands in a volume: a place for files, governed in Unity Catalog as tables are.
A function, ai_parse_document, reads each file: its words, its tables, and where each sits on the page.
Another, ai_extract, takes out the fields Finance names, one row for each invoice.
Each row keeps the path of its file, so anyone can open the invoice it came from.
An AI model does the reading, so what it reads is checked like any other data, as the film Promises and proofs shows.
Jun Park's data project checks each one: is every field read, and do the lines add up to the total?
Then come Finance's own rules: has this number been sent before, and does Finance know the supplier?
Of October's 3,860, 3,734 passed every check.
126 went to a person, each with its reason. Nine had been sent twice.
The function reads, the checks sort, and Rohan's team decides, as it still approves every payment.
A signed contract is different: it's an official document, kept just as it was signed.
Nobody rewrites it as a table. Beside it goes its metadata: the contract's ID, its version, the day it was signed, and where its file is.
The HR system writes that metadata as it makes the document, so nobody has to read it back.
Linh Nguyen's contract for this semester, T-26188, has two files: the offer HR sent on 9 July, and the contract she signed on 14 July.
The offer ended on the 13th of November. Before she signed, HR added a week for marking.
In a folder, the two look alike. By their metadata, they don't.
So if Linh asks when her contract ends, a person or an agent finds the signed version, and cites its file: the 20th of November.
The films Context engineering, and Context and memory, governed, show how a document becomes an agent's context.
Who may read a contract is Ingrid Holm's to decide, in HR. Data protection, a module of its own, teaches the rest.
Best of all is a document nobody has to read back.
Claims for hours worked used to come as spreadsheets by email, and someone typed each one into payroll.
Now the claims app writes each claim as data, the moment it's made: a row any system can read.
With it goes its metadata: who claimed, on which contract, whether it's approved, and when.
What each field means is written in its contract: a YAML file, in an open standard, kept with the app's code.
It's the log of 1853 again: one form, kept by everyone, so nobody has to read it back.
Those logs were kept. More than a century later, climate scientists read them again, into over a million weather reports.
Keep the file and its metadata, and better readers can read it again.
So Noor Rahman, the data architect, gives every document one of three answers.
If we write it, we write it as data, in a standard structure such as JSON or YAML, with its metadata.
If it's official, we keep it as it is, its metadata beside it.
If it's written for people, we read it, with the platform's functions or a scraper, only where a use case needs it, and keep the file.
Every organisation's documents differ, and the standards are there already: don't reinvent the wheel.
Start from the official docs. Investigate, adapt, implement, iterate.
In short: read documents where a use case needs it, keep the file and its metadata, and write what's yours as data.

films.t: Ideas that last, features you test
films.x: Module recap, and keeping up. Data platforms change every month, so a film of every button would soon be out of date. This one looks back on what the module showed, points to the official docs, and follows Jun's team as they test a new feature on Finance's invoices in two days: investigate, adapt, implement, iterate.
c: Mexico, 1944. In the Yaqui Valley of Sonora, in the north, farmers hardly grew wheat any more.
Stem rust, a fungus that chokes the plant, could ruin a whole field of wheat at once.
One field there that year was expected to give only ten bushels an acre: a poor harvest for a season's work.
For a farmer, a ruined field meant a year's work and seed lost, and Mexico bought wheat from abroad for its bread.
And breeding a wheat that resisted the rust was slow: one generation a year, and many years before it reached a farm.
Farmers couldn't wait a decade for every new wheat.
From 1945, a wheat program of Mexico's Ministry of Agriculture, with the plant breeder Norman Borlaug, tried another way.
They grew two generations a year: one in summer, in the highlands near Mexico City, and one in winter, in Sonora, far to the north.
Each season, they crossed plants, tested them in the field, kept the few that did best, and sowed those in the other place.
Many breeders said a wheat should be bred only where it would grow. The team tried it anyway, and measured.
It cut the time to breed a new wheat in half, and the new wheats grew well in both places, and far beyond.
By 1956, Mexico grew all the wheat it needed. In the program's first twenty years, its harvest tripled.
And the testing never stopped: the rust kept changing, so the wheat had to change too.
Data platforms change too, every month. What lasts is the ideas, and a quick, honest way to test what's new.
This module walked the university's platform, from where data is born to who reads it.
In Data that moves, moving data was easy, and agreeing what each field means was the work.
How fresh data must be came from when someone acts on it, and most analysis was fine a day old.
And each claim was written once, on one platform, for everyone to read.
In Data as software, scripts became software: tested, reviewed by the data team, and released the same way every time.
And the platform watched itself, while a person decided what to change.
In From tables to decisions, answers came on demand, and each measure was defined in the open, as each part of the business means it.
And every reader, a person or an agent, read those definitions as itself.
And here, in Documents and closing remarks, each document was read, kept, or written as data.
Each idea is older than the tools that showed it.
The tools change fast: new features every month, new names, new limits.
A film that taught every button would be out of date within months.
So these films stay with what changes slowly: agree what data means, test it, govern it, and serve it when the business acts.
For the how, go to the source: each tool's official documentation and training, kept up to date by the people who build it.
Not on Databricks? The ideas still hold. Check what your own platform offers for each one: most have an answer, under another name.
Don't choose a feature because it's new, or a platform because a film showed it. Choose what answers a real need.
So how do you keep up? With a loop, small and quick: investigate, adapt, implement, iterate.
It's the breeders' two seasons again: the shorter the loop, the more you learn in the same time.
Investigate starts from a real need, not from the feature. Rohan's team typed every invoice by hand, and asked for a better way in a ticket.
Jun read the official docs on the functions that read documents: what they do, what they cost, and where they stop.
Adapt means trying it small, on your own data, in a sandbox, for a set time: two days, on 200 of September's invoices.
Jun compared what the functions read with what Finance had typed: 188 of the 200 matched, and most of the 12 that didn't were poor scans.
Two days told the team what months of guessing couldn't: where it works, and where it doesn't.
Implement means one use case, done properly: in the data project, with its tests, and a way back.
The data team reviewed the change. Then Rohan's team checked October's results, and only then was the ticket closed.
Iterate means watching what happens, and trying again: each month, the team looks at what went to a person, and why.
Not every trial ends in yes. They tried letting the model pick each invoice's cost centre.
But Finance's supplier list already gave it, so they dropped it.
A trial that ends in no costs two days, not a year.
The wheats of the 1950s are long gone from the fields. The method, two places and two seasons, is still used by wheat breeders today.
So keep the ideas, and test the features: small, soon, and on a real need.
That closes this module: moving data, running the platform, serving it to people and agents, and reading documents.
Each once took a whole team. Databricks and dbt now do much of it; what's left for people is agreeing what the data means.
Start from the official docs. Investigate, adapt, implement, iterate, and keep going.

films.s: In the weeds of data crafting
films.x: The series and its method. The opening film of a technical series for analytics engineers. Declare the data model beside the code, then build it with dbt, layer by layer and domain by domain, in four phases (ask, promise, build, keep) and ten steps, from a question to tested, versioned and documented tables.
c: In the 1870s, architects began copying their drawings as blueprints: white lines on blue paper, one copy for every trade on site.
A blueprint says exactly what the building will be: where every wall stands, how thick it is, and what it carries.
It doesn't lay a single brick.
Data has blueprints too.
At a university, four offices once gave four different answers to one question: how many credentials did we award?
So they agreed what a credential is, and wrote it down as a model.
A model answers four questions. What a thing is. What makes it the same one everywhere. What one row holds. And when each thing was true.
Meaning, identity, grain and time.
Version three of the university's model has just been approved.
The series From words to data tells that story. This is all you need from it.
A model can be written down in many shapes: a normalised core, stars, a data vault, anchors, hooks, one wide table per entity.
Each has its champions. Look inside any of them, and you find the same four answers.
This series takes a middle way. Integrate on business keys, keep every version, and serve each entity as one wide row, with stars where people need them.
But an approved model is still a blueprint.
The data arrives from three systems, each with its own keys, its own codes, and every version it has ever had.
Someone has to turn what arrives into what was agreed, and show that it matches.
That's the work of an analytics engineer. At the university, that's Jun.
The building work is transformation: select, join, clean and reshape.
It can be done in notebooks, in stored procedures, or in pipeline tools. Jun's team uses dbt, a widely used tool for it.
Each transformation is a SQL query, in its own file.
dbt works out the order from how the queries refer to each other, builds each result as a table or a view on the platform, and keeps the tests and documentation beside the code.
dbt calls each of these queries a model. It's a useful name, and a misleading one.
A query is one step of the building work. The model is the blueprint.
This series is about keeping the two apart, and connecting them. It's for analytics engineers, and it goes into the weeds.
A year from now, Jun's project could hold three hundred of these files, in four layers, each folder named for its domain.
Most are steps: one tidies a source, one matches a learner's three keys, one stitches their history into a single timeline.
Only the core holds what the blueprint names: a learner, a credential, an award. The marts serve each consumer what it asked for.
So which file is the data model? None of them.
The model lives beside the code.
In YAML: what one row holds, which key makes it unique, how it relates to the rest, and the contract each table promises.
In a conceptual model, with a diagram anyone can read: what each thing means. And in a decision log beside it: why it was decided that way.
The queries make the tables. The YAML and the Markdown say what those tables must be, and the tests check that they are.
Jun works in four phases: ask, promise, build and keep. Ten steps in all.
Ask. Start from a question. Learn what the sources really hold. Define what each consumer needs.
Promise. Name the gaps, and write the contracts. Write the tests, before any code.
Build. Layer by layer. Validate against a number people trust. Review and ship.
Keep. Each fact written once, and a model that evolves without breaking anyone.
An AI agent can help at every step. At every step, a person approves.
The next eight films take the steps in turn.
Scoping a model from a question. What makes a learner the same one across systems, and how keys and hashes make it explicit. Grain and time.
Contracts and tests. Building in layers. Who owns what, across domains. Working with an agent, responsibly. And writing it all down, once.
Everything they show is real code and real data. It runs on dbt Core, with DuckDB, and you can run it yourself.
A blueprint says what a building will be. The building work makes it true.
In data, the model is the blueprint, and dbt is one way to build it.
Declare it. Then build it.

films.s: In the weeds of data crafting
films.x: Scope and owners. John Snow's map showed only what his question needed. Jun's model starts the same way: one question from Planning, with a decision behind it, four things to model, and the person who owns each meaning, named before anyone opens a source.
c: In 1854, cholera killed hundreds of people in a few streets of Soho.
John Snow asked one question: where did the dead get their water?
He marked each death at its address, and the deaths gathered around one pump, on Broad Street.
His map showed only what the question needed.
Jun's model starts the same way: with one question, from Planning.
Step one: start from a question.
How many learners are within 15 credit points of a graduate certificate, by faculty, as at census date?
Behind it, a decision: how many places to offer in each faculty's final graduate certificate units next semester.
A second consumer, the learner's wallet app, will read the same facts, as they are today.
The decision says what done looks like. The census report counted twelve. The model has to reach the same number.
The code and the data on screen are real. They run on dbt Core, with DuckDB, in the series' repository, so anyone can run them.
The university's own platform is Databricks, with dbt Cloud, and the same project runs there too.
Only the connection changes, and one function: the one that turns a key into a hash.
The university's glossary has a term for everything it does: fees, timetables, rooms, staff.
The question touches four: a learner, a credential, an award, and the credit a learner holds towards an award.
Everything else stays out, however central it seems.
Noor agreed that scope with Planning, and wrote down why. Model the university, and you never finish. A question, you can finish.
Each of the four is written down once, in YAML.
The learner: a definition, an owner, and the rule for its key.
The definition is in the business's words, not a system's: a person the university has recorded learning with it, in any of its systems.
Beside it, a diagram drawn by hand: a learner holds credentials, and holds credit towards an award.
The YAML holds the meaning. The diagram lets anyone read it.
Next, what identifies each one in business terms, before anyone opens a source.
A learner is their student ID, which the registrar's office issues. An award is its code. A credential is the ID its issuer gave it.
Each key is tagged with the system it comes from: the student system, the learning platform, or the short-course platform.
And each meaning has an owner. Mei, in the registrar's office, owns learner, credential and award. The learning team owns microcredentials and badges.
The sources will disagree. The owner is the person who decides which meaning wins.
Then a harder call. Is a microcredential a kind of credential, or a thing of its own?
Compare what identifies it: the issuer's own identifier. Compare its life: issued on a date, and perhaps revoked.
Both match any credential. Only the credit points differ.
Same identity, same lifecycle: one entity, with kinds. A different identity, grain or lifecycle, and you split.
A certificate of attendance asks to join. It says someone was there, not what they can do. It stays out.
Jun doesn't write all this alone. An AI agent drafts it, following a skill kept in the project.
Write the question first. List only what it touches. Propose combine or split, with the reasons.
The draft defined the credential, but let certificates of attendance in.
Mei adds one clause: a certificate of attendance isn't one.
The agent drafts. The owner approves the meaning, and the decision goes in the log, with her name and the date.
One question. Four things to model. Two owners of meaning. Nothing else.
Now, the sources.
The model says a learner is one person. The sources say one learner, Aisha, is three.

films.t: What makes it the same one
films.s: In the weeds of data crafting
films.x: Identity and keys. Aisha arrives under three keys, and another Aisha looks just like her. Profile the sources with a query behind every claim, qualify each key, match by rules most trusted first, let a person decide what rules can't, and hash every key the same way everywhere.
c: In the 1880s, a Paris police clerk, Alphonse Bertillon, identified repeat offenders by measuring them.
Each measure went on a card, filed by its numbers.
In 1903, the story goes, a new prisoner at Leavenworth matched the card of a man already inside. Fingerprints told them apart.
Looking alike isn't being the same. Which brings us to Aisha.
Aisha has just completed a graduate certificate in data analytics.
The student system knows her by her student ID. The learning platform, by her account.
The short-course platform, by the email she typed, with a space either side, in mixed case.
Three keys. Each one means something only inside its own system.
None of them says which learner she is.
Before matching anything, Jun learns what the sources really hold. The agent profiles them, and every claim comes with the query that shows it.
Four of forty-two platform accounts have no student ID.
Two students share one family email, and so do their two platform accounts.
Two short-course enrolments point at no customer, as typed. Trimmed and in lower case, every one with an email finds its customer.
A claim without its query is a guess.
First, the key sets written on each source go to work.
Every key now carries the short code of the system it comes from, and that system's owner.
Two systems can use the same-looking key for two different people. Qualified, they can't be confused.
And staging writes every key one way: trimmed, and in one case. Aisha's email loses its spaces and its capitals.
Then: which keys are the same learner? Jun writes it as rules, most trusted first, one block of code for each.
A student ID is a learner.
A platform account is the student whose ID it holds.
An email names a student, but only if exactly one student has it.
Anything left is a learner of its own.
Each key takes the most trusted rule that fits.
Aisha's three keys resolve to her student ID. Across the university, ninety keys become forty-six learners.
The rules are written in words in the model, and in code in two models. Mei, who owns what a learner means, approved them.
But another Aisha has a platform account, and its student ID field holds our Aisha's number, typed by mistake.
The rules merge them. Aisha's wallet now shows six credentials, one she never earned. And every test still passes.
No test knew they were two people, because nobody had written it down.
Mei checks, and records a decision: different people. A person's decision beats every rule.
The merge undoes, and Aisha holds five. The decision is data now: the code keeps them apart, and a test fails if anything merges them again.
Jun hashes each learner's business key.
Sixty-four characters. Add one trailing space, and the hash is completely different.
So one macro builds every hash. It trims each part, writes it in upper case, marks a missing part, and joins the parts with a bar.
The same key gives the same hash, in every model, and on every engine.
And the readable key stays beside the hash. A hash can't be read, or checked by eye.
Codes need the same care. Three systems, three codes, one meaning: studying.
A status map says so, one row per code. The registrar's office owns it, and approves every change.
Now every learner has one key. But one key can still mean many rows, and many versions.

films.t: One row of what, and when
films.s: In the weeds of data crafting
films.x: Grain and time. One question gives twelve on census day and nine today, and both are right. Before any SQL, say in one sentence what one row is and which day it describes, test it as a key, and join every versioned thing at that day.
c: The first of June, 1890. The United States counted its people as they were on that one day.
Counting took weeks, but a baby born after the first wasn't counted. Someone who died after it was.
Each person became a punched card, counted by Herman Hollerith's machines.
One card per person, as at one day. Planning's question needs both.
Before any SQL, Jun's table for Planning gets one sentence.
One row per learner per award, as at census date.
That sentence is the grain. It says what a row is, and which day it describes.
The agent drafts it from Planning's question and the census report. Noor, who owns the model, approves it.
Then it becomes a test: no two rows with the same learner and the same award.
Here's why it matters. In July, a graduate certificate in Health changed its name.
So the award has two versions: the old name, and the new one.
Join the credit to the award on its key alone, and every learner meets both versions.
Eight learners become sixteen rows. A hundred and eighty-five credit points become three hundred and seventy.
Nothing errors, and every row looks right. Only the test on the grain notices.
Join the version that was valid on census day, and there are eight rows again.
Those versions come from the sources. Nothing is overwritten: every change arrives as a new row, with the date it started and the date it ended.
But those dates say when the platform saw a change, not when it was true. Where a system says when something happened, the model uses that.
The core builds its own versions from those dated facts. Aisha's credit towards her certificate has six. Five points in October, forty-five by the end of February, and sixty in July.
So the core's grain is: one row per learner, per award, per version. A test checks that no two versions overlap.
Now two consumers read the same versions, and ask about different days.
Planning asks about census day, the 31st of March. Aisha held forty-five of sixty points, with fifteen to go. She counts.
The wallet app asks about today. Aisha finished in July, and her wallet shows the certificate.
Ask Planning's question, learners within fifteen points of a certificate, as it was on census day: twelve. Ask it today: nine.
Both are right. They answer about different days.
So each output declares its day, and one small macro picks the version valid on it.
A learner lives in three systems, and each keeps its own versions.
Aisha's platform account came first. Her student record took effect six days later. A short-course account arrived in January.
Jun cuts all three at every date on which any of them changed, and stitches one timeline.
On each date, the student system's value wins, then the platform's, then the short course's.
A change that alters nothing the model holds makes no new version. Four dates give Aisha three.
Last, Priya. She withdrew from her certificate on the 27th of March, four days before census.
The student system recorded it on the 3rd of April, a week late.
Dated by when it was recorded, she'd still be studying on census day, and Business would count four. The census report says three.
Dated by when it took effect, Business counts three. As in 1890, the answer describes the day, not the day it was written down.
The platforms only say when they recorded a change. That gap is accepted, and written down.
One row of what, and when. Declared before any SQL, and tested.
Two consumers, one core. Before any more code, write down what each is promised.

films.s: In the weeds of data crafting
films.x: Contracts and tests. Since 1300, English silver has been tested before it's marked. A core model makes the same kind of promise: every gap between what the business expects and what the sources hold gets a decision, the contracts say what's promised, and the tests prove it, written before the code they check.
c: Under a law of 1300, English silver had to meet one standard: sterling.
No piece could leave the workshop until it was tested, then marked.
From 1478, the testing was done at Goldsmiths' Hall: the hall in hallmark.
Buyers still trust the mark, without testing the silver themselves.
A core model makes the same promise. Its tests are the assay, and they come before the mark.
Step four: name the gaps.
Jun's gap register lists them beside each source, while they're open: what the business expects, beside what the source holds, one line per gap.
The business expects a revoked credential to be known as revoked. The learning platform just deletes it.
Every gap gets one of three decisions. Fix it at the source. Write a rule in the model. Or accept it, and write it down.
This one gets two. Anything the platform stops showing is revoked from that day. And the platform is asked for a proper flag.
Jordan's microcredential vanished on the twelfth of August. From that day, it reads as revoked.
Ten gaps, ten decisions. Mei approves the ones about meaning.
Then each gap leaves the register. A rule in the model becomes a decision, in its source's log. An accepted gap becomes a known limitation, on the model. Only a fix still awaited stays open.
Then the contracts. The core is what everything else builds on, so it makes the strongest promise.
The whole core folder gets two settings. Public: other projects may build on it. And a contract, enforced.
The credential's YAML lists every column, its type, and what can't be empty. Its grain: one row per credential.
Let the query and the contract disagree on a column's type, and the build stops before the table is made.
The contract is checked at every build, not read once and forgotten. Noor approves it.
Each consumer gets a contract of its own, on the same core.
Each carries the grain it declared: Planning's as it was on census day, the wallet's as it is now.
Both are enforced, and protected: only this project can build on them.
And each declares an exposure: the dashboard or the app that reads it, with an owner and an email.
Change the credential in the core, and the lineage finds one exposure: the wallet app. That's who to tell.
Planning and the wallet team each approve their own.
Step five: the tests, before the code they check. They say what done looks like.
Every key, unique and never empty. Every relationship, pointing at something real.
Every closed list, from agreed values. Every history, with versions that never overlap.
And one number people already trust: the census report's twelve learners.
A test compares the model's count with the report, and fails on any faculty that differs.
The agent drafts the tests from the contracts and the register. Jun reviews them.
Data tests check the tables. Some logic needs checking on its own, with a few rows made up for the purpose. That's a unit test.
The credit rule, in two made-up rows. A passed unit of study counts from the tenth of January. A microcredential counts from the second of February, until it's revoked on the twelfth of August.
Credit changes twice, so the answer is three versions: fifteen, twenty, then fifteen again.
The microcredential's dates are Jordan's. The rule is proved before a single real row arrives.
Not every failure should stop everything. A test can warn, or it can stop the build.
One short-course enrolment has no email: a walk-in, whose certificate can't reach anyone.
The learning team agreed: warn when there's any, stop when there are more than five. One or two a term are expected. More means something broke.
Today, the build warns once, and carries on.
Freshness works the same way: warn when a source is a day late, fail at three.
Who sets the level? The data's owner, with the reason written down.
112 data tests. Four unit tests. Every promise written down, with its proof beside it.
Each is written before the code it checks, so until that code is built, it can't pass. That's on purpose.
Next, the least code that turns them green, in the right place.

films.s: In the weeds of data crafting
films.x: Layers and CTEs. The tests are written, and they wait for code. Like the stations of Escoffier's kitchen, each layer of Jun's project does one job: staging tidies a table, intermediate holds the steps, the core holds what the blueprint names, and each mart serves one consumer. Inside a model, each CTE is one step.
c: At the Savoy hotel in London, in the 1890s, the chef Auguste Escoffier ran his kitchen as a brigade.
Each station had one job: sauces, roasts, fish, vegetables.
Each prepared its part ahead, and every plate was checked at the pass.
Jun's credential project is a kitchen too: four stations, one job each, and a pass.
The tests are written. Now the code has to pass them, layer by layer.
The agent writes a first draft of each model, runs its tests, and watches them fail. Then it writes the least code that turns them green. Jun reviews every line.
The first station is staging. One model per source table: seven of them.
Staging renames and casts. It trims, and writes each key in one case. It adds the readable key, with its key set, and its hash.
No joins, and no rules. A short-course customer is still called a customer here.
Next, intermediate. Eight models, and each one is a step, not a product.
Match a learner's keys. Stitch three timelines into one. Gather the credentials from three systems. Apply the credit rule.
Here the sources' words become the model's: a customer becomes a learner.
Read the names of one model's steps, top to bottom, and you have its recipe.
Then the core: what the blueprint names. A learner, an award, a credential, and credit towards an award.
Each at its declared grain, public, under an enforced contract.
Jun builds it, and the tests turn green.
The award skips intermediate. It has one source, and nothing to resolve, so staging feeds the core directly.
Noor reviews the core. It's her model, built.
Last, the marts: each built for one consumer, and shaped for how it's read.
Planning's is long and narrow: seventy-three rows, one per learner per award, ready to count by faculty.
The wallet's is wide: everything about a learner in one row, so the app reads it in one lookup.
Each mart builds on the core, never on another mart.
Open Planning's mart. It's written as named steps, each called a CTE, and it reads like a recipe too.
First, import CTEs: one for each model it reads, and nothing else.
Then logical CTEs, one step each, named for what they hold: learners at census, not CTE two.
Last, a final select that lists every column, in the contract's order.
A reviewer reads it top to bottom, and can see where every column comes from.
How each model is stored follows how it's used.
Staging and the steps are views: nothing stored twice, and the agent can query any one of them.
The core and the marts are tables, because people read them all day.
The credential table is incremental. Each run merges only what changed, matched on the credential's key. Run it twice, and the second run merges nothing.
On Databricks, the same file clusters it by learner. And when the logic changes, rebuild it in full.
Planning's rule is written once: near an award means more than nothing left, and no more than fifteen points.
The count by faculty is one macro. And the metric the dashboards ask for, defined in dbt's semantic layer, counts the same column.
Then the pass. Planning's mart against the census report, faculty by faculty: twelve, and twelve. Green.
Each layer has one job. Each CTE, one step.
It's built by one team, in one project. But the registrar owns learners, the learning team owns microcredentials, and Planning wants a project of its own.

films.s: In the weeds of data crafting
films.x: Domains and ownership. In 1858, South Australia made the government's register the title: anyone could rely on it, and only its owner could change it. The credential's core models work the same way. Each fact's meaning has an owner, dbt's access says who can build on what, and grants say who can read.
c: Before 1858, buying land in South Australia meant tracing a chain of old deeds, and hoping none was missing.
That year, a law promoted by Robert Torrens made the government's register the title.
Anyone could rely on it, without checking its history.
Only a registered transfer, signed by the owner, could change it.
The credential's core models work the same way. Their owner publishes them, everyone relies on them, and only their owner changes them.
Everything is green, in one project.
But its meaning has owners. The registrar's office, where Mei works, owns learners, awards and credentials, and the student IDs it issues.
The learning team owns two kinds of credential, microcredentials and badges, and the keys of its two platforms.
So there are three kinds of domain. The systems, and the teams that run them, are application domains.
What the facts mean, learners, credentials and awards, are data domains, named as the reference model names them: student and course.
And Planning and the wallet app are business domains: they decide with the data, and own the marts they build for it.
The project is laid out the same way: sources by system, the core by data domain, the marts and exposures by consumer.
Each group names an owner, and the staging, core and mart models name their domain. Ownership follows meaning, not the code.
So what does a domain publish? A core model, as a product.
Take the learner. Its YAML states its grain: one row per learner per version.
Its owner: Mei, at the registrar's office. Its domain. And its glossary term: learner.
An enforced contract. A version number, so a change never arrives as a surprise. And its documentation.
Noor's group builds it. Mei owns what it means. Everyone else builds on it, not on how it was made.
Who can build on what? In dbt, that's access, and it comes in three rings.
Two came with the contracts. Public, for the core: any project can build on it.
Protected, for the marts: only this project.
The third is private: only models in the same group. That's staging and intermediate.
The wallet team tries to build on an intermediate model. dbt refuses before anything runs, and says why.
Then it builds on Planning's mart. dbt allows it: same project, and the mart is protected.
It's still wrong. That mart is shaped for Planning, and changes when Planning needs it to. Consumers build on the core, not on each other's marts.
Access decides which models can refer to a model. It doesn't decide who can read its table.
On Databricks, grants do that. Planning's marts grant reading to the groups Planning names.
A dashboard can read a private staging table, if a grant lets it. Access doesn't stop it.
Referring and reading are two different doors, opened by two different rules.
Today, it's all one project. One day, Planning may own a project of its own.
Then it names the project it depends on: credentials.
And it refers to the core by project and by name, pinned to a version: the learner, version one.
Only public models cross. Planning can't reach the wallet's marts, or any step inside. The domains meet on the core.
This part is a sketch. References across projects need dbt Cloud, so it doesn't run on DuckDB.
Split into domains, some things must still be shared.
The key sets: one per system, each with its owner.
One macro for every hash. Aisha's student ID gives the same sixty-four characters, in every project.
Hash it another way, in lower case, and she gets a second key. Joins find nothing, and no test fails.
The conventions and the glossary, too. Macros don't cross projects, so the shared ones would move to a package both install.
Without shared keys, domains become silos.
So why not split now? Every project is more to deploy, and more to keep in step.
On the twelfth of October, Noor decided: groups first, in one project, while one team builds the core. Projects later, when teams own their domains.
When that day comes, a domain moves out with its own folders: its marts, its exposures, its seeds and its decisions. Nothing else needs untangling.
Many owners, and many hands. One of them isn't a person.

films.s: In the weeds of data crafting
films.x: Agents and review. An AI agent can read a dbt project, run it and draft a change in minutes. To be trusted, it needs what a new colleague needs, written down: rules, skills and who approves each step. Least access, a query behind every claim, a test it never weakens, and people who sign off.
c: In 1766, Nevil Maskelyne, the Astronomer Royal, published the first Nautical Almanac: tables for finding longitude at sea.
He didn't compute them himself. He posted instructions to computers: people working at home, across England.
Every month was computed twice, by two computers far apart. A comparer checked one against the other, before anything was printed.
Jun has had a computer on the team all along: an AI agent, and a fast one. The checking has to be built in.
The agent can read the whole project, run dbt, and draft changes on a branch.
Before any of that, it reads one page, written for agents. What it may do, and what it must not.
Beside it, five skills, one file each: draft the conceptual model, profile a source, draft a model, reconcile and diff, review the metadata.
And the process: for each of the ten steps, the agent's part, and who approves it.
The work itself is tracked in the team's backlog tool, which the agent can read. In the project, only what's still open is written down, and it's deleted once it's done.
Files in the project, not a long prompt. Versioned, reviewed, and read the same way by people and by agents.
On Databricks, the agent works as its own service principal, never as a person.
It reads the sources, and the core and the marts in production. It writes only to its own development schemas.
It works with counts and small samples. Names, emails and student IDs stay in the database.
Whatever it gets wrong stays where nobody else reads it.
Every claim the agent makes about the data comes with the query that shows it, and the result.
You've seen its claims already: accounts with no student ID, a shared family email, a withdrawal recorded a week late.
Now that habit is a rule, written in the agent's page, with an example to copy.
Where rules can't decide, like that shared email, the agent doesn't guess. It asks Mei, and she records a decision.
A claim that arrives without its query goes back, unread.
Then the agent tidies the learner's timeline. To keep it simple, it dates every version the same way: by when it was recorded.
One test fails: the census reconciliation. Business counts four learners. The report says three.
The withdrawal recorded seven days late now looks like a learner still studying on census day.
The agent's draft sets the test to warn. The build passes.
Jun's review of the draft stops it. The rule is written down: never weaken a test to make it pass.
A failing test is news. Report it, with its failing rows, and let a person decide what's wrong.
The fix puts back the date each change took effect. Business: three. Green.
Before anyone signs off, two checks.
Reconcile: every faculty against the census report. Two, three, five and two. The difference is zero, everywhere.
Diff: build main, then the branch from scratch, and compare them key by key. Counts only; no personal data leaves.
From scratch, because the credential table is incremental, and would hide a change in logic.
In Planning's mart, the shortcut changed one learner's row. In the core, fifty-five versions moved. With the fix, the diff is empty.
The agent marks its pull request ready for review: what it changed, why, what it checked, and the evidence.
CI, the checks that run on every pull request, builds the project on DuckDB. It checks that the generated docs are current, and that the metric still gives the census number.
It parses the project for Databricks too. On dbt Cloud, a CI job builds only what changed, and what depends on it.
Then people. Jun approves the code. Noor signs off the model, and Planning its number.
The agent never merges or approves its own work. The agent recommends; people approve.
It's merged, tested and signed off.
Then the agent reviews the metadata, in the project and beyond it, and finds something no test checks.
The definition of an award now lives in four places. And three of them are wrong.

films.s: In the weeds of data crafting
films.x: Documentation and versions. A definition copied into four places drifts in three. Give each fact one home: meaning in the conceptual model, decisions in a log beside what they're about, what the build uses in dbt's YAML. Generate the rest, sync it one way, and ship a breaking change as a new version with a date.
c: By the 1850s, the note A sounded different from one city to the next, and it kept creeping higher.
In 1859, France fixed it by decree, and kept one tuning fork in Paris as its home.
Other forks were checked against it, and instruments were tuned from those, never the other way round.
Today, before it plays, a whole orchestra still tunes to one note.
A definition can work like that: kept in one place, and everything else tuned from it.
The agent's review of the metadata found it: the definition of an award, in four places.
The wiki, a YAML description, the catalog, and the tooltip on Planning's dashboard.
One says an award is given on paper. One has lost its credit points. One calls every award a degree.
Only the tooltip still says what Mei approved, the words in the conceptual model.
Nothing kept the others in step. They drifted, one small edit at a time.
The fix isn't a fifth copy, or a better one. The definition already has a home. Everything else has to be driven from it.
Meaning lives in the conceptual model: what each thing is, its key, and who owns it.
And where the business glossary already defines a term, that's its home. Data governance says which term applies, and the conceptual model takes its words.
Decisions live in a log beside what they're about, with why and who. The gaps the team accepted live on the model, as known limitations.
Everything the build uses lives in YAML: grain, keys, contracts, tests and owners.
A decision log isn't a copy. It holds why, which a model's YAML has no place for.
So the award is defined once, in the conceptual model.
A script turns each definition into a doc block, on a Markdown page it writes itself. Nobody edits that page.
The YAML doesn't copy the definition. It names it, and dbt shows the definition there.
To change the meaning, change one line, with Mei's approval. Edit the generated page instead, and the check in CI fails.
The agent's review runs again: in the project, no description written twice. The wiki now links to the docs site.
Diagrams drift too.
The conceptual diagram is drawn by hand, for people. It changes only when the meaning does.
The physical diagram is generated: every core and mart table, its columns, types and keys, read from what dbt parsed.
If the YAML changes and the diagram doesn't, CI fails.
Draw the meaning. Generate the structure.
On Databricks, people find tables in the catalog, and read their descriptions there.
So each build pushes the descriptions out to it, for each table and its columns.
Nobody edits them there: a rebuild writes over the edit. Fix it at home, and it flows out.
Upstream, the same rule. A sync checks the glossary on a schedule. When a term changes, it opens a pull request, so the owner sees what the new meaning touches before it reaches the build.
One direction: from the glossary, through the files, out to the catalog and whatever reads it. Tuned from one source, never the other way round.
Written once doesn't mean never changed.
A credential can expire, and a true or false can't say so. So is_revoked becomes status: valid, expired or revoked.
That breaks anyone who reads the old column. So it's a new version of the credential, beside the old one.
Version one came first. Now it's built from version two, which holds the logic, so it can go without touching version two. It has a date to go: the 31st of March, 2027.
The exposures declared with the contracts say who to tell: only the wallet app. It pins version two.
Anyone still reading version one gets dbt's warning, with the date, every time they build.
A breaking change arrives as a choice with a deadline, not as a surprise.
That's the loop. A question, the sources, the consumers, gaps and contracts, tests, layers, the trusted number, review, written once, and change.
At every step, the agent drafted and checked. At every step, a person approved.
And a new question arrives, from the wallet team. The loop starts again, at the question.
Declare it. Then build it.

films.s: In the weeds of data crafting
films.x: The whole process. Finance asks how much tuition recognised credit saves learners. Follow its question through the four phases and ten steps, one real commit per step: the files that arrive to stay, the ones that change, and the temporary ones, deleted when the work is done. The series' closing film.
c: In the fourteenth century, the masons building York Minster drew their windows full size, on a floor of plaster.
From each drawing they cut a wooden template, and carved the stone to match it.
When a window was done, the next was drawn over it. In time, the floor was plastered again.
The drawings were for the work. The windows are what stayed.
A project has both: files for the work, deleted when it's done, and files that stay. This is one new question, from start to end.
A new consumer arrives: Finance.
How much tuition does recognised credit save learners, by faculty, as at census date?
The answer sets next year's revenue forecast, and what a microcredential should cost.
Finance is a business domain: it decides with the data. So it gets folders of its own, named for it, from the first commit.
Step one is the scope. Its conceptual model holds the question; its decision log, the first decision: recognised credit only, read from the public core.
And one file that won't last: Finance's open requirements. The first says what done looks like: match Finance's own number.
Who does the work, and when, lives in the team's backlog tool. The project keeps only what's still open.
Step two: what the data really holds. Finance reads the core, not the sources, so the agent profiles the core.
Recognised credit counts towards every award it could count towards. Aisha's counts towards three.
Added up across awards, that's 385 credit points. In the award each learner is enrolled in, 160.
Which one saves the tuition? No rule can say. A question opens, with the query as evidence, and Finance owns the answer.
Finance brings one thing of its own: the tuition rates it publishes, as reference data it owns.
Step three: the output. First, Finance answers: only the award the learner is enrolled in, on census day.
The answer goes where it lasts: a rule in Finance's conceptual model, and a decision in its log.
And the question is deleted. Git keeps it, and the decision says where it came from.
Then the output, before any code: one row per learner per award they're enrolled in, as at census date.
That's a requirement too, open until a contract enforces it.
Step four: the promise. Finance's mart gets a contract: the columns and types the forecast needs, enforced.
For now it's an empty table, the right shape with no rows, and the forecast is declared as what depends on it.
One gap: the project knows the published rate, not what each learner was charged. Scholarships and discounts aren't in.
Finance accepts it. It becomes a known limitation, on the mart, with a decision that says why.
Step five: the tests, before the logic.
The grain, tested as a key. Learners that exist. Only the award types Finance prices.
A unit test for the rule: credit that counts towards two awards still saves tuition once.
And Finance's own number, from its spreadsheet, as an expected seed that no model may read. A reconciliation compares the two.
Nothing can pass yet. The unit test fails, so dbt doesn't even build the mart.
But the grain is tested and the contract enforced, so the output requirement is done, and deleted.
Step six: the logic.
It reads the core as it was on census day, keeps the award each learner was enrolled in, and prices the credit at that year's rate.
It reads nothing but the public core and Finance's own rates. No other team's model changes.
It's short, because the core already did the hard parts: identity, timelines, and the credit itself.
Every test passes: 67,800 dollars, across four faculties.
Step seven: validate. Faculty by faculty, against Finance's report. The difference is zero.
Then the diff against main, built from scratch: every core table, Planning's mart, the wallet's.
No key added, none lost, no column changed. A new consumer moved nobody else's numbers.
Finance signs off, with every row in front of it.
Step eight: review and ship.
The last open item, match Finance's number, is done: the reconciliation enforces it on every build.
So the item is deleted, and with it Finance's requirements file, and its folder.
A check in CI makes sure of it: nothing stays in requirements unless it's still open.
Jun approves the code, and Finance its number. The agent never merges.
Step nine: the agent reviews the metadata.
Two descriptions were written twice, word for word: the award's code and its name, in Finance's YAML and in Planning's.
The award belongs to the course domain, so each becomes one doc block there, shown everywhere it's needed.
Zero descriptions written twice. The generated pages, the definitions, the diagram and the index of decisions, keep up on their own.
Step ten: operate and evolve. Finance pins the versions of the core it reads.
A new version reaches Finance as a choice with a date, and the lineage names Finance among who to tell.
And because Finance's folders were named for it from the first commit, Finance can move out to a project of its own, whole.
Its marts, its exposure, its seeds, its decisions, and the test and two analyses it was built with.
Four phases, ten steps, ten commits. You can replay them one by one, in the repository.
Some files arrived to stay: the question, the decisions, the contract, the tests, the model.
Some were for the work: three open items, and the file that held them. They're gone. The project says only what's still open.
Every file has a home. Sources by system: application domains. The core by meaning: data domains. Marts and exposures by who decides: business domains.
And every file has a lifetime: written by hand, generated, or kept only while the work goes on.
The next question will start the same way: in folders of its own, with one file that won't last.
That's the series. A question and its meaning, the sources, the consumers, promises and proofs, layers, the trusted number, an agent on the team, written once, and change.
The model is the blueprint. dbt is how you build it.
Declare it. Then build it.

films.x: Two bad mornings at the university: a change only half of it saw, and a number too good to be true. Each ends with what catches it next time.
c: It's 7:58 on the morning before census date.
Ana, the Head of School, has a meeting at nine to confirm which classes will run.
Her dashboard shows yesterday's numbers, with a note: last good data, as of 11:02 last night.
The numbers aren't wrong. They're a day old, and the dashboard says so.
Ana messages Sam: are these numbers safe to use?
Six hours earlier, at 2:40 in the morning, the nightly build begins.
Enrolment changes reach the platform all day, as events or in files. Once a night, dbt builds the numbers from them.
Before anything is built on them, dbt tests them. One test checks that every enrolment has a status it knows.
Tonight, some have a status it has never seen.
So the build stops there. Everything downstream is skipped, and the dashboard keeps the last good numbers, with that note.
An alert is filed for the morning. Nothing wrong reached anyone, so nobody needs to be woken.
A good platform fails loudly, and safely.
At 7:59, Sam, the data engineer on call, is already reading the alert.
Sam replies: yesterday's numbers are safe. I'm checking today's, and I'll be back to you by 8:45.
Say what you know, and what you don't. That's how trust survives a bad morning.
Every number on the dashboard has a lineage: the steps that built it.
Sam follows it backwards, one step at a time.
From the dashboard, to the data product behind it. Then to the model that joins enrolments to their units.
Then to staging, where the test failed. The rows that failed it were kept aside, so they can be looked at.
Upstream, in bronze, the rows are exactly as the student system sent them.
Fifteen enrolments in Data Science 101 have a new status: waitlisted.
Bronze keeps what arrived, even what nothing downstream understands yet. Nothing was lost. Something was new.
Sam asks the student system team: did enrolments change last night?
Ben replies: yes, waitlists went live. It's in our release notes.
Then Sam calls the registrar's office. Mei says: yes, we introduced waitlists, and we emailed every School.
Two weeks earlier, both had announced the change.
The registrar's office emailed every School. The student system team published release notes.
Each notice reached its own people. Neither reached the platform, or the people who rely on its numbers.
Ben knew what changed. Mei knew what it meant. Neither knew the numbers depended on it.
So, is a waitlisted student enrolled? Sam doesn't guess. It's a business question.
Mei decides: no. Enrolled means holding a seat on census date, and a waitlisted student doesn't hold one yet.
The sketch, our model of what things mean, gains a new status.
Now the fix is small. In dbt, waitlisted becomes a known status, one that doesn't count as enrolled.
A colleague reviews it, like any code. Tests run on just what changed, and they pass.
The skipped models run again.
Had the waitlist been counted, the dashboard would have shown Data Science 101 at 108% full.
That's believable. Classes do fill up. Nobody would have questioned it, and Ana might have booked a bigger room for students without a seat.
Time travel lays last night's table beside this morning's: 94% yesterday, 96% today.
At 8:40, the note disappears. At nine, Ana confirms the classes.
Later that week, the four of them meet: Mei and Ben, who produce the data, and Sam and Ana, who use it.
They agree a data contract for enrolments.
It lists the fields, the allowed statuses and what each one means, and how fresh the data must be.
It names an owner on each side, technical and business. Changing it needs both sides to agree.
And the platform keeps checking it: on every load, at the door, and on every proposed change, before it ships.
Three weeks later, Ben's team adds another status: deferred.
In their test environment, before release, the contract check turns amber, and all four owners are told.
Mei defines what deferred means. Sam's team adds it. The contract becomes version 1.1.
On Monday, the dashboard simply updates. No note, no alert, and nobody woken.
Changes will keep coming. That's a university doing its job.
The platform's job is to make each one visible, to everyone it touches, in time.
Seen by both sides, before it ships.

films.x: Two bad mornings at the university: a change only half of it saw, and a number too good to be true. Each ends with what catches it next time.
c: It's 10:05 on a Tuesday, in the middle of admissions season.
The planning committee is deciding how many first-year places to offer next year.
On the screen, one number: applications for next year, up 38% overnight.
It's good news, and nobody questions it. The committee approves six hundred extra places. Rooms are booked, and tutors will be hired.
This is one version of Tuesday. Let's go back to Monday.
Sam, the data engineer, looks after the platform behind that number.
Through Sam's screen, it's a gold painting: applications for next year. On Monday, 8,200 so far.
Beside it sits its contract card. One line matters this week: how much the total may change overnight.
Leila, who manages the admissions office, helped set it. On a closing date, applications really do jump, by up to about 15%.
So above 10%, a test raises a warning: worth a look, but the data goes through.
Above 25%, it raises an error: this must not reach a decision, so the build stops.
A test on the number itself, not just on each row, with levels the business helped choose.
At eleven on Monday night, the admissions system syncs with the application portal.
Tonight, the sync times out and restarts. It copies the whole week's applications again, 3,100 of them, and gives every copy a new ID.
The admissions system now holds each of those applications twice. The platform copies what the source holds, faithfully.
At two, the nightly build begins, and the checks run, one row at a time. Every ID is unique. No field is empty. Every course exists.
Then the total reaches its test: 11,340. Up 38% in one night, when the real growth was forty.
The needle swings past amber, into red.
Every row was valid. Only a test on the total could see that there were too many.
What happens next depends on that test. Here are three versions of the same Tuesday.
In the first, there's no test. 11,340 reaches the painting, and the committee approves six hundred places.
Three weeks later, the copies are found. The places are cut again, the rooms released, and nobody trusts the dashboard.
In the second, the test is only a warning. It turns amber, and the number is published anyway.
The warning lands in a channel with forty others. Nobody reads it before ten, and the committee makes the same decision.
In the third, the test is an error. The build stops before gold.
The painting keeps Monday's 8,200, with a note: last good data, as of 2 am on Monday. Checking an unusual change.
David, who chairs the committee, moves the decision to Wednesday. A day late, and right.
A wrong number gets acted on. A late number, clearly labelled, simply waits.
At our university, this test is an error. So this is the Tuesday that happens.
So why not make every test an error?
Because on a closing date, a jump of 14% is real. Stopping it would hold back good data, and teach people to ignore alarms.
So this number has two levels. Amber, for worth a look. Red, for must not reach a decision.
A warning only helps if someone reads it, so each one has an owner.
Choose the level by what a wrong number would cost.
That cost is easy to count once something goes wrong. The value of a right number, on an ordinary day, is much harder to see.
At 8:15 on Tuesday, Sam follows the thread upstream, from the painting, through silver, to bronze.
In bronze, 3,100 pairs of rows are identical, except for their ID and when they were created.
The uniqueness test checked the ID, and every ID was unique.
But in the real world, an application is one applicant, for one course, in one intake. That's its business key.
Test uniqueness on what makes a thing unique in the real world, not only on the system's ID.
Sam messages Rosa, on the admissions system team. Her team finds the restart within the hour.
The copies are in the admissions system itself, so that's where they're removed. And the sync is changed, so it's safe to run twice.
The platform doesn't patch its copy by hand. It loads the affected week again, from the corrected system, so its copy matches the source.
Silver and gold are rebuilt from it.
Time travel lays Monday night's total beside today's: 11,340 then, 8,240 now. Forty more than Monday, as it should be.
On Wednesday, the committee plans with the right number.
The incident leaves a new test behind: one application per applicant, course and intake.
Syncs will time out again. When in doubt, keep the last good number, and say so.
Stale and labelled beats fresh and wrong.

films.x: Fitness for use. In December 2025, the graduation list passed every check and seated the Great Hall well, and still 41 degree certificates were printed again. In January, Malia Fonoti, Mei Tanaka and Jun Park ask who uses the list, for what, and what goes wrong when it's wrong, and agree a level for each use.
c: Duisburg, 1569. The mapmaker Gerardus Mercator publishes a new chart of the world, made for sailors.
At sea, a pilot steered by compass, on a bearing: one fixed angle to north, held hour after hour.
But on the charts of the time, a straight line between two ports wasn't a bearing a ship could hold.
Steer the angle the chart showed, and the ship slowly left the line.
On a long crossing, it could miss the coast it was making for, and its crew spend days more at sea, short of water.
Sailors needed a chart they could steer by, not just look at.
Mercator stretched his chart towards the poles, a little more at every degree, so every course on one bearing is a straight line.
On his chart, a pilot could rule a line between two ports, read its angle, and steer it.
Thirty years later, Edward Wright worked out the stretch exactly, and most charts for sailors are still drawn this way.
The price was chosen on purpose: far from the equator, every country swells.
Greenland looks as big as Africa, which is fourteen times larger.
Right for steering, wrong for comparing countries: one chart, made for one use.
Data is the same. In December 2025, a university's graduation list seated its Great Hall well.
And still, 41 of its degree certificates had to be printed again.
So the people who use the list, answer for it and build it wrote down what it's for.
Now each use has its own level, agreed with the people who use it.
December 2025, at the university: six ceremonies in the Great Hall, for 2,031 graduates.
The graduation list says who graduates, at which ceremony, with which award, and the name printed on each certificate.
It goes to the printer about four weeks before the first ceremony. After that, any change means a certificate printed again.
That December, the list passed every check on it.
Still, 41 certificates were printed again: 26 had a wrong name, 9 a wrong award, and 6 graduates were missing from the list.
Each cost about 120 dollars with its courier, and a graduate might cross the stage holding an empty folder.
The same list had seated the hall well: every ceremony's count was right to within a few seats.
Next December, Andrés Peñaloza will cross the same stage, with a Master of Data Analytics.
The student system holds his name as Andres Penaloza, without its accents.
For seating, that's one graduate and one seat: right. On his certificate, it isn't his name.
So, was the list good? That depends what it's for.
In January 2026, three people sat down with the list.
Malia Fonoti, the graduations officer, who uses it most.
Mei Tanaka, in the registrar's office, who answers for its names and awards.
And Jun Park, who builds it.
They didn't start by asking if it was good.
They asked who uses it, for what, and what goes wrong, for whom, when it's wrong.
The seating plan needs each ceremony's count. Within 2% is good enough: a few seats spare, or a few more chairs.
The certificates need every name, award and date exactly right. Zero wrong: one mistake is a certificate printed again.
The printed programme needs the same names as the certificates. A change after it's printed goes on a slip.
And the government's count of awards, which Planning sends, needs each award counted once, exactly.
One list, four uses, four levels.
The quality pioneer Joseph Juran called quality fitness for use.
Data is no different: good enough always means good enough for a use.
For each use, they named the few things it can't do without: its critical data.
Seating needs each graduate once, their ceremony, and whether they'll be there.
A certificate needs the name as printed, the award, and the date it was conferred.
Then they asked six questions of each. Is it complete? Unique? Valid? Consistent? Accurate? On time?
These are DAMA's six dimensions of data quality. An ISO standard names fifteen; six are enough to start.
Each use leans on different ones, as Mercator's chart chose angles over sizes.
Seating needs the list complete: every graduate who crosses the stage, once.
A certificate needs it accurate: the name its graduate really has.
Each level was agreed with the people who use it: Malia for the ceremonies, Planning for the government's count.
And Mei owns every level, because she answers for the list.
How a check warns or stops, and whom it tells, is set in advance too: Rules that run and Too good to be true show how.
Jun wrote it all down beside the data, in the file that describes the list.
Each use is a quality rule, written in words: its dimension, its level, who agreed it, and what a failure costs.
The columns each use can't do without are marked as critical data.
In dbt, every check on the list names its dimension and its owner.
And on Databricks, each critical column carries a governed tag, so whoever finds the table sees what its uses depend on.
If quality keeps failing anyway, look first at your governance, who owns the data and decides, and then at your tools.
Mercator's chart said what it was for, in its title: for the use of sailors.
The graduation list now says what it's for, too: four uses, each with its level.
Next, the team looks at a hundred of its records, one by one.
Ask what it's for before you ask if it's good.

films.x: Measuring quality. The graduation list passed every check, yet 41 certificates were printed again. On a Friday in February, Malia Fonoti, Mei Tanaka and Jun Park look at its hundred most recent records: 79 are perfect. Then the platform profiles all 2,031 graduates, and only then does Jun write the first checks.
c: Dublin, 1899. A young chemist, William Gosset, joins a large brewery.
It wants better barley: which kind to grow, and how, for the best beer.
But a trial means sowing a few plots and waiting a whole season, so it gives only a handful of results.
And a handful can mislead. The brewery could choose the wrong barley and live with it for a year, or turn good barley away.
The mathematics of the day worked for large numbers of measurements. Nobody could say how far a few could be trusted.
The brewery couldn't wait for large numbers it would never have.
So Gosset worked out how much a few results can tell you, and how sure of it you can be.
Before he could prove it on paper, he tried it by hand: 3,000 measurements on 3,000 cards, shuffled, and drawn four at a time.
In 1908 he published it, with tables anyone could use, as Student: the brewery let its staff publish, but not under their own names.
Now a few careful trials were enough to decide, and his tables said when more were needed.
In his paper, eleven pairs of trials showed that seed dried in a kiln probably gave a little more grain, and almost certainly worse barley.
His way is still used wherever people can't measure everything: in medicine, in farming, in factories.
And for data: a few records, looked at closely, can say how good a whole list is.
At the university, the graduation list passed every check. Yet in December, 41 degree certificates were printed again.
So, on a Friday in February, three people looked closely at a hundred of its records.
79 were perfect: an honest number, and a map of where to look, before a single new check was written.
Friday, 6 February, two o'clock, at the data team's bench.
Malia Fonoti runs the ceremonies. Mei Tanaka, in the registrar's office, answers for names and awards. Jun Park builds the list.
In January, they agreed what the list is for, and what each use needs. A certificate needs every name exactly right.
Jun brings December's list, the last one built in full, and its hundred most recent records.
For each, the fields a certificate and a ceremony need: the names, the award, the ceremony, and the date the degree is conferred.
They go through them one by one, and mark every field that's wrong. A record with nothing marked is perfect.
Two hours later: 79 perfect.
21 have at least one error, 26 errors in all.
15 are in names: accents lost, names cut short, given and family names swapped.
6 are in awards, 3 in ceremonies, 2 in dates.
Thomas Redman, a pioneer of data quality, calls this the Friday afternoon measurement.
It needs no special tools: a hundred records, the people who know them, and an afternoon.
December's list has 2,031 graduates. Can a hundred records speak for them all?
It's Gosset's question again: how far can a few be trusted?
If the hundred are like the rest, the answer is good to about eight either way: between 71 and 87 perfect in every hundred.
Not exact. But enough to act on: about one record in five is wrong.
Why the most recent? They show the list as it's made now, not as it was made years ago.
And everyone understands 79 of a hundred.
It also raises a puzzle. December's 41 reprints were about 2 certificates in 100.
The hundred say 21 records in 100 have an error: over 400 on December's list.
So someone had been putting most of them right by hand before the list went, and nobody counted that work.
The hidden factory, a later film, follows it.
A hundred records say how good the list is, not where to look among two thousand.
So Jun has the platform describe the whole list.
A notebook shows a quick profile in one click. For one the team keeps and refreshes, he sets up Databricks' data profiling.
It reads every row and describes each column.
How many values are empty, how many are different, which are shortest and longest, and which come up most.
He profiles December's list, all 2,031 graduates.
Two things stand out.
The longest family name is exactly 30 characters: the length of the field in the student system. Names cut short.
And among the most frequent family names, the same name twice: once as written, once in capitals.
So Jun adds counts of his own, as custom metrics.
41 family names exactly 30 characters long.
312 in capitals only, every one of a student admitted before 2020.
And not one name with a letter outside A to Z. Eight in the hundred had lost their accents. Here, every accent is gone.
The hundred had none in capitals: all of them were students admitted since 2020.
Only the profile, which reads every row, could see them.
The hundred said how good. The profile said where to look.
Only now does Jun write checks, starting with what the profile showed.
A family name exactly as long as the field may have been cut short.
A family name in capitals only.
And a list of more than 200 names without a single accent.
Eight in the hundred had lost theirs, so a list with none isn't chance.
Mei owns all three. Before any ran, she and Malia agreed their level.
Each holds the list for a person to look; none stops it on its own.
Jun writes them in the project, with dbt. From Monday, they run every night.
The platform's monitoring watches the rest, such as whether each table arrives on time, as Quality on the platform showed.
But some of the hundred's errors, no check of the list can see.
The swapped names, the awards, the ceremonies and the dates were all allowed values. Allowed, and wrong.
To find those, the list needs something outside it to compare with. That's the next film.
Back in Dublin, Gosset never tried every barley. A few careful trials were enough, and his tables said when more were needed.
The team did the same with its list: a hundred records, looked at by the people who know them, then the whole list described.
79 is where they start. Each time they measure again, the number will say whether their changes worked.
And because they measured first, the checks go where the errors are, not where checks are easy to write.
Look at a hundred records before you write a single check.

films.x: Accuracy and references. In February 2026, every name on the March graduation list passed the checks that say a name is allowed. Asked in the portal, the graduates corrected 88 of them, and a check against the exam boards' approved lists found two awards missing. Only a reference outside the data says what's true.
c: Japan, in 1800.
