Ino Tadataka, a retired merchant of 55, set out from Edo, today's Tokyo,
to map the coast of Ezo, the northern island now called Hokkaido.
The maps of the time were drawn largely from estimates: a cape could sit miles from where it really lay.
And with Russian ships appearing in the north, the government, the shogunate, wanted a true map of that coast.
His teams measured it on foot: each stretch with a rope or a chain, and its direction with a compass.
But every stretch adds a small error.
The errors pile up, unseen, because each measure looks right on its own.
A map made only from its own measures can agree with itself, line after line, and still put a cape miles out.
The survey needed a reference its errors couldn't reach.
So, by day, they measured the coast; and on clear nights, they measured the stars.
A star's height, as it crosses the south, says how far north you stand, and no error in the walk can change it.
Where the walk and the stars disagreed, they corrected the walk.
His teams walked for seventeen years.
In 1821, three years after he died, they finished the map of all Japan, the base of the country's maps for decades.
His length for one degree of latitude, north to south, is within a fraction of one per cent of today's.
At the university, in February 2026, every name on the graduation list passed the checks that say a name is allowed.
Eighty-eight were still wrong.
The list needed its stars.
The graduates themselves put all 88 right, before a single certificate was printed.
February 2026.
The list for the March ceremonies holds 1,064 graduates.
Every night, Jun's checks ask whether each name is allowed:
not empty, nothing but letters, spaces, hyphens and apostrophes,
and at most 30 characters, the length of the student system's field.
All 1,064 pass.
In data quality's words, every name is valid.
But valid only means allowed.
Zoë Lefèvre's name, without its accents, is allowed.
So is a name cut short, or a given name where the family name should be.
The team's first checks, from a hundred records, raise two doubts:
twelve names exactly 30 characters long, and not one accent on the whole list.
But no check can say which of the twelve were cut short, or whose accents are missing.
That's a question about the world, not about the data.
Ino had the stars.
A list needs a reference too: something outside the data that knows the truth, and that the data's errors can't reach.
The list has three, from the closest to the truth.
The graduate, who knows their own name.
The identity document seen at enrolment, checked once by the registrar's office.
And a record kept apart: the exam boards' approved lists, which say who completed each award, and when.
The closer the reference, the more it can tell you, and the harder it is to reach.
A graduate can tell you anything about their name, but you have to ask, and wait.
The boards' lists are there every night, and know nothing of spelling.
Checking data against a reference measures its accuracy: whether it's true.
So the registrar's office asked.
From Monday 9 to Friday 20 February, as graduates registered for the March ceremonies,
the portal showed each one their name, exactly as it would be printed,
and two buttons: “This is my name”, and “This isn't my name”.
Zoë Lefèvre saw hers without its accents, pressed “This isn't my name”, and typed it as she writes it.
1,013 of the 1,064 answered: 95 per cent.
925 confirmed their name as it was.
88 corrected it: 51 had lost their accents, 19 had given and family names swapped,
11 were cut short, and 7 were misspelt.
All 88 had been allowed.
A certificate carries a graduate's legal name,
so Mei's team checked each correction against the next reference: the document seen at enrolment.
84 matched.
Four graduates had changed their name since, and each sent the document that shows the new one.
The list took each name as its graduate confirmed it, with the date.
The 51 who didn't answer were printed as the student system held them.
One was among the twelve exactly 30 characters long, and the document settled it: that name really is that long.
A check can raise a doubt.
Only a reference can settle it.
Then the awards.
A graduate of a double degree, like Arts and Laws, has two awards, and two certificates.
On Monday 23 February, Jun's new check compared the list with the exam boards' approved lists, award by award.
The boards had approved 1,101.
The list held 1,099.
The missing two were Bachelor of Arts awards,
for two graduates of Arts and Laws whom the student system held with Laws only.
Every row on the list passed its checks: what was wrong was what wasn't there.
It was found three days before the list went, and both Arts certificates were printed.
Every other award, and every date, agreed.
The boards' lists could see the gap because they're kept apart,
made from the boards' own decisions, not from the student system.
A copy of the student system would have agreed with the list, and both would be wrong:
consistent, in data quality's words, not accurate.
And like Ino's stars, each reference sees some things and not others.
The stars fixed how far north, not how far east: that needed an exact clock his teams could carry, and they had none.
The boards' lists can say an award is missing, not how a name is spelled.
So every check now says which reference it uses.
Beside each check in the project, Jun writes its owner, what it measures, and, for an accuracy check, its reference.
The name checks measure validity: they have no reference but the rule itself,
so they can say a name is allowed, and no more.
The awards check measures accuracy, against the boards' approved lists.
For names, the reference is the graduate, and the list keeps the date each name was confirmed.
And the test it runs names its method: reconciliation, award by award.
And the scorecard counts them apart: allowed, and true.
A check is only as true as its reference.
Say which one it uses, and whoever reads the result knows what it can tell them, and what it can't.
Ino's teams walked the coast by day, and checked it against the stars by night.
The walk said how far they had come.
The stars said how far north they really were.
On Thursday 26 February, the March list went to the printer
with 88 names put right by the graduates themselves, and two awards found in the boards' lists.
Every name had been allowed all along.
Now 1,013 of them had been confirmed by the person they belong to.
A check says it's allowed.
Only a reference says it's true.

films.x: Timeliness. On Wednesday night, 17 June 2026, the student system's nightly file didn't come. The graduation list was built from the night before's: every check green, and 23 graduates missing. Malia Fonoti, Sam Okafor and Mei Tanaka agree how fresh each use needs it, and the list says how old its records are.
c: November 1970: the coast of East Pakistan, now Bangladesh.
Farming and fishing families live on low islands, where great rivers meet the sea.
On the twelfth, a cyclone comes ashore in the evening, with the high tide.
Forecasters warn of danger, and as it nears, the radio broadcasts a great danger signal.
On the islands it means little: survivors said later they took signal number one to be the worst.
Most people know a storm is coming, yet almost nobody takes shelter.
That night a storm surge, the sea driven inland by the wind, sweeps over the islands.
At least three hundred thousand people die, perhaps half a million.
A warning people can't read, or don't act on, is no warning. The next one has to reach every village in time.
In 1972, the Bangladesh Red Cross Society starts the Cyclone Preparedness Programme, run with the government from 1973.
Volunteers from the coast's own villages carry each warning the last mile.
They go house to house with megaphones, and lead people to shelters.
Their flags rise with the danger, one, then two, then three: a signal the whole village can read.
In November 2007, Cyclone Sidr strikes the same coast, with winds as strong as 1970's, though at low tide.
Warnings have gone out for days, and the highest signal has flown since the day before.
More than 40,000 volunteers carry them, and a million and a half people are in shelters.
About 3,400 die: still too many, and about one for every hundred in 1970.
Data has a last mile too.
In June 2026, the night's file doesn't come, and the graduation list is built without it.
Every check passes. 23 graduates are missing, and nothing says so.
This time, someone notices in time, and all 23 are on the list.
Each night at two, the student system sends its nightly file: the day's names and results, and the awards the exam boards approved.
At three, the night's update builds the graduation list.
On Wednesday night, 17 June, the file didn't come: a full disk on the student system's side held it.
At three, the list was built from what was there: the file of the night before.
689 graduates, and every check green.
Even the check against the boards' own lists passed: they come in the same transfer, so they were a day old too.
Missing: 23 graduates the boards approved on Wednesday.
Late data looks complete.
Each check looks at what's there. None can see what hasn't arrived.
Thursday, 8 am. The list is due at the printer at five.
Sam Okafor, who runs the platform, sees in Databricks' monitoring that the student system's tables are late.
dbt's freshness check says how late: the student system's data is thirty hours old.
There was a level, a warning after a day: set by the builders, agreed with nobody, and never run at night.
A level its users never agreed is a signal nobody understands.
Sam calls the student system team, and Malia Fonoti, who sends the list. Malia holds the send.
At 11:40 the file arrives; at 12:10 the list is built again, with 712 graduates.
Malia's team checks the 23 new names, and at 3:20 the list goes.
The December before, six graduates were left off, and nobody saw. Their certificates were printed late, and posted.
On Monday, Malia and Sam meet Mei Tanaka, who owns the list.
The platform can see that a table is late. Only its users can say when late is too late.
The certificates can't wait: they need yesterday's awards on the list when it goes to the printer.
Seating the Great Hall can: it's counted a week before, from a list a few days old.
Planning's count for the government comes after the year's end: weeks are fine.
One list, three clocks. The strictest sets the level: a day old at most, at the send.
A nightly file meets it. For fresher data, Hot, warm, cold shows how it moves.
Malia agrees it, Mei owns it, and it goes beside the list's columns, in dbt.
Rules that run left timeliness in pencil, with no checks. This is its first rule.
From now on, the list says how old it is.
Old, counted from when? Every record has three dates.
When it happened: the board approved this award on Wednesday.
When the student system saved it: that afternoon.
And when its file arrived: Thursday, at 11:40.
The first is the one that matters. But each table says it in its own way, and when no board meets, there's none to read.
The last is the easiest, and says the least: for December's list, a file came on time, full of the day before's records.
So the list goes by the second: the date every load already uses to find what's new.
Every row carries its sources' age: the newest record each one had saved.
Each source has its own. That Thursday, it would have said: student system, Wednesday, before two; portal, Thursday, before two.
It's shown wherever the list is, first of all in the printer's file.
Like the volunteers' flags, it's a signal everyone can read.
Too good to be true labelled a number from the night before. Here, every list says its age, on good nights too.
Data that says its age can be trusted to be old.
Data that doesn't, can't.
Then Sam checks the age where it starts: at each source.
dbt reads the same date there: the newest record each source saved, not when its file arrived.
One level on each: older than twenty-four hours, the check fails.
Each night, the update runs that check first.
If it fails, Sam and Malia hear at once, and the list is still built, saying its age.
That's the warning: nothing stops, and the people who need to know, know.
The send to the printer is a job too. It checks the list's own age.
It sends only if the check passes; if not, the list waits, and Malia is told why.
The data isn't stopped. The send is.
The volunteers can't stop a storm. They make sure the warning arrives in time, in words people understand.
A list can't make a late file come. It can say how old it is, and the send can wait until it's fresh.
Since June, no graduate has been left off a list by late data.
Agree how fresh it must be, and always say how old it is.
Fit for use ends here: a use, a measure, a reference and a clock. Next, Quality as a habit.

films.x: Hidden work and root causes. Before every ceremony, Malia Fonoti and a colleague checked every name on the graduation list by hand: about 320 hours a year, and the same errors came back. In August 2026 the team counts that hidden work, traces each error to where it's born, and fixes it there, with its owner.
c: Washington, 1899.
More than six million letters and parcels a year end up in one office: the Dead Letter Office.
A dead letter is one the post can't deliver, and can't send back.
Most often, people have moved on without leaving an address.
Or a letter to a city gives no street and number, or a town is spelt the way it sounds.
In one room, clerks, many of them women, work out where each should have gone.
The best known, Patti Lyle Collins, works out about a thousand a day.
It's skilled work, unseen by the senders, and it never fixes the next letter.
Nearly three million a year are destroyed: news someone never gets.
The fix has to start where the address is written, not where it ends up.
In 1943, with experienced clerks gone to the war, big cities get zones: a number the sender writes, so new clerks can sort by it.
In 1963, the post brings in the ZIP Code: five digits on every letter, written by the sender.
Now anyone, and soon machines, can sort a letter by its number.
By 1969, 83% of Americans use it, and it has saved the post billions since.
The fix moved to the start: written once, by the person who knows the address.
At the university, two people put the graduation list's names right by hand before every ceremony, in a copy.
So every new list brings the same errors back.
Count that work, fix each error where it's born, and a name is put right once, for every list after.
Malia Fonoti runs the graduations. Before each list goes to the printer, she and a colleague check every name by hand.
On Monday 20 October 2025, they download December's list from the platform into a spreadsheet: 2,031 names.
Each is checked against the documents seen at enrolment; where it doesn't match, they phone the graduate.
They correct the spreadsheet, and on 13 November it goes to the printer.
In December, 41 certificates still have to be printed again.
Yet in February, a close look at a hundred of the list's records found 21 with an error.
One record in five, but only 41 certificates in 2,031?
Like the readers in Washington, Malia's team puts the rest right at the end, unseen.
Thomas Redman, who has spent his career on data quality, calls this a hidden data factory:
the extra steps one team adds to put right the data another team makes.
Decades before, in factories, Armand Feigenbaum called it the hidden plant.
It's careful work, and until the errors stop, it's needed.
But it hides three things.
The hours, because nobody counts them.
How good the data really is, because the printer sees only what gets past.
And the cause, because no fix reaches the place where the errors are born.
Redman's advice: count it, then take what you find to the people who make the data.
In August 2026, Noor Rahman, the data architect, counts it with Malia, three ways.
The hours, from the team's own calendar: about 240 for December's list, 50 for March's, 30 for July's.
320 hours a year: two months of one person's work.
The rounds, from Databricks' system tables:
its query history and audit log show the list queried and downloaded on three Mondays, one before each list.
And the corrections: December's copy, as it went to the printer, against the list the platform built the night before.
517 names had been changed by hand, and 26 more had got past them: the names printed again.
So 543 of 2,031 names were wrong when the list left the platform: about one in four.
A right name takes about two minutes to check. A wrong one, about twenty: find the document, phone the graduate, type it again.
So the wrong names took about 170 of December's 240 hours.
Redman's rule of ten, a rule of thumb: a record with an error costs about ten times as much to finish.
Beatriz Fonseca de Albuquerque Cavalcanti graduates twice this year: a graduate certificate in March, a master's in December.
Her family name has 33 characters.
In February, the portal showed it cut short, and she corrected it: March's certificate was right.
In August, her master's joins December's list, cut short again.
With Mei and Malia, Noor and Jun ask why, five times.
Why is it cut? The list takes the student system's name, unless she confirms it for that ceremony.
Why is it still cut there? Her correction went to March's list, not to the student system.
Why? Only the registrar's office changes the student system, and nothing sent it there.
Why was it cut at all? The family name field holds 30 characters.
Why 30? It was set when the system was built, and it fitted most names then.
Two causes: a field too short, and no way back.
Inside the platform, Unity Catalog's lineage draws the same path, column by column:
from the name on the list back to the student system's family name.
Before the platform and after it, people have to tell you.
To find every cause, the team draws a fishbone, as Kaoru Ishikawa taught: the problem at its head, the causes along its bones.
Four bones: people, process, systems, and interfaces, where data passes from one system to another.
People: paper forms before 2015 had one box for the whole name, split by whoever typed it in: 35 swapped.
Process: every fix made in a copy, with no way back.
Systems: the 30-character field, 39 names cut short; and until 2019, an online form that took only A to Z, in capitals: 312 names.
Interfaces: the nightly file to the platform, in an old encoding that turned é into e.
143 names stored right lost their accents on the way in.
Nobody did anything wrong. Each cause made sense when it was made.
As Fixed where it starts showed: fix it where it starts, with its owner.
On the night of Monday 14 September, the student system team, with Sam, changes two things:
the nightly file keeps every letter, and the family name field holds 100 characters.
From that day, every correction is made once, in the student system, by Mei's office; the graduations team keeps no copy.
Old names are put right as each graduate confirms theirs, those graduating first.
And Jun adds checks in dbt where the names are born: on the student system's records, each night, owned by Mei.
A family name exactly 30 characters long, or in capitals only, holds for her office: a list to work through.
A night's file with not one letter outside A to Z stops the update: the list keeps the night before's names, and Sam is told.
A doubt about one name waits for a person; a file losing letters for everyone stops.
By the morning of Tuesday 15 September, 161 names on December's list have their accents back, and nobody typed them.
The check holds Beatriz's name, and Mei's office writes it in full, once, for every list after.
Each round's hours go on the scorecard, beside the checks, so everyone can watch them fall.
The post stopped placing letters one by one, and put a code on them at the start, written by the person who knew.
At the university, each name is now put right where it's born, by the people who own it.
Count the work spent fixing data by hand. Then fix where it's born.

films.x: When a person reports an error. On Monday 12 October 2026, Andrés Peñaloza sees his name as it will be printed on his certificate: Andres Penaloza. He presses "This isn't my name". Mei Tanaka's team answers within two working days, fixes it in the student system itself and tells him, and his kind of error becomes a check.
c: India, 1974: the last years of a campaign to end smallpox.
Smallpox passed from person to person: it killed many who caught it, and scarred most who lived.
That year it came back hard: more than 116,000 cases by the end of May.
It hid in villages and city streets, far from any clinic.
A case nobody reported passed it to the next family, and the next: a chain.
Vaccinating everyone couldn't reach everyone, and it found the ones missed.
Every chain had to be found, and stopped where it was.
So India's health workers, with the World Health Organization, changed what they did: search, and contain.
More than a hundred thousand of them went house to house.
Anyone who reported a case was promised a reward, and every report was answered at once.
Guards stayed at the sick person's door, day and night, and everyone around was vaccinated: the chain stopped there.
And whoever reported it was paid, so people kept reporting.
In May 1975, a year on, India found its last case.
In 1977, India was declared free of smallpox, and in 1980, the world.
At the university, a name printed wrong on a degree certificate is a case too.
The certificate is printed again, and a graduate crosses the stage holding an empty folder.
A report is worth only what happens next: answer it, fix it where it started, and tell them, and the next is found before it's printed.
Monday 12 October 2026: the portal opens for December's graduates, to check their name as it will be printed.
That evening, Andrés Peñaloza reads his: Andres Penaloza.
No accent on the e. No tilde on the n.
He presses "This isn't my name", and types it as he writes it.
No check had ever held it: it's short, and every letter is allowed.
His record dates from 2018, made by an old online form that took only A to Z, in capitals.
When he came back for his Master's, the capitals were typed again by hand, as ordinary letters, and it looked right.
People find errors no check can see.
So make it easy to say so, where they see the data.
His report is a row of data: who, the name shown, the name given, and when.
And the portal says what happens next: "The registrar's office will answer by Wednesday 14 October."
The report goes straight to the people who own names: the registrar's office, Mei's team.
Their promise: an answer within two working days.
Every report is kept in a model of its own, with its owner, when it's due, and when it was answered and told.
Answering in time is about what people do, not whether the data is right.
So it's tracked and reviewed every week, never failed as a check.
Each morning, an alert on Databricks tells the registrar's office which reports are due that day.
In India, every report was answered at once: a promise kept is what makes people report again.
Wednesday 14 October: Mei's team checks his name against the passport seen at his enrolment.
It matches, and they correct it in the student system itself: not in the list, and not in a copy.
That night, the update carries it to the list, the portal and the printer's file: every copy at once.
Fixed in the list, it would be undone by the next night's update.
Fixed in a spreadsheet, it would be wrong again next year, as The hidden factory showed.
Like guards at the door, a fix where the error started stops it there.
Then the portal tells him: "Your name will be printed as Andrés Peñaloza. Thank you for telling us."
A report that disappears teaches people not to bother.
In India, every reporter was paid, so the next one reported too.
In October, 64 graduates reported their name.
61 were put right within two working days, and three waited for a document. Every one was told.
And the people who make the data hear what it cost: a graduate who had to find their own name wrong.
The admissions team, who made the old forms, now get a note each month.
October's note: 38 names from the old online form, and 11 from the paper forms.
So from November, admissions asks every student who comes back to check their name against their passport.
Thomas Redman calls them data's customers and its creators: tell the creators what an error cost, and the next one isn't made.
Read together, the reports show where errors are born: of the first 19, 12 came from the old form, like Andrés's.
Each kind of error a person finds becomes a check, so nobody has to find it again.
Jun adds one: a name the old form made, still in plain letters, A to Z, not yet confirmed by its graduate.
It can't see a missing accent. But it can see where a name was born.
It holds each one for Mei's team, and dbt keeps them in a table her team reads.
On its first night, it holds 83.
The registrar's office writes to each: our old form dropped accents, so please look closely at your name.
Within a week, seven had given back the accents the old form took.
Mei logs it in the issue log, as Rules that run showed.
As in India, where everyone around a case was vaccinated, before the chain could spread.
In India, after the last case, the reward rose to a thousand rupees, four months' pay, and every report was answered.
None was smallpox: that's how they knew it was gone.
At the university, every report is answered, fixed where it started, and told, and each kind of error becomes a check.
Andrés's certificate will read Andrés Peñaloza.
Answer every report, fix it where it started, and tell them.

films.x: Descriptions and agents. In October 2026, Malia asked the graduations team's agent which December graduates hadn't confirmed their name, and it answered 412 at once. An empty date meant two things: 38 hadn't confirmed yet, and 374 had confirmed on the paper form. Nothing written said so, and the agent can't ask.
c: Around the year 2000, people writing for the United Nations, the European Union and NATO used spell checkers.
A spell checker marks a word it doesn't know, and offers one it does.
Some checkers' word lists had co-operation, with a hyphen, but not cooperation, without one.
So when a writer typed cooperation, the checker marked it wrong, and the first word it offered was Cupertino, a city in California.
Writers in a hurry took it.
A NATO report of 1999 named the Organization for Security and Cupertino in Europe, and readers had to guess what was meant.
By 2006, hundreds could be found on these organisations' websites.
A confident machine, a gap in what it read, and nobody reading after it.
Translators had to start checking what the machine was sure of.
In 2000, the European Commission's English translators wrote about it in their magazine.
Among the European Union's writers and translators, the fault got a name: the Cupertino effect.
The name was a warning: read what the checker offers before you take it.
And the checkers' makers added to their word lists, so cooperation was a word they knew.
By 2007, checkers no longer routinely offered Cupertino for cooperation, and readers got the word the writer meant.
At the university, in October 2026, an agent read an empty column, and answered 412, with confidence.
Once the data said what empty means, it answered 38, and 374 graduates weren't asked again for a name they had given.
Thursday 22 October 2026.
In three weeks, the list for December's ceremonies goes to the printer.
Malia, who runs the ceremonies, asks the graduations team's agent which December graduates haven't confirmed their name.
It reads the list, and answers at once: 412.
No doubt, and no question back.
Malia drafts an email to all 412: please confirm your name before it's printed.
Then, before she sends it, she reads the answer again.
412 is a fifth of the list.
In March, 95 graduates in every 100 answered within the portal's two weeks.
A fifth still silent, ten days in, doesn't fit what she knows.
So before she writes to anyone, she asks Mei, who answers for the list.
The agent had counted the graduates whose confirmation date was empty.
Mei knows that empty means two things there.
38 graduates haven't confirmed their name yet.
374 confirmed it on the paper form, before the portal opened in February, and the paper form has no date in the list.
The column's description said only: date the graduate confirmed their name.
Nobody had written down what empty means.
Mei could have told anyone who asked, but the agent can't walk over to her desk.
It reads what's written, and answers as if that were all there is.
Its 412 was a Cupertino.
So a column's description is part of the data's quality.
One international standard for data quality calls this understandability: data its users can read and interpret.
Empty meaning two things is a fault in the data, and so is a description that doesn't say so.
So the team fixes the data first.
Noor, the data architect, finds where the paper form is recorded, in the student system.
From it, Jun adds a column that says how each name was confirmed: portal or paper, and empty means not yet.
Then he writes the description in Mei's words, for a reader who can't ask.
What it means: the day of the graduate's answer in the portal, for that ceremony, once it's accepted.
What empty means: not confirmed in the portal; the new column says if it was on paper.
And who answers for it: Mei, in the registrar's office.
dbt writes it into Unity Catalog on every run, where the agent reads it.
So the team wrote down what the agent needed to read, as the checkers' makers added to their word lists.
Asked again, the agent answers 38, and shows what it counted: graduates with no confirmation of either kind.
Malia writes to the 38.
Jun's check from Report, fix, tell had read empty the same way; pointed at the new column, its 76 names become 7.
Jun asks his own agent, Genie Code, to read the list and the checks it already runs.
It profiles every column, drafts descriptions for the rest, and proposes three new checks.
Each draft is a start: it can say what a column's name suggests, not what only its owner knows.
So Jun reviews each one, and Mei sets the levels.
The first finds a name on the list that isn't the name its graduate gave in the portal.
Mei makes it stop the printer's file until a person settles each name.
It finds three: names changed since enrolment, still waiting for a document.
The second checks that the two confirmation columns agree, and holds for Jun if they don't.
The third would fail every night a graduate hadn't confirmed yet.
Jun says no: that's about what people do, not whether the data is right.
It becomes a count Malia follows each week, and the agent's trusted answer to her question.
The agent proposes; people decide.
What spared 374 graduates an email they didn't need was Malia reading the answer before she acted.
Read an agent's answer as you'd read a new colleague's: what did it count, and does that fit what you know?
Ask it to show its working, and when the answer doesn't fit, ask the person who answers for the data.
Context engineering showed that what an agent reads decides what it writes, and Context and memory, governed, how to keep that right.
This film's step comes first: a column's description is part of the data, and its quality is the data's quality.
On Monday, pick the table your agent reads most.
For each column, write what it means, what empty means, its unit, and who answers for it.
Where empty means two things, fix the data, not only the words.
Let agents draft and propose; let people review and decide.
The Cupertino's cure had two halves: complete what the machine reads, and read what it offers before you take it.
Describe your data for a reader who can't ask.

films.x: Continuous improvement. In December 2025, 41 degree certificates were printed again from a wrong list. Instead of one big clean-up, Malia, Mei, Jun and Sam met for fifteen minutes every Thursday, made one small change, measured it and kept it with a check. A year later, it was 3.
c: Mexico, 1945. A programme run by Mexico's government with the Rockefeller Foundation is working to grow more food.
On wheat, a small team: young Mexican agronomists, and a plant scientist from the United States, Norman Borlaug.
Their enemy is stem rust, a fungus that covers wheat's stems in rust-red spots.
The stems weaken, the grain shrivels, and a whole field can be lost.
It had ruined harvest after harvest. Farmers lost their crops, and Mexico had to buy much of its wheat abroad.
A wheat that resists the rust can be bred, but slowly.
One harvest a year is one generation a year, and finding the right wheat takes many.
Every year of waiting was another year of ruined fields. The breeding had to go faster.
So the team grew two generations a year.
In winter, in the Yaqui Valley in the north-west, near the sea.
In summer, in the highlands near Mexico City, more than two thousand metres up, and over a thousand kilometres away.
After each harvest, they carried the seed to the other field and sowed it again.
Each round, they looked at every plant, saw which ones the rust left standing, and kept the best.
Small steps, twice a year, every year.
It halved the time to a new wheat. By 1948, they had four new wheats that resisted the rust.
Farmers came to the fields to see, more than 800 on one day in 1954, and sowed the new seed.
By 1956, Mexico grew all the wheat it needed.
At the university, in December 2025, 41 degree certificates had to be printed again: the list they came from was wrong.
Each one, a graduate who might cross the stage holding an empty folder.
A year later, after one small change a week, each one measured, it was 3.
In January, after December's 41, the first idea was a big project: clean every name on the list, once, before March.
But a clean-up fixes the names once, and the next list brings the same errors back.
So Mei, who answers for the list, asked for something smaller.
Every Thursday at ten: fifteen minutes, standing at the bench.
Malia, who runs the ceremonies. Mei, whose office makes the names right.
Jun, who builds the list, and Sam, who runs it every night.
Three questions. What did this week's results say?
What one small change will we make?
And how will we know it worked?
The results come from the checks that run every night.
And from what people count: reports, hours of hand work, and the hundred records.
Quality engineers call it plan, do, study, act: a loop drawn by Walter Shewhart and taught by W. Edwards Deming.
Many say check for its third step. Deming preferred study: compare what happened with what the plan expected, and learn from it.
Borlaug's team ran the loop twice a year: sow, look, keep the best, sow again.
Here is one turn of it, from Thursday 1 October 2026, before December's round of hand checks.
Last December, two people checked every name by hand: 240 hours.
Since September, names are fixed where they're born, and each night the checks hold the doubtful ones.
So Malia asks: do we still need to check every name by hand?
Plan: check by hand only the names a check holds or a graduate reports, and let the hundred records look at the rest.
They'll know by two measures they keep already: the round's hours, and the perfect records in the hundred.
And they say what they expect: far fewer hours, and at least 95 perfect records.
Do: from Monday 19 October, the team checks 78 names by hand, not 2,140.
Study: the round takes 26 hours, not 240. And on Friday 6 November, 97 of the hundred records are perfect.
Both as the plan expected.
Act: they keep it, and write it into the round's steps.
With agents, study matters more. An agent can draft the whole change, for a person to approve.
People learn by doing the work. Handed to an agent, that understanding can stay hidden.
So a person still has to understand the plan, and know enough to help with the doing.
Then study the results against the plan, and act on what they show.
The order mattered: measure, simplify, standardise, and only then automate.
They measured the hand work first, in August: about 320 hours a year.
They simplified it: only the names a check holds.
They standardised it: one way to settle a held name, in the student system, against the document seen at enrolment.
Then they automated: each night the checks hold names, in a list the registrar's office reads each morning.
Automate first, and you only do the wrong work faster.
The last step of every change is a check that keeps it.
Without one, a change lasts only until someone forgets it.
The hand checks are kept by the hundred records, now every month, at a level agreed with Malia.
Below 95 perfect, the next round checks more by hand.
Every change of the year has its keeper.
The scorecard shows only last night's checks.
So a last step of each night's run in dbt now keeps every result, in a table.
On Thursdays, one dashboard on Databricks reads that table, beside what people count.
It shows the whole week: a check that holds more names each night is something to look at.
Certificates printed again: 41, 14, 6. Perfect records: 79, 88, 97. Hours by hand: about 320 a year, now about 40.
Fifteen minutes is enough because the people who use the list and the people who make it stand at the same table.
Malia brings what the ceremonies need. Mei's office brings the names, made right at the source.
Jun and Sam bring the checks, and the night's run.
When a change needs someone else, such as admissions, who make each student's first record, they're asked to that Thursday.
In Mexico, the farmers came to the table too.
In 1955, they helped buy land for a new research station, and taxed their own wheat to add more.
Wednesday 9 December 2026, ten in the morning, in the Great Hall.
Andrés Peñaloza crosses the stage.
Mei reads his name from the list: Andrés Peñaloza, as he says it.
His certificate says Andrés Peñaloza, every letter.
This December, 3 certificates were printed again, not 41.
Two graduates had changed their names after the list was sent, and one hadn't confirmed hers.
On Thursday 17 December, the four look at the three, and pick the next small change.
Borlaug's team didn't stop in 1956 either.
Round after round, its wheats got better, and by 1963 Mexico was selling wheat abroad.
Quality isn't a property of data. It's whether data is fit for a use.
Say what good means for each use. Measure it. Check it against the truth and the clock.
Fix it where it's born. Answer the people who report. Write it down for readers who can't ask.
And get better, a little, every week.
One small change a week, measured, then kept.

films.x: Why enterprise architecture. Tomás starts as an enterprise architect at a publicly owned energy utility. He's handed an org chart, a list of 140 systems and a backlog, and none of it explains the place. The film shows a way of looking: an organisation in layers, from why it exists down to what runs it.
c: Nineteen years after conquering England, William the Conqueror still didn't know exactly what he ruled.
At Christmas 1085, he sent surveyors across most of the country.
Who holds this land? What is on it? What is it worth?
Ploughs, mills and meadows, then and now.
Their record became the Domesday Book.
Before you can govern a place, you have to know what it is.
Today, Tomás starts as an enterprise architect at an energy utility owned by the regional government.
It runs the poles and wires for the region, owns a few hydro and wind farms, and sells power to homes and businesses.
By lunchtime he has a badge, an org chart, a list of a hundred and forty systems, and an invitation: the transition program.
Everyone asks what he thinks.
He doesn't know what to think yet. He doesn't even know what to ask.
Everything he's been given is true. None of it explains the place.
The org chart shows who reports to whom, not what the utility must be able to do.
The system list shows what was bought, not what it's for.
The process manual runs to four hundred pages, last revised six years ago.
And the strategy is five words on a slide.
Each is a piece of the picture, cut from a different puzzle.
Enterprise architecture is a way of looking at an organisation in layers, from why it exists down to what runs it.
Three questions hold the layers.
Why does it exist, and for whom?
How does it work: who does what, with which information?
And what runs it: which applications, on which technology?
Each layer is worked out from the one above.
Start from the bottom, and you'll describe every system perfectly, and still not know what they're for.
There's no shortage of methods.
TOGAF gives a way to do the work. ArchiMate, a language to draw it. Zachman, a grid to sort it.

Business architecture brings capabilities and value streams, process frameworks bring catalogues, domain-driven design shows where meanings change, and data management shows who looks after information.
Each has its champions. Under the vocabulary, they agree on more than they differ.
This series takes what they agree on.
And it starts rough.
A canvas on a wall: who the utility serves, what they need, and how it's paid for.
Sticky notes can be argued with in an afternoon.
Later, they become a capability map, then value streams, and finally a model in a formal notation.
Notation is earned.
Draw too precisely too early, and people correct your drawing instead of your understanding.
Tomás sets himself two rules.
Every note names where it came from: the annual report, the regulator's decision, the owner's statement of expectations, an interview.
And every note stays a draft until the person who owns that part of the business says it's right.
A map nobody has confirmed is one person's opinion, drawn neatly.
Why would a data architect care?
Because every data rule is a claim about the organisation.
Take this one: an estimated meter reading stands only until the next actual reading.
Which process creates it? Who owns it? Which goal does it serve?
Without the map, a rule is a guess, and when it's wrong, nobody knows who should fix it.
With the map, the rule has a home.
Over eleven films, Tomás builds the map, one layer at a time.
Seven films to understand the utility: who it serves, why it moves, what it must be able to do, how value reaches people, who does what, and what runs it.
Then four on what it means for data: the questions that matter, rules with a home, a change in strategy, and a map that people and agents can read.
The surveyors' first questions still work.
What is this place? Who holds it? What is it worth?
Tomás writes the first note.

films.t: Who it serves, and how it pays
films.x: Customers and offerings. Before any capability or process, find out who the utility serves, what they're trying to get done, what hurts, what it offers, and how each offering pays. Two canvases hold it, and a canvas only means something if it fits.
c: In 1882, Thomas Edison opened a power station on Pearl Street, in New York.
His customers didn't want electricity. They wanted light.
Gas lamps were hot, smoky, and could start fires.
So Edison sold steady, clean light, priced to compete with gas, and measured it with a meter whose zinc plates were weighed.
He knew who he served, what they were trying to do, and how it would pay.
Tomás's first note asks why the utility exists.
The annual report answers in five words: safe, affordable, reliable, clean, ours.
But for whom? He goes to see Farah, the utility's customer advocate.
They start with two kinds of canvas: one for each kind of customer, and one for each thing the utility offers.
Who pays, who uses and who decides are often different people.
A tenant uses the power and pays the bill. The landlord decides whether there are solar panels. And the regulator decides the price.
Farah names the segments: households, households in hardship, businesses, and homes with solar, which buy power and sell it back.
The minister and the regulator matter just as much, but they aren't customers. They'll have their own place on the map.
Tomás starts with households, one canvas at a time.
What are they trying to get done?
Keep the lights and the heating on.
Not worry about the bill.
And, for many, do their bit for the climate.
A job is what the customer wants, in their words, not what the utility sells.
What goes wrong today? Bills that are too high.
Bills based on a guess.
A power cut with no warning, and no idea when it ends.
And what would be a win? Knowing when the power will be back.
A bill they understand.
Paying less, because of their solar panels.
Now the other side: what the utility offers, named the way a customer would name it.
Electricity supply. A connection to the network. Outage updates by text. A hardship plan.
Then, for each pain, what takes it away.
Smart meters replace guesses with real readings.
A text gives the time the power will be back.
A payment plan spreads a large bill.
A canvas only means something if it fits.
Every pain needs something that relieves it. Every gain needs something that creates it.
On the canvas for homes with solar, one pain has nothing: waiting months to connect new panels.
An unmatched pain is either a missing capability or a customer the utility has decided not to serve. The canvas has to say which.
Farah is clear: they serve them. It's a missing capability, and it goes on the list.
Then, how each offering pays. Not one canvas for the whole utility, but one for each offering, because each has its own economics.
The network earns what the regulator allows, through a charge on every bill. Its biggest cost is poles, wires and crews.
Retail supply earns from tariffs, and its biggest cost is buying energy on the wholesale market.
The hardship plan is paid for by the government, because a public utility is measured by public value, not only by profit.
These canvases aren't the architecture. The architecture is derived from them.
Segments become stakeholders. Pains and gains become reasons to change. What relieves a pain becomes a capability. Key activities become processes.
Revenue and costs have no box of their own in the model. They stay as tables, tied to what they pay for.
And later, the same blocks will tell a data team what each number is for.
Farah confirms the households' canvas. The rest stay drafts, for now.
Tomás's first note has an answer: to keep the region's homes and businesses powered, affordably and fairly.
Next, he asks why it has to change.

films.x: Motivation. A minister, a regulator and a valley community pull the utility three ways at once. Ama, the regulatory lead, sorts who cares, what pushes on them and what it means here; then goals with outcomes someone can check, and principles that settle the pull.
c: On the ninth of November, 1965, a single relay near Niagara Falls switched off a line it should have kept on.
Within minutes, the fault spread across the north-east of America and into Canada. Thirty million people lost power.
Every utility had watched its own wires, and none could see the whole.
So the utilities set up a council and wrote rules for all of them to keep.
A shock, what it revealed, what had to become true, and a rule to hold to.
Tomás's new note asks why the utility must change. Three letters answer at once.
The minister expects lower bills, a dividend, and net zero by 2045.
The regulator has cut what the network may earn for the next five years.
And a valley community objects to a new line that would carry power from a wind farm.
Each letter is right. They pull in different directions.
He takes them to Ama, the regulatory lead. Ama starts with who cares.
The customers from Farah's canvases are only some of them.
The minister owns the utility. The regulator sets its prices. The community lives beside its lines. And the staff keep it running.
Each is a stakeholder: someone with an interest in what the utility does.
Then, what pushes on them. Ama calls these drivers.
Decarbonisation. Affordability. Ageing poles and wires.
And rooftop solar, which turns customers into generators.
A driver is a pressure, not a wish. It's there whether or not anyone plans for it.
A driver says nothing until someone works out what it means here.
Ama calls that an assessment, and every one has a source.
A third of the poles are over fifty years old.
The network was built for power that flows one way.
Household bills rose eighteen per cent in two years.
Without the evidence, it's just an opinion.
Now, what must become true. Goals.
Keep bills affordable. Replace ageing assets before they fail. Connect renewable power.
A goal is a direction. An outcome says how anyone will know it's been reached.
The network charge on a household bill no higher in real terms in 2030.
New solar connected within ten working days.
If no one can say how an outcome will be checked, it isn't one yet.
Then the goals collide. Connecting the wind farm needs a new line.
A new line costs money that bills must repay. And it runs through the valley.
Every goal is right, and they can't all win.
If the loudest letter decides, the next decision will go another way. That's what principles are for.
A principle is a rule every choice is checked against.
Ama has three. Use what we have before we build.
Every option is costed for the customers who pay for it.
And customer information stays with the business that collected it.
"Be sustainable" is not a principle, because nothing could ever fail it.
Checked against these three, the new line isn't the first option. Upgrading the old line, with batteries in the valley, is.
Drawn together, it's a chain.
Stakeholders feel drivers. Assessments say what they mean here. Goals answer them, and outcomes say how anyone will know.
Principles stand beside it all.
Every outcome is a number someone will one day have to measure.
What counts as a working day? Connected, from when?
Ama confirms the drivers and the assessments. The goals go to the board, as drafts.
Tomás's note has an answer, and something to check every answer against.
Next, he asks what the utility must be able to do.

films.t: What it must be able to do
films.x: Capabilities. Tomás's first capability map is the org chart again. Grace shows him that teams, processes and systems change, and what the network must be able to do stays. Three levels, one owner each, and a heat map with evidence that shows where it hurts.
c: In the Andes, in the 1400s, the Inca sent messages across their empire on foot.
Every few kilometres along the roads stood a small post, and a runner waited there: a chasqui.
Each ran his stretch, then passed the message on: spoken, or knotted into cords called khipu.
Relay by relay, a message could travel more than two hundred kilometres in a day.
Runners served their turn and went home. Roads were mended and rebuilt.
What lasted was an ability: to move a message across the empire, whoever carried it.
Tomás's next note asks what the utility must be able to do.
He starts where most people start: with the org chart.
Network Operations. Customer Service. Finance. Technology. Regulatory Affairs.
Each box becomes a capability, and the map is done in an hour.
It looks complete. It's the org chart again.
Grace, who owns network operations, reads it.
"Network Operations is my team," she says. "Two years ago, it was two teams. Next year, it may be part of another."
The org chart changes. What the network must be able to do doesn't.
A team is who does the work. A capability is what must be done, whoever does it.
Tomás tries again, and walks into two more traps.
"Run the outage system" names a system. It says with what.
"Dispatch through the control room" names a process. It says how.
Under both is one ability: manage outages.
A capability survives a restructure, a new system and a new process. If a box wouldn't, it isn't one.
Grace helps him lay them out in levels.
Level one is the whole utility: eight boxes, with the support ones beneath.
Level two opens one of them. Operating the network means monitoring it, controlling it and managing outages.
Level three opens one more. Managing outages means finding faults, dispatching crews, restoring supply and keeping customers informed.
Three levels are enough to talk about. Deeper, and nobody reads it.
Next, an owner for each: one person who answers for it.
Grace takes the network's. Ama takes meeting the utility's obligations.
The head of retail takes selling energy and serving customers.
Generating power has no owner yet. Until someone answers for it, it's a guess.
An owner is a person, not a team: someone who can say, yes, that's right.
Now the map can show where it hurts.
They colour each capability by how well it works today, with evidence, like every note on the wall.
Operating the network: green. Faults are found and fixed within target.
Maintaining assets: amber. Two poles in five haven't been inspected in ten years.
Connecting customers: red. New solar takes thirty-four working days to connect. The goal is ten.
A heat map shows where it hurts, so it shows where the money should go.
Tomás wants to open every box. Grace opens only the red one.
Connecting customers takes three abilities: assessing network capacity, approving connections, and installing meters.
Approvals and meters are quick. The wait is in assessing capacity.
The network was built for power that flows one way. Nobody knows how much solar each street can take.
So the money goes to one capability, whichever team or system ends up doing the work.
On the map, capabilities fill the strategy layer.
Above them, the goals they serve. Below them, the teams, processes and systems that do the work.
Those will change. The capabilities stay. That's why they're the spine.
Every measure and every data rule will need a home, and most will hang from one of these boxes.
Even a number nobody has yet: how much solar each street can take.
Grace confirms the network's capabilities, Ama hers, and the head of retail theirs.
Generating power stays a draft until its owner is found.
Tomás's note has an answer: eight capabilities, seven owners, and one that hurts.
Next, he follows one power cut from the first call to the lights coming back on.

films.x: Value streams and processes. A branch brings down a line on a stormy night, and forty homes go dark. Tomás follows one household's call: a value stream from their side, the teams behind it, a process map in levels, and detail only at the step whose rule depends on order.
c: Mumbai, a weekday morning. A home-cooked lunch goes into a tin, and the tin to a dabbawala.
On its lid, a few painted marks say where it's going: the station, the building, the floor.
By bicycle, train and on foot, it changes hands several times, and reaches a desk across the city by lunchtime.
Before the pandemic, about five thousand dabbawalas carried some two hundred thousand lunches a day, with almost no errors.
The detail lives where the tins change hands: marks, read at every sorting.
The customer sees only three things: lunch leaves home, lunch arrives, the tin comes back.
Tomás's next note asks how value reaches people.
At ten past two on a stormy morning, a branch falls on a line on Hill Street. Forty homes go dark.
Four minutes later, one household calls the faults line, and Tomás follows that call to the lights coming back on.
On its way, it will pass through three teams, and a rule nobody has written down.
Farah, the customer advocate, draws the night from the household's side.
The household sees no teams and no systems. It sees a few stages, in order.
Someone knows the power's out. Help is on its way. The lights come back. And someone says what happened.
Each stage ends with something the household gets.
That's a value stream: how value reaches a customer, seen from their side. This one: get the power back.
A utility has only a handful; meter to cash is another.
Under each stage go the capabilities from his map that make it possible.
Finding faults. Dispatching crews. Restoring supply. Informing customers.
The work itself passes through three teams: the contact centre, the control room and the field crews.
The household sees none of them, and feels only the hand-offs that go wrong.
As with the dabbawalas' tins, the detail belongs where the work changes hands.
A value stream shows what reaches the customer; a process, how the work gets done.
Grace shows him the utility's process map. Every process sits in one of four groups.
Strategic processes set direction. Operational ones deliver to customers. Support keeps the rest running. Evaluation measures and improves.
Restoring supply is operational. Evaluation measures it: how long, and how often, customers are without power.
Like capabilities, processes have levels.
Level one is the map. Level two is one process: restore supply.
Level three is its steps. Take the call. Find the fault. Decide who goes first. Send the crew. Repair. Switch back on. Confirm.
For most of these steps, a box and an arrow say enough.
Before going deeper, Tomás draws its edges.
Who supplies it, what comes in, what goes out, to whom: a SIPOC, in Six Sigma's terms.
In come calls, alarms from smart meters, and where each crew is.
What comes out: power back on, a time to tell customers, and a fault record.
The fault record, with its start, end and cause, goes to the regulator.
Only one step needs more detail: deciding which crew goes first.
Tonight the storm has caused three faults, and two crews are free.
On Hill Street, a wire is down. On Riverside, twelve homes, one with someone on life support. On the east side, twelve hundred homes.
Left to habit, both crews would go to the biggest fault.
The rule says otherwise: wires down first, for safety. Then life support. Then whatever brings back the most homes.
Order and state: that's where a process earns detail, step by step, in a notation such as BPMN.
At two in the morning, the rule needs three facts.
Which wires are down: from the calls.
Who is on life support: from a register.
How many homes each fault cuts off: from the network model, which isn't sure which homes hang off which transformer.
Wherever order, state or timing matter, that's where the data rules are.
At twenty to four, Hill Street's lights come back on, with a message: a branch on the line, now cleared.
Farah confirms the stages, and Grace the steps.
The rule for who goes first is written down at last, and Grace owns it.
Tomás's note has an answer: value reaches people in a few stages; the detail belongs at one step.
Next, he asks who does each step, and what "customer" means to each of them.

films.t: Who does it, and where meaning changes
films.x: Actors, roles and domains. Tomás finds roles filled by people, partners and an AI agent, and one word, customer, that means two things: a connection point to the network, and an account to retail. The film shows who does the work, and how to translate where meaning changes.
c: Japan, the 1890s. Tokyo buys its generators from Germany. They make power at fifty cycles a second.
Osaka buys American ones, at sixty.
The two grids grow until they meet in the middle of the country. Both sides call it power, but they can't simply be joined.
In March 2011, after the earthquake and tsunami, the east loses a large share of its power stations. The west has power to spare.
But it can send east only what a few converter stations can translate: about one gigawatt. Around Tokyo, the power is cut in turns.
Making one side match the other has been studied, and judged far too costly. So Japan builds more converters.
The same word means something different on each side of a line. What crosses is translated at the edge, and that's where it can fail.
Tomás's next note asks who does the work, and where meaning changes.
He writes a name on each step of the night on Hill Street. Priya took the call. Sam decided who went first.
Grace crosses the names out. Next week, someone else is on the night shift.
A step is done by a role: the call-taker, the duty controller, the crew leader.
Whoever fills a role is an actor: a person, or a team. Actors come and go; roles stay.
Roles sit in teams: the contact centre, the control room.
But the crew that fixed Hill Street isn't the utility's. It's a contractor's: a partner.
What a partner must do is written in a contract: on site within two hours, under the utility's safety rules.
Partners change. The contract goes on the map, because it says what the next one must do too.
One more actor worked that night, and it isn't a person.
An AI agent reads every outage report as it arrives: calls, texts, alarms from smart meters.
It groups them into faults, and proposes which matters most.
Its rights are written down, like anyone's. It may group reports and propose. It may not send a crew.
A wire down, or someone on life support, goes straight to the duty controller. The agent recommends; a person decides.
Then Tomás asks a simple question: how many customers do we have?
Retail says three hundred and ten thousand: people and businesses with an account, who pay a bill.
The network says five hundred and forty thousand: connection points, the places where power is delivered, whichever retailer they buy from.
When a family moves out of fourteen Hill Street, retail closes one account and opens another. The network's connection point doesn't change.
Both numbers are right. They count different things, with the same word.
Ama, the regulatory lead, explains what keeps them apart.
In many markets, the rules separate a network from retail, even inside one group. The utility's own principle says it too: customer information stays with the business that collected it.
The network knows who has just applied to connect solar panels. To a retailer, that's a list of people to sell batteries to.
It must not cross.
So Tomás draws the edge. On one side, the network. On the other, retail.
Each is a domain: a part of the organisation, modelled as an organisation in its own right.
Each has its own customers, its own capabilities, and its own words. The network says connection point, feeder, outage. Retail says account, tariff, bill.
Meaning changes at a domain's edge. Customer is one word, for two things.
Tomás's first instinct is one definition of customer for everyone, kept in one place.
It would fit neither side. And it would carry what the network knows straight across the wall.
Instead, each domain keeps its own meaning, and the edge gets a translation: a short, agreed list of what crosses, and how.
Which connection point. Which retailer serves it. Planned outages. And who there depends on power for life support.
When someone on life support moves into a home, retail hears first.
The network must know before the next storm, because its rule for who goes first works from that list.
If the message is late, the rule works from the wrong list.
As at Japan's converters, the edge is where the translation is built, and where it can fail.
Grace confirms the network's roles, and the head of retail confirms theirs. Ama confirms the edge, and what may cross it.
The agent's rights go on the map, with an owner: Grace.
Tomás's note has an answer: roles do the work, and people, partners and agents fill them. Customer means two things, with a wall between them and a translation at the edge.
Next, at last, he opens the list of a hundred and forty systems.

films.x: Systems and a target. Tomás places today's 140 systems under the capabilities they serve: three for one job, one capability with only a spreadsheet, and one system that serves nothing. Then he draws a target, and the path to it, with a reason for each step.
c: An imagined morning, in 2045, in the utility's own region.
As the sun comes up, the homes on one street trade power from their batteries, house to house.
A transformer's readings start to drift, and a crew is sent before it fails. Nobody on the street notices.
This isn't a forecast. It's a drawing of where the utility wants to go, made as carefully as a drawing of today.
And today, it runs on a hundred and forty systems.
Tomás's next note asks what runs the utility today, and where it's going.
On day one, the systems were a list: what had been bought, over forty years.
Now there's a map to place them on. Each system goes under the capability it serves, from evidence: who uses it, and for what.
Most of them land where you'd expect.
Under managing outages, there are three: an outage system, a network control system that also handles outages, and a storm tool someone built in 2015.
Under assessing network capacity, the capability that hurts, there's no system at all: a spreadsheet, kept by one engineer.
And one system serves no capability anyone can name. It still costs a licence every year.
Overlaps, gaps and shadow systems: a list could never show them. A map does.
Below the applications is the technology they run on: two data centres, a cloud, and the radio network the field devices talk over.
Each layer serves the one above. The business needs a capability; applications serve it; technology runs them.
Change a capability, and you can follow it down. Switch off a server, and you can follow it up.
For the first time, the drafts become one model, in ArchiMate's notation.
Each block of the early canvases finds its element. A customer segment becomes a stakeholder. A pain reliever, a capability. A key activity, a business process. A key resource, a resource.
The whole map, layer by layer: why the utility exists, what it must be able to do, how the work flows, who does it, and what runs it.
Modelling tools can keep it. The ideas don't depend on them.
Where it's going is a second drawing: the target, on the same map, so the two can be compared.
Two capabilities are new: predicting faults, and trading power locally.
One outage system instead of three. A model of the network's capacity instead of a spreadsheet. And the licence nobody uses, gone.
Laid side by side, the differences between the two are the gaps. Each gap is a piece of work.
Merge three outage systems into one. Build the capacity model. Switch off the system nobody uses. Add sensors, and predict faults. Open local trading.
The path is a third drawing: plateaus, the steady states in between, and the order in which the gaps are closed.
The order matters. Trading power on a street needs to know how much that street can take, so the capacity model comes first. Predicting faults needs sensors, so the sensors come before it.
By 2028, one outage system and a capacity model. By 2033, fault prediction. Local trading, after that.
Each choice on the path is written down with why: what was decided, what else was considered, and who decided.
Keep the newest outage system, and fold the storm tool into it. Considered: keeping all three, or buying a new one. Decided by Grace.
Three years on, someone will ask why the storm tool was switched off. The answer will be there.
Grace confirms the network's systems as they stand today. The target and the path go to the board, as drafts.
Tomás's note has an answer: today, placed on the map; a target, drawn as carefully; and a path between them, with reasons.
The map of how the utility works is drawn, for now.
Now, at last, he can open the backlog from day one, and ask which questions matter.

films.x: Questions and measures. Tomás reads his backlog of 42 requests with one test: who will decide what with the answer, and when? Half reach a goal and half reach nothing. Traced down from the goals, each decision needs a question, and each question a measure, defined once, with an owner.
c: Kerala, on India's south-west coast, a January morning in 1997.
Sardine boats head for the beach markets with their catch. The markets close by eight, and a boat can reach only one.
Each skipper must choose one while still at sea, without knowing what the markets will pay.
At Badagara, eleven crews find no buyers, and their catch goes back into the sea. Within fifteen kilometres, twenty-seven buyers leave with no fish.
Within weeks, mobile phones reach the coast. At sea, a skipper calls buyers in several markets, agrees a price, and only then chooses where to land.
The question was always the same: what will each market pay? It mattered because the skipper would act on the answer, by choosing where to land.
The phones brought that answer in time.
Tomás's note asks which questions matter.
On day one, the reporting team handed him their backlog: forty-two requests for reports, dashboards and extracts, most of them marked urgent.
Then, he couldn't tell which mattered. Now there's a map, and the skipper's test for every request: who will decide what with the answer, and when?
The first asks which lines fail most often. Grace's planners need it every spring, to decide which lines to renew first.
That decision belongs to maintaining assets, and it serves a goal: replace assets before they fail. The request reaches the top.
The next asks for a dashboard of every outage, refreshed every minute, for the screen in the lobby.
It's as live as the skipper's call, but who decides what with it? No one. It reaches nothing.
He traces all forty-two. Twenty-one reach a decision and a goal. Some get there through an obligation: the regulator decides with them.
The other twenty-one reach nothing: a report someone needed once, a dashboard nobody acts on, an export nobody can explain.
Each goes back to whoever asked for it, with one question: what would you decide with it?
Now the other way, from the top. A goal implies decisions. A decision needs questions answered. A question needs a measure.
Take replacing assets before they fail. Its outcome said only a better network, and nobody could check that.
Its decision is which lines to renew first, and its question is the one the planners asked.
The measure: interruptions per customer, per year, line by line.
From the top and from the bottom, they meet at one decision. Now the goal can be checked.
Keeping bills affordable has a measure for the network charge, but none for the people who pay it.
Retail decides whom to offer help, before a household falls too far behind. Its question: how many are falling behind?
The hardship register counts only those already getting help.
Farah, who speaks for customers, has asked for that number for years. A goal without a measure can't be steered.
Connecting renewable power does have a measure: new solar connected within ten working days.
Two reports count it, and disagree: thirty-four days, and twenty-one.
They start and stop the clock at different moments. Both are right. Neither is the measure.
So Grace writes one definition down: from a complete application to the new meter, in working days, Monday to Friday, not public holidays.
Now everyone who counts it gets the same number.
Each measure gets a home on the map: the capability whose work it measures.
Interruptions, under maintaining assets. Days to connect, under connecting customers. Households falling behind, under serving customers.
And each gets that capability's owner: Grace for the first two, the head of retail for the third.
An owner says what the number means, and acts when it moves.
Now, what to build. Twenty-one requests could become twenty-one reports, each kept by someone different.
Grouped by capability, and by the domain they belong to, they need four data products: three on the network's side of the wall, one on retail's.
Each answers many questions, has one owner, and stays on its own side of the wall.
Back on the coast of Kerala, the phones spread, district by district.
On boat after boat, the skipper now knew what each market would pay before choosing where to land.
The waste stopped, and prices along the coast evened out. Crews earned eight percent more, and fish cost four percent less.
Grace confirms her measures and their definitions. The third goes to the head of retail, as a draft.
Tomás's note has an answer: the questions that matter are the ones someone will act on, in time, traced to a goal, with a measure and an owner.
But a measure is only as true as the data beneath it, and the rules that data must keep. Next: where each rule belongs.

films.x: Objects, owners and rules. A bill goes wrong on Tomás's first day. The rule that should have corrected it lives in a nightly script, and is written four more ways elsewhere. Each rule gets one home on the map, at its step, with an owner and a reason, and tests or a tracking table made from it.
c: Tartu, Estonia, today. A baby is born, and the birth is entered once, in the population register.
Days later, the parents get an email from the Social Insurance Board. A family benefit is theirs, if they accept it.
They never applied.
No office asks the parents again. Each one asks the population register, over X-Road, the exchange Estonia's public offices share.
By law, no office may build a second database of the same data, and every database is listed, with the office that owns it.
Each fact has one home and one owner. It's asked for once, and everyone who needs it asks there: once only.
Tomás's note asks where each rule belongs. On day one, he was shown one: an estimated reading stands only until the next actual reading.
Beside it was a bill, flagged wrong.
Farah brings the household behind that bill. In June, they were away for three weeks, and their smart meter stopped sending readings.
The bill estimated those weeks from last year: four hundred and twelve dollars eighty.
When the meter came back, it sent the readings it had stored. They had used almost nothing.
The actual readings arrived. The bill was never corrected.
The rule existed. Years ago, an analyst in metering wrote a nightly script, as a stopgap.
It found estimates with an actual reading behind them, and queued their bills to be corrected.
In March, billing moved to a new system. The script kept writing to the old queue, which nothing reads now.
It ran every night, reported no error, and corrected nothing: about nineteen hundred bills since March.
It lived on the wall between the network and retail, and belonged to neither side.
Tomás finds the rule written four more ways.
In the regulator's retail code, the meter system's settings, the billing team's notes and the complaints team's spreadsheet.
The regulator's code says why. The others each say how, a little differently. None of them is its home.
He wants for rules what Tartu has for a birth: once only.
Day one's rule is really two rules, one on each side of the wall.
The network's: an estimate is replaced when the actual reading arrives, and the replacement is sent to the retailer. Grace owns it.
Retail's: a bill based on a replaced estimate is corrected on the next bill. The head of retail owns it.
Between them, the replaced reading crosses the wall on the agreed list, where the script once reached across unseen.
Each rule has a reason: a regulation, a principle, or the service level of the step it serves.
Grace's comes from the metering rules; retail's, from the regulator's retail code.
A rule with no reason can't be changed safely. One with no owner can't be fixed.
Ama corrects day one's draft too. Fair, accurate bills was never one of the utility's goals. It's an obligation, in the regulator's code.
A rule builds on facts, and facts on concepts.
So it's written in the business's words, about what it governs: a reading, an estimate, a bill, a connection point.
Each becomes a data object, in the domain that owns it: readings and connection points on the network's side, bills on retail's.
The industry's model gives the starting words, such as usage point for a connection point.
The map keeps the utility's own words beside them.
Each rule is attached to its step in meter to cash: the network's to reading, retail's to billing.
Attached, not inside: a rule isn't the process.
The step also says what to expect of the data. Timeliness, from its service level: an estimate replaced within two working days.
Completeness, from its steps: every estimate replaced, or explained. Validity, from another rule: every reading marked actual or estimated.
In ArchiMate 4, the standard the map follows, a rule is a requirement, one of the motivation elements.
The parallelogram on every rule card is the requirement's symbol.
ArchiMate has no element called a rule. The map makes data rules and business rules two kinds of requirement.
Its reason is a driver, linked by an influence: for retail's rule, the regulator's retail code.
Its home is the step that applies it, linked by a realisation: billing, in meter to cash.
Its owner, and the data objects it applies to, are linked by an association.
ArchiMate says where a rule sits, not how it's checked. The checks come from the rule.
Written in a set form, a rule says what it applies to, what must be true, its owner, its reason, its home, and what happens when it fails.
A rule about the data, such as every reading marked actual or estimated, gets tests: they check the data is right.
They're generated from it, one way: a dbt test, a data contract's quality rule, a shape for linked data.
Nobody edits a check by hand.
Retail's rule is about what the business does: the data can all be right while a bill goes uncorrected.
So a tracking table is generated from it instead, listing every bill not corrected on the next bill.
It tracks what the rule promises, not whether a job ran.
The first uncorrected bill would have been listed the morning after the move.
Each morning, the list goes to the owner's team, not a shared mailbox.
Written like this, the concepts, how they relate, and the rules about them are, generally, an ontology.
It's ready for OWL, a language machines reason with.
As the film Meaning machines can read shows, the glossary, the models, the ontology and the checks are all views of that one map.
But OWL reasons only from what is said. To it, a correction that never happened is simply unknown.
Finding the uncorrected bill stays the tracking table's job.
The household gets a hundred and forty-four dollars forty back, and the nineteen hundred bills are found and corrected.
Grace and the head of retail confirm their rules.
In Tartu, the benefit is paid, and nobody was asked twice.
Tomás's note has an answer: each rule belongs in the map, written once, at the step where it applies.
Each has an owner and a reason, and its checks are generated from it.
Rules hold while the organisation holds still. Next: when strategy moves.

films.x: Change, owners and contracts. The government orders a social tariff for every eligible household from 1 July, and the minister's office asks what it will take, by tomorrow. Tomás walks the change down the map, layer by layer, to the owners, rules and contracts it touches.
c: Kenya, 2007. A man working in Nairobi sends part of his wages to his family, upcountry.
The money goes with a bus driver or a friend, and not all of it arrives.
A mobile network sets a new strategy: to carry money, as well as calls.
In March, it launches M-Pesa: money sent from a phone, confirmed by a text message.
That strategy fits in a sentence. Making it real takes much more.
The central bank lets it run, with customers' money held in trust at a bank.
Shops that sell airtime become agents, changing cash into mobile money and back.
Customers register with an identity card, and a short menu works on the simplest phones.
That one sentence reaches every layer, down to the shop counter, where people meet it.
Tomás's note asks what a change in strategy means for the data.
In November, the government, the utility's owner, sends a direction.
From the first of July, every eligible household gets a social tariff, a discount on its bill, automatically, with no forms.
Who is eligible is known to another organisation, the social services agency, not to the utility.
The minister's office asks what it will take, by tomorrow.
As with M-Pesa, the sentence is the easy part.
Tomás walks it down the map, layer by layer.
