In motivation: a new driver, the direction, under a goal the utility already has, keep bills affordable.
And an outcome to check: eligible households on the tariff.
In strategy, three capabilities: selling energy, serving customers, and meeting obligations.
In business: a new product, a new step in billing, and a new partner, the agency, with an agreement.
In information: a new business object, eligibility, with its dates.
And in what runs it: the billing system, the customer system, and a secure exchange with the agency.
Every element it touches has an owner. So the walk is also the list of who must agree.
The agency already knows who is eligible. Once only, as in Tartu: don't make a household prove what the government already knows.
So the agreement asks for the least. The utility sends its account holders' matching details. The agency answers only: eligible, from this date.
Never which support a household gets.
And the agreement starts today: agreeing it will take longer than changing the systems.
Tomás's first draft sends the list to the network too, to take the discount off the network charge.
Ama checks it against the third principle: customer information stays with the business that collected it.
The list would cross the wall. She crosses it out.
The decision is written down, with why: retail applies the whole discount, and nothing new crosses the wall.
Checked against the principles first, a hard call goes the same way every time.
Eligibility brings new rules, and each gets a home, an owner and a reason.
The discount applies to every bill from the date the agency gives. Its reason is the direction.
An answer is kept only until the next match. Its reason is the agreement.
And only billing reads it. In the catalogue, the call centre sees on the social tariff, and nothing more.
Then down to the counter, where households meet it: a line on the bill, a letter, and the call centre's answer.
Farah asks who the match will miss: tenants whose account is in a landlord's name. The agency knows them; the utility doesn't.
Found now, not in the first bills, they get a second route: an application, later in the year.
Bills now carry a discount line, so the accounts and bills product gets a new column for it. Amount due keeps its meaning: what the household pays.
A new column breaks nothing that reads it, so the contract stays at version one. A second version is the last resort, for removing or redefining a column.
Lineage finds everyone who reads it: a measure, a report for the regulator, and a collections job. Each owner hears of it before the first bills.
The exchange with the agency gets its own contract too: what goes, what comes back, and how often.
The path is drawn in plateaus, in the order their dependencies allow.
By the first of July: the match, the bills and the call centre's answer. By December: the second route. Next year: the outcome, measured.
By the morning, the minister's office has one page: what changes, who owns each change, what's ready by July, and what isn't.
What a mapped organisation answers in a day, an unmapped one finds out in production.
On the first of July, the first bills carry the discount. About nine in ten eligible households get it without asking.
And the head of retail confirms the measure Farah has asked for since 2024: households falling behind. Now the goal can be steered.
In Kenya, within a few years, most households had someone using M-Pesa, and money sent home arrived in minutes.
Tomás's note has an answer: a change in strategy lands in every layer, and walked down the map, it's a list of owners, rules and contracts, in order.
But a map that's used every week goes stale. Next: a map people and agents can read.

films.t: A map people and agents can read
films.x: Keeping the map. Tomás's map is used every week and goes stale in slides. He moves it into one tool that brings in what other systems hold, keeps each element once with an owner, reviews every change and generates every view from it. An agent reads it too: it drafts, and people confirm.
c: May 1976. The double-hulled canoe Hōkūleʻa leaves Maui for Tahiti, more than four thousand kilometres south, with no compass and no charts.
Its navigator, Mau Piailug, from Satawal in Micronesia, finds his way by the stars, the swells and the birds.
His map is in his memory: a star compass, the points on the horizon where the stars rise and set.
After thirty-one days, the crew sights Mataiva. Three days later, in Papeʻete, more than seventeen thousand people are waiting.
Few still held this knowledge. It passed only from navigator to apprentice.
Mau chose to teach it beyond his own island, so it wouldn't be lost. A young Hawaiian, Nainoa Thompson, learned it from him, and taught others.
Any map lives only while people use it, keep it true, and teach it to the next navigator.
The navigator's test: could someone else sail by it?
Tomás's last note asks how to keep the map alive.
It's used every week now: for the skipper's test, to give rules a home, and to answer the minister.
That's when a map goes stale.
It lives in slides, and in a modelling tool only Tomás edits.
Its applications were typed in by hand from the IT service management tool, and many have changed since.
Its views are copied into decks, and the copies drift. The glossary and the catalogue keep their own words.
A stale map is worse than none, because people trust it.
If Tomás left tomorrow, nobody could sail by it. It fails the navigator's test.
So he moves the map into an enterprise architecture tool that everyone can reach, with a database and a graph.
Much of what it holds is already kept somewhere else.
Strategy in documents, goals and initiatives in the project management tool, applications and servers in the IT service management tool.
The tool brings each one in with its source's ID, and keeps it in step, so nobody retypes it.
The rest is written in the map itself: capabilities, rules, decisions, and the links between everything.
Even the business glossary fits: each term is a business object, defined once by the business.
So keeping a map true is a data integration job, as well as a modelling one.
Each element is kept once: a capability, a step, a domain, a business object, a rule, a measure.
Each has a stable ID. Names change, but IDs don't, so everything else points to the ID.
Then its name, its definition, its owner, and its relationships, named as ArchiMate names them.
And his two rules from day one, on every element: its evidence, with a date, and whether its owner has confirmed it.
Decisions are kept too, each saying why.
A small map could keep all this as text files in a repository: the simplest approach.
With many sources, and many people in their roles, the utility needs the tool. Either way, the ideas are the same.
Every version of the map is kept, with who changed what, and when.
A change is proposed as a draft, and nothing changes until it's approved.
The owner of that part approves it: Grace for the network's, Ama for the obligations.
Checks run on the map itself, on every change.
Every element has an owner. Every rule, a reason and a home. Every measure, a definition.
Generating power still has no owner, and the check says so, every time.
Everything people read is generated from the map, one way.
The ArchiMate views, the glossary, the conceptual model, the ontology, the tests and tracking tables, and the heat map.
Each one answers the questions of the people who read it.
In dbt, each model carries its owner, its domain and the IDs of its rules.
In Databricks, each table shows its owner, its tags and its description, beside its lineage.
Nobody edits a view. A fix goes to the map, and every view follows.
Now an agent can read the map.
Given a request, it applies the skipper's test, and finds the decision, the capability and the owner, or nothing.
Given a change, it walks the layers, as Tomás did for the social tariff, and lists the owners who must agree.
Given a column in the catalogue, it finds the rule behind it, with its owner and its reason.
Every answer cites IDs and evidence, so a person can check it.
The agent is on the map itself: software, filling a role, with its rights written down, like the outage agent's.
It may read everything, and draft changes. It may not confirm one.
Where two sources disagree, it doesn't choose. It asks the owner.
Its owner is Tomás.
Agents draft, people confirm, every version is kept: the rule that keeps data models true, applied to the map.
Then the regulator changes the retail code, the rules every energy retailer must follow.
When an actual reading replaces an estimate, the bill must be corrected within ten working days, not on the next one.
The agent finds the one rule whose reason is that clause: retail's half of day one's rule.
It drafts the rule's new words, and lists what they touch: the billing team's tracking table, and two views.
The head of retail, who owns the rule, confirms it.
From the next morning, the tracking table shows each bill not corrected within ten working days.
Next spring, Zofia starts as a data engineer.
Her first day, like Tomás's, brings a badge, a page of acronyms and a list of systems.
This time, there's also a map.
She asks the agent who owns the readings data, and which rules it keeps.
Back come an owner, Grace, and two rules, each with its reason, and links to check them.
By the afternoon, she has drafted her first change, for Grace to confirm.
In 2007, on Satawal, Mau made five Hawaiians master navigators. Nainoa was one of them.
Mau died in 2010. What he taught lives on.
Fifty years after that first voyage, Hōkūleʻa is still sailing, navigated by people Mau taught, and by people they taught.
Grace confirms Zofia's change. The map passes the navigator's test.
Tomás's last note has an answer: a map stays alive while people use it, keep it true, and can pass it on.
Layer by layer: who it serves, why it moves, what it must do, how value reaches people, who does the work, and what runs it.
Then, for data: the questions that matter, rules with a home, and a change walked down every layer.
The map holds what the organisation means. Turning that meaning into data is where From words to data begins.

films.x: Who owns what. A ticket asks the data team for all customers and gets three answers, each right about something. Nobody in the business ever said which one the report meant. Tomás writes down who owns what: the business owns what its data means, and the data team keeps how it's stored, moved and checked.
c: Iran, at the edge of the desert. For more than two thousand years, villages here have lived on water that nobody sees.
It comes through a qanat: a tunnel dug from the foot of the mountains, which brings groundwater to the surface by gravity alone.
A line of shafts marks its path. They let the diggers in, and the earth out.
There's never enough water for every field at once. Each family's crop lives or dies by when the water reaches it.
And the tunnel is fragile. One cave-in can cut off a whole village.
People needed to know whose water it was, and who would keep it flowing.
So each part has its own people. The water belongs to its shareholders, in shares of time. In one town, a share was ninety-six minutes of the flow, every twelve days.
A water master, the mirab, keeps the turns.
And the diggers, the muqannis, build and repair the tunnel. They're paid for the work. The water isn't theirs.
With each part in its own hands, the water has been shared this way for centuries, and the fields stay green.
In Gonabad, the Qasabeh qanat still flows, thirty-three kilometres long. In 2016, UNESCO listed eleven qanats as the Persian Qanat.
At the utility, the data team is the digger. It keeps the channel. The water, and what it means, belongs to the business.
Tomás, the utility's enterprise architect, has drawn its map, layer by layer: why it exists, how it works, and what runs it.
This series looks at one part of it: what the business owns about its data.
It sits in three layers: the capabilities, in strategy; the work, in business; and the concepts the business uses, in the information layer.
The series after it take the map down to the data and the platform, and they start from here.
A ticket reaches the data team: all customers, by district, for the annual report.
There are three answers.
Billing has three hundred and ten thousand accounts.
The network has five hundred and forty thousand connection points.
And the data team's own customer table has three hundred and fifty-two thousand.
Last year, the annual report gave one number, and the regulator's return another.
In parliament, the minister was asked which was true, and couldn't say.
Each count is right about something. But which one is a customer?
The data team's first idea is to pick one, or to fix its own table until it's right.
Tomás asks who decided what that table counts.
An analyst built it three years ago, for a report due that week: one customer per address, with accounts and connection points merged.
Nobody in the business had said which customer the report meant, so someone had to choose.
But an account belongs to the head of retail: someone who pays a bill.
A connection point belongs to Grace, who runs the network: a place where power is delivered.
The merged table's meaning had no owner. Nobody in the business had ever confirmed it.
In the village, the diggers don't decide whose turn it is.
So Tomás writes down who owns what.
The business owns what its data means, who creates it, the rules on it, the quality it needs, and the decisions it serves.
The data team owns how it's stored, moved and checked.
Like the shareholders and the diggers: one owns the water and its rules, the other keeps the channel.
Both matter. A channel nobody keeps silts up, and water nobody owns is fought over.
Business architecture has many parts. The BIZBOK Guide puts four at its core: capabilities, value streams, information and the organisation.
Around them sit stakeholders, products, policies, initiatives and more.
It covers much more than data: products, partners, finance, how the organisation is designed.
These films take only what matters for data, and say so.
What the business needs to know. Who creates it, and who owns it. The processes it's born in. The rules and expectations on it.
One film each, in that order.
The ticket goes back with one question: which customers does the report mean?
Ama, who owns the utility's obligations, asked for it. She decides, with the two owners.
The report counts both, each by its own name: accounts, as retail defines them, and connection points, as the network does.
The data team builds both counts from those definitions, and tests them.
The merged table is retired. Its rule was never the business's.
Ama checks the counts before the ticket closes.
This year, the annual report and the regulator's return agree, and each number says what it counts.
One more thing goes on the map: the data practice itself, drawn like any part of the business.
The data team is a business actor. What it offers are business services, like answering data requests.
People reach that service through tickets: its interface.
Account and connection point are business objects. What they mean stays with their owners.
Film by film, the practice fills in: its glossary, its owners, its processes and its products.
In the village, the diggers keep the channel, and the shareholders decide whose water it is.
At the utility, the data team keeps the channel. What flows in it, and what it means, is the business's.
Tomás's next note asks what the business needs to know.

films.t: What the business needs to know
films.x: The business's concepts. Tomás needs the concepts behind each capability on the utility's map. He starts from the industry's reference models, not a blank page, and confirms each one with the people who use it, in their words. One concept nobody holds keeps new solar waiting, so the business defines it first.
c: In the desert villages of Iran, the water of a qanat, a tunnel from the mountains, is owned in shares of time.
A share can be sold, split, or left to your children.
But a share didn't mean the same everywhere.
On one qanat, the water came round every six days. On another, every twenty-two.
In the 1960s, as land passed to the farmers who worked it, the government asked for written deeds to the water.
In some villages, the deeds added up to more than twenty-four hours of water a day.
Owners fought, sometimes violently, and some villages broke apart.
Before anyone could count the water, a share had to mean the same to everyone who held one.
In Mahan, near Kerman, one qanat's owners measured every share against the day itself.
A day of its water was fifteen shares, and each share came round every twelve days.
Each share was ninety-six minutes, so fifteen make exactly one day: the shares add up to the water.
Another qanat there, shared by three men in the 1860s, passed bit by bit to some seventy families.
Because a share meant one thing, it could be sold, inherited, split as fine as thirty seconds, and still add up.
At the utility, the business needs the same: each thing it counts, defined once, in its own words, before anyone builds it.
Tomás's next note asks what the business needs to know.
He starts from the capabilities on his map: the eight things the utility must be able to do.
Each one needs some information, creates some, or changes it.
Those are the business's concepts. They go in the information layer, beneath the capabilities that use them.
He doesn't start from a blank page.
Utilities share reference models, written by their industry's standards bodies.
The IEC, which sets the world's electrical standards, keeps the Common Information Model, CIM.
It names what a utility works with, from its cables and meters to its customers, and how they relate.
One of its standards lists what a distribution utility does, and the business objects each part uses.
Its 2020 edition draws them in ArchiMate, the language of Tomás's map.
The Smart Grid Architecture Model shows where each part sits, from the power station to the home.
And Europe's market role model names who does what in the electricity market.
Other industries have their own, from BIAN for banks to HERM for universities.
Tomás takes CIM and the IEC's list as his first draft, and the map says where each element came from.
A reference model isn't the utility's own until its people confirm it, so every element starts as a draft.
He goes through the capabilities one at a time, with the people who run each one.
Connecting customers needs a connection request, the network's capacity, a connection point and a meter.
Serving customers needs accounts, bills and complaints.
Operating the network needs meter readings and outages.
Some of these a capability creates; others it only reads.
Most of them, CIM already names, so the first draft comes quickly.
But CIM's words aren't always the utility's.
CIM calls a connection point a usage point. Europe's market role model calls it a metering point.
Grace's people call it a connection point, and so do their forms, their reports and their customers.
So the map uses the business's word, and keeps the reference model's beside it, for when data is exchanged.
As in Mahan, the measure is shared, and the words are the people's own.
Each word gets one definition in its domain, written with the people who use it.
The network's words sit with the network, and retail's with retail.
A word both use, like location, sits in a shared domain, so each word's owner is easy to find.
Then the capability that hurts: connecting customers. New solar takes thirty-four working days to connect.
The wait is in assessing the network's capacity, and that needs one number: how much solar each street can take.
No system holds it, no report shows it, and nobody owns it.
Grace's engineers name it hosting capacity: the solar a street can take before its voltage or its cables pass their limits.
It goes on the map in their words, with Grace as its owner, and no data yet.
The data team will build it later. First, the business says what it means.
Each concept on the map is a business object, with a name, a definition, a domain and an owner.
The glossary is drawn from them: one term for each, grouped by domain.
It doesn't need a tool to start. A table is enough, as long as every term has an owner.
Later, each table and report the data team builds will point to the terms it holds.
On the data practice's map, the glossary's domains appear: the network, retail, and what they share.
Meter readings and hosting capacity join the network, and bills join retail. Location sits in the shared domain.
The connection point and the account were already there. Now each sits in its domain, with its owner.
In Mahan, a share means the same to everyone who holds one, so the water can be counted, and shared.
At the utility, each concept now means one thing in its domain, in the words of the people who use it.
Tomás's next note asks who creates each one, and who owns it.

films.t: Between the business and the systems
films.x: What data architecture is. At the utility, three people say they work on information architecture and mean three things. Inés Duarte, the new data architect, settles on DAMA's data architecture, then follows one word, connection point, into the six systems that record it, and gives the line between them an owner.
c: In 1971, Chile's new government took over factories across the country.
Its development agency, CORFO, had to run them.
But its figures on what they made took about six months to collect.
By the time a problem showed in them, it was half a year old.
The people in charge needed to see what each factory was doing now, not six months ago.
CORFO asked a British expert on how organisations steer themselves, Stafford Beer, to help.
Their project, Cybersyn, would link the factories to Santiago.
Before any computer was used, engineers went to the factories.
They walked each one with the people who worked there, and drew how it worked.
Only then did they choose what to measure.
Each factory would report about five numbers, such as how much it produced and how many workers were absent.
Each number had its place in the drawing, so everyone knew what it meant.
Inés Duarte, the utility's new data architect, finds the same problem: plenty of data, and no agreed picture of what it means.
She starts where the engineers did: with how the business works.
This is Tomás's map of the utility: six layers, from why it exists down to what runs it.
He drew it in The map before the data, with the people who own each part.
Business architecture for data then drew what the business owns about its data: its concepts, their owners, and the rules on them.
Each concept is a business object, defined once, in the business's words.
Under the business sits the fourth layer, information, and data architecture works there, between the business and the systems.
Inés has just joined as the utility's data architect. That layer is hers.
In her first meeting, she asks who here works on information architecture.
Three people say they do, and each one means something else.
The web team means how the website is organised and labelled: its menus, its pages, its search.
That's a real discipline, and not this one.
An analyst means a model of the company's information, and how it flows between its parts.
Tomás, who learned TOGAF, means a phase of its method.
So Inés writes down what this team will mean: data architecture, as DAMA defines it.
DAMA's body of knowledge knows the old distinction: data as facts, information as data with meaning.
But it criticises splitting them. Data is a form of information, and information is a form of data.
So it uses the two words as one, and calls the discipline data architecture.
TOGAF names data architecture as one of its four domains, but groups it with the applications.
ArchiMate puts what the business means in its business layer, and how a system records it in its application layer.
It has nothing in between.
Tomás's map draws a layer there, as many architects do.
Inés starts with one word: connection point, where a home or a business meets the network.
The business defined it once, and Grace, who runs network operations, owns it.
Six systems record it, each in its own way.
The network map calls it a service point. Meter data, a metering point. Billing, a premise.
Customer service, a supply address. The outage system, a service location. And the data platform keeps a table of its own.
In January, a storm cut power to 3,400 connection points.
Outage texts went out by supply address, matched from the outage system's locations.
180 households never got one: the two systems wrote their addresses differently.
They sat in the dark, not knowing whether anyone knew.
Who owns the line between the word and its six records? Nobody.
That line is what data architecture is for, and it's why it's an architecture of its own.
Data outlives the applications that hold it. The connection points are older than every one of those systems.
Billing moved to a new system in March. The points stayed the same.
One concept serves many applications, so no single application can own it.
Meaning belongs to the business, and storage to the systems. Someone has to own the join.
DAMA makes that a discipline of its own.
So Inés draws the line: each record, joined to the word it stands for.
And she decides that every system that needs a connection point carries the network's ID for it.
Outage texts are now matched on that ID, not on addresses.
In the next storm, all 2,100 households on the list got their text.
This adds a layer to the data practice on the map.
The business layer holds the concepts, as business objects with owners.
Data architecture adds the information layer under them.
Each system's record is a data object, and a line says which business object it realises.
One word, six records, six lines, and each line has an owner.
Next, this layer shows where each fact is born, how it travels, and who owns which data.
In Chile, the engineers drew each factory before they chose a single number.
The drawing came first, so a number meant the same thing to everyone who read it.
Inés drew the business first too: one word, its records, and a line with an owner.
So the next outage text reaches every home on the list.
But how do records become decisions? There's a famous pyramid about that, and it's only half right.

films.x: How records become decisions. Grace reads one measure every month, and it seems to come from the systems. Inés Duarte takes apart the famous pyramid of data, information, knowledge and wisdom, keeps what it gets right, and redraws it with arrows both ways: the question decides what's recorded.
c: In 1972, Chile's government was linking the factories it ran to Santiago, in a project called Cybersyn.
Every afternoon, their numbers came in by telex.
But a number alone didn't say whether anything was wrong.
Was today's cloth a good day or a bad one? That depended on the factory.
And with every factory reporting every day, one in trouble would be lost among the ones that were fine.
The people in charge needed to see the factories that needed them, and only those.
So the project's software, Cyberstride, worked out from each factory's own history what was normal for it.
It compared each day's numbers with that, and passed on only what had changed.
A warning was to go first to the factory's own manager, with time to put it right.
Only if it stayed wrong would it go on to Santiago.
On 21 March 1972, the software printed its first results.
Stafford Beer, who designed Cybersyn, telexed that it really worked.
Instead of a wall of figures, the people in charge would see a few warnings, each beside its factory's normal.
At the utility, Grace reads one measure every month: interruptions per customer, per year.
It looks like a number the systems produce. But it exists only because someone first decided what an interruption is.
There's a famous picture of how records become decisions: a pyramid.
Data at the bottom, then information, then knowledge, and wisdom at the top.
No one person invented it. In 1934, a poet asked where the knowledge we have lost in information had gone.
Writers on management drew the levels in the 1980s, and a systems thinker, Russell Ackoff, made them famous in 1989.
Read from the bottom up, data becomes information, information becomes knowledge, and knowledge becomes wisdom.
Half of that is right.
First, a number needs context.
Forty-one interruptions means nothing until you know: on which line, over what time, and among how many customers.
Line by line, over a year, per customer: now it says which lines fail most often.
Second, people decide.
The measure doesn't renew a line. Grace decides which ones to renew first, and answers for it.
Inés keeps both.
What's wrong starts with how it's drawn.
It looks like a factory: data goes in at the bottom, and wisdom comes out at the top.
But nothing is recorded until someone decides what to record.
Before the outage system logged a single interruption, someone wrote down what one is.
Power lost to a connection point for more than five minutes.
A shorter cut counts as a momentary one, in a measure of its own.
So the outage system records when each cut starts and ends, at every connection point.
The question came first, and decided the data.
In Chile, too, the drawing came first, and chose the numbers.
There's no such thing as raw data, either.
A meter reading looks raw: a number, every half hour.
But someone chose the half hour, chose kilowatt hours, and chose to keep one decimal place.
A book of essays on data puts it in its title: raw data is an oxymoron.
Every record was designed by someone, for some question.
The levels aren't separate things, either.
As DAMA says, data is a form of information, and information is a form of data.
The same record of a cut is data to the outage system, and information to Grace.
And the top is vague.
People who've studied the pyramid find little agreement on what wisdom is, or how a system could hold it.
In practice, the top is a person, deciding.
So Inés redraws it, with arrows both ways.
Down: a decision asks a question, the question needs a measure, and the measure needs a definition.
The definition decides what's recorded.
Up: the records answer the measure, the measure answers the question, and a person decides.
On the data practice on the map, interruption becomes a business object, defined once and owned by Grace.
The outage system's record of each cut is a data object that realises it.
And the measure traces to both: what it counts, and where the counts come from.
In Chile, the numbers never came raw from the factories.
Someone drew each factory, chose what mattered, and worked out what was normal for it.
Then the software sent on only what changed, and a person decided.
Grace's measure works the same way: defined first, recorded to fit, and read by someone who acts.
So it counts the same way every year, and the lines that fail most are renewed first.
But each cut is recorded by more than one system. Which record is the fact? That depends on where it's born.

films.x: Where the platform sits. Ravi Menon has just taken over the utility's data platform, drawn on the map as one more application. When a measure built on it for the regulator goes wrong, nobody can say whose rule it is. Drawn as a platform, it carries every domain's logic, and every rule on it has an owner in the business.
c: Japan, 1601. A year after the battle that ended a century of war, Tokugawa Ieyasu is the most powerful lord in the land.
His seat is Edo. The emperor's city, Kyoto, is about five hundred kilometres west by road, and between them, many domains, each ruled by its own lord.
A traveller on foot took about two weeks from Edo to Kyoto, and orders and news went no faster than the people who carried them.
To govern from Edo, Ieyasu needed his letters, officials and goods to cross the country in days, not weeks.
Early in 1601, he gave each station on the road to Kyoto an order: keep thirty-six horses, and carry official travellers on to the next station.
With it came his seal, and one line: without this seal, no horses.
Over the decades that followed, five great roads ran out of Edo, most along older routes, with stations along the way: the Gokaidō.
Relayed from station to station, an official letter now crossed from Edo to Kyoto in three or four days.
And the road served every domain: lords travelling to Edo, couriers, merchants and pilgrims, each on their own business.
At the utility, Ravi Menon has just taken over the data platform. Like that road, it carries every domain's business.
But on the map it's drawn as one more application, and when one of its numbers goes wrong, nobody can say whose rule it is.
Drawn as a platform, it serves every domain, and every rule on it has an owner.
Tomás's map has six layers. This series works in the bottom two: the applications, and the technology they run on.
Here are the hundred and forty systems from Today, and where it's going, each with its own job: billing, outages, meter data, finance.
Above them, the information layer: what the data means, and where each fact is born.
And among the applications, one box: data warehouse. That's the data platform, drawn as one more application.
Ravi asks Tomás to move it. But first, a word that means two things.
Databricks calls its product a data platform, and so do other vendors. At the technology layer, it is one: many components, sold as one product.
Your data platform is more: a service the utility runs for all its domains.
It's built from that product and the components around it: identity, the network, integration, orchestration, reporting tools, and what watches it all.
And from a team, with rules and support, that keeps it running for everyone.
In this series, Databricks is the product. The data platform is the service.
Take billing. It has one purpose: to bill customers. Its rules are built into it: tariffs, estimates, discounts.
Its owner is the head of retail, who decides what it does. It's measured by retail's outcomes: bills right, and on time.
The data platform has no purpose of its own. It gives shared capabilities: bring data in, store it, process it, serve it, and govern it.
On it, many owners build their own logic: the network, retail, finance.
And one more: the enterprise domain, for measures that cross domains, for performance and analysis.
That's the test. One purpose, with its logic built in: an application. Shared capabilities, on which many owners build their own: a platform.
Serving every domain isn't the test on its own. The finance system serves finance, procurement and people.
But it's an application suite. Each part has one purpose, and its logic is built in, the way its vendor designed it.
The line is where the logic lives: inside the system, or brought to it by its owners.
The stations of the Tōkaidō kept the horses and porters ready. They never wrote the letters they carried.
On a data platform, the logic runs on it, in each domain's data products, never in the platform's own components.
And its owner is always the business, never the platform team by default.
That's easy to say, and hard to see, because the platform brings the data in and runs the code.
One of the enterprise domain's measures: minutes without power, per customer. It goes to the regulator.
It's built on the platform from three systems: outages, the network map, and the old storm tool.
In March, it jumps from about eight minutes to nineteen.
A major storm counted. The rule that leaves major storms out came in the storm tool's export, and an update in February dropped it.
Whose rule was it? The code was the platform team's. The storm tool had no notes, and the person who set it up had left.
Tomás's map and the catalogue find its owner: the measure belongs to the enterprise domain, and for the regulator's measures, that's Ama.
Ama raises a ticket, and writes in the glossary which storms don't count, as the regulator's method says.
The data team builds the rule on the platform, with a test, and reviews the pull request.
Ama checks the number in test before her ticket closes. March is back to nine minutes.
The roads had an owner too: the shogunate. Its officials rode free, others paid their way, and the stations and nearby villages carried the burden.
A data platform has a business owner too: a sponsor, with a platform product owner.
But it answers to every domain that uses it. It decides less of what's built on it, and answers for how well it serves them all.
It's measured by its users' outcomes: how many build on it, how fast a first data product ships, how reliable it is, and what it costs.
That's why enterprise architecture matters most for a data platform.
It's the one system that crosses every domain, and every layer: business, data, applications and technology.
It can't be designed from inside any one of them.
Here's the data practice, on Tomás's map.
In the technology layer, the platform's services: storage, compute, the catalogue. Databricks realises them, as system software.
In the application layer, the measure's data product: its pipeline and models, one application component, owned by the enterprise domain.
Where others read it, its output port, is an application interface. Its tables are artifacts, kept on the platform.
The platform's components hold no rule. The product on them does, with its owner.
The Gokaidō carried every domain's letters and goods for more than two and a half centuries. What they said was always the sender's business.
Drawn as a platform, Ravi's does the same: every domain builds on it, and every rule on it has an owner Tomás's map can find.
Next: what's inside the platform.

films.x: Agents in the architecture. A website chat agreed 212 payment plans that billing never saw: an agent nobody put on the map. Tomás finds every agent at work, and draws each in a role of its own, with its tasks and how far it may go, its own identity, a hand-off and a person who answers.
c: Babylon, about 620 BCE. At the heart of the city stands the temple-tower of its god, Marduk: Etemenanki.
Its new king, Nabopolassar, finds it in ruins. In his own words, it had become very weak, and had been allowed to collapse.
For the people of Babylon, the house of their god lay broken at the centre of their city.
It had to stand again: the king writes that Marduk commanded him to raise it, its top to rival the heavens.
No one crew could build it: its base was about ninety metres on each side, and every brick was made and carried by hand.
So no one was told to build the whole tower. Surveyors measured the ground with a rod, and master builders stretched ropes for its plan.
The work was split into tasks: moulding mud bricks, firing them in kilns, carrying baskets, and bringing bitumen, a natural tar, by river.
And the king answered for the work: at its foundation, he carried bricks on his head himself.
When he died, in 605 BCE, the tower stood about fifteen metres high.
His son, Nebuchadnezzar, finished it with people from many lands, and their god's house stood again at the heart of the city.
Today, the utility's work has many hands too, and some of them are agents.
Given a task, a role and someone who answers, an agent helps. Given a whole job, it can harm the people it serves.
Tomás's new note asks where agents belong on the map.
His map shows the whole utility in six layers, from why it exists down to what it runs on.
Two of its applications are agents: the outage agent proposes which fault matters most, and the map agent drafts changes.
Each is software in a role, with its rights written down and an owner: Grace for one, Tomás for the other.
This series adds what's around them: the AI platform, AI in the architects' own work, and a map kept alive.
How an agent works is the AI agents module's; here, the map shows where agents work, and who answers for them.
Then Farah brings a household, behind on their bill. They asked the website's chat for more time to pay.
The chat said yes: a plan over three months, and no late fee.
Two weeks later, their bill came with a late fee, and a warning that their power could be cut.
The chat is an agent: its vendor switched it on in an update to the contact centre's software.
Nobody put it on the map. It was given a whole activity, payment requests, so it agreed plans.
But agreeing a plan is a billing officer's decision, under the regulator's rules for households who can't pay.
It wrote each plan in the contact centre's notes, which billing doesn't read: 212 plans in six weeks.
How many agents work here? The IT service management tool can't say: it lists applications, not what's switched on inside them.
So Tomás looks where agents leave traces: vendors' release notes and contracts, logs of calls to language models, and each team's answer.
He finds three more: a crew planner the network's analysts built, and a meter agent that drafts a work order when a meter goes quiet.
And the field app's assistant, which answers crews' questions from the manuals.
Inside billing, an assistant works on each officer's sign-in: a helper, with that person's rights, not an agent of its own.
Six agents and a helper, where the map showed two.
On the map, an agent is drawn as ArchiMate 4 draws software that works beside people: an application, assigned to a role.
A role of its own, never a person's.
In a billing officer's role, the chat would hold every right an officer holds, and no one could tell its work from theirs.
And it covers tasks, never a whole activity: the activity, and the decisions in it, stay with the people who own them.
Helping a household that can't pay is a process, written down, and its owner is the head of retail.
For each task, its owner sets how far the agent may go: inform a person, draft for them, verify their work, or run the task alone.
Answering a question about a bill: run. It may do that alone.
Taking a request for more time: draft. It writes the request for a billing officer, and tells the household when they'll hear back.
Telling the officer what the household owes, and has paid: inform.
Agreeing the plan: not at all. That stays with the officer.
Checking that the plan follows the hardship rules: verify. It checks, and the officer decides.
How an agent earns more is the AI agents module's Five stages, not a switch.
It works under its own identity, never a person's: one for each set of rights it needs.
One may read bills. The other may only write requests into billing's queue.
So every log says which agent did what, and it can be stopped on its own.
Its role says when it hands over, and to whom.
Anyone who mentions hardship, illness or life support goes to a person, the same day, and the agent says so.
Farah asks what the map couldn't say: when the agent is wrong, who answers for it?
Not the vendor, which answers to the utility under its contract. Not Tomás, who draws the map.
The head of retail, who owns the process and set its tasks, answers for it, as for anyone in that team.
AI frameworks, such as NIST's and ISO's, ask the same: a named person accountable for each AI system.
And it never approves. Approving is a person's job.
One by one, every agent goes on the map: its role, its tasks and how far, its identity, its hand-off, and who answers.
The crew planner drafts rosters, a supervisor approves them, and Grace answers for it.
The vendor's setting that let the chat agree plans is switched off. It drafts them now.
With every change, a check runs on the map: no agent without a role, an identity, a hand-off and a person who answers.
The field app's assistant is flagged: its vendor hasn't said which identity it uses.
And the 212 plans? Billing honours every one, refunds the late fees, and calls each household.
Many scholars think Babylon's tower may have inspired the story of the Tower of Babel, in the Book of Genesis.
In the story, the builders all speak one language, until they can no longer understand each other, and stop building.
Babylon's real builders came from many lands, and spoke many languages.
What they shared was the plan: a task for each, and a name that answered for the work.
Tomás's note has its answer: each agent in a role of its own, with its tasks, its identity, a hand-off and someone who answers.
Next, the platform they all run on.

films.x: The platform under the agents. Six agents each reach a model their own way, and when a provider retires one, the crew planner stops and nobody can say who else is hit. Ravi sorts what's shared from what's each agent's own, and puts every call through one gateway.
c: Babylon, more than 2,600 years ago. Its king, Nabopolassar, is rebuilding the city's temple-tower, and its walls.
The city stands on the Euphrates, inside two great walls, built, like most of Babylon, of mud brick dried in the sun.
By one estimate, the inner wall alone holds nearly a hundred million of those bricks.
But mud brick doesn't stand up to water. In the king's own words, heavy rains and downpours had carried the wall away, and its foundations had become a heap of ruins.
For the people inside, a wall the rain could carry away kept out neither enemies nor the river.
Building it again in mud would only wait for the next rains: whatever faced the water needed a brick the water couldn't wash away.
So the brick is fired: baked hard in kilns, and laid in bitumen, a natural tar that keeps water out.
Nabopolassar surrounds the city's wall, on the outside, with an embankment of baked brick.
And the temple-tower is wrapped in the same baked brick: its core of mud brick sits inside a skin nearly sixteen metres thick.
The embankment protected the city against the river's waters, and it lasted: two and a half thousand years later, archaeologists found his bricks still in place.
At the energy utility today, six agents are on Tomás's map, each in a role of its own.
Under every one are the same few things: a model to answer with, tools to act with, memory, and search.
Like the fired brick, those can be made once and shared, while what each agent is for stays its own.
Ravi Menon, the platform lead, brings Tomás a note.
What should our agents share, and what is each one's own?
Together, they follow each agent to the model that answers for it, and find a different way every time.
The website chat uses its vendor's model, inside the contact centre's software.
The crew planner calls a provider directly, with a key kept in a script.
The map agent uses a model built into the map's own tool.
The other three each found a way of their own.
So nobody can say which model answered a customer, or what all of it costs.
Then a provider retires the model the crew planner calls. Its notice goes to the analyst who set up the key, who has since moved to another team.
Three months later, on a Monday morning, the crew planner stops drafting rosters.
The dispatchers build the week's rosters by hand, and fourteen planned jobs slip.
310 households, told when their power would be off for that work, have to be told again.
Ravi asks which other agents call that model. Nobody can say.
Ravi sorts what the agents use with the test from Platform and solution architecture.
One purpose, with its logic built in: an application.
Shared capabilities, on which many owners build their own: a platform.
A model, which writes an agent's answers, serves no single purpose: the chat and the crew planner could use the same one.
The same goes for tools, which let an agent look something up or do something.
And for memory, which keeps what an agent needs from one step to the next, and search, which finds the right page in the utility's documents.
They're shared capabilities, so they're the platform's.
What each agent is for is its own: its purpose, its instructions, and the logic of its tasks. That's an application, and its owner answers for it.
On Tomás's map, the platform's capabilities go at the foot, as services it offers every agent: reach a model, call a tool, remember, and search.
The agents stay in the application layer, each in its own role, with someone who answers, and each using those services.
Drawn once, under all of them, the platform shows what every agent stands on.
And the map can answer part of Ravi's question: which agents use which service.
Then Ravi's team puts a gateway in front of every model: one door that every call, from every agent, goes through.
Each call comes in under the agent's own identity, the one its place on the map gives it.
The gateway writes every call down: which agent, which model, when, and what it cost.
It keeps each agent within limits, so one stuck in a loop can't run up the bill, or crowd out the rest.
And it reaches only models the utility has terms with: where its data is kept, and that it isn't used to train anyone's model.
Even the vendor's chat is set to reach its model through the gateway.
Months later, another provider retires a model.
This time, the gateway's log shows which agents call it: three of them.
Ravi's team tries the replacement on each agent's own checks, and each agent's owner looks at the results.
Once the owners agree, all three move to the new model in an afternoon.
No roster is late, and no household is told twice.
The platform has its owner too: Ravi's team runs it, sets its limits, and holds the contracts with the providers.
Each agent's owner still answers for what it does: the head of retail for the chat, Grace for the crew planner.
And every month, the gateway's log shows each team what its agents cost.
On Databricks, that gateway is Unity Gateway, built on Unity Catalog.
In one place, it sets which models each team may use and the limits on each, and keeps track of every call and what it costs.
It can split calls between two models, to try a new one, and fall back to another if one fails.
The functions agents use as tools are kept in Unity Catalog too, under the same permissions as the data.
Databricks' own models and other providers' go through the same gateway.
In Babylon, the same baked brick and the same bitumen went into the river wall and the temple-tower.
What each was for, holding back a river or raising the house of a god, was its builder's.
At the utility, every agent now stands on one platform, and each keeps its own purpose.
Ravi's note has its answer: agents share the platform's models, gateway, tools, memory and search; each keeps its own purpose, instructions and logic.
Next: what an agent may read.

films.x: The person behind the role. Linh graduated from the university and came back for a master's, under a new student number. Now five records in four systems hold one person, and none of them knows the others. Keep the person apart from her roles, and ask four questions to know what needs mastering.
c: In 1686, Sweden's church law asked every parish priest to keep a book of every household: who lived there, when they were born, whether they could read.
When someone moved, they carried a certificate to their new parish, and the next book took them in.
In 1947, the register gave everyone a number for life.
One person, written down once, followed wherever they went.
Today, at the university. Linh Nguyen graduated here in 2022.
Last year, she came back to study health informatics.
She applied online, and got a new student number.
Nothing linked it to the number she graduated with.
Now the university has five records of her.
Two in the student system, under the old number and the new.
One at the alumni office, which knows only the old one.
One in HR, which pays her to tutor a first-year unit.
And one at the research office, for a project she joined this year.
So her application asked for a transcript of the degree the university gave her.
And the alumni office invites her back, for a master's. She's already doing one.
Five records, five Linhs, and nobody sees that she's one person.
Linh is master data: one of the things the university is about, shared by every process and system.
The lists that sort her, like “casual tutor” or a country, are reference data.
What happens to her, an enrolment or a payslip, is transactional data.
And the definition of a learner is metadata.
This series is about the first two, and the next film tells them apart.
Noor, the university's data architect, opens the university's own model.
It has a learner. A good one, with keys from three systems and a decision for every match.
But a learner isn't someone. It's how someone relates to the university, for a while.
The model has no person. She says so, and writes it down.
So she draws four things apart.
The person: someone, once.
The roles: student, tutor, researcher, each with a start, an end, and an owner.
The contact points: an email or an address, each with a purpose, and some shared by two people.
And the identifiers: a student number belongs to the student system, a staff number to HR.
None of them is the person.
Enterprise architects draw it the same way: a person, a team or an organisation is an actor, assigned to one or more roles, for a time.
Then Noor and Mei write down who keeps what.
For each role, which system creates it, and who owns it.
For each piece of the person, which system is trusted.
The registrar's office keeps the legal name.
Linh keeps her own preferred name, and her home address.
HR keeps her work details.
And Mei's office looks after the person: who someone is, and whether two records are one.
Every industry has a Linh.
A nurse admitted as a patient, in the same hospital.
A bank customer who guarantees a friend's loan.
A household where the account holder moved out, and the person who stays needs the power on.
Different words, the same four things.
The data management body of knowledge, DAMA, calls this reference and master data.
It names four ways to keep it: a registry that only links, a copy for analysis, a master that systems read back, or one place where people are created.
The series picks one later, and shows the tools that do it.
People aren't the only master data.
The university also has employers and partner universities, awards and units, campuses and rooms.
A hospital has patients, practitioners and wards.
A bank, customers, accounts and the firms it trades with.
A utility, meters, connection points and poles.
A shop, products, suppliers and stores.
Which of them need mastering? Ask four questions.
Is it a thing the business is about, not something that happens?
Is it used by more than one process?
Is it created or changed in more than one place, so the copies can disagree?
And does it matter when they do: money, safety, the law, or someone's trust?
Four yeses: master it.
Eight more films follow, in four parts.
Who someone is. Roles and lists. Sharing it safely. And keeping it right.
This time, when Linh applies, the university finds her first.
It adds a role, not a person.
Her degree is already there, and the alumni office sees she's back.
Know the person, not just the role.

films.x: Matching and the golden record. A duplicate check proposes three pairs of records, and Mei's office decides each one: Linh's two student numbers, linked with a reason; her HR record, its birth date one digit off; and two students called Aisha, who are two people. The golden record keeps every source, so any link can be undone.
c: In 1548, Martin Guerre left his village in the south of France, and his wife, Bertrande.
Eight years later, a man came back as Martin. He knew the house, the family, their stories, and they took him in.
His uncle came to doubt him. In court, a hundred and fifty witnesses couldn't agree.
On appeal, as the judges leaned his way, a man with a wooden leg walked in: the real Martin Guerre.
Two people, taken for one, because so much matched.
First, two words.
Master data is the things the business is about: Linh, an award, a supplier, a meter.
Many rows, always growing, and matched across systems.
Reference data is the short lists that sort them: countries, role types, statuses. Few rows, rarely changing, often from outside.
Would you ever ask, “is this the same one as that?” Then it's master data.
If you only pick a value from a list, it's reference data.
And a list that gets owners and a life of its own, like faculties, becomes master data.
What matching builds is a master record, often called a golden record.
An ID of its own, which never changes and is never reused.
For each detail, the best value, labelled with where it came from.
And links to every record it came from, each kept as it arrived.
So it can be explained, value by value, and undone, link by link.
Linh came back to study under a new student number.
This term, for the first time, the registry runs a duplicate check across the university's systems.
Fifty thousand records would make over a billion pairs.
So it compares only records that share something: an email, a number, or a birth year and a family name that sounds alike.
It proposes pairs for Mei's office, the steward of the person. Here are three.
The first pair is her two student numbers. Same name, same birth date.
Out of a hundred, it scores 93: over the line where a pair links on its own.
But in this first term, Mei's office checks the automatic links too, to test the rules.
And Linh's application says she studied here before.
So Mei links them, and writes down why.
The registry merges the two numbers in its own system.
The second pair is harder: her new student number, and HR's record of her as a tutor.
Each thing compared adds weight, or takes it away.
Given name, the same: plus 3.2. Family name, the same, but common: plus 2.
Birth date, one digit apart, maybe a typo: plus 2.4. Email, different: minus 0.4.
Together, 74: between the lines, so a person decides.
If the birth dates agreed, it would score 93, like the first pair.
An AI helper drafts a note for Mei, with the names hidden: birth dates one digit apart, and the HR email on the university's domain.
It suggests; Mei decides. She asks HR, and they check her contract: a typo.
She links them, with that reason.
Which birth date to trust is the next film's question.
The third pair looks easy: a learning platform account with Aisha Karimi's student number.
But the account is Aisha Rahman's, and the number was typed in by mistake.
Link them, and one student sees the other's results. Two people, taken for one.
A false merge costs more than a missed match.
So Mei keeps them apart, and her “not the same” binds the matcher.
Two decisions, and Linh's five records point to one person.
Nothing was destroyed: each record stays as it arrived. So if a real Martin ever walks in, any link can be undone.
And no rule says two student numbers are never one person. A student who comes back has two.
Hospitals match people too. Merge two patients by mistake, and a test result follows the wrong one.
So they keep each identifier with the system that issued it, and undoing a merge is part of the job.
Where the data is transformed, a query proposes the pairs without comparing everyone, and the decisions table becomes the person's queue.
A test fails when a pair waits more than a week: the queue has an owner, and a limit.
On the platform, the master records and their links, each with who decided and why.
Decide a match once, with a reason, and keep it.

films.x: Survivorship. Linh's five records are linked to one person, and their values still disagree: four spellings of her name, two birth dates, four emails. The model picks one with a single order, hidden in the code. Jun writes a rule for each field in one place, and every value keeps its source.
c: Plymouth, December 1831. HMS Beagle is about to sail around the world.
At sea, the time back home tells a ship how far east or west it has come.
So it carries clocks. And clocks drift.
With two that disagree, you can't tell which one is wrong.
The Beagle carries twenty-two.
In port, each one's drift is measured and written down.
The two thought best are the standards, and the others are checked against them.
Which clock to trust is decided before the clocks disagree.
Today, at the university.
Linh's five records are linked now: Mei's office decided they're one person.
So the person needs one name, one birth date, and a way to reach her.
But her records don't agree.
Four ways of writing her name. Two birth dates. Two mobile numbers. Four emails.
Which value wins?
The university's model already picks one.
For the learner, it takes the student system first, then the learning platform, then short courses.
One order, for every field, inside the code, where the people who own the data can't see it.
For the person, the quick fix is to let the newest value win.
But HR sends its whole file again every teaching period, so its values always look new.
Her birth date becomes HR's typo, and her old mobile comes back.
Her transcript would print her name as HR typed it.
Newest isn't truest.
Her legal name is Nguyễn Thị Linh: family name first, with its accents, as on her passport.
The student system checked it when she enrolled.
Her old record lost the accents, and HR turned it round: Linh Nguyen.
The name she goes by, Linh, she set herself.
Both are hers, for different things.
Her transcript carries her legal name.
Her class lists and her ID card, the one she chose.
So the person keeps two names, and each needs its own rule.
So Jun writes the rules down, field by field, in one place, where the steps that build her record read them.
Like the Beagle's standards, each field has the source it trusts most.
Her legal name, from the student system, which checked her passport.
Her preferred name, from Linh herself.
Her birth date, from the student system.
If another system sends a different one, it waits for Mei.
HR's still has the typo, so Mei pins the right one, with a reason, until next year.
Her mobile: the newest one she confirmed, not the newest one sent.
Every other field falls back on the same order: the most trusted source, then the newest confirmed value, then the most complete.
Master data tools let people set rules like these on screens of their own.
In the simplest form, they're a file like this one, and the code and the tests are written from it.
An email column holds one email. Linh has four.
Her student email, for her studies. Her staff email, for her tutoring.
A personal one from 2019, and a newer one from her application.
None of them is wrong. Each is for something.
So each is kept as a contact point: its purpose, its source, and the day she last confirmed it.
HR writes to her staff email. The alumni office, to a personal one.
Now each value in Linh's record says where it came from, which rule chose it, and how old it is.
The values that lost are still there, one click away.
So if anyone asks why her record says 14 March, the answer is right there.
Her transcript, her class list and the alumni office all read from it.
Rules change too.
The alumni office asks for a new one: for personal email, the one people confirmed most recently.
Before it runs, a dry run lists every value it would change.
1,284, Linh's among them.
Mei checks a sample, and the registrar, who owns the data, approves.
Then it runs, as version two, with its date.
A bank knows two names too.
Statements carry the account holder's legal name.
The app greets them by the one they chose.
A shop keeps a billing address and a delivery address, each for something.
Different places, the same question: which value, for what, and who says so.
In October 1836, the Beagle came home.
After five years around the world, its clocks were out by just thirty-three seconds.
Which clock to trust was settled before they disagreed, and checked at every port.
Linh's rules work the same way: written down before her records disagree, and tested every night.
The rule is declared, not hidden in the code.

films.x: Roles with dates. Each night, the university's systems write over how they saw Linh the day before. So when Planning asks about last year, she counts as a student months before she came back. Noor and Mei give every role an owner, a start and an end, and any question can be asked as at a date.
c: In the Roman Republic, an ambitious citizen climbed a ladder of public offices, each held for one year.
Marcus Porcius Cato was quaestor, then aedile, then praetor, and in 195 BC, consul.
Each office had its year, and his name: one man, a sequence of roles, each with a start and an end.
His last office was censor. Censors wrote down every citizen, their age and what they owned: the census.
At the university, census date is the 31st of March: the day it counts who's enrolled, for its official numbers.
Planning has a question for that day. How many of our students also work here?
And the alumni office, which invited Linh back for a master's she was already doing, asks: which of our alumni are studying again?
Each night, every system tells the platform how it sees Linh that day.
The student system says enrolled. HR says casual staff. The research office, project member. The alumni office, graduate.
Each answer is true for a day, and written over the next.
So when Planning asks again about last year's census date, to compare, every answer still says today.
Linh counts as a student in March 2025, four months before she came back.
Yet each office knows when its role starts and ends.
So Noor and Mei give every role the same shape: the person, the kind of role, the office that owns it, when it starts, and when it ends.
Linh's roles become bands, under her.
Applicant, then student, from 2019 to 2022. Then alumna.
Casual tutor, from 2023.
Applicant again in 2025, and student again, from July.
And researcher, from March to December this year.
Some follow each other, and some run at once. The person under them stays the same.
So far, her tutoring is one band, since 2023.
HR sees it differently: it offers her work one teaching period at a time, a new contract each semester, for one unit.
So the tutor role starts and ends every semester.
In January, between contracts, she isn't staff. On census date, she is.
Now Planning draws one line across her bands, at census date.
Student, tutor and researcher are open, and so is alumna.
So Linh counts once, as a student who works here: one person with three roles, not three people.
Move the line back a year, and she's a tutor and an alumna, not a student.
Last year's number stays as it was.
And the alumni office's question becomes a filter: alumni with an open student role.
Linh is back, since July 2025.
Each role also says what it relates to.
Her student role, a master's in health informatics. Each tutor contract, one unit in one semester. Her researcher role, one project.
People relate to each other, too. On the project, Ana Ruiz supervises Linh.
That relationship has its own dates, and ends with the project. Both people stay.
An energy company has the same problem.
The account holder moves out in June, and his role ends that day.
The person who stays depends on life support at home. Her need goes on, and so does the risk.
Kept on his account, the need would close with it. Kept on her, it stays.
On the platform, it's one table, with a row for each role.
Each row holds the person, the role type, its owner, what it relates to, and the dates it's valid from and to.
Jun builds it, with two tests. A role can't end before it starts, and every role belongs to a person.
Then any question can take a date: census date, last year, or today.
Each row also keeps when it was recorded, so a contract entered late still counts from the day it began.
Today, Linh is a student, a tutor, a researcher and an alumna.
In December, the project ends. One day, she'll graduate again.
Roles come and go.
A role has a start and an end. The person stays.

films.x: Reference data. Linh's tutor role has three names in three systems, a list of statuses is typed again in two tests, and a count lists her country three times. Jun gives each list one home, with an owner and the date each value applies from, and everything reads from it.
c: Airlines know each airport by three letters.
Toronto's main airport is YYZ, after the old station code of Malton, where it stands.
Ho Chi Minh City's is SGN. The city took that name in 1976, and its code still says Saigon.
A code outlives its reason, because changing it costs everyone who uses it.
A university runs on lists like these.
Linh studies here, and tutors a first-year unit.
HR calls her a Casual Academic. Payroll calls her CAS. The learning platform calls her a tutor.
Three names for one role, and nothing written down says they match.
HR's own list of roles lives in a spreadsheet, attached to an email.
And no one has written down which kinds of identifier the university issues.
Her status is ENR in the student system, and active on the learning platform.
One file maps both to studying.
Then two tests type the list of statuses again, by hand.
Her country of birth is Vietnam in HR, Viet Nam in the student system, and VN at the research office.
So a count of people by country lists her country three times.
These are reference data: short lists that sort and describe everything else.
Some are the university's own, like role types. Others come from outside, like countries, or airport codes.
Each value has a code that systems store, and a label that people read.
Jun, the analytics engineer, gives each list one home.
Role types, identifier types, relationship types, consent purposes, and countries.
Each is a table: every value with its code and label, who owns it, and the date it applies from.
HR owns tutor, and the registrar's office owns student.
Beside it, each system's own names are mapped: Casual Academic, CAS and tutor all mean tutor.
Now the tests read their allowed values from the list, instead of typing them.
Change the list once, and every test that reads it follows.
On the platform, each list is one table, and its lineage shows the tables and reports that read it.
Next year, HR will call the role Sessional Academic.
The change is a pull request, and HR, who owns tutor, approves it.
The new name applies from the first of January.
The old one isn't deleted. It's ended, because Linh's past contracts still use it.
Some lists belong to someone else.
Countries come from the international standard, ISO 3166, loaded on a schedule.
Like the project's glossary, the list is copied, never typed again.
Viet Nam appears once, with one code: VN.
And the count by country lists her country once.
Some lists describe people, like titles or gender.
Those stay short and inclusive, and are asked for only with a purpose.
A title can tell whether someone is married. If it isn't needed, it isn't asked.
Every industry runs on lists like these.
A bank's customer types decide which checks each customer goes through.
A hospital's relationship types decide who may be told about a patient.
Get a list wrong, and the wrong thing happens to a real person.
Now Linh's role, her status and her country each come from one list.
Like an airport code, a value can outlive its reason. But now everyone knows who keeps it, and from when it applies.
A list has an owner, a date and one home.

films.x: Purpose and consent. A fundraising email reaches Linh as a student, although she told the alumni office not to ask her for donations: her no was on her alumni record, and the student system never heard it. Write each role's purposes beside its data, and keep the person's wishes with the person.
c: About two thousand years ago, India's Charaka Samhita, a book of medicine, set down an oath.
A teacher gave it to each new student, by the sacred fire, before teaching them anything.
One line says: the peculiar customs of the patient's household shall not be made public.
A healer comes into a home to heal, and sees how the family lives.
It stays in that home.
What you learn for one purpose isn't yours for every purpose.
Today, at the university. Advancement, the alumni office, plans an appeal for a new scholarship.
Owen, who runs it, asks the registry for this year's top students, to feature them.
Their results were collected to teach them and award their degrees, not to raise money.
But nothing in the data says so, and the list goes.
The same month, the appeal's email goes to the faculty's students and alumni.
It reaches Linh, as a student. She's back for a master's.
When she graduated in 2022, she asked the alumni office not to ask her for donations.
They wrote it on her alumni record. The student system never heard it.
Her records are linked now, but the wish was written on one of them, not on her.
So the university writes its own oath, as data: what each role's data is for.
The student's results: teaching and awards.
The alumna's details: news, events and fundraising.
The tutor's pay: employment.
The researcher's data: her project, as she agreed.
Each purpose comes from one list, with an owner and a date.
A team may use a role's data only for a purpose written on it.
So the appeal can open the alumna's door, and no other.
And Linh's wishes go on the person, not on a role.
Each one is data: what she asked, for which purpose, when, to whom, and how to change it.
Her no to fundraising closes the alumna's door too.
A no she gave the alumni office now holds wherever she appears, until she changes it.
Where the data is transformed, Jun writes each purpose as a tag on the columns.
A test fails if a column with personal data has no purpose.
Then two policies on the platform read the tags.
One hides every column tagged for teaching from the appeals team.
The other leaves out anyone whose wishes say no.
Each is written once, and every table with those tags follows it.
So the next appeal goes to alumni, as their role allows.
It selects 2,140 of them.
37 come off, because their no sits on the person, and Linh is one of them.
The top students' results stay with teaching.
Then Linh asks the university what it holds about her.
That used to mean four offices, each searching its own system.
Now Mei's office starts from the person, and the links find every role.
Each value comes back with where it came from, and what it's for.
A correction goes to the office that keeps the value.
Her answer is ready in days, not weeks.
If she asked to be forgotten, each role would keep only what it must.
Her degree for good, and her project's data for as long as its rules require.
Every industry has these doors.
A shop's loyalty card was given for discounts, not to decide who gets credit.
A hospital patient agreed to one study.
The next study asks again.
What the healer saw stayed inside the house.
The university keeps each role's data inside its purpose, and Linh's wishes with her.
Data given for one role isn't free for every role.

films.x: Sharing master data. Linh wants to apply for a PhD, and the application still creates a new person before anyone looks. There are four ways to share one person across systems, each costing more than the last. The university chooses the lightest that stops a third number: search before you create.
c: Before 1874, every pair of countries that exchanged letters needed a postal treaty of its own.
A letter's price depended on its route.
That year, in Bern, twenty-one countries signed one treaty instead.
They became one postal territory, with one rate for a letter, and each kept the postage it collected.
Nobody built a post office for the world. Each country kept its own, and they shared the rules.
Today, at the university, Linh Nguyen wants to apply for a PhD.
Last time she applied, she got a second student number, and nothing linked the two.
The application still creates a person first, and nobody looks until later.
And four systems need to know who she is: the student system, HR, the research office and the alumni office.
Noor, the data architect, lays out four ways to give them one person.
A registry only links. It knows which records are one person, and asks each system for the rest.
A copy for analysis gathers everyone in the lakehouse, so reports count each person once.
A master that systems read back keeps the person in one place, and each system reads her from it.
Or one place creates every person, and the systems only read.
The university already has the first two: Mei's links, and the copy in the lakehouse.
At best, both find Linh after the fact. Neither stops a third number.
The last two do, but every system that reads back has to change.
So which is the lightest way that still works?
New people come in at two doors: the application and HR.
So those two read the person back. The research and alumni offices only add roles, so links are enough for them.
Like Bern: no post office for the world. Each system keeps its own, and they share the person.
Others need a heavier way. A bank's customer hub is read by every product system.
Many countries keep one population register, and agencies ask it instead of keeping their own.
And one change at the door: before the application creates a person, it searches for one.
It compares the name, the birth date, the email, and any number from before.
A clear match adds a role. A likely one waits for Mei's office to decide.
Only when nobody matches is a new person made.
Noor and Mei write down who may create a person: only the application and HR, after a search.
The research and alumni offices never do. They add roles to people already there.
In October, Linh applies for her PhD.
The search finds her: the same birth date, the same email, and the student number she gave.
So the application adds a role, applicant, to the person she already is. No new number, and nothing to merge later.
The same week, another Linh Nguyen applies. It's a common Vietnamese name.
But she was born in another year, writes from another email, and has never studied here.
Only the name agrees. So she becomes a new person, with her own number, and none of Linh's history.
Behind the search is the person, published as a data product, and owned by Mei's office.
A contract fixes its shape, and a new version marks any change to it, so nothing that reads it breaks by surprise.
The data platform builds and tests it, and governs who may read it.
A synced table serves it to the application, while the applicant waits.
In Bern, each country kept its post office, and they shared the rules.
Here, each system keeps its records, and they share one person.
Choose the lightest way that solves the problem.

films.x: A master data hub. Over a weekend, 1,240 changes reach the university's hub from four systems. Its rules match nearly all of them, and 8 too close to call wait for Mei. She decides each one with a reason, and can undo it in one step. Five questions to ask any hub close the film.
c: Monday morning. Mei, whose office decides who someone is, opens the hub.
Earlier in this series, the university wrote down its rules: when two records are one person, and which value wins.
The hub, a master data solution, puts those rules to work, every day.
Over the weekend, 1,240 changes came in from four systems.
The rules dealt with nearly all of them.
1,180 matched someone the university already knows.
52 were new people.
8 were too close to call, so they wait for Mei.
She starts with the one someone is waiting on.
On Saturday, Rafael Souza applied to come back for a master's, like Linh last year.
Before it makes a new person, the application now searches for one.
It found a likely match, but not a sure one.
So instead of a new student number, his application waits for Mei.
The hub shows why the rules gave it 74.
The same given and family names add a lot.
Birth dates one digit apart, probably a typo, add a little.
A new email takes a little away: his student one closed when he graduated.
74 is in the band where a person decides.
If the dates agreed, it would be 93, and linked without asking anyone.
An AI helper has read the case, and drafted a note.
