On the form, he wrote that he'd studied here: a bachelor's, finished in 2019.
The old record says the same thing, in other words.
The helper reads meaning, not only spelling.
It suggests they're the same person. It doesn't decide.
Mei decides. She links them, and writes down why.
The hub keeps her name, the time, and her reason.
Her decision teaches the helper, too.
And it can be undone: unlinking is one step, and every version is kept.
Then the change is published, not pushed: each system reads what concerns it.
His application moves on under his old number, with his degree already on file.
The alumni office stops inviting him back.
And it never sees his birth date. It doesn't need it.
His record shows where each value came from.
His names and his birth date come from the student system, checked when he first enrolled.
His email comes from the application: the newest one he's confirmed.
The typo stays on the application, but it doesn't win.
On Friday, Leila, a steward in admissions, checks fifty of the week's automatic links, mostly ones that only just passed.
She sees each pair of records, but not what the rules decided, so she isn't swayed.
This week, one was wrong, and Mei unlinks it.
If more than three were wrong, automatic linking would stop.
Every match would wait for a person, until new rules were agreed.
Whatever the hub, at a university, a hospital or a bank, ask it five questions.
Can it explain every match, and every value?
Can every decision be undone?
Do people decide what's unsure, and check what isn't?
Does each office see only what it needs?
And do systems read the changes, instead of being overwritten?
Rules act. AI suggests. People decide.
And everything can be explained, and undone.

films.x: Keeping master data. In 2024, a clean-up at the university merged two thousand duplicate records of people. A year later there were eleven hundred new ones, because nothing had changed how records were made. Now the application checks at entry, and Mei's office measures every day. The film closes the series.
c: Around 256 BC, in what is now Sichuan, the governor Li Bing split the Min River in two, without a dam, to water the Chengdu plain.
Its shape sends most of the river's gravel down the outer channel.
And every dry season, the inner channel is closed off and dug out, down to a mark buried in its bed.
Stone horses, it's said, at first, and later iron bars.
Its rule is six characters long: dig the riverbed deep, keep the weir low.
More than two thousand years later, it still waters the plain.
It wasn't cleaned out once and left. It's kept, every year.
At the university, in 2024, a clean-up project merged two thousand duplicate records of people.
It took a team of four, for six months, and it finished on time.
For a while, the duplicates were gone.
A year later, there were eleven hundred new ones.
Every intake made more.
Graduates came back to study, and people applied through two routes, each giving them a new number.
Linh's second number, in July 2025, was one of them.
The clean-up fixed the records. It didn't change how they were made.
In 2026, the application started searching before it creates a person.
A clear match adds a role to someone already known. A likely one goes to Mei's queue.
New duplicates fell under fifty an intake, and stayed there.
Like the river's shape, the search keeps most of them out. Mei's queue digs out the rest.
So keeping the person right isn't a project that ends. It's everyday work.
Mei's office has its own iron bars: five measures, each with a limit.
New duplicates per intake.
How long the queue's oldest case has waited.
Roles past their end date, like a tutor whose term contract ended, but who's still active.
Values with no source.
And requests for what the university holds about someone, answered on time.
Each has a test for its limit. Every night, the platform works them out, keeps them, and shows them on a dashboard.
One Monday, an alert: the oldest case had waited twelve days.
It was waiting for HR to confirm a birth date, one digit apart.
Mei rang HR, and the case was decided that morning, with its reason.
The alert pointed at a case, not at a person to blame.
Lists from outside change too. This year, the government's list of visa types added one.
An agent drafted how it maps to the university's fee categories, with its evidence, as a change to the list.
The list's owner, the admissions office, checked it and approved it.
The agent proposes. The owner decides.
Yusuf, who leads data governance, reads the same measures on his scorecard, beside every other domain's.
Owners, limits, and a way to change them: the person now has all three.
Every industry knows this picture. A bank cleans up its customer records every three years, and the duplicates come back every time.
One check at entry ends the cycle.
February 2027. Linh starts her PhD: a new role, on the person she already is.
That intake made thirty-eight new duplicates. She isn't one of them.
And at Dujiangyan, every spring, when the repairs are done, the water is let back in.
Clean it once, and it decays. Keep it, and it lasts.
Nine films followed Linh, until the university knew her as the same one, everywhere.
Who someone is: decide each match once, with a reason, and declare which value wins.
Roles and lists: give each role a start and an end, and each list an owner and one home.
Sharing it safely: use each role's data for its purpose only, and share the person the lightest way that works.
Keeping it right: make every change one you can explain and undo, and stop duplicates at the door.
Master data is one of the things data governance looks after.
And it needs the rest of governance: someone who decides, one meaning for each word, access for a purpose, and rules that run.
The next series follows Yusuf as he puts each of these in place, for all of the university's data.

films.x: Where governance comes from. In 2008, a bank couldn't add up how much it stood to lose: the numbers were there, and nobody could put them together. People who look after shared data had met over the same problem since 1980. In 2009 they wrote down what they knew, the DMBOK, with governance at its centre.
c: Autumn 2008.
As the financial crisis spreads, a bank's board asks its risk team one question: if another bank fails, how much do we stand to lose?
The answer is somewhere in the bank, in every business line, each with its own systems and its own names for the same customers.
By Monday, nobody can add it up.
It wasn't just one bank.
The regulators later found that many banks couldn't add up their risks quickly or accurately.
The numbers were all there.
Nobody could put them together, or say which to trust.
It wasn't a new problem, either.
In the 1970s, companies began sharing data between departments.
That raised new questions: who owns this data, and who may see it?
A new job grew up to look after it: data administration, with a dictionary of what each piece of data meant.
In 1980, in Los Angeles, the people doing that job started meeting, to share what they'd learned.
Their association, DAMA, soon had chapters in city after city.
Every organisation had been learning the same lessons alone.
Now they could learn them together.
In 2002, after accounting scandals, a law in the United States made chief executives sign for their company's figures,
and answer for the controls behind them.
Someone at the top now answered for the numbers, and for how they were made.
In 2009, DAMA published what its members had learned, as a body of knowledge for data management: the DMBOK.
It draws the work as a wheel: architecture, modelling, security, quality, metadata, and more.
At the centre, like a hub, is governance.
The other areas only fit together, and stay in balance, when someone has the authority to decide.
Other guides cover the same ground, or part of it.
This series takes what they agree on, and shows it at work.
After the crisis, the banks' regulators wrote principles for their data, and the first was governance: a condition for all the rest.
Someone had to own the bank's risk data, and answer for its quality.
Ten years later, only two of thirty-one of the world's biggest banks met them all.
Their programmes were often underfunded, narrow, and short of attention from their boards.
Making data add up takes more than systems.
It takes decisions, money, and attention from the top.
As data grew, so did the questions about how it's used.
In 2017, the DMBOK's second edition gave more room to ethics: not only whether we can use data, but whether we should.
In 2018, a European law made organisations answer for the personal data they hold, and be able to prove it.
Governing data now meant answering to the people it's about, too.
Now machines learn from data, whatever it teaches them.
So the people training them have to ask: where did this data come from, and who decided we could use it?
In 2024, a revision of the DMBOK added governance and ethics for AI.
The same year, Europe's law on AI asked for governance of the data that high-risk systems learn from.
And a third edition is being written, with new sections on AI governance, data ethics and sustainability.
Its makers call it a living body of knowledge.
It's planned for 2027.
So why does the DMBOK still matter today?
Because the question it answers never changed.
In 1980, in 2008, and in every system that learns: who decides about this data, and who answers for it?
The book keeps growing, but governance stays at the centre.
Today, at a university, a new data governance lead is about to meet the same question.

films.x: Why data governance. Yusuf starts as the university's data governance lead and inherits a shelf of thirty-four policies. The same week, two reports disagree on how many awards were conferred, and nobody has decided which goes to the government. He listens first, then asks every policy one question: where does it run?
c: Surgical teams have long known the steps that keep patients safe.
Check it's the right patient. Give the antibiotic before the first cut. Count every sponge before closing.
The steps were written in guidelines, but in a busy operating room, they were often skipped.
Patients paid for it: infections, mistakes, and deaths that could have been avoided.
Something had to change.
In 2008, a study in eight hospitals, in eight countries, tried one change.
Three times in every operation, the team paused, and a nurse read a short checklist out loud.
Each step was confirmed, and the nurse could hold the team until it was done.
Deaths after surgery nearly halved, from 1.5 to 0.8 in every hundred patients.
What worked was all of it together:
one agreed list, a copy in the room where the work happens, and someone who checks every step, every time.
Today, Yusuf Demir starts as the university's data governance lead.
He inherits a shelf of thirty-four policies, and a maturity score: 2.1 out of 5.
A chart of who's responsible for what, with half its names still to be confirmed.
And the minutes of a council that meets once a month.
His brief: fix governance before the next submission to the government.
The same week, two reports disagree.
Planning's census report says 4,812 awards were conferred this year.
The draft submission to the government says 4,867.
Which number is right?
The data team checks both numbers.
Both are right, each by its own meaning of award.
On Monday, the word changed: microcredentials of at least six credit points now count.
One report ran before the change, the other after.
But the government counts awards by its own definition, and no one agrees which number matches it.
So the data team takes it to Yusuf, in data governance: who decides?
Mei owns what award means here. Jun builds what the model says. Planning reports what it's given.
And the chart says: to be confirmed.
Like an operating room before the checklist: everyone knows their own step, and no one checks them all.
Policy 12 says that business terms are defined consistently.
It doesn't say who decides, or how a decision reaches the work.
That's what governance is for: deciding who decides, and making sure each decision reaches the work.
Like the surgical checklist: a rule, a copy where the work happens, and someone who checks.
Governance sets the rules and checks they're kept. Management does the work.
Yusuf doesn't write a thirty-fifth policy. He asks everyone the same question: what slows you down?
For Jun, the rules arrive after the work is built.
Mei approves the words, then never sees where they're used.
Sam could protect a column in minutes, if anyone said which.
Planning doesn't know which number to trust.
The people who wrote the binder weren't the problem. They wrote what they were asked for.
Governance is people's work. Tools can carry out what people agree, but they can't make them agree.
So he opens the binder, with one question for every line: where does it run?
Some lines can run in the work itself, as a field no one can leave empty, a check that runs every night, or a label.
Some are decisions: someone owns each one, and writes it down where the work can find it.
And some can go.
Behind every line that stays, there's something worth keeping, and someone to keep it.
Rules, each with an owner, that reach Jun before he builds.
One glossary every report reads from, so Mei sees where her words are used.
A class for each kind of personal data, so Sam knows which columns to protect.
And a list of who owns what, so Planning knows who answers for each number.
Owners decide. Stewards keep it all up to date.
The teams who do the work use it, and governance checks it's kept.
Over nine more films, Yusuf follows one symptom at a time to what's worth keeping, and to who decides and acts.
Then three draw it all as one model, on the university's architecture map.
And six build it, with dbt and Databricks.
A policy that doesn't run anywhere is a wish.

films.x: Decision rights. Every area of the university's data should have an owner and a steward, but three owners and half the stewards are still to be confirmed, so decisions are made in email, or not at all. Yusuf confirms each name, says who decides what, and every change of meaning goes first to its owner, by name.
c: Japan, the 1960s. A car maker's engine line moves on, past a row of workers.
Any worker who finds a problem pulls a cord, or presses a button, within reach.
A lamp lights on the andon, the board above the line, and the supervisor comes at once, to help.
If it can't be fixed before the job is done, the line stops, and the team fixes it together.
Every worker could stop the line, and they did.
It was within reach, and it brought someone who could decide, at once.
A right to decide about data needs the same.
Today, Yusuf opens the binder called Who decides.
Its policy says every area of data, like students or courses, has an owner and a steward.
Its register lists eight areas. Three owners, and half the stewards, are still to be confirmed.
So decisions are made in email, or not at all.
How award maps to the government's definition has gone round a thread of twenty-three replies. Nobody has decided.
Then he asks the data team who they ask, when a meaning isn't clear.
Noor, the data architect, shows him the list on their board: who we ask, area by area. Every area has a name.
For award, they ask Mei Tanaka, in the registrar's office.
They wrote it down as they built, because they needed someone to ask.
Yusuf takes each name to its office to confirm it, and asks for the names still missing.
On the way, he sorts out three roles, whatever a policy calls them.
The owner answers for what the data means. Mei decides what an award is.
The steward keeps it right, day to day. Mei also decides whether two records are the same learner, and writes down why.
One person can hold both roles.
The custodian runs the platform it lives on. Sam's team can change any table, but doesn't decide what an award means.
Each area decides what its own words mean.
Governance sets only the few rules they all share, such as one glossary, and one way to classify data.
When two areas disagree, or someone needs an exception, the council decides, by its next meeting.
If it can't agree, the deputy vice-chancellor decides.
Everything else, the owner decides, where the work is.
Then Yusuf and Noor make the owner required.
Anything new that other teams will read has a sign-off sheet. One line on it is never left blank: who answers for what it means.
Jun's new report for Planning comes back with that line empty, and a note saying what to add.
He asks Planning. Clara Jensen will answer for it, and signs.
The council's oldest action, name the data owners, is closed.
Next, every change request gets a routing slip, filled in from the register.
Yusuf keeps the register: change a name there, and every slip follows.
Jun's next change request maps award to the government's definition.
Its slip sends it first to Mei, by name, to settle what award means, in the glossary.
Then Noor's team builds it, and reviews the code. Owners are told, not asked to review.
Like the cord on the line: the work calls the person who decides, at the moment it matters.
When Mei decides, her decision is written down where the work is: what, who, when and why.
She already keeps a log book of which records are the same learner. The mapping will go in the course area's decision book.
Each area keeps its own, so the next person can find why.
Not in an email thread nobody can find.
Mei didn't ask to be an owner. She was named because she always answered.
So Yusuf asks her manager for the time it takes: two hours a week.
He keeps her scope small and clear: award, not every word her office uses.
And she has someone to ask: Yusuf, or the council, when owners disagree.
A role without time is a name in a spreadsheet.
On the line, the cord brought someone who could decide. Here, every change of meaning asks its owner.
A decision right is real when the work asks for it.
Then Mei opens Jun's change request, and asks a question nobody expected.
Which award does she own? She has found it defined in five places, and they don't agree.

films.x: One meaning for each word. Mei owns what award means, and finds it defined in five places, with three meanings. When award changed on Monday, only one of them changed. Yusuf brings the terms' owners together to keep one glossary they trust; the others are retired or read from it, and reports agree.
c: In 221 BC, the king of Qin conquered the last of his rivals, and became China's first emperor.
But each old state had its own script, its own measures and its own cart widths.
A measure of grain held more in one state than in the next, so taxes and prices were in doubt.
The empire needed the same script, measures and cart widths everywhere, so it set them by law.
Now a measure of grain had to hold the same everywhere, so taxes and prices could be trusted.
The empire even decided which words its officials used: “the king's order” became “the emperor's edict”.
Far to the south, a county office kept a list on a wooden board: each old word, and the new word to use instead.
In 2002, archaeologists found the board in an old well, with thousands of the county's own records.
Those records use the new words almost every time, so a word meant the same in the county as in the capital.
The board was a glossary, and it was used.
A university has the same problem: one word, defined differently in many places.
It needs one glossary that everyone trusts, and every tool reading from it.
Mei owns what award means, and she has found it defined in five places.
Yusuf goes to look. There are five glossaries.
The business glossary on the platform, with the words Mei approved. The data team copies from it.
Planning's spreadsheet.
An appendix to the registrar's policy.
The faculties' dashboards, each with its own description.
And a glossary tool bought in 2019, with six hundred terms.
Between them, three different awards.
Each was made for a good reason: a team needed words it could use, so it wrote its own.
So they disagree. One counts microcredentials, three don't, and one says an award is a degree.
Two can only be found by the people who made them.
And the biggest is the one nobody opens: the 2019 tool, last opened fourteen months ago.
When award changed on Monday, only one glossary changed. The other four never heard.
Five glossaries are no glossary. Nobody knows which to trust, so everyone keeps their own.
So Yusuf brings the terms' owners together, to keep one glossary.
Not the biggest. The one they can trust, and every tool can read: the glossary on the platform, beside the data.
Like the Qin board, it sits where the work is done, so it gets used.
Each term there has a definition, an owner, a status, and the date it last changed.
It holds the business's words.
A data dictionary describes each table and column. A catalog helps people find the data, and shows both.
The other four are retired, or made to read from it.
The 2019 tool is retired. Its terms with an owner move across; the rest are archived.
Planning's spreadsheet links to each term, instead of keeping its own words.
The registrar's policy now says: award, as defined in the business glossary.
The faculties' dashboards show the glossary's words, read from the platform, so they can't say anything else.
The data team's copy already worked this way: it says where its words came from, and it's checked against the glossary every night.
Every copy is made from the glossary, one way, never the other way round.
Without a nightly check, a change like Monday's is found months later, in a dashboard, when a number moves.
On Monday night, the check found it, and sent a change notice.
Like the Qin board, it shows the old words and the new ones.
And what the new words touch, and who owns each part.
A list of learners near an award, and its dashboard. The wallet app.
Mei approved the new meaning. This time, she could see where her words are used.
Jun saw a number in the words: six credit points.
A number in a meaning is a rule too. So it's kept in one place, as a business rule every report reads.
Monday's words weren't written at a desk.
Mei and the faculties argued them out in a workshop: should a microcredential count, and from how many credit points?
The glossary keeps what they agreed. It doesn't make the agreement.
And the people who kept the other glossaries lose something they built.
So they're thanked, and their best definitions move into the one that stays.
Policy 12 said reports count by the glossary's definitions.
Now each word has one home, and every tool reads from it.
Like the Qin board, it's used.
Reports agree, a change reaches everyone it touches, and people can trust the numbers.
Many glossaries are no glossary. Keep one, and sync every tool from it.

films.x: Who may see what. Clara in Planning needs each learner's status to plan next term's places. The old path would have given her the whole learner table, names and emails included, with no end. Now each column's owner says if it identifies a person, one rule hides what she doesn't need, and her access ends on a date.
c: West Germany, April 1983.
Every resident is to answer the census, so the country can plan housing, schools and transport.
But the same law lets each town hall add the answers, by name, to its records on each resident.
With computers, answers like these add up to a picture of each person, and nobody knows who will see it, or what for.
Hundreds of groups call for a boycott.
The Constitutional Court stops the count.
The country still needs a way to count, without knowing who said what.
The court rules that, in principle, each person decides what is disclosed about them, and how it's used.
The court doesn't forbid counting.
It draws a line.
Names and addresses are kept apart from the answers, and removed as soon as possible.
And answers given to be counted never go into the town hall's records.
In 1987, the count goes ahead that way: the country counts its 61 million people, and they keep their privacy.
Counting people is one permission.
Knowing who they are is another.
In a university's data, the court's line runs between columns: who may see each one, for what, and until when.
The university has a census too.
Planning counts its learners, and its list of those near an award has no names: counting doesn't need them.
Clara, in Planning, wants to know which of them are still studying, to plan next term's places.
For that, she needs each learner's status, from the learner table.
Yusuf opens the next binder.
Policy 6, Data protection, says personal data is classified and protected.
It doesn't say which data, or how.
Until now, a request like Clara's went one way.
A form.
An approval, by email.
Three weeks later, the whole learner table, names and emails included, granted to her by name.
And nothing ever ended it.
The platform team checks who can read that table today: forty-one people.
Nine have moved to other jobs, and still see every learner's name and email.
Nobody did anything wrong.
The path just had no end.
Now the path starts somewhere else: at the column.
Every column other teams read carries a class: what it tells about a person.
Direct, if it identifies someone by itself, like a name or an email.
Pseudonymous, if it only can with something kept elsewhere.
Or none.
Each owner writes the classes in a register, column by column.
And every change is checked: a column with no class goes to its owner, with a question.
One reached Mei: a credential's code.
It looks harmless, and most are.
But an award's code holds the student number.
Nothing can be assumed insignificant.
Mei classed it direct: the court's line, drawn at the column.
The class travels with its column, as a label, into every table the column reaches.
One rule reads the label: the registrar's office sees direct personal data, and everyone else sees stars.
The platform team applies it by label, not table by table.
So the email is masked in every table it reaches, and in tables built tomorrow.
Clara's request goes to the registrar's office, which owns the learner table.
Mei says yes, for her office: to plan next term's places, until 15 December.
The access goes to a Planning group, not to Clara by name, and ends by itself on that date.
Clara sees each learner's code and status.
Student numbers, names and emails are stars.
The learner code names no one by itself.
But with the registrar's list, it leads back to a person.
So it's still personal data: even codes come with a purpose and an end date.
The data team's AI agent sees stars too, and works from counts and samples.
Clara asks Yusuf why the names are stars.
He tells her why, as the court did: Planning counts learners; it doesn't need to know who they are.
And he shows her the way to more: if a purpose needs names, she asks the registrar's office, and says what it's for.
A no without a way forward is how tables end up copied into spreadsheets.
Clara's plan goes to the faculties, and on 15 December her access ends by itself.
Later that month, Yusuf's review takes minutes: he reads the access list itself.
The forty-one names are two groups now, each with a reason to be there.
Policy 6 now says which data, and how: owners class each column, and decide who may see it, for what, and until when.
The platform team protects each class, and Yusuf reviews who has access.
Like the census of 1987, Planning gets its numbers, and learners keep their privacy.
Classify once, at the column, and protect it everywhere.

films.x: Data quality rules. The university's policy says data quality is monitored, but monitored means a yearly survey of how each owner feels about their data. Yet the data team runs 160 checks every night. Yusuf gives each check an owner and a dimension, each owner sets its level, and the scorecard is read from what ran.
c: Fustat, in what is now Cairo, in 861.
Egypt's harvest depends on the Nile's summer flood.
When the flood is low, the fields stay dry, and a land tax set by guess would take the grain a farmer's family needs to eat.
A fair tax needs a measure.
On Roda Island, a new Nilometer is finished: a well open to the Nile, and a column marked in cubits.
The keeper reads the water every day, and the officials get the readings.
At sixteen cubits, the tax is due in full.
Below it, it isn't.
So farmers pay what the river allows, and officials know the tax before the harvest.
That's what a quality score should be: a measure every day, a level set in advance, so those who decide know which data to trust.
At the university, binder nine says data quality is monitored.
Here, monitored means a survey.
Each spring, every system's owner rates its data from one to five.
The short-course platform: four.
Average: 3.9.
David asks: can we trust the number we send to the government?
The survey can't say.
Like a guess at the flood, it measures how people feel about their data, not the data.
Yusuf needs a measure.
But like the keeper, the data team already measures, every night.
As the night's update brings in each system's data, a hundred and sixty checks run.
Every learner has an ID.
No learner appears twice.
Planning's number matches the census report.
Each check passes, warns or fails.
But a result names only the check.
Not whose it is, or what kind of quality it checks.
So Yusuf asks for two things on every check.
An owner: whoever owns the data it checks.
The short-course checks belong to the learning team.
And a dimension: the kind of quality it checks.
There are six common ones: completeness, uniqueness, validity, consistency, accuracy and timeliness.
A check for empty values is about completeness; for duplicates, uniqueness.
Jun writes both into the rule register, beside every check.
Now the scorecard writes itself, from last night's checks.
A row for each area, a column for each dimension, and in each cell, how many checks passed, of how many.
Under it, what didn't pass, and whose it is.
And David's question has an answer.
Planning's number matches the census report, faculty by faculty.
That check is Planning's, and last night, it passed.
Each check needs its sixteen cubits.
But who sets the level?
Not governance: its owner.
An enrolment with no email: one or two walk-ins a term are normal, and the learning team follows them up.
So they chose: warn on any, and stop the night's update above five.
Planning chose the opposite.
Any difference from the census report stops it, because that number goes to the government.
Each owner signs the rule, with its level and reason; the data team writes it into the check.
A rule its owner doesn't understand gets ignored, then switched off.
At Thursday's office hours, Tom reads the learning row.
One amber cell he knows: a walk-in from February, whose certificate still can't reach anyone.
And one he's never seen: emails typed with spaces and capitals, warning every night for a year.
The night's update cleans them, so nothing broke.
Nobody owned the warning, so nobody read it.
Now it's his team's.
Following up the walk-ins isn't a check.
It's about what people do, not the data, so it never stops the update: it's a list the learning team works through.
One night, five more walk-ins arrive with no email.
That's six, over the learning team's five, so the check fails.
Everything built from the short courses stops, and keeps yesterday's numbers, Planning's too.
In the morning, the scorecard has one red cell, and the learning team an issue, with a date.
Tom knows what it means.
His team chose the level.
Their list shows the six.
By noon, they've registered them, with their emails.
That night, the cell is green.
Binder nine's line runs now: every rule a check, with an owner, a level and a reason, and a scorecard read from what ran.
From now on, a rule without an owner and a dimension is sent back.
Like the Nilometer, the scorecard is a measure, not a guess.
The university knows each morning which data it can trust, what's held back, and who fixes it.
Where problems like these start is the next film.
A quality rule is a check with an owner.

films.x: Fixing data at the source. One cell on the university's quality scorecard is still amber, and the first answer is the old one: it's cleaned downstream. Yusuf follows one email back to where it's typed, a sign-up form on a phone. Tom's team fixes the form, the clean-up can go, and its rule stays as a check.
c: Vienna, 1847. The city's general hospital has two maternity clinics.
In the first, where doctors and their students work, about one mother in ten dies of fever.
In the second, where midwives work, about one in thirty.
Women in labour beg not to be sent to the first clinic.
Nobody can explain the difference. Something has to change.
Ignaz Semmelweis, a young doctor in the first clinic, looks for what's different.
The doctors and students come to the ward from the autopsy room, with traces of the dead on their hands. The midwives don't.
So he has everyone wash their hands in chlorinated lime, a bleach, before they examine a mother.
Within months, deaths in the first clinic fall to the level of the second.
Hundreds of mothers who would have died go home.
The fever showed in the beds. It started on the doctors' hands, on their way in.
Where a problem shows is often not where it starts.
Today, Yusuf opens binder 15. Its policy says the root causes of data quality issues are addressed.
But on the quality scorecard, one cell is still amber.
Short-course emails, with spaces and capitals.
The issue goes to their owner, Tom's learning team. The first answer is the old one: it's cleaned downstream.
Every night for a year, the data team has trimmed each email and written it in lower case.
Without it, one learner could end up with two wallets.
And every system that reads these emails cleans them again.
It's a mop under a leak. It works every night, and the leak never stops.
Yusuf follows one email back to where it's made.
From the wallet, through the data team's clean-up, to the short-course sign-up form.
The form keeps each email as it's typed, in a plain text box, so phones start it with a capital.
And picking a suggestion can leave a space at the end.
More than one email in three arrives that way.
Nobody typed anything wrong. As in Vienna, it shows downstream, but it starts here, at the form.
This time, the issue has an owner, a cause, a date, and a check that proves it's closed.
Tom's team makes the box an email box, so phones stop adding the capital.
And the form trims each email, writes it in lower case and checks its shape, before it's saved.
Nobody has to type more carefully. The form does the work.
Like the basin in Vienna, the form stops the problem on its way in.
Tom's team corrects the old emails in their platform. Then the data team's clean-up can go.
No system cleans them again, and every learner keeps one wallet.
The rule stays, as a check that should never fail: a promise to everyone who reads them.
If it ever fails, the form has broken, and its owner hears first.
The cell turns green: not because the emails were cleaned, but because they were right where they were typed.
One night, the learning platform sends something no rule names.
Half the new badges arrive with zero credit. Most are microcredentials that should carry five.
Every check passes. The value is there, and it's a number.
But the wallet shows them as plain badges, with no credit.
Monitoring knows each table's usual shape: when it arrives, how many rows, how many empty, how the values spread.
Usually, one badge in twelve has no credit. Last night, one in two.
As in Vienna, the numbers show something's wrong before anyone knows why.
It tells the owner on record: the learning team.
The cause is last week's update to the learning platform. Tom's team fixes it there, and sends the badges again.
Then the surprise becomes a rule: a microcredential carries credit. A check, with an owner.
Next time, it's stopped before it reaches a wallet.
Prevent what you can, where it starts. Check what you know. Watch for what you don't.
And every surprise you confirm becomes a rule.
Nobody blamed Tom's team. The form did what it was built to do. They got the evidence, and help to change it.
Back in Vienna, Semmelweis was right. But the washing was slow, and it hurt the skin.
Germs weren't known yet, so his only proof was his numbers. He waited years to publish them.
And when doctors doubted him, he blamed them, in angry open letters.
Washing became the rule only after his death, once germs were known.
It's basic hygiene now, and it saves mothers and babies every day.
A fix at the start lasts when it's easy to keep, and when people get the evidence, not the blame.
Fix the cause. Then make the fix a check.
That's what data governance brings: less cleaning, data everyone can trust, and an owner who hears first.

films.x: Change control. The word award has just changed, and Jun must change what the reports count. The university's change board meets once a month, after the draft submission, and answers its form from memory. Jun's team starts a record of who uses what, and his change request carries an impact note the owners fill in.
c: At ten to five in the morning, on the third of September 1967, every car still on Sweden's roads stopped.
Drivers crossed to the right, and waited.
At five, they drove on.
Swedes call it Dagen H, the day of right-hand traffic.
Until then, Sweden drove on the left, but its neighbours drove on the right,
and most Swedish cars were built for the right, with the wheel on the left.
When overtaking, drivers couldn't see what was coming, and many crashed head on.
Something had to change.
Switching sides would be safer, but many feared the switch itself: one driver who didn't know could meet another head on.
Everyone had to know.
So a commission prepared for four years.
New signs went up on the right, covered until that night.
A booklet reached every home, and the change's sign was even on milk cartons.
The change was huge, and it surprised no one.
In the next two months, half as many people died on the roads as a year before.
Everyone knew what would change, when, and what they had to do.
A change to data can surprise no one too, if everyone it reaches knows the same three things.
At the university, the word award has just changed: microcredentials of at least six credit points now count.
Mei, who owns the word, signed off the new meaning this morning.
Now Jun must change what the reports count.
The binder says changes are assessed for impact first.
In practice, that's a change board, once a month, and its form is answered from memory.
The next board meets after the draft submission, so the draft would count the old way.
And anyone nobody remembers isn't told.
Jun needs a better way.
To see what a change reaches, you need to know who uses what.
Jun's team keeps the table of every credential learners hold: awards, microcredentials and badges.
But nobody keeps a record of all the reports and apps that use it, or who answers for each.
So they start one: a record of who uses what.
Each owner writes their own line, and Jun's team keeps it.
Now Jun's change request carries an impact note: what it reaches, whether it breaks anything, and who must be told.
His first draft relabels microcredentials of six credit points or more as awards.
From the record, the note lists five things it reaches.
The two reports that count awards asked for it.
Planning's dashboard, Finance's forecast and the wallet app didn't.
Four owners to ask: Mei, Clara, Finance, and Marta, who leads the wallet team.
Planning's dashboard and Finance's forecast both count the credit learners have towards an award,
and part of it comes from microcredentials.
Relabelled as awards, the big ones would drop out, and both numbers would move.
Learners' wallets would show their microcredentials as awards.
The table would look the same.
But changing what existing data means is breaking.
Like switching sides of the road, everyone who uses it must change at once.
Mei, who owns the meaning, decides: this one breaks.
So Jun adds instead.
Every microcredential stays a microcredential, and one new mark says which ones count as an award: yes or no.
Nothing changes for anyone until they choose the new mark.
Now the note lists only what uses credentials: the two reports and the wallet app, with three owners to ask.
And nothing breaks.
Some changes can't be added, like taking a piece of information away.
Then a new edition goes beside the old one, like Sweden's new signs, and the old one stays until a date everyone knows.
The table of credentials already has two editions.
Edition 1 retires on the thirty-first of March 2027.
A new edition is the last resort.
The note says who must be told, and the wallet team didn't ask for this.
So Jun writes to them before the change goes in, in their words, not his.
Like Sweden's booklet, it says what changes, from when, and what to do.
Jun adds who will help.
Half of change control is telling people.
From Wednesday, the draft submission counts with the new mark, and Planning's census report from its next run.
Like the cars at ten to five, the change waits for everyone it reaches: Mei, Marta and Clara each say when they're ready.
It goes in when they all are, today, before Wednesday's draft.
In Yusuf's office, the line about change leaves the shelf.
Every change request now carries an impact note, filled in with the owners.
Every team that starts using data adds its line to the record.
The board meets only when a change needs it.
Governing change this way pays off.
This change went in today, not in a month, and so can the next.
Nothing broke, and the two reports will agree.
Like Sweden's morning, it surprised no one, because everyone knew.
Change control is a step in the change, not a meeting.
One question is left: when a table many teams use is late, who answers for it?

films.x: Data products. On census day, Planning's count of learners near an award wasn't ready at seven, and nobody answered for it. Yusuf, Noor and Clara write down what the table promises, and Clara becomes its owner. Every table other teams use belongs to one product, with an owner, and each product knows who uses it.
c: Istanbul, 1461.
Sultan Mehmed the Second has a stone hall built for the city's most precious goods: the bedesten.
Shops spread into the streets around it.
By the 1520s, nearly eight hundred stand outside its walls.
With so many, a buyer can lose hours searching, pay for poor goods, or be sold short, given less than they paid for.
When no one answers for it, buyers stop coming, and the traders lose them.
A market this big needs order.
In time, each trade has its own street, named after it.
And each has its guild, with rules for what its goods must be.
The guild's officers check the goods, and so does the market inspector.
A master who sells short answers for it.
So a buyer knows where to find a thing, what it will be, and who stands behind it.
And they come back.
Data has the same problem, and the same answer: a product, with a promise, and someone who answers for it.
Today, Yusuf takes down another policy: data is managed as an asset, with clear accountability.
Anil, an analyst in the Faculty of Health, tells him what happened last March.
On census day, Planning's count of learners near an award wasn't ready at seven.
The faculty needed it to plan next semester's places.
Anil asked Jun, who built it.
Jun said Noor designed it. Noor said Planning asked for it. And Planning said Jun builds it.
One table, and nobody who answered for it.
Until someone does, it can happen again.
Yusuf sits down with Noor and Clara, from Planning.
One question: what does this table promise, and who keeps the promise?
They write it on a card, and list it in the university's catalogue.
What it's for, and how to use it. Its owner: Clara, for Planning.
What's in it, column by column, and the checks it must pass.
Its service levels: built every night, and ready by seven on census day.
Where to ask, a version, and a status.
That's a data product: data, with a promise, and an owner who keeps it.
Clara answers for the product: that it's on time, that it keeps its promise, and that its users are heard.
What award means is still Mei's to decide.
As in the bazaar, where the guild's rules said what the goods must be, and each master answered for his stall.
The meaning has an owner, and so does the product. They can be different people.
But Clara didn't ask for this. “I'm not technical,” she says.
So Yusuf shows her who depends on it: the near-award dashboard, and every faculty that plans from it.
What it's worth to them: a number on time, from someone they can ask.
And what comes with it: Jun still builds it, Noor designs it, Sam runs it, the data team reviews changes, and she's told what they touch.
She answers for the promise, not the code.
Not every table is a product.
The data team keeps thirty-three tables. Ten are used by other teams, and each of those belongs to one of six products.
The rest are steps, which only the data team needs.
Every change is checked, like goods in the bazaar: a table other teams use must belong to exactly one product, or the change goes back.
Some products stay close to one system, some join several, and some serve one use.
Each product also knows who uses it: not from a mailing list, but from the record of who uses what.
The registrar's learner records are used by three other products: the wallet's, Planning's and Finance's.
Mei publishes them for everyone to build on, and she knows who does.
And a product has a life.
It's a draft until its owner says it's ready, and active while people rely on it.
When it's no longer needed, it's deprecated: it gets a date to go, and its users are asked to move.
An old edition goes the same way.
The first edition of the registrar's credentials has no users now, so at the end of March 2027 it's retired.
Now Anil finds Planning's product in the catalogue, among the others: its promise, its owner, and where to ask.
Like a buyer in the bazaar, he knows where to find it, what it will be, and who stands behind it.
If it's ever late again, Clara answers for it.
The policy runs in the work now: a product, an owner, and a check.
Order kept the bazaar's buyers coming back. Governance does the same for data: people find it, trust it, and build on it.
Own the product, not only the meaning.
Next, Anil makes a list of his own, for the faculty's advisers. It will need an owner too.

films.x: AI for governance. Anil's first change, a list for the faculty's advisers, comes back with four gaps and waits for Jun, the one person who knows the rules. So Yusuf and Noor write the rules as a checklist an AI agent follows on every change: it finds, drafts and flags, and people decide. The agent is governed too.
c: Imagined: the university, a few years from now.
Before going home, Anil Kurian, an analyst in the Faculty of Health, adds a column to a list: each learner's date of birth.
Nothing marks it as personal data, so nothing hides it: anyone who can open the list would see when each learner was born.
In the wrong hands, with a name and an email, it can help someone pretend to be that learner.
Someone has to catch it, and today, that means waiting for the one person who knows the rules.
At three that night, an AI agent reads the change against governance's written rules.
It doesn't edit the change, or approve it. It leaves a note: where, the rule, who decides, and a fix to consider.
At eight, Anil reads it, agrees, and marks the column as personal data.
No one had to wait, and no one saw a date of birth they shouldn't.
What this shows: rules written plainly enough to check, applied by an agent to every change, at any hour, and a person who decides.
Back to today, and Anil's first change: the list itself.
Every learner studying for one of the faculty's awards, how far each is from finishing, and a name and an email to call.
The checks send it back, with four gaps.
Each says what's missing. None says what's right for this list, or who decides.
So Anil asks Jun, who knows the rules, and waits.
Every change nobody else owns waits for Jun, and the advisers wait for their list.
So Yusuf and Noor write governance's rules as a checklist: the steps an agent follows on every change.
It's one page, in plain words, for anyone to read.
The rules no longer live with one person.
Start from the glossary: take each definition from it, or have governance confirm there's none. Find the owner. Run the checks.
Classify every column, with evidence. Check each rule about the data; track the ones about what people do.
Name what it touches. Then report, once, to the people who decide.
And it never approves, edits the glossary, weakens a check, or shows a value from the data.
It's the page the agent followed on the night we imagined.
The data team's AI agent reviews Anil's change. Two things pass.
Then three findings, each with where it is and the rule, and what the checks couldn't say: a draft, and who decides.
One: nobody answers for it, so no owner would be told what a change touches.
Two: ten columns don't say whether they identify a person.
It counts, and shows no values: all seven rows of the email column look like an email.
Three, which no check could find: the faculty wrote a rule, only its own awards, and nothing checks it.
The draft checks that every row's faculty is Health.
Where the agent wasn't sure, it said so.
Two columns look alike: long codes. One stands for a learner.
The other has two values for seven learners, and its description says it's made from the award.
Maybe not a person at all. But when in doubt, the checklist says, draft the stricter class, and ask.
Anil confirms: a course, not a person.
So it's classed as identifying no one, with Anil's reason in the review.
Then the meaning is written first: the faculty puts its classes and its rule in the glossary, and Yusuf names the new owner.
Jun, in the data team, reviews the change against them, and the owners are told what it touches.
The advisers get their list.
The agent decided nothing. It brought each decision to the right person, with the evidence.
Binder 26 says: AI use follows the organisation's data policies.
The agent is governed too, by the rules for AI helpers.
It has its own identity, reads only what Sam grants it, and writes only in its own workspace.
It works from counts and small samples, never bulk personal data, and only reads the glossary.
And it can't approve: the data team does, and the agent owns nothing.
That's why, on the night we imagined, it only left a note.
So the binder's line goes green: it runs, in the agent's access, its checklist, and the data team's approval.
An agent can only follow what's written down, plainly enough to check.
Remember policy 12's last line: “Staff take care to use terms correctly.” No agent can check care.
And the checklist itself is open: anyone can read it, and argue with it.
A change to the checklist is reviewed like any other: data governance approves it, and the next review follows it.
People trust a review they can read, question and overrule.
That night, a few years from now, is made of what you've just seen:
a checklist in plain words, rules for AI helpers, a register of who owns what, and people who decide.
What data governance gains: every change checked against the same rules, at any hour, and no one waiting for one person.
Personal data marked before anyone sees it, and each decision made by the right person, with the evidence, written down.
An agent checks what's written. People decide.

films.x: Getting people to take part. The university's two reports agree, by a meaning Mei and the faculties argued out. Getting people to take part is the key challenge. When a check stops Anil, an analyst, its page says why and how to fix it. Stewards share what broke, and a new rule only warns until a date everyone knows.
c: Bogotá, 1995.
In the city centre, drivers stop on the zebra crossings, so people on foot have to weave between the cars.
It's dangerous: more than a thousand people a year die on the city's roads.
Fines alone haven't changed the habit. The city needs another way.
The new mayor, Antanas Mockus, sends mimes into the streets.
When a car stops on a crossing, the people around it whistle.
A mime steps in and, without a word, invites the driver to back up.
If the driver still won't, a traffic officer writes a fine, and the people watching applaud.
The fine still came. But it came last, in an order meant to teach.
It worked.
By 1996, three drivers in four were keeping the crossings clear.
People on foot could cross in front of the cars, not between them.
Most people keep a rule because they understand it, and because the people around them keep it.
The fine is for the few.
It's the same with data. When most people keep the rules, everyone who uses the data can trust it.
Today, the university sends its awards to the government.
The submission and Planning's census report agree: 4,867 awards, counted by the glossary's meaning.
How that maps to the government's definition is a decision Mei owns, and has written down.
The glossary's meaning wasn't written at a desk: Mei and the faculties argued it out.
Agreeing is hard. It's one part of the key challenge in data governance, and its first priority: getting people to take part.
To understand the data and its rules. To look after their data, and answer for it.
To make the decisions that are theirs, and respect the ones that aren't. And to do what their role asks.
All of it is harder without tools that guide people, and show them what their work changes.
Governance has its fines too: the checks that stop the work.
Most of its work comes before them.
Anil is an analyst in the Faculty of Health.
He adds a column to the call list he made for the faculty's advisers, and the governance check stops him.
But it doesn't just say no.
Its message says what's missing, and links a page written for him:
what the rule asks, and why, how to fix it, and who to ask.
Anil fixes it in two minutes.
A check that only says no is a fine with no mime.
Governance used to be a queue of approvals.
Now it keeps office hours, every Thursday afternoon, for anyone a check has stopped.
Once a month, the stewards meet: the people who look after the data in each office and faculty.
They don't meet to approve anything.
They bring what broke, and what helped, so nobody has to learn it the hard way twice.
Yusuf started with the few who wanted to come.
Others joined once they saw it working.
Like the people at the crossing, colleagues remind each other, long before a check has to.
A new rule starts here too.
At October's meeting, Yusuf brings one: every column other teams read says what it holds.
First, why. A reader who can't tell what a column holds will guess, and two guesses make two numbers.
The stewards agree it, and set a date.
Until then, the check only warns.
Each warning links its page, and names the day it's required: the first of December.
Four weeks in, the warnings are gone.
There's nothing left for the date to stop.
The mime came before the fine.
And the maturity score of 2.1?
Yusuf opens binder 29. Its policy says governance maturity is assessed every year.
Nobody assesses it again.
Governance is measured from the work instead, every day.
From each night's checks: how much of what other teams read has an owner, a glossary term, a class and a description.
Which checks failed last night, and whose they are.
And from people: who came to office hours, and who came back.
A score said how governance looked on paper. These say whether it's used.
Bogotá measured its crossings the same way: by how many drivers kept them clear.
So what does a governance team do all day? Like the mimes, it teaches.
Governance sits at the centre of data work, where every other part of it meets.
As those parts get easier to run, the centre matters more, and the people in it most of all.
Someone has to show how the pieces fit.
So every new analyst starts with a path: short films, and labs to practise on.
And the stewards pass it on. Anil shows a new colleague the page that helped him.
And the binder? Of its 215 lines, 92 now run in the work, 64 are decisions someone owns, and 59 are gone.
Change models, from Kotter's eight steps to ADKAR, agree on what people need:
to know why, to want it, to know how, to be able to, and to see it last.
The last is the hardest.
In Bogotá, within about ten years, the habits had faded: the campaigns weren't kept up.
So governance can't be a project that ends. It has to be something the university can always do.
Scattered tools have long made governance hard to organise, and hard to see. That's changing, as the rest of the series shows.
Kept up, governance does for data what the mimes did for the crossings.
Most people keep the rules before a check has to stop them.
Nobody has to guess what the data means, so the numbers agree.
And a check stops only the few, who fix it in minutes.
Governance is people's work. Tools remember what people agreed.

films.x: Governance that lasts. The project that paid for the university's data governance ends in June, and the deputy vice-chancellor can't see what it does. Yusuf and Noor put governance on the architecture map: one capability, eight beneath it coloured by evidence, and seven services people can ask for, each with a promise.
c: Holland, around 1300.
Farmers have drained the wet, boggy land behind the coast, and as it dries, it sinks, lower than the water around it.
Dikes keep the water out.
But a dike is only as strong as its weakest stretch.
Where one stretch isn't kept up, the water breaks through, and floods everyone behind it: fields, homes, animals, the winter's food.
And a dike is never finished: it settles, it wears, and storms break it.
They need a way to keep every stretch up, every year.
So the people behind the dikes form water boards.
Each landowner keeps a stretch of dike: the more land, the longer the stretch.
Every year, the board walks the dikes, and fines anyone whose stretch isn't kept.
Whoever relies on the dikes pays for them, and has a say.
Behind kept dikes, people can farm and live, safe from the water.
Rijnland's board has kept its land dry since 1255, in a country where a quarter lies below the sea.
It's the same with data.
A project can put governance in place.
Kept up every year, it lets everyone trust the data.
December.
The submission went in, and both reports gave the same number.
Now David Mensah, the deputy vice-chancellor, is planning next year's budget, and the project that pays for Yusuf's team ends in June.
He isn't against governance, but he can't see what it does.
What would the university lose without it?
Yusuf's project report lists everything the project did, and nothing after June.
Without the team, rules nobody keeps up would drift, like a dike nobody walks.
And next year, the two reports could disagree again.
David needs to know what governance does, not what the project did.
Yusuf takes the question to Noor, the data architect, and her map.
He starts with three cards at the top: the governance team, the glossary, and the stewards' meeting.
Noor tests each one.
A team is who does the work. A capability is what must be done, whoever does it.
A capability survives a restructure, a new system and a new process. If a box wouldn't, it isn't one.
A team can be reorganised, a glossary replaced, a meeting changed.
So each moves down the map.
A water board isn't its members, or its spades.
It's keeping the land dry.
So one card stays at the top: govern data.
Under it, they write what the university must be able to do, in its own words.
Define what words mean.
Decide who owns what.
Protect who sees what.
Keep data fit for use.
Change without surprises.
Provide data products.
Help people take part.
Each was put in place this term.
Then they check the list against two frameworks, as checklists, not as the map.
The checklists find one more: keep records only as long as they're needed.
Nobody does it yet.
They colour each capability by how well it works today, with evidence, like every note on the wall.
Green where it runs, amber where people still have to remember, red where nothing happens yet.
Five are green: the work itself shows they run, every night.
Two are amber, still checked by hand: who uses what, and who may read each table.
One is red: learner records are kept for seven years, and nothing checks it, or removes what's older.
A heat map shows where it hurts, so it shows where the money should go.
The water boards walk their dikes every year.
Here, checks run through the work every night.
But nobody asks for a capability.
People ask for help.
So under each, they write the services people can ask for, named the way they'd ask.
What does this number mean?
Define or change a term.
Let me see this data.
Can I trust this product?
Fix it where it starts.
What will this change touch?
Help me do it right.
Each has a promise.
A new term, for one, is decided within ten working days.
Like the water boards, whoever relies on a service has a say in it.
Each year, its users review its promise.
David reads one page: seven services, their promises, and what it costs to keep them.
Most of it is people's time, and the tools they use.
Governance gets a line in the budget every year: the capability's, not the project's.
So the money goes to one capability, whichever team or system ends up doing the work.
And next year's new work starts with the red card.
In Holland, floods brought big projects, and projects end.
Keeping the land dry never did.
Here, the project ends in June, as planned.
What it built stays, because something keeps it.
Next November, the two reports can agree again.
Kept up every year, governance gives everyone who relies on the data one meaning, one number, and someone to ask.

films.t: Who does what, end to end
films.x: One service, end to end. Three faculties count a completion three ways, so Health looks nine points behind. Clara, in Planning, asks for the term to be defined, and Noor and Yusuf follow her request: each step done by a role, each role filled by a person or an agent, and the glossary run as a product.
c: Madrid, 1892.
Ricardo Palma, a writer from Lima, joins the meetings of the Royal Spanish Academy, which makes the dictionary of Spanish.
He brings more than three hundred words used every day in the Americas, and asks for them to go in.
Most are turned down, among them the word for ‘to budget’.
People look in the dictionary to see if a word is right, so words left out count as wrong.
And the millions who use them have no way in.
Seventeen years later, Palma is still asking a friend in Madrid what became of ‘to budget’.
Something has to change.
In 1951, the academies of the Americas form an association, and Spain's academy soon joins their work.
Today, they make the dictionary together.
Members of each academy propose words from where they live.
A commission drafts each change, the Spanish Academy approves it, and every other academy gives its view before it goes in.
Twenty-three academies make one dictionary, free online, for more than six hundred million people.
Each year's update lists what changed.
And ‘to budget’ is in it.
It's the same with data.
When anyone can ask for a term, and every step has someone to do it, everyone can use the same words.
January.
Clara, in Planning, compares how many learners complete their awards, faculty by faculty.
But three faculties count a completion three ways.
Business, when the last mark is in.
Science, when the examiners confirm the marks.
Health, when the award is conferred.
So the same learners look nine points less likely to complete in Health.
Before, a question like this went round by email, and nobody decided.
Now there's a service for it: define or change a term, decided within ten working days.
Clara asks.
Noor and Yusuf follow her request from start to finish, through the rooms where it happens.
Mei, the steward, drafts what completion means, with an example.
An agent checks that the draft has everything a term needs, and lists what it touches: three reports, and two dashboards.
The registrar, the owner, decides.
Mei writes it once, on Noor's map, and the map publishes it to the glossary.
And every copy follows, one way: the data team's copy, the dashboards, and the assistant that answers questions in plain words.
Ask, draft, check, decide, publish, follow.
Each step is done by a role: the one who asks, the steward, the reviewer, the owner.
Whoever fills a role is an actor: a person, or a team. Actors come and go; roles stay.
Here, one actor is software: the agent fills the reviewer's role, with its rights written down.
It may read the glossary and the record of who uses what, and write its note.
It may not decide, or change a word in the glossary.
People decide.
The academies work the same way: their members change, and the steps stay.
Each step reads something, and writes something for the next.
The request: which term, why, and who it affects.
The draft: a definition, an example, an owner, and its status, proposed.
The agent's note: what's missing, and what the change touches.
The decision: who decided, when, and why.
Then the term, and its copies, each saying where it came from.
On the map, each of these is information the service keeps, with a home of its own.
On his first day, Yusuf found a chart of who's responsible for what, with half its names still to be confirmed.
Now it's drawn from the map: every step, its role, and who fills it today.
In February, Mei takes three weeks' leave.
A colleague fills her steward's role, and the chart changes that day, and back again when she returns.
Nobody retypes it.
A steward is a role with time to do it, not a name on a chart.
And the glossary itself is run as a product.
It has an owner: Yusuf, for data governance.
Its users: people, reports, the tables that link to it, and agents.
And a promise: every term has an owner, a definition, an example and a status, and a change is decided within ten working days.
Each week, it lists what changed.
And it counts who reads each term.
This year, nine terms nobody read are retired, each with its owner's yes.
Like the dictionary's yearly list, the week's list shows everyone what's new.
All along, Clara could see where her request was, without chasing anyone.
It was decided in eight working days.
Now the faculties count a completion one way, and the nine points between them are gone.
Palma had to ask a friend what became of his word.
Clara can see where hers is.
A service followed end to end gives anyone a way in, a step for every role, and words everyone can use.

films.x: One home for every piece. A planner's request waits nine days with the wrong person, because a page on the data platform still names the table's old owner. Yusuf counts seven places that hold governance's pieces, and Noor gives each piece one home and an owner, with every copy synced one way and checked every night.
c: Korea, under the Joseon kings.
Every day, historians at court write down what's said and done.
When a king dies, one office makes the record of his reign, his annals, from their notes, and prints them.
Every copy is the same, kept in four archives, and nobody may change one, not even a king.
In 1592, war comes up the roads, and three of the four archives burn.
Only Jeonju's copy is left.
If it burns too, 175 years of the kingdom's memory are gone: what was decided, by whom, and why.
Something has to change.
Two local scholars carry it into the mountains, and guard it, in turns, for more than a year.
After the war, the court prints the annals again, from that one copy.
Five sets, far apart: one in the capital, four high in the mountains.
Every few years, a historian climbs to each archive, airs the books, and writes down what he finds.
The annals survive, complete: 472 years, twenty-five kings, 888 books.
Today, anyone can read them online, free.
Jeonju's copy could rebuild the rest because every copy was made from one source, one way, and nobody wrote in one.
It's the same with data.
A copy can be trusted when it's made from its home, one way, and checked.
February.
A planner in the Faculty of Business asks to read Planning's list of learners near an award, to plan next year's courses.
On the data platform, the table's page names its owner: Jun.
So her request goes to Jun, and waits.
But Jun only built it.
Since October, its owner is Clara, in Planning.
Nine days later, Jun sees the request, and passes it on.
Had he said yes, someone who isn't the owner would have decided who may see it.
The page was typed by hand when the table was built, and nobody kept it in step.
Sam runs the data platform, and wants its pages to name the right owner.
So Sam asks Yusuf where governance's pieces live.
Yusuf counts seven places.
The architecture tool, which holds Noor's map.
The glossary.
The document library, with the policies and the council's minutes.
The data team's repository: owners, classes, tables, checks, decisions, and each product's promise.
The data platform: who may read what, and the record of who read it.
The catalogue, where people find products.
And the tracker, for issues and requests.
Some pieces sit in more than one place.
One copy no longer matched the others: it had drifted.
Noor puts each place on her map, as an application, with what it holds.
Then she sets one rule.
Every piece has one home, where it's changed, and an owner, who decides it.
Every other place keeps a copy, and says where it came from, and when.
A product's owner, for one, lives in the data team's repository.
The catalogue and the platform's page copy it.
As with the annals, nobody writes in a copy.
A fix goes to its home, and every copy follows.
Then the flows between them, each one way.
Definitions go from the map to the glossary.
From the glossary, they go to every tool that reads them: the data team's copy, the dashboards, and the assistant.
The map's concepts, a learner or an award, go to the data team's tables.
Each column's class goes from the repository to the platform, where it sets who may read it.
Each product's promise goes from the repository to the catalogue.
Nothing flows back.
A copy is never a home.
But a copy can still drift from its home, if someone types into it, or a sync stops.
So every night, a check compares each copy with its home.
The first night, it finds the old owner's name on the table's page, and wrong names on two more pages, typed by hand last year.
The sync puts them right by morning, and the check tells each owner what changed.
Drift is something a check finds, not something a person remembers.
The historians climbed to each archive, and wrote down what they found.
Here, a check does it every night.
Each team still works in its own tool.
What changes is that everyone knows which copy is theirs to change, and which only to read.
The planner's next request goes straight to Clara, who decides it in a day.
And Noor's map becomes the plan for the next series, Governance you can use: each of its films builds a part of it, in the tools.
The annals lasted because every copy came from one source, one way, and was checked.
Give every piece of governance one home, and every copy can be trusted.
Everyone reads the same thing, and every request reaches the person who decides.

films.x: Governance in the code. At the university, the rules used to arrive after a table was built, and a table could reach other teams with no owner. Jun shows where the data team's dbt project keeps owners, classes, contracts, tests and decisions, and the checks that hold every pull request to them.
c: Today, in the data team's room.
Jun Park builds in ten steps round a loop, from a question to a new version, as the team's poster shows.
Now he opens a pull request, a change put up for review: a new table for Planning, the awards conferred this year, by faculty.
When Yusuf asked what slowed him down, Jun said: the rules arrive after I've built it.
One rule is that every table other teams use has an owner, someone who answers for what it means.
For four months, the council's minutes carried the same action: name the data owners.
Without an owner, nobody answers for a number.
On census day, the Faculty of Health couldn't plan its places: Anil was sent from Jun, to Noor, to Planning, and back to Jun.
The rules couldn't stay in minutes nobody acted on.
Now the rules live in the project, beside the code, and a check runs them on every pull request.
In a minute, it answers Jun: no owner, and how to add one.
He adds two lines, and the check turns green.
It goes to the data team for review, with nothing missing.
An action the council carried for four months is now a check that takes a minute.
And for Jun, the rules arrive first, while he can still fix them.
Governance puts a pin where each decision enters the loop:
a term at the question, a class of personal data at the sources, an owner and a contract at the gaps,
a rule at the tests, an approval at review, a version when it changes.
In dbt, each pin is a line beside the model's code.
The learner table names its owner, Mei, and the term it holds.
Each column says whether it identifies a person, and each test has an owner.
All of it is reviewed with the code.
Groups and access decide who may build on what.
The data team's first layers are private to its group.
Its core tables are public, for any team, and the marts protected, for this project only.
Build on a private one, and dbt stops before anything runs.
Jun's new table reads only public tables, so it builds.
But who may read it is the platform's to decide, in the next film.
Every table other teams use has a contract: these columns, these types.
Each build checks it, and a mismatch stops the table being replaced.
A change that would break a reader becomes a new version, beside the old one, with a date to go:
credentials' first version goes on 31 March 2027.
And exposures name who uses each table, and who answers for each use.
Contracts like these are agreed team to team, with whoever reads the data or sends it, and don't wait on governance.
Only the canonical tables, the shared core, also have an enterprise contract, in an open standard.
Data governance's information architect writes it first, and the data team builds to it.
A check compares the two, and if they differ, data governance looks at how the change got there.
Each pull request also says what it touches.
The meaning comes first: on Monday, Mei changed what award means, in the glossary.
On Tuesday, Jun's first draft relabelled microcredentials of 6 credit points or more as awards.
The impact check wrote it into the pull request: five reports and apps depend on it, four owners to tell.
The data team's review said a change of meaning breaks, even when the columns don't.
So Jun added a column instead: counts as an award.
The check called it additive, with three owners to tell.
A renamed column would fail: a breaking change needs a new version.
Owners don't review pull requests: they decide what words mean, in the glossary, before any code.
So a script writes the reviewers file: the data team for the code, and data governance for its own files.
GitHub asks them on every pull request, and a check fails if the file falls behind.
Decisions are files too, with who decided, when and why.
Every message says what to add, and where, and links a page on how, with who to ask.
A new rule warns first.
Every column other teams read must say what it holds: until the first of December, that's a warning with its date, then an error.
Week by week, the warnings fell from forty-one to none.
When Anil added a column, the check showed him how to classify it.
And an agent reviews every pull request, against the same rules.
It follows a skill the team wrote: run the checks, read what they can't, and draft what's missing.
On Anil's first pull request, his faculty's call list, it found no owner, ten columns with no class, and a rule with no test.
It drafted each, with counts as evidence, never values, and said who decides.
The agent never approves. People decide, and the data team approves the code.
Jun's table goes in, with its owner, its classes, its contract and the data team's yes.
On Noor's map, the project is the home of owners, classes, contracts, tests and decisions,
and their copies flow one way, to the platform and the catalogue.
The rules don't arrive after he's built it any more.
They arrive with every change.
The project carries governance with the code.

films.x: Access, masks and audit. At the university, access to the learner table was given by hand, to people, with no end date: forty-one could read every name and email. Sam shows how the platform now tags each column from the project's classes, masks them with one policy, and gives access to groups, until a date.
c: Today, in the platform team's room.
Sam Okafor runs the data platform, where the university's tables are kept and read.
Yusuf asks him who can read the learner table, with every learner's name, email and student number.
When Yusuf first asked what slowed him down, Sam said: tell me which column, I'll protect it in minutes.
Nobody could tell him, so access was all or nothing, given by hand:
a form, an emailed approval, and three weeks later, the whole table, to one person, with no end date.
Sam finds forty-one people who can read it.
Nine have moved to other jobs, and still see every learner's name and email.
Something had to change.
Now each build tells the platform which columns identify a person, from the classes in the project.
One policy shows stars in those columns to everyone outside the registrar's office, on every table, even tables not built yet.
And access goes to groups, until a date.
By the end of December, two groups can read the learner table, not forty-one people.
Each new table is protected as it's built.
And Sam protects a column in minutes, because the project tells him which.
On the platform, the project's tables sit in the university's catalog, a schema for each layer the project builds.
But people look for data by area, not by layer.
So each table carries its area as a tag, from the domain its model names,
and the Discover page lays the tables out by area: student, course, planning, finance, and more.
Who may read a table is a grant, and a grant goes to a group, never to a person.
In the project, each column's class says whether it identifies a person: direct, pseudonymous or none.
After each table builds, dbt writes the class to the platform, as a tag on the column.
The tag is governed: an admin created it once, with only those three values, so nobody can tag a column "maybe".
Change a class in the project, and the next build changes the tag.
For tables the project doesn't build, the platform's classifier finds columns that look personal, for their owner to class.
Then one policy masks every column tagged direct, in the whole catalog, for everyone but the registrar's office.
It isn't set table by table: a table built tomorrow, with an email in it, is masked as soon as it's tagged.
A policy can filter rows the same way; this one masks.
Clara reads the learner table, and sees each learner's status, and stars where the names and emails are.
The registrar's office sees the values, and so does the identity that runs the build.
The learner code is pseudonymous: the student number, scrambled the same way in every table, so tables can be joined without names.
Scrambled isn't anonymous.
With the registrar's list, anyone can scramble every number on it and match them.
So the code is still personal: the policy leaves it readable, for counting, and reading it takes a purpose and an end date.
Access goes to groups, never to people.
Mei, for the registrar's office, said yes to Clara: to plan next term's places, until 15 December.
So Sam doesn't grant the table to Clara.
