He grants it to a Planning group, and Clara joins the group in the university's directory, until that date.
The platform reads its groups from there.
When someone changes jobs, the directory moves them, and their access follows.
On 15 December, her access ends by itself.
The platform also draws each column's lineage.
Pick the learner's email, and it shows every table it flows into, down to the column.
Tags can follow lineage by themselves.
Here they don't need to: every table the email reaches is built by the project, which classes it there too,
and the check stops a table that doesn't.
And the platform keeps a log of who read each table, and when.
So Sam can answer what Yusuf wanted to know: who read the learner table this month.
Each December, the access review reads the grants themselves: who can read each table, through which group, and who's in it.
Forty-one people gave way to two groups:
the registrar's office, which keeps the learners' records, and the data team, which builds the tables.
Clara plans next term's places with the statuses she needs, and stars where the names are.
On Noor's map, the project says what each column is, and the platform holds the line:
classes become tags, tags meet one policy, and groups carry the dates.
Sam protects a column in minutes now, because the project tells him which.
The platform enforces what the metadata says.

films.x: Glossary and metrics. At the university, award was kept in five glossaries with three meanings, and two reports counted it two ways, 4,812 and 4,867. Now award has one page on the platform, every copy is checked against it each night, and awards conferred is counted once, for people, reports and agents.
c: Monday, in the registrar's office.
Mei Tanaka owns what award means: the qualifications the university confers.
Today, the meaning changes: microcredentials, the certificates of short courses, count too, from 6 credit points.
When Yusuf asked what slowed her down, Mei said: I approve the words, then never see them used.
Until now, award was kept in five glossaries, lists of what words mean, with three meanings between them.
So two reports counted awards two ways: Planning's census report said 4,812, the draft submission to the government 4,867.
The university could have sent the government a number it couldn't explain.
Something had to change.
Now award has one page, on the platform, and every copy is checked against it each night.
The 6 credit points are kept once, as a setting.
And awards conferred is counted once, for every report and every agent.
That night, the check finds Monday's change, and on Tuesday morning, Mei sees everything her words touch.
On submission day, both reports say 4,867.
Her words reach the work, and the university sends one number.
On the platform, each term of the glossary is a page.
Award's page has its words, its owner, Mei, and its domain, course.
It lists the tables that hold it, and where its words come from.
It's published from Noor's map, where each term is kept, so a change is made there, never on the page.
People read it beside the data.
So does the platform's assistant, and it cites the page when it answers.
The data team keeps its own copy of each term, beside the models, so the tables that hold award describe it in the same words.
The copy names its source: the glossary's term, and the day it was synced.
Each build then sends the descriptions on to the catalog, one way, never back.
Every night, a check compares each copy with its term in the glossary.
On Monday night, award had changed.
So the check proposed the change, in a pull request: the old words and the new, and what the new words touch.
Three tables, eight definitions that name award, the code that builds them, and three reports and apps to tell.
On Tuesday morning, the data team reviewed the code, and Mei was told what it touches.
This time, she saw where her words are used.
The new words hold a number: 6 credit points.
So it's kept in one place, as a setting: min award credit points, 6.
Jun's new column, counts as an award, reads it, and every count of awards reads the column.
If Mei and the faculties ever agree on another number, the glossary changes first, then one line, in a pull request the data team reviews.
A count is a meaning too: which credentials count, and in which year.
So awards conferred is counted once, as a metric view: a count the platform defines once, for every tool that asks.
It counts the credentials that count as an award, by the year they were issued.
The project builds it like its models, so every change to it is reviewed.
The draft submission reads it, and so does Planning's census report.
Neither counts awards its own way any more.
And the platform's agents read the same meaning.
Clara asks Genie One, the platform's assistant, how many awards the university conferred this year.
It answers 4,867, from the metric, and cites award's page for what an award is.
It prefers the page to its own guess, and shows where its answer came from.
An agent the data team builds on the metric gives the same answer.
People and agents read one meaning, so they get one number.
Meaning comes in three layers: what a word means, how a number is counted, and how things relate.
Each has one home.
The words live on Noor's map, and the glossary copies them.
How things relate lives there too, copied into the project.
And the counts live in the project, which the platform serves as metric views.
Every copy is checked against its home, or built from it.
Mei sees her words used now, in every table, count and answer that holds them.
She decides what award means, once, and the platform carries it everywhere it's read.
On submission day, the draft and Planning's census report both say 4,867, counted by the same metric, with the same words.
One meaning, read by people, reports and agents.

films.x: Quality checks and monitoring. At the university, a failed check named no owner, a warning ran for a year unread, and data quality was a survey, 3.9 out of 5. Now each check names its owner and its level, checks run where data is typed and loaded, monitoring watches the rest, and every result lands in one scorecard.
c: In Planning's room, Clara Jensen checks the numbers before they leave.
The census numbers go to the government, and the lists to the faculties.
When Yusuf asked what slowed her down, Clara said: which number do I trust?
Checks ran every night, but a failed one said only its name, not whose data it was.
A warning that emails were typed with spaces and capitals had run for a year, and nobody owned it.
And data quality was a survey: people rated their data, 3.9 out of 5.
So a broken night could change a number on its way to the government, and nobody knew whose it was to fix.
Something had to change.
Now every check names its owner, the kind of quality it checks, and the level its owner chose.
Monitoring watches for what no rule names.
And each morning, every result goes into one scorecard, with an issue for each owner.
On the 19th of October, five more enrolments arrived with no email.
That made six, more than the five the learning team allows.
Everything built from them stopped, so nothing wrong went out: Planning kept the day before's numbers.
By noon, the learning team had added the six emails, and that night, all 160 checks passed.
Now Clara knows each morning which numbers to trust, and who answers for each.
In the project, each check is a dbt test, and each test names its owner and the kind of quality it checks, its dimension.
The owner comes from the folder: every test on the short-course data is the learning team's.
The dimension comes from the kind of test: a test for empty values checks completeness.
The level is in the test, as its owner chose: warn on one enrolment with no email, stop above five.
The decision log says who chose it, and why.
And a test without an owner or a dimension doesn't get in.
After each night's build, two scripts read dbt's results.
One writes the scorecard: for each area and each dimension, how many tests passed.
On the 19th, learning's completeness was six of seven.
The tests on what was built from the stopped data didn't run: they count as not run, not as failed.
The other script writes each owner an issue to answer: what didn't pass, and why the level is there.
A cause to fill in, and a date to answer by.
A dbt test, on what the data team builds, is one place to check.
There are three more along the data's way: where it's typed, where it's loaded, and on the platform's tables, as monitoring.
Each catches what the others can't, and each tells the data's owner.
Prevent what you can, where it starts.
Check what you know.
Watch for what you don't.
Emails used to arrive as typed, with spaces and capitals, and every night the data team cleaned them.
From the 2nd of November, the sign-up form checks each email as it's typed.
A test on the source, as the data team reads it in, checks every email recorded since, and stops the build if one isn't clean.
It should never fail: if it does, the form has broken.
Once the old emails are corrected, the clean-up goes, and the test checks every row.
Each night, the platform team's pipeline loads each system's files.
Its expectations, rules on each table, check that a row can be loaded at all.
An enrolment with no ID can't be told apart from another, so it's kept out, and counted.
The count reaches its owner like any other result, and the row is fixed where it's kept, in the short-course platform.
One night, half the new badges arrived with no credit.
Every test passed: no rule said a microcredential carries credit.
Monitoring caught it.
The platform learns when each table usually arrives, and how many rows it brings, with no rule to write.
And a profile of the badges counts, each night, how many carry no credit: usually one in twelve.
That night, one in two.
An alert went to the owner on record, the learning team.
Once they'd confirmed it, the surprise became a test.
The pipeline's counts and the monitors' results land on the platform, by table.
Each table's owner is in the project, so the scorecard reads them too, in a table under the tests'.
Every result reaches one owner, not a shared inbox.
And quality is measured, not surveyed: last night, 160 of 160 tests passed, one with a warning.
So did the platform's 22 checks, and every test had an owner and a dimension.
This morning, Clara opens the scorecard before the numbers leave.
One amber cell: an enrolment with no email, that the learning team is following up.
Everything else passed, and every cell has an owner.
Clara knows which numbers to trust, and who answers for each.
Rules you write, and monitoring for the rest.

films.x: Open standards. Data products whose promises are files in open standards: each owner writes the product's file, data governance writes the core tables' contracts first, a check holds the code to them on every change, and any catalogue reads a copy.
c: Today, in Noor's room, Noor and Clara go over Clara's product.
Noor designs the university's data and its six data products: data with a promise, and an owner who keeps it.
Clara's is the count of learners near an award, ready by seven on census day.
But the promises were typed by hand into a catalogue, where people look for data, and the tables changed every week.
So the catalogue could promise a column the table no longer had.
And on census day, a faculty's report could break, just when it's needed to plan next semester's places.
And each catalogue kept its promises in its own format: change the catalogue, and every promise is typed again.
Something had to change.
Now each promise is a file, kept with the code, in two open standards that any tool can read:
one for the product, and one for the contract of each core table it's built on.
Data governance's information architect writes that contract first, and the data team builds to it.
A check stops the two drifting apart.
When credentials needed a new column, its contract got the line first, Jun built it, and no report broke.
All ten tables other teams read have a promise that's checked on every change.
And whichever catalogue shows them, the promises stay the university's.
Each product starts as a short file its owner writes.
Clara's says what the product is for, and how to use it.
It names her as its owner, the table it offers, and its service levels: built every night, and ready by seven on census day.
And it says where to ask.
The data team builds the table. Clara keeps the promise.
The contract is the promise about the table itself:
each column, its type, whether it's always there, whether it can identify a person, and the tests it must pass.
Only the core tables have one: the shared tables that every product is built on.
Data governance's information architect writes it first, in the Open Data Contract Standard.
The data team builds the model to it.
Side by side, each line of the contract has its line in the model.
On every pull request, a check fails if the model has drifted from its contract, or if the contract breaks the standard's rules.
Then data governance looks at how the change got there: the contract changes first, and the code follows.
Clara's own table has no enterprise contract: its promise is in its code, the data team's.
So it can change without waiting on governance.
Not every table is a product.
Of the data team's thirty-three tables, ten are read by other teams, and each is in exactly one of six products.
The same script checks that too.
A new table other teams read, in no product, stops its pull request until a product takes it in.
Clara's table keeps its promise in its code: change the model, and its contract changes with it.
But some changes break the readers.
Rename a column in Clara's table, and the impact check fails: it's breaking, so it needs a new version.
So the old version stays, with a date to go, and the new one goes beside it.
Credentials already has two: the first retires on the 31st of March 2027, and its contract says it's deprecated, on its way out.
Better still, add: a new column breaks nobody.
Each product also says who reads it, from the record of who uses what: Planning's census dashboard reads Clara's table.
And it names what it's built from: two of Mei's products, the learner records and the awards.
So when one of them changes, Mei knows who to tell, before anything ships.
Both files are written in open standards: one for data products, one for data contracts.
They're kept by Bitol, at the Linux Foundation: free for anyone to use, and versioned.
Tools that know them can read the files, and a check holds every file to the standard's rules.
The project keeps the versions its catalogue reads today, and moves when the catalogue does.
On the platform, the university's catalogue is Ontos, from Databricks Labs.
It imports each contract from its file, and lays the products out by domain, each with its team.
Governance doesn't review each product before it's published: its owner publishes it, and rules check them all.
Each night, a policy checks every product: an active one with no owner is tagged, and governance is told.
And it can link each column to the business term it holds.
But a Labs project comes as it is, with no formal support.
So the files stay at home, in the project, and the catalogue holds a copy.
On census day next March, a faculty will open Clara's product in the catalogue, read its promise, and plan from it by seven.
If the catalogue has changed by then, the promise hasn't:
it's a file, in an open format, kept with the code, and any tool that knows the standard can read it.
A contract in an open format outlives the tool.

films.x: Finding and asking for data. At the university, people asked around for data and passed copies by email, with nobody's yes and no end date. Now every product sits in one catalogue: you read its promise, ask its owner with a reason and an end date, get access that ends by itself, and partners read shared tables without copies.
c: Today, in the Faculty of Health, Anil Kurian plans the faculty's places.
Its health informatics certificate ends with a hospital placement, arranged months ahead.
So Anil works out how many to offer: one for each learner a unit from finishing.
In September, nobody owned the table with that number, and he didn't know whom to ask.
So he asked around, and a colleague sent him a copy.
It counted one learner near the certificate.
Planning's census report, the university's official count, said two, and nobody could say which was right.
So the faculty offered one place, and a learner a unit from finishing would have waited a semester.
And the copy stayed in his inbox: a code for every learner, which can lead back to their name, sent with nobody's yes, and no end date.
Something had to change.
Now the university's data products sit in one catalogue, like a shop window, each with its promise and its owner.
You find what you need, read what it promises, and ask its owner, saying why, and until when.
This morning, Anil found Planning's product in a minute, and asked.
Clara, its owner, said yes by the afternoon, until the end of January.
Her table agrees with the census report: two.
So the faculty offers a second place, and no one waits a semester.
Anil deleted the old copy.
The catalogue is Ontos, the Databricks Labs project the platform team runs.
Its marketplace shows every product that's live, each with its domain and its owner.
The university calls it the marketplace, though nothing is sold.
Anil types near award, an idea on Noor's map.
The catalogue finds the product linked to it: Learners near an award, owned by Clara, in Planning.
Before he asks, Anil reads its promise, from the files kept in the project.
What it's for: planning support for learners near an award.
How it counts them, as at census day, matching the census report.
When it's ready, and where to ask.
And its contract, column by column.
Two columns hold codes that can lead back to a learner.
So reading it takes a purpose, and an end date.
So he asks, on the product's page.
The form wants two things: why, and for how long.
He writes: to plan next semester's places in the certificate's last unit.
And he asks for ninety days.
Had he started on the platform, its request button would have brought him here too.
Every request comes to one place.
The request goes to Clara, the product's owner, not to whoever built the table.
Governance promises an answer within five working days.
She answers by the afternoon.
His reason is what the product is for, so she says yes, for ninety days, until the 31st of January.
She could have given fewer days, or said no, with her reason.
Either way, the request is the record: who asked, why, who said yes, and until when.
Access goes to a group, never to one person.
Clara's yes puts Anil in the product's readers' group, in the university's directory of accounts, until his date.
On the platform, that group was given the table once, when the product went live.
A week before the date, the catalogue reminds him.
On the date, the directory takes him out of the group, and his access ends.
Clara can see every reader, why, and until when.
Anil also adds the faculty's placements plan to the record of who uses what, in the project.
So when someone next changes Clara's table, the impact check names the Faculty of Health beside Planning's census dashboard.
Both hear about it before the change ships.
A reader who's known is a reader who's told.
Outside the university, the same rules hold.
A partner university counts the faculty's certificate towards its degrees, so it asks for Mei's Awards:
each award, its credit points and its faculty, and no one's personal data.
Mei says yes, and Sam shares it through OpenSharing, an open way to share tables with another organisation, on any platform.
The partner reads the table itself, not a copy, with a key that ends on a date, and the same contract.
Partners on Databricks can also find it in a private exchange of the Databricks Marketplace: a shop window only they see.
This morning, Anil asked in a minute, and Clara answered by the afternoon.
The faculty offers a place to each learner a unit from the certificate, so no one waits a semester.
The old copy is gone, and on the 31st of January, his access ends by itself.
And Clara knows who reads her table, why, and until when.
Finding and getting data is part of governance.

films.x: Identity as the boundary. Every night at two, a job loads the registrar's records onto the university's data platform. It signs in with Jun Park's personal token, from a workspace open to the internet, so to the platform, the job is Jun. What should every request prove, and where should its rights come from?
c: China, about 2,300 years ago.
Seven kingdoms are at war, and each keeps armies on its borders, days from the capital.
The king can't be at every border, so his orders travel with messengers.
The most dangerous is an order to raise troops.
If anyone could bring one, a forged letter or a messenger's lie could put an army on the march.
Soldiers could die for an order nobody gave, or be turned against the king himself.
And the commander at his post sees only the man who brings it.
The commander needs a way to know an order truly comes from the king.
The answer is a tally: a small bronze tiger, cut in two along its back.
The king keeps the right half, and the commander takes the left to his post.
An order to raise troops comes with the king's half, and counts only if the two halves fit together.
So the commander needn't trust the messenger, only the match.
One tiger, now in a museum in Xi'an, carries its rule in forty characters of gold.
For fifty soldiers or more, the halves must match, and only then may they march.
Only a beacon fire, an attack at the border, lets him act without it.
The power to send soldiers stays with the king, however far the order travels.
A request to a data platform is an order too: read these records, change that table.
It should count only when it proves who sent it, so every request starts with one question: who is it, really?
Sam Okafor runs the university's data platform.
Every night at two, a job loads the registrar's records onto it.
It signs in with Jun Park's personal token, so to the platform, the job is Jun.
And the platform has one workspace, open to the internet.
For years, security meant a wall round the network, and whoever was inside it was trusted.
But a stolen password works as well inside the wall as out.
So the platform trusts no request for where it comes from.
Each one says who it is, and proves it, and is checked against what that identity may do, and what's usual for it.
It gets the least it needs, and the next request is checked again.
This is zero trust: not trusting no one, but trusting nothing without proof.
On the platform, there are three kinds of who.
A person: Mei Tanaka in the registrar's office, or Jun, who builds the data project.
A workload: a job or a service that runs with no one at the keyboard, like the nightly load.
And an agent: an AI assistant doing a task someone gave it.
Each gets a name of its own, an identity, and a person who answers for it.
A job never borrows a person's name, and neither does an agent.
The films of AI agents in data work show how an agent gets its own.
Then what each one does shows under its own name.
Next: what may each one do?
Sam's team once found 41 people who could read the whole learner table, each given it by name.
Nine had moved to other jobs, and still could.
So rights go to a role, never to a person.
The roles are on the university's map: a data owner, an analytics engineer, a data steward.
Each role is a group, holding what the role's work needs, and no more.
Join the group, and you have its rights; leave it, and they're gone.
And who may use the registrar's data is Mei's to say, as its owner.
People join, move and leave, and their groups have to follow.
The university's directory takes it from HR's records, so nobody has to remember.
A joiner gets an account on the first day, and no access yet.
First, they sign a confidentiality agreement: six lines, in their own voice.
Everyone who works with the data signs it, signs again every year, and stays in a group only while theirs is current.
An agent signs nothing: its owner signs for it.
A mover leaves the old group as they join the new one, so no right travels with them.
A leaver's account is turned off on their last day, and every right goes with it.
But the nightly job runs as Jun: when he moves, it stops, or goes on with whatever he may do next.
Before Sam builds anything, he thinks like an attacker.
Four questions: what are we working on? What can go wrong?
What are we going to do about it? And did we do a good enough job?
What can go wrong starts with the oldest trick: being someone else.
The tallies had that weak spot too.
In 257 BC, Qin had Handan, the capital of Zhao, under siege.
Wei's king sent an army to help, then, afraid of Qin, told it to wait.
Lord Xinling, a prince of Wei, wanted it to march, and had the king's half taken from his rooms.
At the camp, Jin Bi, the general, fitted the halves together, and they matched.
Still he doubted: would the king send one man in a single chariot to take his army?
He was killed, and the army marched: Handan was saved, by an order the king never gave.
A match proves someone holds the half, not who they are, or that the king sent them.
So the platform keeps Jin Bi's doubt: who is it, from where, on which device, asking for what, and is that usual?
And since a proof can be stolen, each identity gets only the least it needs.
For the nightly job, what can go wrong is plain: a copy of Jun's token is Jun.
So what are we going to do about it? The nightly job gets a name of its own: registrar-loader.
Sam owns it, and answers for it.
Its rights come from a role written for it: the loader role.
It may read the registrar's nightly files and write the registrar's tables, and nothing in any other area.
Mei, who owns that data, agrees, before the job ever signs in under its new name.
This is where most security work starts.
NIST's Cybersecurity Framework puts it first under Protect: every user, service and device known, checked, and given the least it needs.
In the Warring States, a bronze tiger let a commander trust an order without trusting the man who brought it.
On the platform, every request can say who it is, and get the least it needs.
Did we do a good enough job? Not yet: tonight, the job still signs in with Jun's token.

films.x: Signing in without secrets. Every night at two, a job loads the registrar's records, and it signs in with Jun's personal token, made in 2024 with no end date. Whoever holds that token is Jun to the platform, and Sam finds it in three places. Which ways of signing in leave no secret for anyone to keep?
c: London, 2 May 1990.
In the City, the money markets still run on paper.
Treasury bills and certificates of deposit are promises to pay a set sum on a set day: the government's, and the banks'.
When a bank sells one to another, a messenger walks it across the City, and comes back with the payment.
Much of that paper is made out to the bearer: whoever holds it can cash it.
That morning, in a quiet street near the Bank of England, a man with a knife takes one messenger's case.
Inside are 301 bills and certificates, worth 292 million pounds.
To whoever holds them now, they're as good as cash.
If they're cashed before word of the theft gets round, the money is gone.
And every messenger in the City carries that risk, every day.
The paper itself has to stop being worth stealing.
The Bank of England has been building an answer since 1988.
On 1 October 1990, it opens the Central Moneymarkets Office.
The paper goes into a vault at the Bank, and stays there.
Who owns each one is kept in the Bank's records.
A sale changes the record, once both sides have approved it.
Forty-four banks and firms are in it from the first day.
The Bank says why: to avoid the risk and the cost of moving paper around the City, as the theft in May had shown.
Paper kept at the Bank stays off the streets, and no messenger carries it.
A password, a token or a key is bearer paper too: to whatever it opens, whoever holds it is you.
At the university, a nightly job still carries one.
Like the Bank's records, the platform can know who the job is, so that nobody has to carry a secret at all.
Every night at two, a job loads the registrar's records onto the university's data platform.
Sam Okafor, who runs the platform, has given it an identity of its own: registrar-loader.
But it still signs in the old way, with Jun Park's personal token.
Jun made it on 14 March 2024, to get the job running, and it has no end date.
To the platform, whoever holds that token is Jun.
They can read what Jun can read, from anywhere, at any hour, for as long as nobody notices.
And it isn't in one place.
Sam finds it in the job's settings, in an old notebook, and in a file on Jun's laptop.
Every copy works as well as the first, and nobody can say how many there are.
When Jun moves to another team, the job will stop, or go on with whatever Jun may do there.
Nobody did anything wrong: it was the quickest way to start, and it has worked for more than two and a half years.
But every night, the job carries bearer paper through the streets.
To sign in, the job has to prove it's the job.
Sam lays out the ways it can, from worst to best, with one question: who holds a secret, and for how long?
At the bottom, a person's token, or a shared account's password.
The job runs as someone else, with everything they may do.
One up, a token of the job's own.
Only its own rights now, but still bearer paper, often with no end date.
Then a secret in a vault, which the job reads as it starts, and a machine changes every month.
Nobody types it, but while it's valid, a copy still works.
Then a certificate: a key the job keeps, and never sends.
It proves who it is by signing, so the key itself never crosses the wire.
But the key is still kept somewhere, and must be renewed before it ends.
Near the top, a note from where the job runs.
That place signs a short note, this job, from here, now, and the platform, which trusts the signer, lets it in for that run.
At the top, an identity the platform gives the job.
The job runs on the platform's own machines, so the platform knows which job it is, and vouches for it.
On these two rungs there are still passes, but the platform makes a new one for each run, nobody sees it, and it ends within the hour.
That's the goal: nobody makes, keeps, copies or changes a secret.
Sam moves the nightly job up.
On the platform, it now runs as registrar-loader, and the platform vouches for it.
Its rights are the loader role's, decided when it got its name, before it ever signed in.
Its code reaches the platform from the build service, which signs a note for each run, so no secret is stored there either.
Then Jun ends his token.
The copies in the settings, the notebook and the laptop are worthless paper now.
Sam asks what a thief would find tonight.
Before: Jun's token, everything Jun can read, from anywhere, with no end date.
Now: a pass with one job's rights, that nobody stored, and that ends within the hour.
And when Jun moves team, nothing breaks: the job was never his.
Where a system can't climb yet, such as one that only takes a password, the password goes in a vault.
A machine changes it, and the exception is written down, with its owner.
Every new job starts at the top.
People sign in too, and their ladder is much the same.
At the bottom, a shared account: nobody can tell who did what, and nobody can leave without changing it for everyone.
A password alone can be guessed, used again on other sites, or typed into a fake page.
A code by text message is better, but a phone number can be moved to a thief's phone, and the code typed into a fake page too.
An app on your own phone is harder to steal, but a convincing fake page can still pass on your code, or get your yes.
At the top, a passkey, or a security key you plug in.
It's a key that stays on your device.
You unlock it with your face, your fingerprint or a PIN, and those never leave it either.
It answers only the real site, so a fake page gets nothing.
And the platform keeps only the matching half, which opens nothing on its own.
Nothing to remember, and nothing to type.
At the university, everyone signs in once, with a passkey: Sam, Jun, and Mei Tanaka, who owns the registrar's data.
Agents climb the job's ladder too: each signs in as itself, never on a person's token.
In 1990, the City's paper stopped travelling, because the Bank kept the record of who owned what.
The nightly job stopped carrying a secret, because the platform knows who it is.
There's nothing to leak, nothing to change on a schedule, and nothing that breaks when someone moves on.
The best secret is the one nobody holds.

films.x: Boundaries, paths and keys. The nightly job no longer runs on Jun's token, but the platform still has one door on the open internet, one room for everything, a way straight to the files, and backups any admin could delete. If someone got in, how far could they go, and what would keep that small?
c: Ragusa, on the Adriatic coast, in the 1370s.
Today it's Dubrovnik, in Croatia.
Then, it's a small republic of merchants, behind high stone walls.
It lives by trade, and its ships sail the whole Mediterranean.
Sailors, merchants and goods come in every day, through only a few gates.
But ships can bring more than goods.
In 1348, they brought the plague: a sickness that spread fast, and killed within days.
It killed thousands in the city, and kept coming back.
At the gate, nobody could tell a sick traveller from a well one.
Shut the port, and the city loses its living.
Leave it open, and the sickness walks in, to every family behind the walls.
The city needs a way to stay open without letting the sickness in.
On 27 July 1377, the Great Council, the nobles who made the city's laws, passed a new one.
Anyone coming from a place with plague must first spend a month apart: on the islet of Mrkan, or in the town of Cavtat, down the coast.
Only then may they enter the city.
No one from the city may go to them: whoever does, stays the month too.
Later, health officers watch every ship and every gate.
The port stays open, and the city keeps its living.
When the sickness comes now, it's held on an island, not let loose in the streets.
Ragusa is the first city known to have made it a law.
Other ports followed, and the wait grew to forty days: the word quarantine comes from the Italian for forty.
The university's data has the same problem: people and jobs must reach it every day, and whoever breaks in shouldn't reach it all.
It needs what Ragusa had: a few doors, each with a rule, and a place apart for what isn't trusted yet.
At the university, the nightly job no longer carries Jun's token.
But Sam Okafor, who runs the data platform, asks what an attacker would: if someone did get in, how far could they go?
Today, the platform's door is on the open internet: anyone, anywhere, can reach it.
Inside, one workspace holds people's experiments and the nightly job's real records.
From there, every area's data is in reach: the registrar's records, learning, planning, HR and finance.
A way runs straight to the files in storage, past the catalog that checks who may read what.
Data can be sent anywhere.
The backups sit beside the data, where any admin can delete them.
And the cloud provider keeps the data's key, which the university can't take back.
Nobody chose this: the platform started small, and grew.
First, Sam writes down who secures what.
The cloud provider secures its buildings, its machines, and the network between them.
The platform's makers secure its software, and how it checks every request.
The university secures the rest: who gets in, what each may do, its settings, its keys and its copies.
Whatever the contract says, the data is the university's to protect, and the walls are the university's to draw.
They follow the areas on the university's map, each with the owner Who decides wrote down.
A wall doesn't make anyone inside it trusted: every request is still checked, as Who is it, really? showed.
But walls keep the ways in few and the rooms small, so a mistake, or an intruder, stays where it started.
Then, the doors.
The platform's door comes off the open internet: people and jobs reach it only by a private path, from the university's own network.
The platform reaches the storage by a private path too.
And the way out is watched: data may leave only for places on a short list.
Storage keeps files, and knows nothing of who may see which column: no masks, no rules.
So the catalog becomes the files' only door: it checks every request, and applies every rule on the way.
The back door, straight to the files, stays shut.
Only an admin account, switched on to read the storage, opens it, as Power you switch on shows.
Like Ragusa's walls: a few gates, and at each one, a rule.
Next, one workspace becomes three: development, test and production.
In development, people try new things; in test, a change is tried as it will run.
Production holds the real records, and runs the nightly load.
Each reaches only its own data.
Development and test get made-up or masked data, never a copy of production's.
So a mistake in development stays there, and an intruder there finds no real records.
A change moves one way, along one reviewed path, which From a branch to production builds.
Like the islet off Ragusa: what isn't trusted yet waits apart, and comes in only through the gate, after the wait.
Now, the locks themselves.
The data is kept encrypted, on disk and on the move: unreadable without its key.
So what matters is who holds the key.
Until now, the cloud provider did.
Now it's the university's own, kept by its security team in a vault of its own.
The platform may use it, but never take it out, and those who run the platform can't delete it.
The security team can take it back: then nobody can read the data, not even the cloud provider.
Lose that key, and the data is lost with it: so every use is recorded, and a deleted key is kept ninety days, which nobody can cut short.
In Ragusa, for centuries, the gates were shut each evening, and their keys taken to the rector, the head of the republic, until morning.
Everyone knew who held them.
Last, the copies.
An attacker who gets in often deletes the backups first, then locks the data, and asks for money to unlock it.
So every night, a copy of production's data goes to a place apart, with admins of its own.
Each copy is locked for thirty days: nobody can change or delete it before then, not even an admin.
And once a month, Sam's team restores one, to prove it works: a copy nobody has restored is a hope, not a backup.
A lock that strong cuts both ways: a copy can't be deleted early, even when it should be, and Deleted means deleted comes back to that.
Sam walks the attacker's path once more.
From the open internet, there's no door to find.
With a stolen way in, there's only what that one person may reach, in one workspace, through the catalog's checks.
No back door to the files, nowhere to send them, no key to take, and no copy to delete.
In 1377, Ragusa stayed open to the world, through a few gates, each with its rule.
The university's data stays open to the people and jobs that need it.
Few doors, each with a lock you can see.

films.x: Admin accounts. Sam's and Jun's everyday accounts, the ones that open their email, can read every file in the storage, change the admin settings and restore any table, every hour of every day. Whoever takes one of those accounts takes all of it. How do they keep that power off until a task needs it?
c: The United States, in the 1870s.
A bank keeps its money in a vault, a strong room behind an iron door.
The door's lock opens to a row of numbers, turned on a dial.
Only a few of the bank's men know them.
But robbers have found a way round the iron.
At night, they go to the home of a man who knows the numbers.
They hold his family, take him to the bank, and make him open the vault.
No lock can stop that: the right numbers, from the right man, open the door.
So every banker who knows them, and his family, is in danger.
The vault has to stay shut, even to the man who knows the numbers.
In Rochester, New York, a lock maker, James Sargent, builds clocks into a vault's lock.
Each evening, the bank sets the hour it may open.
Until that hour, no one can open it, even with the right numbers.
In May 1874, the first is fitted to a bank's vault, in Morrison, Illinois.
One Friday night in May 1875, in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, eight robbers hold the Deland family at home,
and take Fred Deland, who knows the numbers, to his bank.
He turns the dial, but the bolts that hold the door won't move:
the new time lock, put on three days before, holds them.
The robbers take a few bonds from a desk, and flee; the vault stays shut.
Now, taking a banker from his home at night opens nothing.
Sargent's lock sells in the thousands, and banks soon expect one.
The university's platform has the same problem.
Sam's and Jun's everyday accounts hold its greatest power, every hour of every day.
Whoever takes one of those accounts takes all of it.
It needs what the bank had: great power, shut until it's needed.
Most work on the platform goes through the catalog.
It checks every request, and shows each person what their role allows, masked where it must be.
Some work can't go through it.
The storage: the files under every table.
There, no mask and no filter applies: every name and every date of birth, in the clear.
Walls, doors and keys shut that back door.
The admin settings: what the whole platform allows, such as who may sign in, and how.
And restoring a table: putting it back as it was, over everyone's work since.
That's great power over data.
In data governance, the platform team are its keepers: they keep the platform running, and don't decide what the data means.
Until now, that power sat in Sam's and Jun's everyday accounts:
the same accounts that open their email, and every link in it.
Some had gone to others too, each for one task, and never come back.
So each data specialist gets a second account, of their own: an admin account.
Jun's is his alone.
It's never shared, and never used for email or the web.
It signs in only with a passkey, and only for a task.
His everyday account keeps his daily work: writing code, testing it, watching the jobs run.
And the admin account?
It has no power either, until it's switched on.
That makes two locks.
A stolen everyday sign-in doesn't reach the admin account.
And whoever steals the admin account finds its power off, and can't switch it on alone.
A second account isn't always practical: it can cost a second licence.
In that case, the power stays in the everyday account, but switched off, until a task needs it.
That's one lock, not two: still far safer than power that's always on.
To switch it on, Jun says what for.
Which power: only the one the task needs, to read the storage, change the settings, or restore a table.
A reason, in words someone else can check.
And a time: what the task needs, four hours at most.
Another specialist approves: Sam approves Jun's, Jun approves Sam's, and no one approves their own.
The moment it's on, the platform team gets an alert.
Everything the admin account does is recorded, under its own name.
When the time is up, the power switches off by itself; or Jun switches it off as soon as he's done.
A time lock opened at its hour, for whoever had the numbers.
This power opens only for a task, and only when someone else says yes.
Like the first bankers with a time lock, Sam and Jun find it slow at first: it keeps them out too.
It costs a minute, and a yes.
One morning, the two o'clock load has stopped.
It met a row it couldn't read, in last night's file from the registrar's office.
To find it, Jun must open that file, in the storage.
His everyday account can't: the back door is shut.
So he switches on his admin account's power to read the storage, for one hour.
His reason: open last night's file.
Sam reads it, and approves.
The alert reaches the platform team, and matches the morning's task.
Jun opens the file, and goes straight to the row, number 9,317.
A date of birth that doesn't exist: the thirty-first of February.
He tells the registrar's office which record to fix, by its student number, and switches off:
fourteen minutes of his hour.
The record keeps it all: who switched on, why, who said yes, what was read, and when it ended.
That night, the load runs clean.
And Jun asks what every switch-on is worth asking: could the next one be avoided?
Now the load sets a row it can't read aside, in a table the catalog guards, for the registrar's office to see.
Who gets an admin account?
Only the data specialists who keep the platform running: here, Sam and Jun.
Never business users, like Mei Tanaka in the registrar's office.
Never analysts, like Clara Jensen in Planning.
Their work goes through the catalog, which shows each of them what their role allows.
If they need more, they ask the data's owner for access, not for power.
And never an agent.
An agent can propose a task that needs power; a person decides, and does it with their own admin account.
AI agents in data work shows how agents get their rights.
One exception: two emergency accounts, locked away for the day nothing else works.
Who did what shows how they're watched.
In Great Barrington, in 1875, the right numbers, from the right man, weren't enough:
the vault opened only at its hour.
On the platform, the right account isn't enough either.
Its power is off, until it's switched on for a task, and someone else says yes.
Whoever takes Jun's everyday account gets his everyday work, and nothing more.
Great power is a separate account, switched on for a task.

films.x: Sign-in, groups and admin power. The university's workspace was given 214 people by hand, and nineteen who had moved on still got in. Eleven admins worked from the accounts they read email with, everyone signed in with a password and a text code, and Jun's token had no end date. How does every key end with the stay?
c: Moss, on a fjord in Norway, in the 1970s.
A factory here makes locks, and ice skates.
Tor Sørnes leads its research.
Hotels have a problem with their keys.
Guests forget to hand them in when they leave, or lose them on the way.
And a key still opens its door, whoever holds it, long after the stay has ended.
Anyone who found one, or kept one, could let themselves into the next guest's room, while that guest slept.
A key has to stop working when the stay ends.
Sørnes makes a lock that a punched plastic card opens.
Inside each lock is a pattern card, put in from inside the room.
For each new guest, the hotel puts in a new pattern, and gives the guest a card punched to match.
The last guest's card opens nothing.
In 1978, the first go into a big new hotel in Atlanta, which had been troubled by burglaries.
Now a lost card opens nothing once the next guest arrives, and changing the lock takes only a new card.
By 2011, the company says, its card locks are on six and a half million hotel rooms, in 166 countries.
A key that ends with the stay.
At the university, a place on the data platform could outlive a person's job, and an admin's power outlived the task.
And a personal token had no end date at all.
This film builds the answer from three earlier films, in Microsoft Entra ID and Azure Databricks.
Sam Okafor keeps the university's data platform.
Its tables already give their rights to groups from the university's directory, as Governed in Unity Catalog showed.
But who could come in at all was a list kept by hand.
The workspace had been given people, one by one: 214 of them.
Nineteen had moved to jobs that didn't need it, and still got in.
Four groups had been made inside the workspace, and the directory knew nothing of them.
Eleven people were its admins, on the same accounts they read their email with.
A fake page that caught one of their sign-ins would catch an admin.
Everyone signed in with a password and a code by text message.
And Jun's personal token, made in 2024 with no end date, ran the nightly job.
Like the hotel keys before the card, each still opened its door, long after the stay.
The university's directory is Microsoft Entra ID, and HR's records feed it.
When someone joins, their account is made, already in their team's groups.
When they move, their groups change; when they leave, their account is turned off.
Now Azure Databricks reads the directory for itself: its people, and its groups, groups inside groups too.
Sam switches on its automatic identity management, once, for the whole account.
Each workspace is then given groups, never people.
Production is given the data team, the registrar's office, and the readers each area's owner allows.
The four groups made by hand are gone: their people are in the directory's groups now.
Groups are changed in one place only: the directory.
Each time someone signs in, Databricks reads their groups again.
So when someone moves to another team, the platform follows at their next sign-in.
And when someone leaves, Databricks turns their user off at its next sync, and nothing can sign in as them.
Everyone signs in the same way, once, through the directory.
A rule there, a Conditional Access policy, lets no one reach Azure Databricks without a passkey: a sign-in no fake page can catch.
It lives on their own phone, in the Authenticator app, or on a security key.
Mei Tanaka, who owns the registrar's data, signs in with her phone: her face unlocks the passkey, and she's in.
There's no password to type, and none a fake page could use.
The same rule asks for each person's confidentiality agreement, as Who is it, really? showed.
No one reaches the platform before accepting it, and everyone accepts it again each year.
The directory keeps who accepted it, and when.
Great power goes to groups too, and no one is in them.
Every admin role, in the Databricks account, in each workspace and in Azure, belongs to a group whose name starts with admin.
Only two people can switch one on, Sam and Jun, each from a second account kept for it, signed in only with a security key.
The switch is Microsoft Entra privileged identity management: those accounts are eligible for the groups, never in them.
On 19 October, Sam needs to know who still has personal tokens: the account's token report, which only an account admin can read.
So he switches on the account's settings group for one hour, and types why.
Jun approves.
Within seconds his admin account is in the group.
And an alert reaches the platform team: who, which group, why, who approved, until when.
Databricks reads his groups as he signs in, and for this hour, he can read the report.
Then he signs out, and when the hour is up, the directory takes his admin account out of the group.
Like a new pattern in the hotel's lock, each switch-on opens one stay, and ends with it.
The report shows seven personal tokens: six people's, for their command lines, and Jun's.
But the command line can sign in through the browser now, with the same passkey.
The Databricks CLI keeps its own short passes, each an hour long, in the computer's secure store: nothing to copy, nothing to paste.
So the six sign in that way, and end their own tokens.
Jun's runs the nightly job, until Workloads without secrets gives the job its own way in, and ends it on 3 November.
That afternoon, Sam switches on the workspaces' settings for thirty minutes, Jun approves, and Sam turns personal tokens off.
Now no one can make a personal token, or use one.
In the hotels of the 1970s, a new pattern for each guest meant a lost card opened nothing.
At the university, a place on the platform now ends with the job, and admin power ends with the task.
And no personal token is left to outlive anyone.
People sign in once, with no password to steal; power is borrowed, not kept.

films.x: Workload identity. Every night at two, a job loads the registrar's records, and it still runs on Jun Park's personal token, with copies in its settings, in a notebook in GitHub and on his laptop. How can it prove who it is each time it runs, with nothing anyone could copy?
c: The Netherlands, in the middle of the 1990s.
Cars stand in every street, and every year about one in two hundred of them is stolen.
The trouble is in the ignition: the key only turns a switch.
A wire behind the steering wheel can close it too, and so can a copy of the key.
For the owner, that means a morning with no car: no way to work, a claim to make, and a car that may never come back.
A car has to know its own key, not just a turned switch.
In 1995, the European Union decides: from October 1998, every new car sold must have an electronic immobiliser.
It's a small chip in the key.
When the key turns, the car asks the chip, by radio, for its code.
Without the right answer, the engine won't run.
A wire starts nothing now, and nor does a key cut to the same shape.
In the Netherlands, new cars with one go from about one in five in 1994 to all of them by 1998.
And car theft falls by about forty percent, for no more than fifty euros a car.
Far fewer owners wake to find their car gone.
And for data: a job that proves who it is each time it runs, with nothing anyone could copy.
At the university, the nightly job still starts with a copy of a person's key.
This film gives it a way in of its own, in Microsoft Entra ID, Azure Databricks and GitHub.
Every night at two, a job loads the registrar's records onto the university's data platform.
It already has a name of its own: registrar-loader.
But it still runs on Jun Park's personal token, made on 14 March 2024, with no end date.
To the platform, whoever holds a copy is Jun, with everything Jun may do.
And there are copies: in the job's settings, in a notebook in GitHub, and on Jun's laptop.
If Jun moved team, the job would stop. If someone found a copy, they'd be Jun.
Like a car without an immobiliser, it starts for anyone with a copy.
No secret to lose showed the way up: at the top, nobody keeps a secret at all.
In Microsoft Entra ID, the university's directory, registrar-loader is a service principal: an identity for a workload, not a person.
Sam Okafor owns it.
It's the only member of one group, the registrar's owners, which owns the registrar's catalog.
Azure Databricks reads both from the directory, as it reads people.
So its rights come from a group, never from a person, as Who is it, really? decided.
Sam sets the job to run as registrar-loader, and takes Jun's token out of its settings.
Now the platform knows which job it is, and gives each run its way in, with nothing anyone keeps.
On Tuesday 20 October, at two, the load runs under its own name for the first time.
The record says registrar-loader now, not Jun.
And if Jun moves team, nothing breaks.
The job's code is in GitHub, and until now, Jun deployed each change from his laptop, with his token.
Now GitHub Actions deploys it, and keeps no token either.
For every run, GitHub signs a short note: this repository, this environment, now.
Azure Databricks checks GitHub's signature, and one thing more: does the note say exactly what registrar-loader's policy names?
Sam set that policy once: the platform's repository, in its production environment, and nothing else.
When they match, the platform gives the run a pass as registrar-loader, good for an hour.
Run from anywhere else, the same code gets a note that says where, and no pass.
The note is good for minutes, for that one run, and nothing is stored in GitHub to steal.
Where a workflow changes Azure itself, Microsoft Entra ID trusts the same note, the same way.
Like the car asking its key, the platform asks each run where it comes from, and a copy can't answer.
Who may change production, and who approves, is From a branch to production's.
On Azure, a resource can have an identity of its own too: a managed identity.
Azure looks after its credentials, and nobody ever sees them.
Network, storage and keys gives the catalog one: the only identity that may read the registrar's files.
And on the platform, people linked their Git folders to GitHub with their own personal tokens.
Jun's could reach every repository he can, and it had no end date.
Now each link goes through the Databricks GitHub app, installed on the platform's repository alone.
It acts for each person with passes that end after eight hours, and renew themselves.
When a tool works in GitHub, it gets an app with only what it needs, never a person's token.
One door still wants a password: the student system, where the registrar's records come from.
It offers no other way in yet.
So the password lives in one place: a key vault in Azure, for this job alone.
The platform reads it through a secret scope, and only registrar-loader may read it.
If a notebook prints it by mistake, the platform shows only the word redacted.
Once a month, a small function changes it, at the student system and in the vault, signing in as its own managed identity.
And the exception is written down: why, who owns it, and when it's looked at again.
On No secret to lose's ladder, it's a lower rung, kept only until the student system can climb.
But what about the copies already made?
On Tuesday 3 November, Sam turns on GitHub Secret Protection for the repository.
Secret scanning reads the whole history, every branch, back to the first commit.
It finds Jun's token in a notebook pushed in March 2024, and checks whether it still works.
It does.
The job hasn't used it for two weeks, so that morning, Jun ends it.
The copies in the notebook and on his laptop open nothing now, and Sam closes the alert: revoked.
The token stays in the history, but it opens nothing.
From now on, push protection stops a push with a secret in it, before it lands.
Anyone who pushes past it gives a reason, and the platform team gets an alert.
That afternoon, as People and groups showed, personal tokens are switched off on the platform.
In the Netherlands of the 1990s, a car that asked its key meant a wire started nothing, and far fewer cars were stolen.
At the university, the two o'clock job proves who it is each time it runs, with nothing anyone could copy.
One password is left, in one vault, changed by a machine, and a secret pushed into the code is stopped at the door.
A workload proves who it is without a password.

films.x: Doors to the data. Production's files sit in Azure storage, and Unity Catalog is meant to be the only way to them. Sam Okafor finds nine ways around it: two account keys, a link signed with one, and six people with a role on the storage. Every door is open to the internet. He shuts all but one.
c: Rome, in the year 97.
Nine aqueducts bring the city its water from the hills, most of the way in channels under the ground.
In the city, it fills distribution tanks, and pipes carry it on:
to public basins and fountains, to baths, and to houses that hold a grant from the emperor, for so much water.
That year, the emperor Nerva makes Sextus Julius Frontinus the water commissioner,
an office, he writes, that concerns the city's health, and even its safety.
Frontinus measures the water where it enters the channels, and finds about ten thousand measures more than the records give out.
On the way, it's being drawn off.
Water-men, who tend the pipes, divert it for private use, and sell it.
Landowners along the way tap the channels to water their gardens.
Under the pavements, secret pipes are bored here and there, with branches to the shops along them.
So only a little reaches the public basins and fountains, which should run day and night for the people,
and some stop altogether.
Nobody can say who draws what.
The water has to go where it's owed, and someone has to know where it goes.
Frontinus holds the city to its rules.
No one may draw water from the channels.
Whoever holds a grant draws it only at a distribution tank, through a bronze nozzle stamped with the size granted,
and every grant is in the records.
The secret branch pipes come out, and so much lead comes back that he estimates the theft by it.
And the gangs who keep the channels, often sent off to private work,
now write down the day before what each will do, and the records keep what each did.
Frontinus wrote that the supply almost doubled, as though new springs had been found.
More basins and fountains ran for the people, the city was cleaner,
and those who had drawn water in fear now drew it by grant, free from care.
A data platform's files are its water, and its catalog is the tank:
the one place to draw, where each grant is checked and every rule applied.
Every way to the files around it is a hole in the channel.
At the university, the data platform runs on Azure Databricks, in three workspaces now: development, test and production.
Production's files, every table's data, sit in an Azure storage account, a container for each area.
Unity Catalog is meant to be the only way to them.
Sam Okafor, who runs the platform, counts the ways to the files that skip it.
Two account keys, each of which opens every file.
A link signed with one of them, made in 2024 for a supplier's one-off file, and good until the end of 2027.
Six people with a role on the storage, each given for one task, and never taken back.
Nine ways in, and not one asks the catalog.
In the files, no grant, mask or filter applies: whoever reads them sees every row.
And the workspaces and the storage all have a door on the internet, open to any address.
Nobody did anything wrong: each was the quickest way to finish a task.
First, the doors in.
Sam gives each workspace a private endpoint: a door inside the university's own network,
so people and jobs come in by a private path.
The machines that run the jobs reach Databricks by a private path too, and so does the build service.
While every team moves to it, for two weeks, an IP access list lets in only the university's own addresses.
Then Sam switches public access off in all three workspaces:
the platform has no door on the open internet.
Then the ways out.
Serverless compute, which Databricks runs for the university, could reach anywhere on the internet:
a notebook could send a table anywhere.
Production gets a network policy with restricted access: only the catalog's own storage, and a short list.
For a week it runs in dry run: it blocks nothing yet, and Sam sees what it would have blocked.
Then it's on: data may leave only for places on the list.
Now the files themselves.
Sam switches the storage's public access off: it's reached only by its own private endpoints.
He switches off its account keys, and the storage refuses anything signed with them:
the two keys and the supplier's link open nothing now.
The six people's roles go; each now gets what they need through the catalog, under their group's grants.
One identity keeps a role on the files: the catalog's own, its access connector,
an identity Azure gives it, with no secret anyone holds.
In Unity Catalog, a storage credential holds it, and an external location for each area points to its container.
So every read of the files goes through the catalog, which checks the grant, and applies the masks and filters.
Like Rome's tanks, the catalog is the one place to draw.
One more wall.
By default, every workspace reaches every catalog:
a notebook in development, with a grant, could read production's real records.
Sam binds each catalog to its own workspace:
production's five, registrar, learning, planning, HR and finance, to production alone;
test's to test; development's to development.
The storage credential and the external locations are bound the same way.
Now a grant isn't enough: from a workspace it isn't bound to, a catalog isn't there.
The files keep one more door, and it stays shut.
Some work needs the files themselves.
One morning, the nightly load stops on a row it can't read, and Jun Park must open last night's file.
On the storage, one group holds one role: read and list, nothing more.
It's for admin accounts only, and no one is in it.
Jun switches on his admin account's power to read the storage, for one hour, with a reason, and Sam approves.
Jun comes in by the private path, reads that one file, and switches off.
The storage's own log keeps every read, under the account that made it, and the platform team gets an alert.
Had he forgotten, it would have shut by itself when the hour was up.
Like the gangs in Rome, the work is written down before, and recorded as it's done.
Last, the keys.
The files were always encrypted, with a key the cloud provider kept for the university.
Now the key is the university's own, kept by its security team in a vault of its own.
The storage may use the key, never take it out.
The people who run the platform can't delete it or turn it off, and every use is recorded.
The vault makes a new version every year, and the storage picks it up within a day.
A deleted key is kept ninety days, and nobody can cut that short.
The workspace's notebooks, queries and disks use a key from the same vault.
And the security team can take the key back:
then nobody can read the files, the cloud provider included.
In Rome, water was drawn only at the tank, through a stamped nozzle, and the gangs' work was written down.
At the university, the files are reached only through the catalog,
behind private doors, with a short list out and a key of the university's own.
And the one way around it is switched on for a task, and watched.
No path to the data skips the catalog, except the one you switch on and watch.

films.x: A reviewed path to production. The nightly job signs in with no secret now, but whatever reaches main goes straight to production, and anyone on the team can push to it. Sam sets the rules first, Jun's change is sent back and fixed, and production waits for Noor's yes. Who may change production, and how?
c: South Africa, 1993.
After decades of apartheid, the parties negotiating its end have to agree how a new constitution will be written.
In April 1994, all South Africans will vote together for the first time.
The winners will hold most of the seats in the parliament that writes it.
The smaller parties fear what a winning majority could write: rights a later vote could take away, courts that answer to a party.
And the party expected to win won't accept a constitution written by negotiators nobody elected.
The way a constitution is made has to win everyone's trust first.
So they agree the principles first: 34 of them, from rights for everyone to judges no party controls.
They write them into a temporary constitution, in force from 27 April 1994, and nobody may change them.
The new parliament, sitting as the Constitutional Assembly, will write the final text.
It will count only once the new Constitutional Court, which didn't write it, certifies that every part keeps every principle.
On 8 May 1996, the Assembly adopts its text, with 86 percent of its members.
On 6 September, the Court's judges, all agreeing, decline to certify it.
In nine respects, it falls short.
Among them, the rights in it could be changed too easily.
And the officials who check on the government and its money aren't protected enough from it.
In five weeks, the Assembly fixes all nine, and on 11 October it adopts the amended text.
On 4 December, the Court certifies it.
President Mandela signs it on 10 December 1996, and it comes into force on 4 February 1997.
Nearly thirty years on, it's still the country's constitution.
Every side could trust it, because no side could put it into force alone.
Elected people wrote it; judges who hadn't written it checked it against promises fixed before; and it counted only once both were done.
A change to production can work the same way.
At the university, a job loads the registrar's records every night at two.
In Walls, doors and keys, its one workspace became three: development, test and production.
In Workloads without secrets, its deploy got a key with no secret in it: the job's own identity, registrar-loader.
But nothing guards the way in.
Whatever reaches main, the branch in GitHub that production is built from, goes straight to production.
Anyone on the team can push to it, at any hour, and nobody else has to read the change.
One unread change could stop every student's record from loading, or send it where it shouldn't go.
And anyone who stole one of the team's sign-ins could do the same.
Production needs one way in, with a gate.
So before the next change is written, Sam sets the rules, as South Africa fixed its principles first.
A ruleset on main: every change comes as a pull request, and nobody pushes to main, rewrites it or deletes it.
A code owner approves each change, and the last push is approved by someone who didn't push it.
The checks must pass.
And nobody may bypass it, not even an owner of the organisation.
Who owns what was decided in Who decides.
The code owners file names the platform team for the job.
The platform team and the release approvers own the workflows, and the file itself.
GitHub reads that file from main, not from the pull request, so no change picks its own reviewers.
And the ruleset isn't in the code at all: no pull request can loosen it.
Jun has the next change.
One morning in Power you switch on, the load stopped on a row it couldn't read.
Jun switched on his admin account to open last night's file.
Now the job should set such a row aside, and load the rest.
Jun writes it on a branch, and tries it in development, in a copy under his own name, on made-up records.
Then he opens a pull request.
The checks run: the job's tests, and code scanning.
Sam reviews it.
One line writes each set-aside row to the job's log, names and all.
A log keeps whatever it's given, outside the table's masks, for 30 days.
Sam asks for that line to go.
Jun takes it out and pushes again, and Sam approves this last push.
Sent back, fixed, checked again.
Jun merges it.
Merging doesn't put it in production.
The deploy runs on GitHub's machines placed inside the university's network.
So it reaches the workspaces by the private path from Network, storage and keys.
It goes to test first.
It signs in as registrar-loader-test, deploys the bundle, the job and its settings as files, and runs the job once on test's records.
It passes.
Then production waits for a release approver: Noor Rahman.
Whoever started the run can't approve it, and only main may deploy here.
Noor sees what changed, who reviewed it, and the test run, and approves.
Now the workflow asks Databricks to sign it in as registrar-loader.
Databricks lets in only this repository's job in the environment production: the one that waited for Noor.
The bundle deploys from main, in production mode, and the job runs as registrar-loader.
There, people may look at it, never change it.
Two people said yes, and a machine did the rest.
One way in is easy to miss: code nobody at the university wrote.
The deploy runs two actions, small programs from other people: one fetches the code, one installs Databricks' tool.
They run right beside the production key.
An action named by a tag or a branch runs whatever the name points to that day, and the name can be moved.
Code scanning reads the workflows too, and flags the one that isn't GitHub's own.
Sam pins both, GitHub's own too, to the commit he checked, its version written beside it.
A commit can't change.
Dependabot proposes each new version, and any fix for a known flaw in the job's libraries, as a pull request, reviewed like any other.
And the workflow's own token can only read: only the two deploying jobs may ask to sign in.
At two on Wednesday morning, the job runs the reviewed code.
A week later, a row is unreadable again.
The job sets it aside, and every other record is in by a quarter past two.
The registrar's office fixes the row by half past nine, and nobody switched on any power to see it.
As in South Africa, the rules came first, someone who hadn't written the change checked it, and it counted only once both were done.
In an emergency, the same path, faster, or an admin account switched on, approved and recorded.
An agent's change takes the same path, as Every change through review shows.
Production changes only through a reviewed path.

films.x: Seeing who did what. Sam has locked the platform's sign-ins, doors, admin power and changes. Now the security review asks him to show they held over the last 90 days, but the answers sit in four records, and one keeps only a month. Where should the record live, and what should ring a bell at once?
c: Australia, 1953.
David Warren is a chemist at the Aeronautical Research Laboratories, and he knows aircraft fuel tanks.
He's asked to help find out why two Comets, the world's first jet airliners, have crashed.
In 1954, two more break up over the sea, and no one on board survives.
No one is left to say what the crew saw or heard.
So the experts can only guess.
And while they guess, the planes fly again, full of passengers, and the next one may fail the same way.
The next crash can't leave everyone guessing.
In April 1954, Warren writes a short note.
A small box could record the voices in the cockpit, over and over, so the last hours are always kept.
It would sit in the tail, where a crash is least likely to reach it.
Pilots fear a spy in the cockpit, and his boss tells him to get on with fuel tanks.
By 1958, his team's box keeps four hours of voices and the instruments' readings.
After one more crash that no one can explain, Australia is the first country to require recorders on its airliners, from 1963.
Now, when a plane is lost, investigators can hear its last minutes, find the cause, and fix it on every other plane.
A data platform needs a recorder too.
Without one, when something goes wrong, the team can only guess what was touched, and the way in stays open.
With one, they can see who did what, close the way in, and show what didn't happen.
At the university, Sam Okafor has locked the platform's sign-ins, doors, power and changes.
Now the security review asks him to show they held, with three questions about the last 90 days.
Who signed in, and from where?
Who switched on admin power, and what did they do with it?
What changed production, and who approved it?
The answers are in four records, and each keeps its own time.
The platform's audit table keeps a year.
GitHub's audit log keeps six months, but who pushed or copied code, only a week.
The directory keeps its sign-ins, and each switch-on of power, for a month.
And the storage keeps a log only where someone has asked it to.
So for two of the questions, part of the answer is already gone.
So every record is now sent, as it's written, to one store apart, kept by the security team.
A locked copy is kept for a year: until then, no one can change or delete it, not even an admin.
Switching a record off is recorded too, and if one goes quiet, someone is told at once.
Everyone is in it under their own name, agents too, as AI agents in data work shows.
The record is about people, so it's kept like personal data: read by few, for a reason, and every search is recorded.
Warren's pilots feared a spy in the cockpit.
A record of who did what is read to find out what happened, not to watch the people in it.
A few moments ring a bell at once, and someone always answers it.
The first is power.
One morning, last night's load has gone wrong, and Jun has to put the learner table back as it was.
He switches on his admin account's power to restore a table, for an hour, with a reason, and Sam approves.
The platform team gets the alert at once, and checks it matches a known task.
The record keeps the rest: the switch-on, the restore, made by Jun's admin account, and the switch-off, twenty minutes later.
The other bells: a risky sign-in, an emergency account used, a record gone quiet.
Few bells, so none is ignored.
One evening, at twenty to ten, the bell rings for a risky sign-in.
Jun's session is in use from another country, at an hour he never works.
Jun is at home, and his laptop has been shut since six.
A browser add-on he'd used for a year had changed hands, and its last update copied his sign-ins.
Whoever holds a copied session is Jun, until the session ends.
So the first step is to end it.
The security team's on-call switches his account off, and ends all his sessions: in the directory, in GitHub, and on the platform.
Twelve minutes after the bell, GitHub and the platform refuse it.
Then they read, in the one store, what the copy did.
In GitHub, it downloaded the platform's code as a file.
No push, no change to a rule, no approval.
On the platform, nothing: it has no door on the open internet.
The code holds no secret and no learner's data.
That night, the add-on is taken off every browser; the next morning, Jun is back at work on a clean laptop.
Nothing was changed, so nothing has to be put back: the record is how they know.
The next day, a review without blame asks what made it possible, not who.
Now browsers take only add-ons the university approves, and GitHub takes requests only from the university's network.
A leaked secret gets the same steps: end it first, then read what it did.
Every admin power here is switched on for a task, and approved by someone else.
But what if the sign-in service fails, or a wrong rule locks every admin out?
For that, the directory has two emergency accounts.
They belong to no one, and their power is always on.
So they sign in only with security keys, kept in two safes, in two buildings.
No rule that could lock everyone out applies to them, and any sign-in rings every bell.
Every 90 days, two people open a safe, sign in, check it works, and lock the key away.
The bell rings then too, and everyone knows it's the test.
The last lock is on the data itself.
A table's own history can undo most mistakes, for seven days.
But what if a mistake is found too late, or someone deletes a table and its history?
Every night after the load, a copy of production's data goes to a place apart, with admins of its own.
For 30 days, no one can change or delete it, not even an admin.
Once a month, the team restores one beside the real table, and checks they match.
As Walls, doors and keys says, a copy nobody has restored is only a hope.
Three months on, the review asks its three questions again.
Sam answers them in an afternoon, from one place.
Of every sign-in, one was wrong: a copied session, stopped in twelve minutes.
Admin power was switched on 23 times, each with a reason, an approval, and a record of what was done.
Production changed 11 times, each change reviewed, and each release approved.
And every night at two, the job signed in as itself.
Warren's box doesn't keep a plane in the air.
It means no one has to guess what happened.
The record does the same for the platform.
If you can't see it, you can't say it's protected.

films.x: Agreements before access. A study in the Faculty of Health asks for the records of 2,614 learners. A plain yes would hand over names, results and who gets extra time. So two papers come first: each person's confidentiality agreement, and one for this use, signed by the owner. Access is made from it, and ends with it.
c: England, 1939.
At Bletchley Park, Britain's codebreakers set to work on the enemy's coded radio messages.
By 1945, almost nine thousand people work there, three in four of them women.
Each of them learns the war's best-kept secret: the enemy's messages can be read.
Ships crossing the Atlantic are steered away from submarines, because the submarines' orders have been read.
If the enemy found out, it would change its codes, and the ships would sail into them.
One careless word, from any one of thousands, could give it away.
Something has to come before the secret.
