So the people who run Bletchley put a promise first.
Before anyone is told what the work is, they sign the Official Secrets Act: a promise to keep what they learn to themselves.
Then each is told only what their own part needs.
What they read goes only to a few named commanders, by an officer who waits while it's read, then takes it back and destroys it.
And nothing done with it may give the secret away.
It holds.
The enemy never learns its messages are read, and the ships keep their warning.
And all those thousands keep it for almost thirty years, until 1974.
A university holds secrets too, and a study may ask for them.
A no fails the learners it could help; a yes with nothing written could expose them.
So, as at Bletchley, two papers come first, and access comes last.
The study gets what it needs, and not one learner is named.
Monday, 5 October 2026.
Anil Kurian, in the Faculty of Health, wants to study how its learners progress, and where they need support.
So he asks the registrar's office for the records of the faculty's 2,614 learners.
Mei Tanaka owns them, for the office.
Who may see it gave every access a purpose and an end date, and The marketplace put the asking in one place.
But a purpose and a date don't say what the study must never have, where it may work, or what may leave it.
Left unsaid, names could sit beside results, and who gets extra time, and why, could travel wherever the work goes.
So two papers come first: one each person signs, and one for each use.
The first is each person's own: a confidentiality agreement.
I keep what I see to myself.
I use it only for the work it's given for.
I keep no copy where it isn't allowed.
I answer for the data I'm given.
I report anything that goes wrong, at once.
And it holds after I leave.
Everyone who works with the university's data signs it before any access: staff, contractors, researchers, the data team.
It's renewed every year, and Yusuf Demir, in data governance, keeps them.
Access comes through groups, never to a person by name, and a person stays in a group only while their promise is signed and current.
An agent signs nothing: its owner signs, and answers for it, as AI agents in data work shows.
Anil renewed his in February.
As at Bletchley, the promise comes before the secret, and outlasts the work.
The second is for this use: a data sharing agreement, written line by line.
Its purpose: how learners in the Faculty of Health progress, and where they need support.
From the registrar's learner records: 2,614 learners.
It may have each learner's course and results, their year of birth, and a code in place of who they are.
Never anything that names a learner, and nothing about their health.
Only the study's group, each member with a signed promise.
Only on the platform, in the study's own space, with nothing downloaded.
What may leave: totals, with any count under ten hidden.
It ends on 30 June 2027; then the study's copy is deleted, and the totals stay.
Statistics offices call these questions the Five Safes: people, project, setting, data and outputs.
Mei signs as the owner, who answers for the data, as Who decides set out; Anil signs for the study.
Yusuf keeps it in the register of agreements: what was agreed, by whom, and until when.
As at Bletchley, the data reaches only the people named, stays where it's kept, and leaves only in a form that names no one.
Only now comes access, and it's made from the agreement.
Its terms are written again where the platform reads them: the agreement's contract.
The columns: course, results, year of birth, learner code. The group: the study's. The end: 30 June 2027.
The platform team makes the grant from the contract, never by hand, so it can't give more than the agreement says.
Every grant names its agreement. No agreement, no grant.
In November, the faculty asks the study for the names of learners who need support, to call them.
That's a new purpose, and the study's agreement doesn't stretch to it.
The support team asks Mei for an agreement of its own.
Wednesday, 30 June 2027.
The grant ends by itself, on the date the agreement set.
The study's copy is deleted, and Yusuf closes the agreement in the register.
The totals stay, with every count under ten hidden.
Anil's promise doesn't end: it holds after the work, and after he leaves.
At Bletchley, the promise came first, and the secret held for almost thirty years.
At the university, the study learned what it needed from 2,614 learners' records, and not one learner was named.
Access is the end of an agreement, not the start.

films.x: Data classification. Anil's agreement lets his study have each learner's course, results, year of birth and a code, and nothing that names a learner or touches their health. But the platform reads columns, and Mei's register asks only whether a column identifies someone. What does each column tell about a person?
c: Chile, 2012.
Every packet of food lists its numbers on the back: energy, sugars, fats, sodium, in grams per hundred.
In small print, in a busy shop, a parent can't tell which foods are loaded with sugar.
Is thirty-three grams a lot?
And about one child in four starting school is obese, at risk of diabetes and heart disease later.
Parents need a label they can read at a glance.
That year, Congress passes a law proposed by five senators, from left, centre and right.
The Ministry of Health sets limits for sugars, sodium, saturated fats and calories.
From June 2016, a food over a limit carries a black octagon on the front of its pack, the shape of a stop sign: high in sugars.
Its maker, who knows the recipe, puts it there.
And no food with one may be sold in a school, or advertised to children.
In the first year and a half, households bought about a quarter less of the drinks that carried one than expected.
Makers took sugar and sodium out of many foods, to lose the octagon.
The numbers are still on the back. The front says which to be careful with.
A university's tables list every value too. What they need is the front.
Tuesday, 13 October. Anil Kurian is studying how the Faculty of Health's learners progress.
Yesterday, Mei Tanaka, in the registrar's office, signed his agreement.
In plain words, his study may have each learner's course and results, their year of birth, and a code in place of who they are.
Never anything that names a learner, or anything about their health.
But the platform reads columns, not plain words.
Mei's register asks each column one question: does it identify a person?
By itself, that's direct: name, email, student number. Only with a key kept elsewhere, pseudonymous. Not at all, none.
Course and results: none. Date of birth and exam support name no one either: none.
So the study could have both. But the agreement allows only the year of birth, and nothing about health.
Mei takes it to Yusuf, in data governance, who keeps the list of classes.
He keeps those three, and adds two.
Indirect: it names no one alone, but with other columns it can single out one person.
In a course of twelve learners, a birthday points to one.
And special: it tells something that could harm a person if it got out, like health, disability or faith.
Five classes, strictest first. Each column gets the strictest that applies.
Now the agreement's plain words have classes.
Nothing that names a learner: direct. Nothing about their health: special.
A code in place of who they are: pseudonymous. Their year of birth: indirect. Course and results: none.
Columns get classes. Each table gets a level: how much harm if the whole table got out. Its owner sets it.
Public, like published totals. Internal, for the university's own people, like the timetable.
Confidential, for those with a reason, like the learner table. Restricted, for a named few.
Two floors come from the columns. A table with anything that points to a person is never public.
A table with anything special is restricted.
These five classes and four levels are the university's own. Another organisation may choose others.
What matters is one list, and that everyone uses its words the same way.
Back to exam support. Its values name no illness: extra time, a separate room, a reader.
But Mei knows why a learner has them: for a disability.
So the column tells something about their health: special.
A column's name doesn't say what it holds. Its owner does.
And one special column would make the whole learner table restricted, too strict for the help desk and Planning, who read it every day.
So exam support moves to a table of its own, the support table, restricted, for the few who arrange exams.
The learner table stays confidential.
Who names each column? Its owner, once, at the source, where the data is born.
Like the octagon: the Ministry sets the limits, and the maker, who knows the recipe, puts it on.
Data governance keeps the list of classes, and the owner picks one for each column.
A scan can suggest one: this looks like an email. Only Mei knows that exam support is about health.
And a new column with no class doesn't go through. It comes back with a question: what does it tell about a person?
From the source, each column carries its class into everything made from it. Nobody names it again.
Course and results reach Anil's study as they are: none.
Two change on the way. The student number becomes a learner code, made with a key the registrar's office keeps.
The date of birth becomes the year.
A step that changes what a column holds gets its new class from the owner.
Mei names the code pseudonymous, and the year indirect: with a course, it can still point to one.
Exam support never reaches the study.
And Anil's totals by course, any count under ten hidden, get a new class, none, in a public table.
The class goes wherever the column goes, as the octagon goes with the pack.
The octagon took no sugar out by itself.
It named what each pack held, where everyone could see it, and families, schools and makers acted on it.
Mei's classes protect nothing by themselves either.
But now every column says what it tells about a person, and every table how careful to be, before anyone opens it.
Which way to hide each class is the next question.
You can't protect what you haven't named.

films.x: Ways to hide a value. Anil Kurian studies how learners in the Faculty of Health progress. The records, as kept, would show him names, birthdays, and who has a disability; hide it all, and he can't follow anyone. So Mei Tanaka picks a way to hide each column, and the study never sees who they are.
c: Victoria, 1856: the colony is about to elect its first parliament.
Until then, a man said his vote out loud, so anyone could learn it: his employer, his landlord, a candidate.
A vote against them could cost a worker his job, or a tenant his home.
So a man might not dare vote as he wished. His vote had to become his own secret.
That March, the colony passed a secret ballot, worked out by Henry Chapman, one of its lawmakers.
An official marked the voter off the roll, and handed him a printed paper with every candidate's name.
Alone, he crossed out the names he didn't want, folded it, and put it in the box.
At the end, the papers were counted, and the totals announced.
Now a worker or a tenant could vote as he wished: nobody could see his vote, so nobody could punish him for it.
Britain took it up in 1872; by 1892, so had 38 American states.
The roll says who voted, and nothing about how. The box says how, and nothing about who.
Today, at the university, Anil Kurian studies how learners in the Faculty of Health progress.
Their records, as kept, would show him far more: names, birthdays, and which of his own faculty's learners have a disability.
Hide it all, and the study can't follow anyone from one year to the next.
So Mei Tanaka, who owns the records, picks a way to hide each column that keeps what the study needs.
The study follows 2,614 learners, year by year, and never sees who they are.
And for data: show the least that still answers the question.
The study's agreement says what it may have: each learner's course and results, their year of birth, and a code in place of who they are.
And never anything that names a learner, or anything about their health.
Each column already has the class its owner set: direct, indirect, special, or none.
So which way should hide each one? There are nine, and three questions tell them apart.
What does the reader see?
Can it be undone, and by whom?
And what can the reader still work out?
Exam support is about health, and the agreement says never.
So leave it out: the study isn't given the support table.
Names and emails name a learner: the registrar's office needs them, the study never does, so mask them whole.
The columns stay, but for the study every value reads as stars, and stars can't be turned back.
The help desk needs a little more: to check it has the right learner on the phone.
So mask them in part: the last two digits, and the first letter.
Enough to recognise a record, too little to look anyone up.
The date of birth helps the study see how age shapes progress, so generalise it: 14 May 1987 becomes 1987.
The day and month are gone, and can't come back.
But hidden isn't anonymous: in a small course, one year of birth may fit only one learner.
So it stays indirect, and stays behind the agreement.
Last, filter rows: the study gets only the Faculty of Health's 2,614 learners.
That hides no value; it leaves out other people's rows.
The study must follow each learner from year to year, so the student number becomes a code.
The learner code you've seen before scrambles the number, and scrambled isn't anonymous: with the registrar's list, anyone can match it.
So the study's code mixes in a secret key: a keyed hash.
Without the key, the list matches nothing.
With it, the registrar's office can find whose code it is: undone, but only with the key, kept sealed, apart from the study.
So the code stays pseudonymous, behind the agreement.
In Britain's ballot of 1872, each paper had a number, matched to its voter only in a sealed packet, opened only to trace a fraud.
A token is a stand-in, paired with the real value in a vault: only the vault's owner can turn it back, to reach the person again.
This study reaches no one, so it takes the keyed hash.
And encryption keeps the whole value where it's stored or moved: unreadable without the key, all there for anyone allowed to read it.
When the study is done, it may publish totals, with any count under 10 hidden.
Here, learners who left after their first year, by course.
Midwifery's 4 is a small count: in a class that size, people would know who left.
So it reads: fewer than 10.
But the faculty's total is there too: 80, less 38, 21 and 17, gives the 4 back.
So one more count is hidden, and the 4 can't be worked out.
Totals can't be undone, and they still answer the question: about 9 in 10 first-year learners went on to second year.
As in 1856: everyone sees the totals, and nobody sees a vote.
So for each line of the agreement, Mei picks the way that keeps what the study needs.
A code in place of who they are: a keyed hash.
Their year of birth: generalise.
Nothing that names a learner: mask it whole.
Nothing about their health: leave it out.
Only its 2,614 learners: filter rows. And only totals leave, with small counts hidden.
Each new column gets its class from her: the code pseudonymous, the year still indirect.
Later films build these ways on the platform, so each class is hidden the same way, every time.
And an agent helping the study sees what the study sees, never more.
The roll, the box and the totals: each shows the least that still answers its question.
Samuel's row now answers the study's question, and says nothing about who he is.
Show the least that still answers the question.

films.x: Access by design. The registrar's tables got their readers one grant at a time: 163 grants made by hand on 58 tables, a new table waiting six days for its first reader, and nine tables owned by the person who made them. Now they move into a catalog of their own, and Mei Tanaka asks for a plan before a single grant.
c: The Galápagos, in the late 1960s.
Volcanic islands, about a thousand kilometres west of Ecuador, whose animals don't fear people.
Now boats bring visitors, more each year.
Scientists and guides fear what all those feet will do.
Visitors could walk anywhere, a step from nesting birds, iguanas and sea lions.
Nests could be trampled and the lava worn down, and coral is already being carried off.
Birds could leave for good, and many of the islands' animals live nowhere else.
The islands need rules for every visit, before visitors come in thousands.
So the national park, on the Darwin Research Station's advice, plans the visits once, for the whole park.
Most of the park gets no visitors at all.
A few sites near the coast are open, each along its own marked trail.
Every group walks with a trained guide.
And the rules are the same for everyone: keep to the trail; touch nothing, feed nothing, take nothing.
A new boat, a new guide, a new visitor: each fits the plan the day they arrive.
In 1982, twenty-five thousand people visit, and the sites they walk are near pristine.
Flamingos have nested again beside a visited lagoon, for the first time in fourteen years.
In 2025, 290,404 people came, still on the trails, still with a guide.
A university's data has visitors too.
Opened one table at a time, some wait for what they need, and some reach what they shouldn't.
So, as on the islands, its grants are designed once, by area and role.
Every person and every new table fits the plan from its first day.
At the university, the data platform keeps each area's records in Unity Catalog.
In Governed in Unity Catalog, every table sat in one catalog, and its readers were groups.
But each grant was made by hand, on one table, when someone asked.
Fifty-eight tables, a hundred and sixty-three grants, each made on its own.
A new table waited six days, on average, for its first reader.
And whoever made a table owned it: nine belonged to a person, and two of those people had left.
To say who could read what, someone had to read every grant.
Now each area has a catalog of its own, and the registrar's tables are moving into theirs.
Mei Tanaka owns them, for the registrar's office, and asks for a plan before a single grant.
In Unity Catalog, a table sits in a schema, and a schema in a catalog.
Think of the catalog as a room, and each schema as a shelf in it.
To read a table, a group needs three rights: into the room, onto the shelf, and into the table.
USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT.
Like a landing, a trail and a site: all three, or none.
SELECT on a table, without the first two, opens nothing.
One more right lets everyone look without reading: BROWSE.
With it, anyone can find a table, see what it holds and who owns it, and ask for it.
So the plan starts from who reads what, as the islands' plan started from where people may walk.
Every area's catalog gets the same shelves, one for each set of readers.
Staging and intermediate hold the build's own steps, and nobody reads them.
Core holds the area's records; reference, the lists they use; published, totals for everyone.
And the registrar's catalog has one more: support, for the exam support only a few may see.
Then each shelf gets its readers, always a group, never a person.
The registrar's office reads core and reference; the few who arrange exam support read support.
The help desk and Planning read core, and the policies decide what each of them sees.
The data team builds in development, on made-up records, so here it holds nothing of its own.
A grant goes on a catalog or a shelf, never on one table.
A table that needs other readers belongs on another shelf.
A grant on a shelf reaches every table on it: those there today, and every one made later.
When a new version of the credential table arrives, the readers of core read it from its first minute.
Nobody asks, and nobody grants.
When the exam support table arrives, it goes on its own shelf, and only those who arrange exam support can read it.
The help desk, Planning and the study read core, so none of them ever sees it.
Like a new boat at the islands, it keeps the plan from the day it arrives.
Every catalog, shelf and table has an owner, and the owner can do anything with it, even let anyone read it.
Whoever makes it is its first owner.
So the registrar's catalog, and everything in it, is handed to a group: registrar owners.
No person is in it, only registrar-loader, the identity that builds the tables and deploys the plan.
When someone leaves, no table is left without its owner, and no one person can open one up.
Mei still decides who may see the records: she owns them, for the registrar's office.
Two kinds of owner: Mei says who may see them, and the group is who may change them.
In Network, storage and keys, each catalog was bound to its own workspace, so a grant isn't enough from anywhere else.
Anil Kurian's study works in a workspace of its own, studies, where nothing can be downloaded or copied out.
The registrar's catalog is bound there too, but read only.
From there, the study reads the learner table, as far as its grants allow, and can never write to it, whatever a grant says.
What it makes goes in its own space, health progress, made for its agreement and deleted when the agreement ends.
Look, don't touch, as on the islands' trails.
The plan is written once, as two files beside the job's code in GitHub.
Each shelf and its readers take a few lines.
The data team reviews each change to those files, and Mei is told what it touches.
A study's grant is made from its agreement's contract, and names it: 2026-14, until 30 June 2027.
The study's policies go in first, and its grant after them, so it never reads the table unmasked.
Then the path of From a branch to production: test first, then production, once a release approver says yes.
And nobody can grant by hand: only the owners' group can, and its one member deploys only from main.
Anything else takes an admin account, switched on, approved and recorded.
On the islands, the plan came first, and every visitor since has walked inside it.
At the university, the plan comes first too.
The registrar's office reads its records; the study, only what its agreement allows; everyone else can find what exists, and ask.
Every new table, and every new person, fits the plan from its first day.
Design the grants once, by area and role.

films.x: Tag propagation. Mei has named a class for every column of the learner table. The platform has to read them, and every table made from it has to carry them, or a copy shows what its source hides. How do the classes become tags in Databricks and dbt, and follow the data on their own?
c: The early 1990s.
Tropical forests are being cut much faster than ten years before.
In Europe and North America, people campaign against tropical wood, and refuse to buy it.
But no buyer can tell where a plank was grown, or how.
Wood from a forest cut bare looks just like wood from one cared for.
So the cutting goes on: species disappear, and the communities who live from those forests are hit hard.
In 1992, at the Earth Summit in Rio, governments fail to agree to stop it.
Buyers need a way to tell the two woods apart.
In 1993, 130 people from 26 countries meet in Toronto: forest and human-rights groups, timber traders, foresters.
They found the Forest Stewardship Council.
An independent auditor certifies a forest against its rules.
Then every company that buys, saws, makes or sells the wood is certified, and passes the claim on.
A product carries the label only if every company along the chain is certified.
Where certified wood is mixed with other wood, a rule set in advance says how it's labelled.
By the end of 2025, over 171 million hectares of forest are certified, and over 68,000 certificates cover the chain.
And a buyer can tell, from one label, where the wood began.
A university's data travels too, from the learner table into every table made from it.
If its classes don't go with it, a name hidden at the source shows on a copy.
If they do, every copy says what it holds, and is protected for it.
Tuesday, the thirteenth of October.
In Know what you hold, Mei named a class for every column of the learner table, and a level for the table.
Now the platform has to read them.
Sam Okafor, who runs the platform, makes each one a governed tag in Databricks.
Personal data takes four values: special, direct, pseudonymous and indirect.
None is simply no tag.
Level takes four more, from public to restricted, on tables only.
And faculty, with no values, marks the column that holds each row's faculty.
Governed means only those values, set only by those allowed to assign them.
Here, that's the registrar's own loader, from the project's files, so nobody sets a class by hand.
Before Mei confirms them, the platform takes a look of its own.
Data classification scans the registrar's catalog, and proposes what it recognises.
In the learner table, it finds a name, an email and a date of birth.
Mei confirms them: direct, direct and indirect.
It proposes nothing for the student number, a format of the university's own.
And nothing for exam support, in the support table: extra time names no illness.
Only Mei knows it's given for a disability, so she names it special herself.
The scan proposes.
The owner decides, and adds what no scan can see.
Her word goes into the project, in dbt.
Jun Park writes each class beside its column, in the learner table's file.
The data team reviews the code, and Mei is told what it touches.
After each build, dbt sets every class as a tag on its column.
Then the faculty tag, and last, the table's level: confidential.
A column marked none gets no tag, and an old one is taken off.
Change the file, and the next build changes the tags.
This is where the tags start: on the learner table, the first that people read.
Then Sam turns on tag propagation, for the classes and the faculty tag.
Now each tag follows its column through lineage: the platform's record of what each query read, and what it made.
That afternoon, the registrar's loader makes the study's copy: Health's 2,614 learners.
Within minutes, its tags arrive: the learner code pseudonymous, the year of birth indirect, as their sources are.
Course and results bring none.
Nobody tags the copy.
Until its tags are there, a policy can't see them.
So Mei checks the classes are there, and gives the copy its level: confidential.
The study is given its space only the next day, with the copy in it.
And every table Anil makes from it will carry the same classes.
Propagation never lowers a class.
Suppose the copy had made the code itself, from the student number.
Lineage would bring the student number's class: direct.
Mei's file says pseudonymous.
One column, two values for one tag: a conflict.
The platform can't choose, so it applies the value Sam set in advance: special, the strictest.
Like the rule for mixed wood, it's set before anything is mixed.
Nothing shows that shouldn't, but the column now says the wrong thing, and passes it on.
So a value that says less is made once, at the source, by its owner.
The learner table holds the code beside the student number, and every table after takes the code.
And a level doesn't travel at all.
Join a public table to a confidential one, and every table made from them would be a conflict.
Each table's level stays its owner's call.
A tag travels only inside the platform.
A file downloaded, or a copy in another tool, carries no tag at all.
That's why the studies' workspace has downloads switched off.
Inside, tags travel only where lineage can follow: into tables and views the platform's serverless compute makes.
Anil's totals by course are counted from courses and results, which carry no class.
So nothing travels into them.
Mei checks them, and gives them their level: public.
A label on a chair can be trusted because every company passed the claim on, by rules agreed before.
Mei named each class once, at the source.
The platform carries it into every table made from it, and where two meet, a rule set in advance decides.
Next, one policy reads those tags, wherever they land.
Tag once at the source.
The tag follows the data.

films.x: Policies by tag. The registrar's catalog holds 38 tables with personal data: 140 columns to hide, and new tables keep coming. Masked by hand, each new table shows every name until someone remembers it. How can every table be protected from its first minute, with no mask written for it?
c: North America, in the 1970s.
When a truck or a train carrying dangerous chemicals crashed, the first to arrive were firefighters and police.
Their guide gave each chemical a page of its own: a few dozen in all.
To find the page, a crew had to know exactly what was inside,
often from papers in the driver's cab, close to the wreck.
And thousands of chemicals had no page at all.
Guess wrong, and a crew might spray water on a chemical that gives off a poison gas when wet,
with families still in the houses nearby.
Crews needed one book that covered every chemical, before they had to guess.
In 1980, the US Department of Transportation changed the book.
Chemicals that behave alike in a fire or a spill share one guide, written once.
Each chemical's four-digit number leads to its guide,
so a new chemical needs only one line: its number, and its guide.
And a load no one can name gets Guide 111, which assumes every danger.
Today's book, from Canada, the United States and Mexico, has 62 guides for nearly 2,000 numbers.
A crew reads the number through binoculars, from upwind,
and knows what to do, and how far back to keep people, before it goes near.
Data has the same problem: a mask written table by table protects nothing until someone writes it.
One policy for each class, found by its tag, protects every table that holds it, the day it appears.
So a learner's name stays hidden, wherever it lands.
On Tuesday 13 October, Mei Tanaka gave every column of the registrar's data its class, in Know what you hold.
Show the least chose how to hide each one: a name masked whole, a date of birth cut to its year.
Her catalog holds 38 tables with personal data: 140 columns to hide.
By hand, that's 140 masks, set one table at a time, by someone who remembers.
But Grants by design gives each shelf its readers, so a new table is read from its first minute.
A mask set by hand comes later, if at all,
and until then, everyone on the shelf reads every name.
So Sam Okafor, who runs the platform, writes one policy for each class, on the whole catalog.
A policy has four parts.
Where it sits: on the registrar's catalog, it covers every shelf and every table, now and later.
Whom it covers: everyone, except the groups it lets through.
What it finds: each column whose class is direct, by its tag, in any table.
And what it does: mask it whole.
Governed in Unity Catalog wrote one like it.
Sam writes one for each class that's hidden: special, direct, pseudonymous and indirect.
One more decides rows, not values: the study sees only the Faculty of Health's learners.
It sits on the shelf the study reads, core, and finds each table's faculty column by its tag.
A filter needs its column, so every table with learners in it carries their faculty:
one without would show the study every learner.
Each way is a small function, written once, on the catalog's shelf for policies.
Mask it whole: words become three stars, and anything else is left empty.
Mask it in part, for the help desk: the last two digits, and the email's first letter.
Generalise: a date of birth becomes the first of January of its year.
A mask gives back the column's own type: a date stays a date, or the query fails.
Filter rows: a yes or a no for each row: is this learner in the Faculty of Health?
The other ways aren't masks.
The learner code is made at the source, with a key the registrar's office keeps.
And exam support is left out: the study has no grant to its shelf.
A policy covers everyone but the groups it lets through:
owning a table isn't enough, nor is an admin account.
Who's on each list is Mei's decision: her office sees the learner table whole.
The builder, registrar-loader, is let through too, or every table it built would hold stars.
The help desk is let through the policy that masks names whole,
and given the one that masks them in part.
Each reader gets one mask for each column:
two different masks for one person stop the query with an error.
The study is let through the policy for the learner code:
its agreement allows a code in place of who they are.
An agent is never on a list: it reads with its own role's rights, as AI agents in data work shows.
Only compute that applies policies can read these tables: serverless, or Databricks Runtime 16.4 and above.
Older compute is refused.
On Wednesday 21 October, Jun's new model is built for the first time: each learner's progress, year by year.
Its columns bring their classes from its sources, as Tags that travel showed,
and Mei's level comes with it.
It's the 39th table, and nobody writes a mask.
From its first minute, the help desk sees part of each student number, and Planning sees stars.
And the study sees only Health's learners, each by their code.
On the road, a load no one can name gets Guide 111, which assumes every danger.
Here, a table that comes without its level shows no rows to anyone but its builder,
until its owner gives it one.
But a policy hides only what has a tag.
A column no one has classed shows as it is, until the morning check of Proof it held finds it.
The policies are code, kept beside the grants, in the registrar's bundle.
A change is a pull request the data team reviews, and Mei is told what it touches.
It runs in test, then in production after a release approver, as registrar-loader, never a person.
Each file replaces its policy whole, so what the repository says is what runs.
On 14 October, the policies went in that morning, and the study's grant that afternoon:
rules first, then the door.
On the road, one guide is written once, and a new chemical needs only a line.
Here, one policy is written once, and a new table needs only its tags.
So a learner's name stays hidden wherever it lands, and the study sees only its own faculty's learners.
The policy follows the tag, so new tables are protected the day they appear.
Next: Copies that keep the rules.

films.x: Copies of people's data. This autumn, four copies of the learners' records are asked for: one to build with, one for the teaching hospital, an answer that needs both sides' rows, and one to take home. The rules live in the catalog, not in the records, so each copy keeps the protection, or isn't made.
c: France, 1948.
Lascaux, a cave in the south-west, opens to visitors: its walls were painted with horses, bulls and deer about 21,000 years ago.
By the late 1950s, more than a thousand people a day come to see them.
Every one of them breathes out warmth, water and carbon dioxide into the cave's air.
In 1960, with the heat and the lights, green algae spread over the walls, and white crystals form on them.
The visits that let people see the paintings are destroying them, and once they're gone, they're gone for everyone.
The paintings have to be saved, even from the people who love them.
In 1963, the minister for culture, André Malraux, closes the cave to the public.
On the same hill, its two best-known galleries are rebuilt in concrete, down to every bump in the rock.
And painters copy each painting onto them, with natural pigments, the way the first artists worked.
Lascaux II opens in 1983: true to the cave, and none of it is the cave.
About ten million people have seen the paintings there since.
And the cave rests: only a few scientists go in, for about 200 hours a year.
A university's records of its learners are like that cave.
Every copy made of them, to build with, to share or to take home, is one more place they can come to harm.
So, as at Lascaux, each copy keeps the protection, or isn't made, and the work still gets done.
At the university, the learners' records are protected where they're kept.
Know what you hold gave each column a class, and Tags that travel made each class a tag on the platform.
One policy for many tables hides each class, by its tag, wherever the records are read.
So a copy made inside, read through those rules, keeps them: the study's own copy holds only what Anil may see.
But the rules live in the catalog, where the records are read, not in the records.
A copy that leaves the catalog takes the records, and none of the rules.
That's why An agreement first said where the study may work, and what may leave it.
This autumn, four copies are asked for.
Monday, 19 October.
Jun Park, who builds the registrar's models, is changing how the faculty's published totals are counted.
He'd like to try it on the real records: a copy of the learner table, in development.
Azure Databricks refuses to clone a table its policies cover, for anyone they cover.
Cloned by someone they leave out, it would hold every real name, and no column's class, so no policy would match it.
A masked copy is possible, but it's still about real people, and a column nobody has classed yet goes through as it is.
So, wherever they can, development and test get made-up learners, and none of them is anyone.
For size, a script writes 2,614 of them, with production's columns and their classes.
That's synthetic data, and it's easy to write now.
This kind is written without reading a record: only the columns and their classes go in, so it can give no one away.
The other kind is learned from the real records, and the closer it fits them, the more likely it is to give a real person away.
So the university treats that kind as a copy of the real records.
How closely made-up data should follow the real records, gaps and odd cases included, is the harder question, and still an open one.
dbt's unit tests check the counting on rows written for each test: if nine learners leave Midwifery, the count shows as fewer than 10.
dbt's clone and sample bring production's rows in, so they're never used on tables about people.
Like Lascaux II, they stand in for the learners, and not one is real.
Jun's change runs on 2,614 of them, and no record leaves production.
Monday, 2 November.
The teaching hospital where the faculty's learners train asks how many leave after first year, by course, to plan its places.
A new purpose needs a new agreement, as An agreement first says: 2026-21, signed by Mei and the hospital's head of education.
The hospital is on Databricks too, so OpenSharing can share a table with it, as in The marketplace.
But the university's policies don't travel with a share.
Whoever shares a table must be left out of its policies, and the hospital reads it on its own platform, where they never run.
Share the learner table, and the hospital would see every name.
So the share holds one table that already shows no more than may leave: Show the least's totals, small counts hidden.
A share has no end date, so a job made from the agreement removes the hospital's access on 30 June 2027.
Then the hospital asks a harder question: do learners who spend more weeks on its wards do better that year?
The answer needs both sides' rows, the hospital's weeks and the university's results, and neither may hand its rows to the other.
So they meet in a clean room, on Azure Databricks, where neither can see the other's rows, only their columns' names.
The university adds one view, from a shelf no one reads: each Health learner's student number, course and result.
The hospital writes the code that matches the two, and counts, by weeks on the wards, how many learners passed.
Nothing runs until the university approves it: Mei said yes in the agreement, and Jun reviews the code and approves it on 1 December.
The clean room hides nothing by itself: what comes out is what the approved code writes, so the code hides any count under 10.
On 3 December, the hospital runs it, and gets one table of totals, kept for 30 days.
Twelve weeks or more, 91 in 100 passed; four to seven weeks, 84.
Like the scientists at Lascaux: what goes in is approved, and the walls never leave.
Tuesday, 10 November.
Elena Lindgren, Anil's new research assistant, would like to download the study's table, to clean it in a spreadsheet.
But a file on a laptop keeps no rules at all, and the agreement says nothing is downloaded.
So in the studies' workspace, from Grants by design, every way out is switched off.
Downloading results, exporting notebooks, copying a table, downloading a file: each one is off.
The switches are kept as code: turning one back on takes a reviewed change, and the audit log shows it.
And what runs there can reach only the catalog's storage and a short list, as Network, storage and keys set up for production.
No switch stops a photo of a screen; her confidentiality agreement covers that.
So Elena cleans the data where it is, in a notebook in the study's space.
As at Lascaux, nobody takes a piece of the wall home.
Lascaux's paintings have been seen by millions, and the cave still rests.
This autumn, four copies were asked for.
Jun got made-up learners, the hospital its totals and one answer from a clean room, and Elena's download was never made.
Every copy keeps the protection, or isn't made.

films.x: Proving the protection held. Three months after Mei signed the agreement for Anil's study, its first review asks of each promise: can we prove it held? One member moved on and kept her place, and a new mobile column went 31 hours with no class. The records show who could read, and who did.
c: From the 1970s, health workers carried polio vaccine to clinics and villages all over the world.
Polio can leave a child paralysed for life.
The vaccine is two drops by mouth, from a small bottle: a vial.
It had to stay cold the whole way, from the factory to the child.
But heat spoils it, and leaves no sign.
A vial left too long in the sun looks just like a good one.
So health workers threw away vials they couldn't vouch for.
Or a child was given vaccine that no longer worked, and the family thought the child was safe.
Health workers needed to see, on the vial itself, whether the cold had held.
In 1979, the World Health Organization asked for a way to show it.
PATH, a health non-profit, worked for years with a company on one: the vaccine vial monitor.
It's a square inside a circle, printed on each vial's label.
Heat darkens the square, a little at a time, and it never turns light again.
Lighter than the circle, the vaccine can be used.
As dark as the circle, or darker, the vial is thrown away.
In 1996, the first monitors went onto polio vaccine, for a few cents a vial.
Now, at the moment of use, a health worker could see which vials were still good.
UNICEF and the World Health Organization estimate it saves over $14 million a year, in good vaccine no longer thrown away.
And a child got vaccine that still protects them.
Protecting data has the same problem.
A protection that failed looks just like one that held, and a name seen by the wrong person leaves no mark.
This film adds the monitor to Anil's study: proof, whenever someone asks, that each protection held.
So the university can show any learner who asks who could see their data, and who did.
Three months ago, in An agreement first, Mei Tanaka signed an agreement for Anil Kurian's study of 2,614 learners.
Since then, every protection was built, from classes to copies.
Today, Tuesday 12 January 2027, is the study's first review.
Yusuf Demir, who keeps the agreements, asks one question of each line: can we prove it held?
Who: only the study's group may read it.
Never: nothing that names a learner, nothing about their health.
Where: only in the study's own space.
Ends: 30 June 2027.
Four promises, four proofs, each read from a record, not from anyone's memory.
First: who could read the study's tables?
On the platform, the grants answer it: each made from the contract, to the study's group.
No grant names a person, and none was made by hand.
So the question is who's in the group, and that lives in the directory, Microsoft Entra ID.
Every three months, its access review asks Mei, who signed the agreement, whether each member still needs it.
A review left unanswered for a week takes the access away.
Two people are in the group: Anil, and Elena Lindgren, a research assistant who joined in November.
In December, Elena moved to another project.
She still works at the university, so her account works, and nothing took her out.
Mei keeps Anil, and removes Elena; when the review closes, the directory takes her out by itself.
Now Anil tells Yusuf the day anyone leaves the study: the review is the net, not the plan.
An agent working for the study would be on the list too, answered for by its owner, as AI agents in data work shows.
Second: does every personal column have a class, and every class a policy?
Like a monitor on every vial, every column needs its class.
Each morning at seven, a query on the platform looks for two gaps.
A column the platform's classification finds personal, with no class from its owner.
And a class that has to be hidden, with no policy to hide it.
If it finds one, an alert goes to Yusuf and Sam.
On Friday 8 January, it found one.
The exam support team had started keeping each learner's mobile number, to text them their exam arrangements.
The night load brought it into the support table as a new column.
The data project stops a new column with no class, but it doesn't build this table.
A day later, the platform's classification found it a phone number.
At half past nine, Mei classed it direct: it names a person by itself.
The policy for direct masks it from then on, with no new rule written.
But for thirty-one hours, the column had no class.
Where did it go, and who read it?
Lineage is the platform's record of what each query read and what it made, column by column.
The mobile column went nowhere: no query made anything from it.
And the study's protected columns: the student number reaches it only as the learner code, the date of birth only as the year.
Names, emails and exam support never reach it.
Then, who read? The audit log keeps who read each table, and when.
In those thirty-one hours, only the night load read the support table.
And over the three months, the study's tables were read by Anil, and by Elena until 11 December. No one else.
After an earthquake in Yogyakarta, in Indonesia, the power was out for days.
The monitors showed most of the vaccine was still good: 50,000 doses that would have been thrown away.
Proof finds the harm, and it shows where there was none.
The gap was real; the records show no one saw a number they shouldn't.
Last: the agreement ends on 30 June 2027, and access must end with it.
Each member's place in the group was given until that date.
On the day, the directory takes them out, and the grants made from the contract end.
But an ending is a promise too, until it's checked.
On 1 July, Yusuf checks: the group is empty, no grant names the agreement, and the study's space is gone.
Only the totals stay.
Every proof is kept with the agreement, in Yusuf's register.
The monitor on the vial doesn't keep the vaccine cold.
It shows whether the cold held, at the moment of use.
The study's records don't protect its data either.
They show, whenever someone asks, that the protection held:
who could read, who did, where each column went, and that it all ended on its date.
Protection you can't prove is protection you hope for.
Next, Kept for a reason: why data is kept, for how long, and how a person is forgotten.

films.x: Purpose and consent. Linh's tutoring contract ends on 20 November. HR holds her contracts, hours, bank details, a yes to its news, even a photo. Ingrid, who owns HR's data, asks of each piece what it's for, and which reason allows it. What has none goes, the form asks less, and a new use gets a check first.
c: Oregon, 1986.
A new blood test can tell people whether they have HIV, the virus that causes AIDS.
The test needs two things: a sample, and a way to give each person their result.
Oregon's public clinics write down each person's name with the result, and keep both private.
But many of those most at risk stay away.
A private list is still a list of names.
They fear a positive result, one that finds the virus, could get out with their name.
It could cost them their job, their home or their health insurance.
So people with the virus don't know it, and can't protect the people they love.
People have to be able to get tested without fearing for their name.
In December 1986, Oregon's health officials let people choose: their name, or a number.
A number does all the test needs: it matches the sample to the person, so each can come back for their result.
In the four months after, the number of gay and bisexual men tested rose from 42 a month to 108.
And in three and a half months, 85 people with the virus were found, against 36 before.
They could look after their health, and protect the people they loved.
It's the same with data: every piece you hold about a person could get out.
So ask what each piece is for, and keep only what that reason needs.
Then people trust you with what you need.
Today, at the university, Ingrid Holm owns HR's data.
This November, she's getting HR ready for next year's tutors.
Linh Nguyen has tutored here since 2023. Her last contract ends on the twentieth.
HR holds a record of her, as of every tutor, in many pieces.
The university already writes down what its data is for, as For this purpose only showed.
But a purpose can be written for anything.
So Ingrid asks of each piece HR holds: what is it really for, and does that need it?
A reason you can say is one you could tell Linh in a sentence.
If HR can't say why it holds a piece, it shouldn't hold it.
A purpose says what a piece is for. The law also asks what allows it.
Europe's GDPR, the best-known privacy law, names six reasons, and many other laws name similar ones.
She agreed.
A contract with her.
A law that requires it.
A public task, a duty to the public, such as teaching.
To protect someone's life.
Or a fair interest, weighed against hers.
Agreeing is just one of the six.
Linh's contracts, hours and bank details rest on a contract: HR employs her, and pays her.
Her tax number and pay records rest on a law, and so does her date of birth, which payroll needs for her pension.
The tutors' mailing list rests on her yes: in 2023, she ticked “Send me news of tutoring work”.
Her student records are Mei's, kept for a public task: teaching her, and awarding her degrees.
Two pieces have no reason at all: her marital status, and a photo.
Nothing HR does uses them.
They came from the form Linh filled in to apply, in 2023.
Applying is a step toward a contract, so the form should ask only what choosing a tutor needs.
But it asked for her marital status and a photo, which no step used.
And it asked everyone who applied for their date of birth and bank details.
Only payroll needs those, and only once a tutor is hired.
Every piece held is one more that could get out, or be used for something it shouldn't.
So Ingrid's new form drops the two.
Payroll's two come after the offer.
And HR deletes the marital status and photos it already holds.
Like the clinics in Oregon, it asks for what the reason needs, when it needs it, and nothing more.
The 2023 form also said: “I agree to the university using my personal data for HR purposes.”
It sounds careful, but it's the wrong reason.
If Linh had said no, HR would still have to keep her pay records: a law requires it.
And it couldn't pay her without her bank details.
A yes is a reason only where a no is a real choice.
In Oregon, the choice was real: a name or a number, and the same test either way.
So the new form says plainly what HR holds, why, and for how long.
And it asks one real question: “Send me news of tutoring work?”
Say no, and nothing else changes.
Linh's yes is kept on the person, with its date, beside her other wishes.
The list is built each semester from those yeses, and when she says no, it leaves her out.
Then Clara Jensen, in Planning, asks HR for the tutors' records, to plan next year's tutoring.
It's a new use: HR holds them to employ and pay tutors, not to plan.
So before anything is shared, a short privacy check.
What is it for? Does it fit why the data is held?
What's the least it needs? Which reason allows it?
What could go wrong, and for whom? And who decides?
Clara needs hours by unit and teaching period: no names, no pay, no bank details.
A unit with one tutor would show her hours, so small units are counted together.
Ingrid, who owns the data, signs yes until the plan is set, and data governance keeps the check.
In Oregon, the counts that showed the change worked held no names. Clara's plan needs none either.
A use that decides something about a person, such as who's hired again, gets a deeper check, which asks the people it's about.
On the twentieth, Linh's contract ends.
Every piece HR holds about her has a reason it can say.
How long each is kept, and why, comes next.
When she asks what the university holds about her, Ingrid can answer: what, and why.
In Oregon, the clinics asked what the test really needed. A number was enough, and people came.
Keep data for a reason you can say.
Then people can trust you with what you need, and what you don't hold can never be used against them.

films.x: How long data is kept. Until October 2026, the university's platform kept every record with no end date: pay records back to 2016, applications from people never hired back to 2017. Ingrid and Mei write one schedule, by kind of record. When Linh's last contract ends, how long is each record kept, and then what?
c: Washington, 1943.
The country is at war, and every new office makes papers: orders, contracts, payrolls and letters.
They fill steel cabinets, four drawers each, then whole rooms, then floors.
The head of the National Archives calls it a flood: every year, enough to fill a building the size of the Archives.
And most of it has no lasting value: eighty percent, the Archives reckons.
But a paper may be destroyed only if it's on a list that Congress approves,
and a list covers only the papers already there: every new pile needs a new list.
So most papers are simply kept: nobody has time to look, or the job of deciding.
Keeping them all costs millions in rent, staff and steel cabinets.
And when the war's offices close, their papers will be shipped away or lost, the valuable with the useless:
papers someone will need one day, to prove a claim or their service.
Someone has to decide what's worth keeping, before it's too late.
On 7 July 1943, the President signs a law the National Archives drafted with a committee of Congress.
Each office now writes a schedule, once:
for each kind of record, how long it's kept, and what's done with it then.
The Archivist and Congress approve it, and it covers papers not yet written.
So the decision is made before the papers pile up.
One rule: papers about money claimed, by the government or from it, stay until the claim is settled.
Another: no paper may be destroyed any other way.
In 1944, in the Army Air Forces alone, the records program saves 927,000 dollars,
about as much as the National Archives' whole budget that year.
Today, only 1 to 3 percent of the government's papers are kept for good,
where families find their history, and veterans prove their service.
Data piles up the same way: at the university, the platform keeps every record with no end date, because nobody has decided.
Like the schedules of 1943, each kind of record can have its end date, decided before it's needed.
October 2026.
Ingrid Holm, who owns HR's records, looks at what the platform holds, with Yusuf Demir from data governance.
Pay records going back to 2016, and applications from people never hired, back to 2017.
Nothing has ever been deleted: every record is kept as if it were in use, forever.
But a record goes through three stages.
First, it's live: in use, read and changed often, like Linh Nguyen's pay records this year.
Then it's archived: kept cold, read rarely, by fewer people, like her pay records from past years.
Then, at its end date, it's deleted.
Or, for the few with lasting value, it's kept for good, like her degrees and results.
Every year a record is kept past its reason is a year a person's details could leak, or be misused.
But deleting without a plan is no safer: a pay record the law needs could go too.
Deciding record by record would never end, like Washington's lists.
So the university writes one schedule, by kind of record.
Each row names a kind of record, its owner and its reason, how long, and then what.
Each owner decides their rows, Ingrid for HR's and Mei Tanaka for the registrar's, and Yusuf keeps the schedule.
Pay records, the contracts, hours and pay: the law asks for them, so 7 years after each contract ends, then deleted.
Academic records, the degrees and results: kept for good, so a graduate can always prove a degree.
The tutors' mailing list and applications from people not hired have their rows too.
Each reason comes from A reason to keep it; each length is what that reason needs, and no longer.
On Wednesday 14 October, the owners sign it.
Later that month, the first clean-up deletes what's past its date,
pay records from 2016 to 2018, and old applications from people never hired.
How long counts from an event, not from the day a record was made.
For pay records, it's the end of each contract.
Linh has had eight contracts since 2023, one each semester, so her pay records have eight end dates.
Her first contract ended in June 2023: its records are kept until 23 June 2030.
Her last ends on 20 November 2026: its records are kept until 20 November 2033.
For an application, the event is the decision; for the mailing list, the last contact, or a no.
Once the event is recorded, the end date follows by itself.
On Friday 20 November, Linh's last contract ends.
Nobody meets, and nobody has to decide: her records already know their dates.
Decided before it was needed, as in 1943.
Sometimes a record must stay past its date.
A former tutor says she wasn't paid for all her hours in 2019, and her claim isn't settled.
Her pay records from 2019 are due to go in January, with the rest of that year's.
If they went, neither she nor the university could show what was paid.
So the university's legal office places a hold.
A hold names the records it keeps, its reason, who placed it, and who may lift it.
While it's on, the clean-up skips those records, and only those.
A hold is for a claim, an audit, or a case in court, never just in case.
Once the claim is settled, the legal office lifts the hold, and her records go at the next clean-up.
As in 1943: papers about a claim stay until it's settled.
Deleted too soon, a record breaks a promise: a tutor can't show what she was paid.
Kept too long, it's a risk to the person it's about, with nothing in return.
Many privacy laws make it a rule: keep personal data no longer than its reason needs.
So nothing is deleted outside the schedule, and nothing stays past its date, except under a hold.
The date holds for every copy: the platform's tables, the archive, old versions, logs.
How the last copy goes is Deleted means deleted.
In 1943, Washington stopped deciding pile by pile, and decided once, before the papers piled up.
The few worth keeping were kept, and the rest went on time.
At the university, every record now has an end date, decided before it's needed.

films.x: Rights over your data. Linh Nguyen's tutoring contract ends on 20 November. Four days later she asks what the university holds about her, and to leave the tutors' mailing list. Her data sits under six numbers, in documents and copies too. To answer in 30 days, the university must find it all, with a reason for every part.
c: Barcelona, 1998.
By order of Spain's labour ministry, a newspaper prints a short notice.
A lawyer, Mario Costeja González, owes social security, and his property is to be auctioned: sold to whoever bids most.
Years later, its old pages go online, and by 2009, a search for his name shows links to that notice.
Every word is true. But he settled the matter years ago.
Anyone who looks him up, a client or a neighbour, reads of his debts as if they were news.
He asks the newspaper to remove it. It says no: it printed the notice lawfully, as it was ordered to.
He wants the old notice to stop following him, and nobody will let it.
In 2010, he complains to Spain's data protection agency, the public body that upholds its privacy law.
The agency lets the newspaper keep its page, but tells the search engine to remove the links.
The search engine goes to court, and Spain's court asks the European Union's Court of Justice.
On the thirteenth of May, 2014, it rules.
Even true information, lawfully published, can in time become wrong to show under a person's name.
If, with the years, it's no longer relevant, or excessive, the person can ask for the link to go,
unless the public has a strong reason to find it, such as a role in public life.
For him, sixteen years on, there's no such reason.
The page stays. The link from his name goes.
Now anyone in Europe can ask a search engine directly. On the first day its form is open, over twelve thousand people do.
Since then, over two million requests, for eight and a half million links.
A person reviews each one. A little over half come down, and each refusal gives a reason.
At the university, Linh Nguyen's tutoring contract ends on the twentieth of November.
Four days later, she writes: tell me what you hold about me, and take me off the tutors' mailing list.
Her data sits in more places than anyone could list from memory.
If the university can't find it all, her rights are only words.
If it can, she gets what he had to go to court for: an answer, with a reason for every part.
Most privacy laws give people rights over the data others hold about them.
Each fits in a sentence anyone can say.
Show me what you hold about me.
That's wrong. Correct it.
You don't need that any more. Delete it.
Stop using it for that.
Since 2018, Europe's GDPR, the best-known privacy law, gives all four, each with its limits,
and calls the third the right to be forgotten.
Not every law gives all four, or in the same words.
The university's own rules give all four to everyone it holds data about, with an answer within thirty days.
Nobody has to say why they're asking.
A person can ask. The university must be able to answer.
Before it answers, the university must be sure the request is hers.
A request is also a way in: someone pretending to be her could be sent everything.
Linh wrote from her student account, signed in, so it's her.
The university asks for nothing more. A copy of her passport would only be one more thing to keep safe.
Check who's asking with what you already trust, and ask for no more than that.
The privacy office logs her request on the twenty-fourth of November. The answer is due by the twenty-fourth of December.
Now, where is her data?
Six numbers: in HR, the student system and its archive, the alumni office, the research office, and the learning platform.
Around them, more: the hours she claimed, payroll, the tutors' mailing list, and her signed contracts, kept as documents.
Then every table made from them, and copies outside, like a spreadsheet someone exported.
Search by her name alone, and some would be missed: it's written three ways, with accents, without, and once as an initial.
So the search uses every number and every form of her name, in documents and tools as well as tables.
Her person record links all six numbers.
Lineage follows each system into every table made from it.
And the classes that mark personal data show where else to look.
This map was kept before anyone asked, with an owner for each place.
Thirty days is time to answer. It isn't time to start looking.
She asked what the university holds. A copy alone doesn't answer that.
For each part, the answer says, in plain words, why it's held, where it came from, who else gets it, and until when.
Her contracts and the hours she claimed: to employ and pay her. From HR and the claims app. Shared with payroll.
Her pay records: the law requires them. Sent to the tax office. Kept seven years after each contract ends.
Her degree and results: awarding them is the university's task. Kept for good.
Other people's data stays out: her students' names and marks are theirs, not hers.
And it's written for her, not in table names.
Her second ask: take me off the tutors' mailing list.
In 2023 she ticked a box: send me news of tutoring work.
That yes was hers to give, and it's hers to take back, as easily.
But deleting her row isn't enough.
Each semester, the list is rebuilt from HR's contracts of the last two years, taking everyone whose yes is on the person.
Her yes would bring her back.
So her no replaces her yes, on the person, with its date.
The next day, her row leaves the list.
And her no is kept. It's the record that she asked, so nothing that reads the old yes can add her back.
To forget her here, the university has to remember one thing: that she said no.
Suppose she had asked to be forgotten altogether.
Not everything could go.
Pay records are kept because the law requires it, seven years after each contract ends.
For her last contract, that's until the twentieth of November, 2033.
Her degree and results are kept for good, so the university can always confirm them.
Her research project's data is kept as the project's rules require.
Each was decided before she asked, by the records' owners, in the university's retention schedule.
What stays is kept for its reason only, and read only by those who need it.
The answer says what stays, why, and until when.
And where the answer is no, it says why, and how to challenge it.
Like the newspaper's page in Barcelona, it stays, for its reason. It just isn't there for anything else.
In Barcelona, the page was true and lawful, and it stayed.
What went was the link from his name: sixteen years on, it had no reason left.
At the university, every place Linh's data lives was found.
She has her copy, with a reason for every part.
Her no is kept, and what stays is said, with its date.
A person can ask. You must be able to answer.

films.x: Deleting every copy. Linh asked to come off the tutors' mailing list. One night's job deleted her row, but the table kept old versions, a send log kept her number, the mailing tool had its own list, and locked copies held her for a month. Where does each copy live, and when does the last one go?
c: Kanesh, in Anatolia, about 1900 BC.
Merchants from Ashur, weeks away by donkey caravan, bring tin and cloth to sell here.
And they lend each other silver.
Each loan is written on a clay tablet: who owes whom, how much, and by when.
The tablet is sealed inside an envelope of clay, rolled with the witnesses' seals, so nobody can change it unseen.
The lender keeps it: it's the proof of the debt.
But paying the debt doesn't make the tablet go away.
It can sit on a shelf in Kanesh, or in a house in Ashur, for years.
If it turns up later, it can be used to claim the silver again, and the borrower pays twice.
Every borrower carries that risk, for every debt they've ever paid.
Something has to be done.
So, when a debt is paid, the lender hands the tablet back, and it's broken.
And when it can't be handed back, because it's still in Ashur, the lender has a receipt written, sealed before witnesses.
The debt is paid, it says, and any tablet of it that turns up is void: worth nothing.
A paid debt stays paid, and nobody pays twice.
More than twenty thousand tablets have been found in the merchants' houses, and receipts like these are among them.
Data has the same problem.
Deleting a person's data writes the receipt: the table now says they're gone.
But the old copies are still there, like tablets on a shelf, until each one is broken, or can never be used again.
Then a person who asks to be deleted stays deleted.
Linh Nguyen has tutored at the university since 2023.
On 24 November, she asked to come off the tutors' mailing list.
The privacy office logged it as request 2026-117, and approved it.
Every night at one, a job deletes what the privacy office has approved.
On Wednesday the 25th, it deletes her row from the mailing list's table.
The table's history records the delete, like a receipt.
But the platform keeps a table's old versions, so you can go back to yesterday's.
Ask for the list as it was on the 24th, and she's there.
On this table, a delete doesn't even rewrite the file.
To save time, it only marks her row as deleted, in a file that still holds it.
So the job rewrites those files, without her.
The old files are kept for seven days, so a mistake can be undone.
Then the job cleans up, with a command called VACUUM: each night, it removes old files more than seven days old.
On Wednesday 2 December, hers go.
From then on, no query can bring her back.
Deleting her row alone wouldn't last.
Each semester, the list is rebuilt from HR's records, taking the tutors who said yes.
Her yes from 2023 would bring her straight back.
So her no goes where the list is made from: on her record, in HR's system.
Ingrid Holm, who owns HR's records, puts it there that morning.
Then every table made from it follows.
One of them only ever adds rows: the send log, which keeps who was sent each newsletter.
Rebuilding the list never touches it, so it gets its own delete.
And the job never names her.
Her numbers are in a restricted table that only the privacy office and its jobs can read.
The job's code says only: request 2026-117.
Where else is she?
The platform shows every table made from HR's records, and each column's tag says what it holds.
Her email is in the list.
Her staff number is in the send log.
One line leaves the platform: the mailing tool, which copies the list each night.
When her row goes, the tool drops her too, at four that morning.
Its contract says its own backups lose her within thirty days.
Some copies don't show here at all.
Every night, a copy of the platform's data goes to a place apart, locked for thirty days.
Nobody can delete it early, even when they should.
So her row stays in the copies made before the 25th, out of use, until each one is removed by itself.
The last goes on 24 December.
And if a copy is ever restored, the job applies every answered request again, before anyone reads it.
Like the receipt in Kanesh: any copy that turns up is void.
Some of her data must stay.
Her contracts and hours are pay records, and the law says to keep them seven years after each contract ends.
Once a contract has ended, its pay records are open only to HR's records team.
A year after they're written, the table's files go to the storage's archive tier: the cheapest, and offline.
A file there can't be read, even to delete rows from it, until it's brought back, which takes hours.
But cold isn't gone.
So its files are grouped by the year each contract ended.
Every January, a clean-up job brings back the year whose seven years have passed.
Then it deletes that year, whole, unless a hold keeps part of it.
Linh's records go in four steps, from January 2031 to January 2034.
Copies also hide in what people type.
The platform keeps the text of every query for a year, and nobody can edit it.
Had someone typed her email into a query, it would sit there for a year, for the platform's admins to read.
So deletes, checks and searches name the request, never the person.
Agents keep what they're told, too.
An agent's trace records each prompt and each answer, and the gateway that carries them keeps its own table.
So email addresses are masked before a trace is saved, and traces and the gateway's tables are deleted after thirty days.
And the ticket in the repository names no one.
What's written there is hard to take back: an issue keeps its edits, and every commit is copied to every clone.
Wednesday 2 December: her row is gone from the list, the send log, every old file, and the mailing tool.
24 December: the last locked copy goes.
January 2034: the last of her pay records.
Every copy had a date, and every step is on the record.
In Kanesh, a paid debt stayed paid, because its tablet was broken, or void wherever it turned up.
At the university, Linh stays off the list, because every copy of her row is gone, or can never be used.
Deleting is done when the last copy is gone.

films.x: A request, end to end. Linh asks the university what it holds about her, and to be taken off the tutors' mailing list. The answer is due in 30 days. How does the data team find every place she is, say why each part is kept and until when, and prove each step, with her numbers in no ticket?
c: London, June 1676.
Francis Jenkes, a linen draper, sits on the City's council.
At the Guildhall, he stands up and asks for a new Parliament, to mend the City's trade.
Four days later, the King's Council sends him to the Gatehouse, a prison at Westminster, to be kept there until the law sets him free.
It names no day.
He asks the keeper for a copy of the warrant, the order that holds him.
The keeper promises it, and stalls.
His friends offer bail, a pledge of money, so he can wait for his trial at home.
Refused.
They ask a judge for habeas corpus.
It's Latin for "have the body": an order to bring the prisoner before a judge, and say why he's held.
The judge refuses, for one reason only: the courts are on their summer holiday.
In August, Jenkes is still inside, writing of his great loss, and the harm to his health.
Without that order, a person could be held for months, with no judge to hear why.
A prisoner needed a right to a judge that no holiday could close.
In 1679, Parliament passes the Habeas Corpus Act.
Once the order is served, the keeper has three days to bring the prisoner before a judge, and certify the true causes of holding him.
Ten days if the prison is more than twenty miles away, twenty if it's more than a hundred.
The courts' holiday is no excuse: any judge must grant the order.
A copy of the warrant, within six hours of asking.
And a keeper who stalls pays the prisoner a hundred pounds.
The second time, two hundred, and he loses his post.
So a prisoner learns why he's held within hours, and stands before a judge within days, not a summer.
A century later, the United States writes the writ into its Constitution.
Today, a person can ask a university too: what do you hold about me, and why?
Left in an inbox, a request waits, and nobody can show what was searched.
Given a clock, the true reasons and proof, it's answered on time, and the answer can be trusted.
On 24 November, Linh Nguyen writes to the university.
Her tutoring contract ended four days ago.
She's signed in with her student account, on the privacy office's form, so the office knows it's her, and asks for nothing more.
"Please tell me what you hold about me, and take me off the tutors' mailing list."
The privacy office logs it: request 2026-117.
Like the writ, it has a clock: thirty days, so it's due on 24 December.
Ingrid Holm, who owns HR's data, takes HR's part.
The data team gets a ticket in its repository.
It names no one: just the request's number, the date it's due, and the steps.
Her numbers go in one place: a table on the platform that only the privacy office and its jobs may read.
Mei's office keeps Linh's master record, P-10482.
From its links come her numbers in every system: six in all.
In the data project, dbt lists every model built from those five systems: more than thirty.
On the platform, lineage adds the rest: a notebook's table, a dashboard, another team's job.
And the tags from Know what you hold point to each column that names a person, or holds a code for one.
Then a job runs, as its own identity.
Table by table, it looks in those columns, for her numbers, and for the codes made from them.
In the marts built for the wallet, planning and finance, she's there only as a code.
A search for her numbers alone would miss them all.
And none of her numbers is typed into a query, whose text the platform keeps for a year.
Instead, each query joins the table of keys, by the request's number.
Lineage only sees the platform, so the owners of payroll, the claims app, the mailing tool and her signed contracts search their own.
What Linh gets back isn't a pile of tables.
It's a copy of what's held, written for her to read.
For each part: what it is, why it's held, where it came from, who else gets it, and until when.
Like the true causes on the keeper's answer, each reason is a plain one, from A reason to keep it.
A contract, for her contracts and hours.
A law, for her pay records: seven years after each contract, the last until 20 November 2033.
A public task, for her degrees and results, kept for good.
Her research project's data, as long as its rules require.
Anything about other people is left out, such as the marks she gave her students.
On 3 December, each owner checks their part: Ingrid for HR, Mei for the registrar's records, the research office for her project.
Her second ask was done first.
In the night of 25 November, the deletion job takes her row out of the list's table, and out of its log of what was sent.
The mailing tool drops her at its next sync.
That morning, Ingrid puts her no on the person, in place of the yes she gave in 2023.
The list is rebuilt each semester from HR's casual contracts of the last two years, and takes only those whose yes is on the person.
So the next rebuild leaves her out.
The table's old versions hold her row for seven days more, then they're cleaned up, on 2 December, as Deleted means deleted showed.
Deleting her row alone wouldn't have been enough: with her yes still there, the next rebuild would have brought her back.
Every step leaves proof.
In the ticket, each box is ticked with a link.
The search's run shows who ran it: the job, as itself.
The list table's history shows her row deleted, and the old versions cleaned up.
The audit log shows who read the table of keys: only the office and its jobs.
The privacy office keeps a table of every request and the day it's due.
A request near its date shows up there, for the office to work through.
A late answer isn't wrong data: it's work still to do.
On 7 December, Linh's answer is ready, seventeen days early, and she opens it by signing in.
The ticket closes. Her numbers stay in the table of keys until the last locked copy is gone, on 24 December.
In 1679, a keeper answered the writ with the body, and the true causes, within days.
Here, it's what's held, the true reasons, on time, and proof of each step.
Five films, one person's data.
Keep data for a reason you can say.
Every record has an end date, decided before it's needed.
A person can ask, and you must be able to answer.
Deleting is done when the last copy is gone.
And a request is answered on time, with proof.
With Locks before the data and Only what you may see, that's data protection and privacy.
Who may come in, what each may see, and how long anything stays.
Next: AI agents in data work, where agents work under the same rules.

films.x: How we got here. This term, an AI agent joins Jun Park's data team. To some it seems to have come from nowhere: some fear it, some expect magic. Before they work with it, the team learns where it came from: decades of slow work, from a machine that learned in 1958 to models that reason and use tools.
c: Europe, in the 1440s. Every book is copied by hand, letter by letter.
So books are slow to make, and rare.
In 1424, the University of Cambridge's library held 122 books.
And every new copy can add new mistakes.
Something has to change.
The idea that will change it is already four hundred years old.
