She gives Ivy a month to learn the team's work, and one real question to follow through all of it.
It comes from Graham Ellis, the new Director of Facilities: should he ask the University Council for a new teaching building?
His question, agreed with him in writing: do we have too few rooms, or too few at some hours?
In her first week, Ivy writes her first goals, and Helena agrees them.
The first: by Easter, know the whole route of one question's data.
She starts where the data is born.
In the registrar's office, Mei Tanaka keeps the timetable: every class, booked into one of 186 rooms, hour by hour.
Sam Okafor runs the data platform, and the feed from each room's sensor, which counts the people in it every hour.
Yusuf Demir, who leads data governance, set the rule for that feed: counts, never people.
Noor Rahman, the data architect, keeps the map of where data is born and where it goes.
Jun Park builds the models that turn raw data into tables people can trust.
Every day, Ivy spends an hour beside him, changing real ones.
How data moves, and how the map is drawn, have films of their own: The Inner Life of Data, and The map before the data.
Each of them is deep in one part, and right about it.
Ivy learns enough of each to follow: their words, their tools, and what worries them.
And she asks each the same question: who uses this, and for which decision?
In her fourth week, she draws the whole route of Graham's question on one page, starting from his decision.
At the top, the decision: whether to ask for the building, which the University Council weighs in June.
Under it, the question behind it: too few rooms, or too few at some hours?
Then the data that answers it: each room's bookings, beside the people counted in it.
Where that data is born: the timetable, and the sensors.
Who keeps it: Mei, Sam, Jun and Noor. And the rule: counts, never people.
Where the bookings meet the counts, she sees what no one part could.
The two must name each room the same way, and for 172 rooms, they do.
For 14, they don't: those rooms were renumbered in the timetable after their sensors went in.
Joined as they were, those 14 would drop out without a word, and Graham's answer would cover 172 rooms, not 186.
Nobody was wrong: the timetable was right, and so were the sensors. They had never been put side by side.
Ivy didn't need to know the timetable as Mei does, or the sensors as Sam does.
She needed depth of her own, in statistics, and enough of the business, the systems and the data to join them.
That shape has a name: T-shaped. One deep stroke, and a wide bar across the top.
Frameworks map the work: SFIA lists well over a hundred skills, and DAMA's body of knowledge names the roles of data work.
Nobody holds them all deeply, and nobody needs to.
In his book Range, David Epstein argues that specialists win where the rules stay fixed, as in chess.
Where problems are messy, people with range do better.
Like the diggers and the boatmen, the specialists stay essential: Mei and Sam matched the 14 rooms in a day.
But someone has to see across them.
On Thursday 25 March, just before Easter, Ivy's first goal is met: she knows the whole route.
When the team takes up Graham's question the next week, it starts from her page, with all 186 rooms.
From April, the catalog draws much of that route by itself.
Its lineage runs from the raw bookings and counts, through Jun's models, to the page Graham reads.
What it can't draw is the decision, and the question behind it. Those stay on Ivy's page.
In Kaifeng, Ding Wei didn't dig, float timber or cart rubble better than the people who did. He saw the three jobs as one.
Ivy did the same with data: she saw the parts as one, and kept 14 rooms in Graham's answer.
On Monday, keep your depth in one thing.
Learn the words of the others, and spend time with each of them.
Take one real question, and draw its whole route on one page.
Ask, of every part: who uses this, and for which decision?
Go deep in one thing; learn enough of the others to see the whole.

films.x: Working with an agent. Ivy Reyes, in her sixth week on the university's data team, asks the team's agent for a first draft of a model of room use. In a minute it's there: tidy, tested, sure, and wrong about one word. She catches it by reading what the agent assumed and checking the draft against what she knows is true.
c: New York, May 1997. The world chess champion, Garry Kasparov, plays a six-game match against a computer built for chess.
The computer wins: the first time a machine has beaten a world champion in a match.
Many fear what that means for people.
Players spend years learning the game, and many earn their living by it.
If a machine plays better than the best of them, what is their skill worth?
Players have to find what their skill is for, beside the machine.
A year later, in León, in Spain, Kasparov tries another way: play with the machine, not against it.
He and his opponent, Veselin Topalov, each have a computer at hand, running the chess program of their choice.
With the machine checking every tactic, Kasparov finds he can give his thinking to the plan.
In 2005, an online tournament goes further: anyone can enter, in teams, with as many computers as they like.
Grandmasters enter with their computers. A supercomputer built for chess enters on its own.
The winners are two amateur players from the United States, with three computers.
From their own experience, they choose which moves are worth a look, and compare what each program says.
They send the programs deeper where it matters, and then the two of them decide.
In the final, they beat a team led by a grandmaster, and take first prize. The supercomputer, alone, doesn't reach the last eight.
Kasparov drew the lesson: weak players, with a machine and a better process, beat a strong computer alone.
More remarkably, they beat strong players whose process was worse.
The players' skill still counted. What counted most was how they worked with the machines.
Data work has its machine now too: an agent can write the first draft of a data model in a minute.
Many ask what that leaves for the people.
As at the board, it leaves the part that decides: saying what's wanted, checking the draft against what's true, and choosing.
A draft is cheap. Judgement isn't.
At the university, a year from now, the data team has taken up a question from Graham Ellis, the Director of Facilities.
He must decide whether to ask the University Council for a new teaching building.
His question: do we have too few rooms, or too few at some hours?
Wednesday 7 April 2027. Ivy Reyes, a graduate data analyst in her sixth week, is building the first model: how much each room is used.
She asks the team's agent for a first draft: a model of room use, for every room and every teaching hour.
In a minute, it's there.
It's tidy: the model, a description of every column, and four tests, which all pass.
Its answer: the rooms are used 38% of the teaching week, and 93% at the busiest hours.
It looks finished, and it sounds sure.
Ivy is about to open a pull request. First, she reads the agent's notes to the end.
At the end, the agent lists what it assumed.
One line stops her: a booked hour counts as a used hour.
In February, Graham had said what used means: people in the room, not a booking.
The tests pass because they check the form of the data: no room counted twice, no hour left out.
No test can know what Graham means.
So Ivy checks the draft against something she knows is true: the sensors, which count the people in each room, every hour.
In one booked hour in five, they counted nobody. The draft calls every one of those hours used.
Graham would have weighed a new building on bookings, not on rooms people use.
The agent wasn't careless. In timetabling, use often means booked, and it said what it assumed.
It had been given the task, but not the decision, or the words.
So before she asks again, Ivy frames the work.
First, the word. She writes room use into the glossary: the share of teaching hours in which the sensors counted at least one person.
Graham approves it there, as its owner, so every model, and every draft, starts from it.
Then she asks again, and gives the agent three things, not one.
The decision it serves: whether to ask the University Council for a new building.
The words to use: room use, as the glossary has it.
And what counts: teaching hours, eight till six, Monday to Friday, with booked and used side by side.
The new draft keeps the two apart, and says again what it assumed.
Ivy checks it against something she knows is true: one room's week, which she worked out by hand, hour by hour.
All fifty hours match.
Ivy opens a pull request. She's its author, so she answers for it, whoever wrote the first draft.
With it, she keeps the reasoning: what she asked for, what the agent assumed, what she changed, and how she checked.
Jun reviews it. Nobody approves their own work: not Ivy, and never the agent.
He asks which room she checked by hand. The answer is in the pull request.
He approves it, and it's merged. Graham is told what it changes: the first answer to his question.
Next morning, at stand-up, Ivy says what she nearly missed: she'd asked for the task, not the decision or the words.
Helena thanks her for saying it, and the team starts asking that way too.
When an agent drafts, the work doesn't go away. It moves to either side of the draft.
Before it: framing the question, with its decision, its words and what counts, and saying exactly what's wanted.
After it: checking what comes back against what you know is true, deciding, and answering for it.
Employers see it too. In the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025, the core skill they seek most is analytical thinking.
Seven in ten companies call it essential.
AI and big data skills are rising fastest; creative thinking and curiosity are rising too.
An agent can draft, test its work, and say what it assumed. It can't take the decision from you, or the responsibility for it.
How agents work, and how teams govern them on data, have films of their own: What an agent is, and Agents at work on data.
In 2005, two amateurs finished ahead of grandmasters and a supercomputer.
Not by out-calculating the machines, but by choosing what to look at, comparing, and deciding.
Ivy did the same with data: the agent drafted in a minute; she framed the work, checked it and decided.
And Graham's answer counts people in the rooms, not bookings.
On Monday, give the agent the decision, the words and what counts, not only the task.
Read what it assumed, to the end.
Check its draft against something you know is true.
Never approve your own work, and keep the reasoning with the result.
Let the agent draft; you frame, check and decide.

films.x: Learning on the job. Ivy Reyes joins the university's data team in March 2027. For six weeks she pairs with Jun an hour a day on the team's real models, one small change at a time. From April the team keeps two hours every Thursday for learning. In May she teaches what she learned, and by June every job has two names.
c: Angicos, a small town in the dry north-east of Brazil, January 1963.
About 380 adults sign up for evening classes, farm workers, builders and washerwomen among them.
Some twenty students from the university in Natal run them, trained by an educator, Paulo Freire.
Three adults in four in Angicos can't read or write.
In Brazil then, people who can't read can't vote.
They sign papers they can't read, and others read their letters to them.
Adult classes often use children's primers, with lines like Eva saw the grape: nothing about their own lives, and many give up.
Learning to read has to start from people's own lives.
Freire's team starts from the town's own words.
They listen to how people talk about their lives, write down about four hundred, and choose a handful.
Each evening, a culture circle meets: learners, and a coordinator instead of a teacher.
They talk about a picture from their own lives, then take one word from it: belota, a hammock's tassels.
Then they break the word into syllables, and make new words from them.
One small step each evening, by doing, together; and what each person already knows counts.
The fortieth hour, the last class, is on 2 April 1963, and the president of Brazil comes.
The organisers count about 300 who can now read and write; people still argue over how many, and how well.
The method spreads; in January 1964 a national plan sets out to take it across Brazil.
That April, a military government stops the plan, and Freire is jailed, then exiled.
Abroad, he writes Pedagogy of the Oppressed, one of the most-cited books in the social sciences.
Learning data work can feel like those primers: tutorials about nothing in your job.
Skills grow faster on the real work, a small step at a time, beside someone who knows; and what you learn, you can teach.
A year from now, at a university, Ivy Reyes joins the data team on Monday 1 March 2027, straight from a degree in statistics.
Jun Park, who builds the team's models, doesn't hand her a course. He opens the real ones.
For her first six weeks, they pair for an hour a day: one types, the other reads, asks and thinks ahead, and they swap.
Each day, one small change, finished: a check that every room has a name, a clearer description, a better column name.
Both of them wrote it, so someone else on the team reviews it before it goes in: Noor or Sam.
In the fifth week, it's one her own page found.
The match for the 14 renumbered rooms goes in, with a check, so no room drops out without a word.
In six weeks, twenty-five small changes, each one reviewed.
By the sixth week, Ivy writes changes on her own, and Jun reviews them.
Pairing like this was made popular by extreme programming, a way of making software from the late 1990s: two people, one keyboard.
The tools change every month, and their official docs change with them.
Learning saved for a quiet week never happens: there isn't one.
From Thursday 1 April, the whole team keeps two hours every Thursday afternoon for learning, free of meetings.
Helena Novak, the data manager, put it in everyone's calendar, and keeps it free: a meeting asked for then is offered another time.
Each person picks one thing the work needs, and starts from the tools' own docs, dbt's and Databricks', open beside the work.
They try it on the real project, and write down what they learned, in the team's notes beside the code.
Ivy picks the sensors' counts: what one number in Sam's feed really means.
She reads the sensors' guide and Sam's notes, and goes through a week of counts, hour by hour.
On Thursday 13 May, in the learning time, she teaches it to the team, on one page, in twenty minutes.
Each hour's count is the most people the sensor saw at once in that hour.
A zero means it saw nobody; a gap means it sent nothing, and the two are never the same.
And it counts heads; it never knows whose.
Getting ready, she found two things she couldn't explain, and asked Sam: that's when she really learned them.
Logan Fiorella and Richard Mayer found the same.
Students who prepared to teach a lesson, then taught it, remembered more of it later than those who only studied it.
Freire put it this way, years after Angicos: whoever teaches learns in teaching, and whoever learns teaches in learning.
Now the whole team reads a count the same way, not only Sam.
A team where only one person knows how to run something is one absence away from trouble.
In May, the team lists the nine jobs that must keep running, and who can run each.
Five have only one name: the sensors' feed is only Sam's, the room models only Jun's.
So they pair on those too, a job at a time, and write each one down, step by step.
By Wednesday 30 June, every job has at least two names.
Ivy's is the second name on two of them: the sensors' feed, and the room models.
Now anyone can take a holiday, or be ill, and the work goes on.
People who study how adults learn at work find the same, trade after trade.
Jean Lave and Etienne Wenger looked at apprentices, from tailors in Liberia to midwives in Mexico.
Newcomers learn by taking part in the real work: first at its edge, with small tasks that matter, beside people who know.
Anders Ericsson found that skill grows from practice aimed at what you can't do yet, with quick feedback from someone who can.
A rule of thumb says about seventy per cent of what people learn at work comes from doing it.
About twenty comes from other people, and ten from courses.
It's a rule of thumb, not a measurement, but it points the same way.
Courses and docs still count: start from the official docs, then learn it on the work.
In Angicos, adults learned to read from their own words, a small step each evening, in a circle with someone beside them.
Ivy learned the team's work the same way, taught what she learned, and by June she was the second name on two of its jobs.
On Monday, learn on the real work, beside someone who knows.
Take one small step at a time, and finish it.
Put learning time in the calendar, protect it, and start from the official docs.
Write down what you learn, and teach it.
Learn on the real work, beside someone, then teach it.

films.x: Listening first. Graham Ellis, the new Director of Facilities, asks for a dashboard of room use by Easter. In half an hour, mostly listening, Helena and Noor find the decision behind it, whether to ask for a new teaching building, and agree the question with him in writing, beside his words.
c: Pisa, Italy. Its marble bell tower, begun in 1173, has leaned since it was being built, because the ground beneath it is soft.
By 1990, its top hangs about four and a half metres out past its base, and each year it leans a little further.
In March 1989, a medieval tower in another Italian city, Pavia, had suddenly collapsed, killing four people.
In January 1990, Pisa's tower was closed to visitors, for fear it could fall too.
Its stone was fragile: a fall could kill anyone near it, and take from the city the tower people cross the world to see.
And any work was a risk: the slightest disturbance to the ground on its leaning side could bring it down.
The tower had to be made safe, without the work itself toppling it.
That spring, Italy's government appointed an international committee: engineers, architects and experts in old monuments.
Before choosing how, they agreed what saving it would mean: a small change, about half a degree, too little for anyone to see.
But enough to ease the strain on its stone, and steady the ground beneath it.
Their method: draw a little soil from under the high, north side, so the tower would settle back towards it.
They tried it first on a test footing, while lead weights on the north side held the tower still.
From February 1999, they did it under the tower itself, a little at a time, and it began to lean back.
Every day, the engineer in charge signed a note: how the tower had moved, and exactly what to take out next.
By the summer of 2001, its top had come back about 45 centimetres, to the lean it had in the early 1800s.
In December 2001, it reopened to visitors, still leaning, as it always has.
Its engineers expect at least two hundred years before it leans as far again.
At a university, a request for a dashboard hid a decision worth about A$140 million.
Half an hour of listening found it, and one page, agreed in writing, turned it into a question the team could answer.
These three films are about working with the people who ask for data.
Thursday 11 February 2027: Graham Ellis, new this year as Director of Facilities, emails the data team.
“Could I have a dashboard of room use, by Easter?”
It sounds clear: a thing, and a date.
But a request usually names someone's guess at a solution. What it's for, it doesn't say.
Build exactly what was asked, and a team can deliver on time and still help nobody.
So Helena Novak, the data manager, asks Graham for half an hour, with Noor, the team's data architect.
Tuesday 16 February, in Graham's office. They ask a few open questions, then mostly listen.
What will you decide with it? Whether to ask the University Council for a new teaching building: forty rooms, about A$140 million.
By when? His paper is due on 1 June, and the University Council decides on 24 June. Easter was a guess at a safe date.
Who else decides? The University Council, on his advice. And the academics will read it closely: they say the rooms are always full.
What do you already trust? What he has seen on his walks: empty corridors on Monday mornings and Friday afternoons.
What would change your mind? If rooms are short at every hour, he'll ask to build. If only at some hours, perhaps not.
Edgar Schein called this humble inquiry: asking what you don't already know, out of real interest in the other person.
Carl Rogers and Richard Farson called the other half active listening: hearing the whole meaning, then saying it back.
Some teams ask “why?” five times over. Asked bluntly, it can sound like doubt; “what will you decide with it?” gets there kindly.
Near the end, Helena says back what she heard: a decision about a building, and a question about how the rooms are used.
Graham stops her at one word: by “used”, he means people in the room. A booking isn't use.
That one word decides the data: the timetable's bookings, beside the head counts from each room's sensor.
In Pisa, saving meant half a degree, not a straight tower. Here, use means people in the room, not bookings.
Then Noor writes the question down with him, on one page.
“Do we have too few rooms, or too few at some hours?”
Under it go the decision, the dates, who decides, what would change his mind, and what “used” means.
His own words stay at the top, beside the question, so anyone can see how one became the other.
That afternoon, Graham replies to the page: “Yes, that's it.”
Then the request waits its turn, like every other, until the team takes it up on Tuesday 30 March.
In March, Ivy Reyes, a new graduate analyst, follows that question through the team's work, starting from the page.
On 30 March, the team starts from the same page, and by 23 April it has an answer.
Across the whole week, the rooms are booked only 38% of the time.
But between 10:00 and 14:00, Tuesday to Thursday, 93% of them are booked.
And one booked hour in five, the sensors counted nobody there.
So the answer to his question: not too few rooms, but too few at some hours.
The academics were right about the peak, and Graham about Monday mornings: the week's average had hidden both.
A dashboard by Easter might have shown that average, and settled nothing.
Instead, he had an answer to the question his decision turned on, weeks before his paper was due.
In Pisa, the committee didn't start by digging. It first agreed what saving the tower would mean.
Then every day, a signed note said how it had moved, and what to do next.
Graham's request got the same care: the decision found, the question agreed in writing, and an answer in time.
From June, the team's front door, a form, asks five questions like these. A form can ask; listening hears what the answers mean.
On Monday, when someone asks you for a report or a dashboard, ask what they'll decide with it, and by when.
Ask who else decides, what they already trust, and what would change their mind.
Listen more than you talk, and say back what you heard.
Then write the question down beside their words, and agree it with them.
Ask what it's for, and agree it in writing.

films.x: Explaining for a decision. In May 2027, Graham Ellis must put one choice to the University Council, on one page: a new teaching building now, or not yet? Ivy Reyes's first draft runs to twelve pages, with the answer on page nine. With Helena, she starts the page with the decision, and draws the week's picture beside it.
c: In 1950, the United States Air Force measured more than four thousand of its flyers: 132 measurements each.
The figures went to the people who designed what flyers wear and where they sit: suits, helmets, cockpits.
Many designers took one figure from them: the average man, about five foot nine.
He seemed the easiest flyer to fit, and the commonest.
But a doorway built to his height would make about half the men stoop.
In a cockpit it's worse: a control just out of reach, or a pedal too far away, and a pilot can't fly safely.
Cockpits built for him were failing the men who actually flew.
In 1952, Lieutenant Gilbert Daniels was a scientist in the Air Force's anthropology section.
He asked a plain question: how many flyers are average?
He took ten measurements used to size clothing.
On each, a man counted as average if he was in the middle thirty percent: a generous band.
Of 4,063 men, 1,055 were average in height.
Of those, 302 were average in chest too.
Each measurement left fewer: 143, 73, 28, 12, 6, 3, 2.
Average on all ten: not one.
His note, seven pages long, said so in its first lines: it is virtually impossible to find an average man in the Air Force.
Then it showed what a design turns on: the range. From five foot five to six foot one fits nine flyers in ten.
Designers came to fit the range, not the average.
By the 1970s, the Air Force designed its cockpits for the middle ninety pilots in every hundred.
The seats rise and fall, and the pedals move.
A car's seat slides for the same reason.
Data has its average men too: one number that seems to describe everything, and describes almost nothing.
Lead with the decision, show the part of the data it turns on, and the people who decide can see what they're choosing.
At a university, a year from now, Graham Ellis is the Director of Facilities.
He must decide whether to ask the University Council for a new teaching building: forty rooms, about A$140 million.
It was proposed because the rooms are always full.
In February, the data team agreed his question with him, in writing: do we have too few rooms, or too few at some hours?
By late April, they had the answer: too few, only at some hours.
Now he must put it to the University Council on one page, by Tuesday 1 June.
Ivy Reyes, a data analyst, drafts it with Helena Novak, the data manager.
Her first draft runs to twelve pages, in the order the work was done: the data, the method, the checks, and on page nine, the answer.
Its first chart is the week's average: rooms booked 38% of the time.
It's how a thesis is written, and nothing in it is wrong.
Helena asks one question: who will read it, and what will they decide with it?
The University Council's members read a pile of papers before each meeting, and decide on each.
So the page starts where they start: with the decision.
Barbara Minto called it the pyramid: the answer at the top, then the reasons, then the evidence under each.
Ivy's page opens with the decision: a new building now, or not yet?
Then the answer to the agreed question, in one sentence: rooms are short only from ten to two, Tuesday to Thursday.
Under it, three lines: the peak, the bookings nobody used, and what it would take not to build.
The method and the other charts move to the back, for anyone who wants them.
So does one true finding: when people came, rooms were about half full.
The decision doesn't turn on it: a half-full room still holds a class.
Now the chart. The week's average, 38%, hides what the decision turns on.
So Ivy draws the whole week: a heat map, the days down the side, the hours across, each hour as dark as the share of rooms booked.
From ten to two, Tuesday to Thursday, 93% of rooms are booked. Most other hours, about one in five.
The academics who said the rooms are always full were right, at the peak.
So were Facilities, who saw empty corridors on Monday mornings and Friday afternoons.
Like Daniels's count, one picture shows what the average hid.
And booked isn't used: in one booked hour in five, the sensors counted nobody.
Edward Tufte's advice for charts: above all else, show the data.
Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's: know who you're showing, and the one thing they need to see.
So Ivy draws the picture as she writes the page, never after: the page says what to decide, and the picture shows what it turns on.
Helena, who thinks like an architect, keeps the same rule for anything that crosses teams: its route, in one picture.
Beside the picture, what it would take not to build: move about one peak class in six to other hours, and release booked rooms nobody uses.
That meets Planning's forecast to 2030: six percent more students.
What isn't known goes on the page too: how many students there will really be by 2030.
So it says how far the answer holds: even if students grew twice as fast, the peak would be no fuller than it is today.
Before it goes, Ivy tries it on Mei, from the registrar's office, who wasn't in the work.
Mei reads it in two minutes, and says it back.
She stops at one word: utilisation. To her, it means seats filled. On the page, it meant rooms booked.
So the page says booked and used instead, each with what it means, in a line.
Then she asks what the University Council will ask: which classes would move?
The page answers: the registrar's office would plan it with the faculties, from Semester 1 2028.
Everyone gets the same page, with the same numbers: the University Council, the faculties and the registrar's office.
On Tuesday 1 June, Graham sends the page under his own name, with the week's picture beside it.
On Thursday 24 June, the University Council meets.
Its members ask how sure the growth is, and which classes would move: both answered on the page.
They defer the building for two years, and ask for the timetable change from Semester 1 2028, with a review in June 2029.
Afterwards, Graham says the meeting argued about the choice, not about the numbers.
The page didn't decide for them. It let them see what they were choosing.
Daniels didn't design a cockpit. He counted, said plainly what the count meant, and left the design to the designers.
Ivy's page did the same: the decision first, the peak beside the average, and the choice left to the people who make it.
On Monday, start with the decision, then the answer, in one sentence.
Show what it turns on, the peak and the spread, in a picture you draw as you write.
Say what you don't know, in your readers' words, with the same numbers for everyone.
Try it on someone who wasn't in the work. Then let the people who decide, decide.
Lead with the decision; show what it turns on.

films.x: When too much is asked. In July 2027 Planning asks the university's data team for a new forecast model by the end of August, in the same weeks the timetable change needs Jun and Noor. Helena asks what the date is for, puts both asks on the one list, and offers what the team can do well, and when.
c: The Aral Sea, between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was once the fourth-largest lake in the world.
From the 1960s, its two rivers were turned to grow cotton and rice in the desert, on farms many families depend on.
The sea shrank. By 2004 it had lost almost 70 percent of its surface, and its level had fallen almost 20 metres.
Around 1990, it split in two: a small sea in the north, in Kazakhstan, and a larger one in the south.
Fishing towns like Aralsk were left far from the water. The sea grew salty, the fish died, and tens of thousands of jobs were lost.
Storms blew salt and dust off the dry seabed. The drinking water was polluted, and people fell ill.
Bringing the whole sea back would have meant taking the rivers back from the farms.
The whole sea was out of reach, and waiting for it would save nothing.
Kazakhstan chose to save the part that could be saved: the northern sea.
With a World Bank loan, it built the Kok-Aral dam, 13 kilometres long, to keep the Syr Darya's water in the north.
It was finished in August 2005, and works upstream let more of the river arrive.
The water rose much faster than planned. By 2006, the northern sea stood four metres higher, at the level the dam was built for.
By 2007 it was half as salty. The fish came back, and the catch grew forty-fold, from 50 tonnes to about 2,000.
Four fish plants opened, and in 2008 its fish were sold abroad for the first time in years.
The shore came tens of kilometres back towards Aralsk.
The southern sea, which the dam didn't save, went on shrinking. By 2014, its eastern part was dry.
It was a no to the whole sea, said plainly, and a yes to the part that could be saved. And that yes was kept.
In data work, more is asked than a team can do well. A bare no helps nobody, and neither does a yes nobody can keep.
An honest no, with what you can do and when, gets people what they need.
At the university, a year from now, Clara Jensen, in Planning, asks for a new student forecast model, by the end of August.
In the same weeks, the registrar's office needs the rooms' data for the timetable change the University Council asked for in June.
Mei Tanaka and Graham Ellis need it by the end of August, so the faculties can plan next year's classes from October.
Both go on the team's one list, ordered in the open, as the data management module shows.
And both need Jun and Noor, in the same four weeks of August.
A yes to both would mean one of them done badly: a model nobody had time to test, or the rooms' data late for the faculties.
A bare no would leave Clara with nothing.
So Helena Novak, the data manager, does neither. First, she asks.
Roger Fisher and William Ury, in Getting to Yes, tell a position from an interest.
A position is what someone asks for. An interest is why they ask: what the date or the scope is for.
On Wednesday 14 July, Helena and Noor sit down with Clara, and ask what the date is for.
The 2028 budget round closes on Friday 17 September. Planning must put next year's student numbers into it.
The new model would take in applications week by week, to warn of a change in demand early, for the admissions round in December.
So what does the budget need? The current model, with this year's figures in it.
Her position: a new model by August. Her interests: a number to trust in the budget, and earlier warning for admissions.
Helena says it back, and Clara nods: that's what it's for.
Helena puts both asks on the one list, side by side, where Clara and Mei can both see them.
Each with its date, what it's for, and the weeks of work it takes.
The rooms' data takes three of August's four weeks. A new model takes six, and time to test it.
Refreshing the current model takes one week.
The order isn't Helena's to choose. The list is ordered by value, urgency, effort and risk, never by who asks.
Fisher and Ury call that fair criteria: what both sides can check, not who pushes harder.
Then they look for options that serve both interests: the budget by September, and early warning by December.
William Ury calls it a positive no: a yes to what you must protect, then a clear no, then an offer.
The Kok-Aral dam was one: a yes to the part that could be saved, and a plain no to the whole sea.
Helena's yes is to the timetable change, and to work done well.
Her no is to the date: no new model by August.
Her offer: the current model, refreshed with this year's figures, by Friday 27 August, in time for the budget.
And the new model by Friday 29 October, before the admissions round.
Then she asks: would that work?
It's Clara's to choose. If she disagreed, the data council would settle it in the open on Tuesday 27 July.
Clara agrees. Both dates go on the one list, in writing: not now, with a reason and a date.
On Friday 27 August, the refreshed model goes to Planning, and the rooms' data to the registrar's office.
On Friday 17 September, the budget round closes, with Planning's numbers in it.
On Friday 29 October, the new model is ready, reviewed before anyone reads it, in time for admissions.
In November, Clara brings Planning's next request early, with what it's for and when she needs it.
A clear no with an offer, kept, built more trust than a yes nobody could keep.
At the Aral, the dam didn't promise the whole sea. It saved the part it could, and the water came back.
Helena did the same: she asked what the date was for, showed the trade-off, offered what the team could do well, and kept her word.
On Monday, when a date can't be met, ask what it's for.
Put the trade-off on the list, where everyone can see it.
Say no to the date, not the person, and offer what you can do well, and when.
Let the people who decide choose, write it down, and keep your word.
The next film, Less, on purpose, opens a new series: what a team stops doing, together.
Never a bare no: say what you can do, and when.

films.x: Minimalism in a team. In 2027 the university's data team runs 38 old reports, sits in standing meetings about eight hours a week each and gets about 60 alerts a week, most needing nothing. Helena Novak and the team ask who uses each thing, and for what, then stop the rest together, openly and so it can come back.
c: Britain, in 2010.
The government publishes millions of pages on the web, across hundreds of websites, most of them run by one department alone.
To renew a passport or pay a tax, people first have to work out which part of government does it, and which of its sites to trust.
The same advice sits on several sites, in different words. People lose time, and can't be sure which page is right.
And taxpayers pay around 560 million pounds a year for all those websites.
Government online has to become one place, and simpler.
In October 2010, Martha Lane Fox, the government's digital champion, reports on its main public website, Directgov.
Her advice: one website for the whole of government, and one team that answers for what people find there.
Don't move the old pages across. Write only what people need, and archive the rest.
A new team, the Government Digital Service, builds that website.
It reads every page of Directgov, and later of Business Link, the site for businesses, and what people searched for.
It keeps only what meets a real need, and writes that again.
In 2012, it writes down its design principles. The first: start with what people need. The second: do less.
Government should only do what only government can do.
In October 2012, GOV.UK replaces both sites, with far fewer pages: about 3,800 pieces of content.
In tests, people finish 61 tasks in 100, against 46 on Business Link, and a minute faster.
And it's expected to cost taxpayers up to 70 million pounds a year less.
The next spring, London's Design Museum names it Design of the Year.
A data team's work piles up the same way: reports, meetings and alerts, each added for a good reason, and rarely taken away.
Stop what nobody uses, and the time goes back to the work that matters.
But simpler doesn't just happen. Someone has to choose it.
This series follows four ideas for leading a team: minimalism, kaizen, Ubuntu, and decentralisation and emergence.
It begins with minimalism: keeping only what does a job, so that what's left is done well.
At the university, a year from now, Helena Novak leads a data team of eight.
On Tuesday 4 May, they put everything they run and attend on one wall.
There are 38 old reports, and the warehouse's logs show that 17 haven't been opened in a year.
Each person spends about eight hours a week in standing meetings.
And the platform sends about 60 alerts a week. Most of them need nothing.
Each was added for a good reason: a request, a project, a night when something broke.
In 2021, a study in Nature found that when people set out to make something better, they mostly add to it.
They rarely think of taking anything away.
When a university's new president asked for ideas, only about one in ten took something away.
So Helena asks the team to choose, together, what to keep and what to stop.
For each thing on the wall, they ask: who uses it, and for what?
For the reports, the logs answer: 21 are read by about 260 people. The other 17, by nobody, for a year or more.
Before they stop anything, they agree what each kind of thing is for.
A meeting is for deciding together, or helping someone. Not for reading out what the team's board already shows.
An alert is for someone who must act now.
A report is for a decision someone makes.
Then they design the week they want: a 15-minute stand-up each morning, and planning on Monday.
A review with the people who asked, every second Thursday, and a half-hour one-to-one.
About three hours a week each, instead of eight.
From Monday 10 May, that's the week. The other standing meetings stop, like the weekly round of updates the board now shows.
For each of the 17 reports, the team first writes to its last readers, and to whoever asked for it.
Most have moved on. One reader needs last year's figures, and gets a copy.
On Tuesday 25 May, the data council approves the plan: the 21 reports people read will move to the platform, and the 17 won't.
On Monday 31 May, the 17 are switched off, not deleted.
Until the old warehouse closes in December, any of them can be switched back on within a day.
GOV.UK did the same with its old pages: it didn't move them, it archived them, where they could still be found.
Sam, who answers the platform's alerts, goes through them with Noor and Jun, one kind at a time, asking: when this fires, what do we do?
Where the answer is nothing, the alert becomes a line in a summary each Monday morning.
By Monday 7 June, about 12 alerts a week reach Sam, and each one needs someone to act, with a note that says what to do.
The team chooses every cut, and any cut can be undone.
The word minimalism comes from art. In the United States in the 1960s, it named work pared down to its simplest forms.
For a team, two ideas from Japan come closer.
In Japanese aesthetics, kanso means simplicity: plain, with nothing extra.
And lean, which grew out of Japan's car factories, calls work that adds no value muda: waste.
But the team never calls anyone's work waste. Every report on that wall once answered someone's real question.
The designer Dieter Rams put the aim in three words: less, but better.
Less isn't the point. Better is: what stays gets the time, and gets better.
In June, the team measures what came back.
Each person has about five hours a week back from meetings. Across eight people, that's about one person's whole week, every week.
And every alert that reaches Sam now matters.
The time goes to the work people use: rebuilding on the platform the 21 reports they read, each with an owner.
To keep that time, they agree one rule: anything new needs a reader, a reason and an owner.
And at each quarterly review, everything goes back on the wall.
GOV.UK didn't try to fix every old page. It found what people needed, did less, and did it well.
Helena's team did the same. It kept what people use, and got a person's week back, every week.
On Monday, list everything your team runs and attends.
Ask who uses each thing, and for what.
Stop the rest together, and openly: switch it off, wait, then delete.
Measure the time you get back, and protect it.
The next film, One small change at a time, shows how to improve what you keep.
Keep what people use; stop the rest, together.

films.t: One small change at a time
films.x: Kaizen in a team. In July 2027 Ivy Reyes spends two hours every Monday checking her room data by hand, and until she's done, readers may see a wrong number. Helena Novak asks what's in the way and gives her the time. Ivy measures, drops what nobody needs, writes the rest down and automates one step at a time.
c: Colombo, Sri Lanka, in the year 2000.
At the Castle Street Hospital for Women, a public hospital where mothers come to give birth, the director is Dr Wimal Karandagoda.
Too many mothers there catch an infection after a Caesarean, a birth by operation, and too many newborn babies catch one too.
An infection is germs in a wound, or in a baby's body: fever and pain, days more in hospital, and real danger to mother and child.
And there's no money for a fix: at first, the ministry gives nothing for it.
The hospital has to get cleaner with what it already has.
The director brings in a way of working from Japanese factories, already used by companies in Sri Lanka: five steps, called 5S.
Sort out what isn't needed. Set the rest in order. Shine: clean it. Standardise: agree one way, and write it down. And sustain it.
It costs little, and everyone can see the change with their own eyes.
The staff of each ward do it themselves, starting with their own corner of the work.
Then comes kaizen: small changes the staff propose themselves, try, check, and keep or drop.
At first, not everyone wants it. Ward by ward, it spreads through the hospital.
In two years, infections after a Caesarean fall by half, and in newborn babies by more than half.
The way spreads to other hospitals in Sri Lanka, and from 2007, with Japan's aid agency, to public hospitals in fifteen African countries.
Nobody was told to work harder: the people who did the work improved it, a small step at a time.
Data work has its weekly chores too, and when they're done by hand, mistakes slip through and hours go.
The person who does the work can improve it the same way: one small change at a time, each one checked.
Since Thursday 1 July 2027, Ivy Reyes has owned Teaching space use: the team's data on how the university's rooms are used.
Its promise to its readers: refreshed every Monday by seven in the morning, with the week before's bookings and head counts.
At six, a job loads the week's data, and publishes the page.
Then, from half past eight, Ivy spends two hours checking it by hand, and fixing what she finds.
Until she's done, anyone who opens the page may read a number that's wrong. And her Monday morning is gone.
On Tuesday 20 July, at her mid-year conversation, Helena asks what she wants next.
Ivy has two answers: to make her Monday refresh better, and to teach what she learns.
Then Helena asks what's in the way. My Monday mornings, says Ivy: two hours of checks, every week.
So Helena gives it Ivy's Thursday learning time: two hours a week, already hers, now for this.
That's kaizen's first idea: improvement is everyone's job, on their own work, in small steps.
Each small step runs through one cycle: plan a change, do it, check it, then act: keep it, or drop it.
Walter Shewhart drew the cycle as a circle in 1939.
W. Edwards Deming taught it in Japan in 1950, where managers made it plan, do, check, act.
In 1986, Masaaki Imai's book took the Japanese word for this kind of improvement around the world: kaizen, change for the better.
Ivy starts by measuring. On Monday 26 July, she times each step of her refresh: six steps, a hundred and twenty minutes.
Like the staff at Castle Street, she starts with her own corner of the work, and asks of each step: who needs this?
Every Monday, she checks by hand fourteen rooms that once had two names.
But since April, a test in Jun's models has checked the same fourteen.
So one Monday she skips her check, and reads the test instead. It covers all fourteen. She keeps the change.
Then the copy she makes for Facilities: since July, Facilities reads the product's page. She asks, and drops the copy.
Two steps nobody needed are gone: ninety minutes.
Next, she writes the four steps left as one checklist: each step, in order, and what good looks like.
The same steps every Monday show her what changes, and let anyone do it.
To test the checklist, Jun follows it one Monday, and gets the same result in the same time.
Only then does she automate: automate a muddle, and you get a faster muddle.
In September, in her Thursday learning time, she turns one step a week into a check inside the job.
Sam reviews each change before it goes in. And each new check runs beside her own for a Monday, before her hand check goes.
Now the job checks the data before it publishes. If a check fails, the page keeps last week's numbers, and Ivy is told.
By October, her Monday refresh takes ten minutes, checked: she reads what the checks found, and writes a note to readers.
And nobody opens the page to a number that's wrong.
Helena made none of these changes herself. Her part was three things.
She asked what was in the way, each Tuesday. When Sam's week was full, she made room in it for the reviews.
She gave the time: Thursday afternoons, for this, and no meeting allowed to take them.
And she showed the small wins: at the review on Thursday 7 October, she put Ivy's chart in front of the people who use the product.
She named who did the work: Ivy, Jun and Sam.
No target, no programme, no speech about change: questions, time, and a chart.
From Friday 3 September, the team's Friday half-hour makes small changes a habit for everyone: one measure, one change a week.
The data management films tell that story; the data quality films tell one of their own.
At Castle Street, nobody waited for a big reform. The staff changed their own wards, a step at a time, and infections fell by half.
Ivy did the same with her Monday: two hours became ten minutes, checked.
On Monday, pick one chore of your own, and time each step.
Drop what nobody needs, and write the rest down, the same each time.
Automate one step at a time, and check each one before you trust it.
And if you lead, ask what's in the way, give the time, and show the small wins.
Change one small thing, check it, keep what works.

films.x: A team that holds. In February 2027 Helena Novak starts as the university's data manager. Before she judges anyone, she reads the team as a whole, and finds every night alert going to one person, Sam. The team pairs until four can answer them, so when Sam has to leave at a day's notice, nobody calls him.
c: Johannesburg, South Africa, in the 1930s.
In crowded yards of rooms near the city live women who have come from the countryside.
They earn what they can, washing, sewing and selling, for low and irregular pay.
Eight or ten of them, who know and trust each other, form a stokvel: a savings group.
At every meeting, each pays the same sum into one pot, and one member takes it all, in turn, until every member has had hers.
Few Black South Africans had a bank account then, or for decades after, under apartheid.
Banks wouldn't lend to them: their pay was low and irregular, and the law kept them from owning property a bank would take as security.
With no safe place to save and no one to borrow from, one funeral, a term's school fees or a lost wage could ruin a family.
Families needed a way to save and borrow. They didn't wait for a bank: they built their own, out of trust.
Each group agrees its rules together: how much to pay, how often to meet, whose turn comes next, and what happens if someone can't pay.
Every member answers to the others, and almost nobody fails to pay: being trusted is worth more than any one pot.
The most common kind, the burial society, carries a member's family through a funeral.
And when one member falls on hard times, the group carries her.
Behind it is an idea from Southern Africa, Ubuntu, and a saying in isiZulu: a person is a person through other people.
For decades, these groups were many families' savings, their credit and their safety net.
Today, by the National Stokvel Association's count, more than 11 million South Africans belong to one.
Together, they put in over 50 billion rand a year.
A team can hold its people the same way. When everyone pays in, nobody carries the work alone.
And when one of them has to step away, the group holds.
At a university, a year from now, Helena Novak starts as the data manager on Monday 1 February 2027.
Before she judges anyone, she watches.
Every week, she has half an hour with each person: about them, never a status report.
She asks how they are, what's in their way, and what they're proud of.
Then she reads the team as a whole: what it achieves together, and each person's work beside it.
She measures it all against what this team really does, not what her last team did.
Measured against her last team, they might look slow.
But this one takes requests in eleven different ways, and keeps a platform running day and night.
Managing and leading are both her job, but for Helena, leading weighs a little more, every time.
The people are the team's first strength, so their wellbeing comes first.
Wellbeing isn't only comfort. Sometimes one person needs more support, a better tool, encouragement or a push.
That way the team keeps working together, and no big gap opens.
In her first weeks, she finds the gap that matters most.
Every alert the platform raises at night goes to one person: Sam Okafor.
About sixty a week, most needing nothing, and only Sam knows how to answer them.
Sam doesn't complain. But the team leans on one person, and that person has nobody to lean on.
In April, Ivy Reyes, a new graduate analyst, reviews a model the team's agent drafted for her.
It counts booked hours as used ones, when used means people actually in the room.
She catches it, but only just.
At stand-up the next morning, she says it out loud: I nearly let it through.
Nobody blames her. Jun thanks her, and Helena asks what would make it easier to catch next time.
Ivy's answer: what used means, written in the glossary, so the next draft starts from it.
That week, two more people say what they nearly missed.
The researcher Amy Edmondson calls this psychological safety.
It means a shared belief that the team is safe for taking risks with each other, like admitting a mistake.
In hospital teams she studied, some nurses talked openly about mistakes with medicines, and how to avoid them.
In others, people kept them to themselves.
In 51 work teams, those that felt safer learned more, and the teams that learned more did better.
A mistake said out loud, and thanked, is one the whole team learns from.
By June, the platform's alerts are down to about twelve a week, and every one needs someone.
So the team pairs on the platform. Through June, Sam works beside Noor, Jun and Erin Walsh, the platform engineer, one alert at a time.
Each time they answer one together, they write down how: a runbook, step by step, that anyone on the team can follow.
By the end of June, four people can answer every night alert, not one.
From Monday 5 July, they share the nights in a rota, one week in four each.
Sam had answered alone every night until then. Now, three weeks in four, his phone stays quiet.
Across the team, two people can now do each job that matters most.
Desmond Tutu wrote that a person with Ubuntu does not feel threatened that others are able and good.
Sam taught three people his nights, and lost nothing by it.
On Sunday 1 August, Sam's mother is taken into hospital, and he calls Helena that evening.
She tells him to go, and to switch his phone off.
It's his week on the rota, and Jun and Erin take it between them.
Helena moves his other work: the platform's upgrade waits two weeks, and she tells the people who asked, with a new date.
Twice that fortnight, an alert comes in the night. Both are answered from the runbooks.
Nobody calls him.
When Sam comes back on Monday 16 August, Helena's first question is about his mother, not the platform.
Like a stokvel carrying a member through hard times, the team carried Sam, because everyone had paid in.
Every week, the one-to-ones go on, about each person, not their tasks.
In September, Jun says he's fine, but he's teaching two people, building models and taking his turn on the rota.
Helena moves one of his projects to November, and tells the people who asked, before the load can wear him down.
At the quarterly review in October, she gives the team the credit, by name, and answers herself for what slipped.
The team first, then each person, then herself.
Philosophers in South Africa, Mogobe Ramose and Thaddeus Metz among them, have written Ubuntu down as an ethic.
Metz reads it as two things held together: sharing a life with others, and caring how their lives go.
Helena's team shares the work, and cares how each of them is doing.
In a stokvel, everyone pays in, and everyone's turn comes. When one member falls on hard times, the group carries her.
Helena's team did the same: four people learned the nights, and when Sam had to go, nobody called him.
On Monday, pair until two people can do each job that matters most, and write down how.
Protect leave: when someone is away, nobody calls them.
Thank the person who says: I got it wrong.
In one-to-ones, ask how people are, not only what they did.
And if you're new, watch first: judge the team's shared work before anyone's own.
Nobody alone, nobody the only one who knows.

films.x: Letting people decide. From October 2027, the four faculties plan their own rooms from the data, instead of waiting two weeks for each report. Three rules, each with its reason, a template that makes the right way the easy way, and one box that says who decides what. Then Engineering finds what nobody had asked about.
c: Bali, Indonesia, in the 1970s.
For over a thousand years, rice farmers here have shared the water that runs down from the mountains.
Farmers who take water from one canal form a subak: a group that decides, together, how to share it.
Groups along a river meet at a water temple, and agree a calendar: who plants first, and who follows.
Planting in turns shares the water, so the fields downstream don't run dry.
And fields harvested together lie empty together, so the pests that live on rice go hungry.
Then the country set out to grow more rice, fast.
Farmers were told to plant new, quick-growing rice as often as they could, whatever the temples' calendar said.
The planners wanted the country fed, and the new rice gave more grain.
But with every field on its own clock, the pests always found rice next door.
A tiny insect, the brown planthopper, destroyed about two million tons of rice across Indonesia in 1977.
In the dry season, farms downstream waited for water that didn't come.
For a farming family, a lost harvest meant a season's food and income gone.
Someone had to show the planners what the temples already knew.
In the 1980s, the anthropologist Stephen Lansing and the ecologist James Kremer built a computer model of two rivers and their 172 subaks.
It showed that the temples' calendar gave the biggest harvests, balancing hungry pests against shared water.
In 1988 they took it to the bank that had paid for new irrigation works, and the bank agreed.
Officials let the temples set the planting again, and farmers were no longer told to plant as fast as they could.
The pests came under control, and farmers sprayed less.
The bank's final report said no project it had reviewed ran itself as well as Bali's.
And in 2012, UNESCO listed the subak landscape as World Heritage.
A data team can make the planners' mistake: every decision taken in one place, far from the work.
This film follows a team that gives the decisions back, and finds what no central plan had looked for.
A university, a year from now, in September 2027.
In June, the University Council asked for a new timetable from February, with fewer classes at peak hours, and put off a new building.
Each of the four faculties has a timetable officer who plans its classes.
To plan, they need to know which rooms are used, and when. That's in one data product: Teaching space use.
But only the data team worked with it, so every room question came to them.
From July to September, the faculties asked for 27 room reports.
Each took about a day and a half to make, and waited about two weeks in the list.
Helena Novak, the data manager, saw more: when two faculties asked at once, she chose whose rooms came first.
Every room decision in the university now passed through one small team, and through her.
The people who knew the courses were waiting for the people who knew the data.
So she decided to stop deciding: the faculties would read the data themselves.
Yusuf Demir, who leads data governance, drafted the rules for letting the faculties in.
His first list had eleven, each guarding against something that had gone wrong somewhere.
Of each, they asked: what goes wrong here, now, without it?
Three were needed now.
One: room use means one thing for everyone, the share of hours in which someone was counted, so the faculties' numbers add up.
Two: the product's promise holds: counts per room per hour, never a person, so nobody is watched.
Three: before you publish a new measure from it, ask its owner, Ivy, so each new number means one thing, written down first.
The other eight went in a drawer, to come out only when a real problem showed.
The political economist Elinor Ostrom studied fishing grounds, forests and irrigation that people had shared for centuries.
The ones that lasted had a few clear rules, fitted to the place, made and changed by the people who live by them.
Helena agreed the three with the four officers, not for them, and any of them can ask to change one.
Rules say what's right. Tools make it easy.
Ivy and Jun made a template: a page on the platform with booked hours beside counted ones, and room use worked out the agreed way.
An officer copies it, picks their faculty's rooms, and asks their own questions: an afternoon, not two weeks.
Anil, Health's data partner, sat with its officer for her first hour.
Beside the numbers, one box says who decides what.
The faculties decide their classes, and Ivy decides what the numbers mean.
The team keeps the platform, and the registrar's office keeps the timetable.
Data mesh and the book Team Topologies agree: decisions with the people who know the work, on a platform that makes the hard parts easy.
On Monday 4 October, the officers started, and the team stopped making room reports by hand.
Lucy Tran, Engineering's timetable officer, opened the template that Monday.
Engineering books its own teaching labs, so they had never been in the university's room reports.
The labs have sensors too, so Lucy put her faculty's lab bookings beside their counts.
Every Monday morning, nine of Engineering's twelve labs were booked, and the sensors counted nobody in them.
Nobody had asked: no report had ever put the two side by side.
Lucy knew who to ask: two first-year courses had moved their lab classes to Thursdays, and their Monday bookings had rolled over every year.
Lab use was a new measure, so before she shared it, Lucy asked Ivy.
Ivy wrote it in the glossary the same way as room use, and the team built it into the product, for every faculty.
Engineering released the nine Monday mornings, and put its request for two new labs on hold.
Then something nobody planned happened.
Within three weeks, Health had copied Lucy's page for its clinical skills rooms, and Arts for its studios.
One faculty's question had become three, and nobody had sent an instruction.
Lansing and Kremer saw the same in their model. Each year, every subak looked at its four nearest neighbours, and copied the best harvest.
Within about eight years, groups planting together appeared, much like the real temple networks, and harvests rose.
Nobody had drawn them.
By Friday 26 November, all four faculties had sent the registrar's office their plans for February.
Together, they moved one peak class in six, as the University Council had asked.
In October and November the team made no room reports by hand, and the time went back to the roadmap.
Helena's job changed too: less deciding, more watching what emerged, and asking what it taught.
One real problem did show: Health sent its heads of school a copy of its page from three weeks before, and two planned from old numbers.
So one rule came out of the drawer, with its reason: share the live page, not a copy, because copies go stale.
And the template now shows the date of its data in the corner.
Four rules, each with its reason, and still room to decide.
In Bali, nobody planned every field. Each subak decided its own work, a shared calendar timed it together, and the harvests held.
At the university, four officers planned their own rooms, a few rules kept the numbers true, and what nobody had looked for came to light.
On Monday, write few rules, each with its reason.
Make the right way the easy way.
Say who decides what.
Watch what emerges, and learn from it.
And add a rule only when a real problem shows.
A few clear rules, good tools, and trust.

films.x: Ownership. From July 2027 Ivy Reyes owns the university's room data. One Monday the refresh runs on time and every check passes, but forty rooms' counts have dropped. She says so first, fixes what's hers, raises what isn't, and nobody is blamed.
c: Kenya, in the 1970s.
In the hills of the central highlands, rural women tell Wangari Maathai, a biologist, what's going wrong.
Their streams are drying up. Their food is less sure. Each year, they walk further for firewood.
The forests had been cleared, for farms, for tea and coffee to sell, and for plantations of timber.
Each choice made sense to the people who made it.
But without trees, the soil washed off the hills, and the springs ran dry.
The women fetched the water, gathered the firewood and grew the food. So the harm fell first on them, and on their children.
Someone had to bring the trees back, and it would be the women.
In 1977, Maathai started the Green Belt Movement, with the National Council of Women of Kenya.
Groups of women grew seedlings in their own nurseries, from the seeds of local trees, and planted them out.
They were paid a small sum for each tree still alive months later, not for each seedling put in the ground.
So they answered for living trees, not for the planting.
Since then, more than fifty million trees have been planted in Kenya.
They give fuel, food and shelter, and thousands of women earned an income from them.
In 2004, Wangari Maathai became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
Data work has its seedlings too: a job that ran, a report that was sent.
Owning the outcome means answering for what they're for.
At the university, a year from now, Ivy Reyes becomes the owner of her first data product, on Thursday 1 July.
Teaching space use: for every teaching room and every hour, what was booked, and how many people came. Counts, never people.
Zhamak Dehghani's data mesh calls her the data product owner: she answers for what the product does for its readers.
A product with an owner shows how a product gets one. This film is about the owning.
Its promise: refreshed every Monday by seven, with the week before.
Ivy knows its readers by name: Graham Ellis at Facilities, and Mei Tanaka at the registrar's office, with their teams.
And she knows what it's for: next year's timetable will move about one peak class in six, and release rooms nobody uses.
Which ones, they'll choose from her counts.
So what Ivy owns isn't Monday's job. It's that the timetable change is judged on true counts.
Many people do part of the work. Facilities keeps the sensors, Sam the platform, and Jun reviews her changes.
One person answers for the outcome. In a RACI chart, that's the A, for accountable, and there's only one.
Helena gives her the authority to match.
Ivy can hold a refresh, change the model with a review, and tell the readers, without asking first.
On Tuesday 17 August, Facilities upgrades the sensors in forty rooms.
The new ones send a count every quarter of an hour, not once an hour. More detail: a real improvement.
Nobody expects it to change the data, so nobody tells the data team.
On Monday 23 August, the refresh runs at seven, as promised. Every check passes.
At the Green Belt, a seedling in the ground earned nothing until it lived.
So Ivy reads the numbers, not only the tick.
In forty rooms, from Tuesday the seventeenth, the counts have dropped to about a quarter.
In those rooms, booked hours with nobody in them jump from one in five to more than half.
If nobody noticed, the timetable team would release rooms that classes really use.
Ivy doesn't wait to be sure, or to be asked.
At ten past eight, she writes to the readers: the counts for forty rooms look wrong; don't use them yet; the right ones by tomorrow.
Saying it first, before the fix, is part of owning it.
With Sam, she opens the feed for one room.
Since Tuesday, four counts arrive each hour. The model was built for one.
A step meant to drop the odd repeat kept the first count of each hour, and dropped the other three.
The first comes as one class leaves and the next arrives, so the rooms looked nearly empty.
The fix is hers: keep the hour's highest count, as the old sensors sent.
Jun reviews her pull request, as someone other than its author reviews every change.
The days since Tuesday are run again, and on Tuesday morning the readers have the right counts, with a short note.
What happened, what it touched, what's fixed, and what changes.
Some of it isn't hers to fix. The sensors are Facilities'.
So she raises it with Graham. From now on, Facilities tells the data team before a sensor changes.
And she adds a check of her own: each room's counts against its own last four weeks.
A drop like this one now holds the refresh, and tells her, before anyone reads it.
Nobody here did anything wrong.
Facilities made the sensors better. Sam's platform loaded every count. The step was right for the data it was built for.
Each was right about what they saw. What failed was the way the parts fit together.
Sidney Dekker calls it a just culture: when something goes wrong, ask what happened and what must change, not who to blame.
Helena's first question isn't who. It's what happened, and what Ivy needs.
That's why Ivy could say it first: where nobody is blamed, saying it early is safe.
Being accountable means giving an account: what happened, and how the next time goes better.
The women of the Green Belt answered for trees still standing months later, not for the planting.
Ivy answers for true counts, not for a job that ran. In June 2029, the timetable change will be judged on them.
On Monday, know who uses your work, and for which decision.
Watch what it's for, not only whether it ran.
When something's wrong, say so first, even before the fix.
Fix what's yours, raise what isn't, and mend how the parts fit together, never blaming a person.
Measure the work, not the people, the next film, asks how a team can tell its work is getting better.
Own what it's for, not only what you did.

films.t: Measure the work, not the people
films.x: Measures for learning. In 2027 the university's data team reads its measures together every second Thursday, and Helena asks what slowed the work, never who. Waits in how the work was arranged are found and removed, each measure is read beside one that balances it, and asked to count each person's tickets, she says no.
c: In 1997, 541 people died on Sweden's roads.
Most crashes were put down to a driver's mistake.
So the answer was to teach drivers, fine them, and blame them.
But people always make mistakes. A tired driver drifts over the middle line.
On a fast road, that mistake could kill. For hundreds of families a year, it meant someone who never came home.
Blaming drivers wasn't saving lives. The roads had to forgive their mistakes.
In October 1997, Sweden's parliament adopted Vision Zero: no one should be killed or seriously injured on the roads.
Those who design and run the roads would answer for that, not only drivers.
Every fatal crash was studied in depth, to ask how it could have been prevented.
Many people died in head-on crashes, on fast roads with two lanes.
So from 1998, those roads got a barrier of steel cables down the middle.
Roundabouts replaced crossroads, and speeds came down where people walk.
On roads given a middle barrier, deaths fell by about three quarters.
Across the country, while traffic grew, road deaths fell by more than half.
Drivers still had to take care. But a mistake no longer had to cost a life.
Sweden stopped asking who to blame, and measured the roads, to find what in them to fix.
Data work is the same: when work is slow, the cause is usually in how it flows, not in who did it.
Measure the work, read it together, and you find what to fix.
At the university, a year from now, Helena Novak is the data manager.
Managing and leading are two sides of her one role. It did harm to call one good, and the other old-fashioned.
What's hard to see is hard to improve for long. So a leader measures, and there are always dates and plans to keep.
That is management, but it has to fit the work: hours or tickets per person say little about thinking work.
From July, the team's page of measures, from the data management module, shows how the work flows.
Days from a request to its first use: 41 in February, 24 by June.
Sent back: how often work comes back for changes.
Promises met: how often the team's data products keep their promise.
And load: pieces of work open at once, against the team's limit of six.
Each measure has a partner that balances it: speed beside sent back, promises beside load.
Every second Thursday from 15 July, the team reads the page together, for twenty minutes.
Helena asks one question: what slowed the work? Never, who was slow?
In Sweden, they asked what in a road let a mistake kill. Helena asks the same of the work.
At the first reading, they take June's 24 days apart.
Seven of them were spent waiting for access to the data.
Access was asked for only when work started, one dataset at a time, up to five days each.
Nobody was slow. The wait was in how the work was arranged.
From Monday 19 July, access is asked for the day a request is accepted, so it's ready when work starts.
By September, that wait is down from seven days to one.
A second cause: one piece of work in eight came back, read one way and meant another.
Now, before work starts, fifteen minutes with the person who asked agrees what done looks like.
By December, the days are down to 14, and sent back has halved, to 6 in 100.
Most of the gain came from waits like these, found and removed one at a time.
On Thursday 12 August, promises met has reached 82%, up from 58 in March.
On its own, a number to celebrate.
But load stands at nine pieces of work open at once, against a limit of six.
New work had started before old work finished: the team kept its promises by carrying too much.
That can't last: tired people make mistakes.
So the team finishes before it starts: nothing new begins until something open is done.
Two requests get a not now, with a reason and a date.
By mid-September, load is back to six, and promises met keeps rising, to 86% in December.
Accelerate's research, in 2018, found the best teams fast and stable at once, measured side by side.
Each pair keeps the other honest. Speed without sent back can hide rushed work. Promises without load can hide tired people.
On Monday 13 September, the director of digital services, Helena's manager, asks for something new.
A count of tickets closed by each person, each month.
The director wants to know if the team is getting faster, and if anyone needs help: fair questions.
In 1975, the economist Charles Goodhart saw that a number pushed to move stops meaning what it did.
Marilyn Strathern put it plainly: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
Count tickets per person, and people split work small, pick easy tickets, and stop helping each other. And mistakes get hidden.
The SPACE framework warns the same: a count of activity never shows, alone, how well people work.
And W. Edwards Deming estimated that about 94 in 100 problems belong to the system, not to the people in it.
So Helena says no to the count, and shows what instead: the team's page, and what its readings changed.
How each person grows stays in their own goals, agreed with her.
The director takes the page to the quarterly review. No one is ranked.
Sweden stopped blaming drivers one by one, measured its roads, and fixed what turned a mistake into a death.
Helena's team measured how its work flowed, read it together, and fixed what slowed it.
On Monday, measure the flow of the work: days to first use, work sent back, promises met, and load.
Pair each measure with one that balances it.
Read them together, often, and ask what slowed the work, never who.
When someone asks for a number to rank people by, say no, and show the team's flow instead.
When someone falls behind, the next film, looks at the harder case: one person's work, and what surrounds it.
Measure the work together. Fix the system, not the people.

films.x: When work falls behind. In 2027 the university's data team moves its reports onto the platform, and gets faster. Tomás Ortega, who built most of the old reports, speeds up less, and unevenly. Before judging, Helena asks what's in his way, clears it, and reads his gap against the team's own change, over months.
c: Fremont, California, in 1982.
General Motors closes its car plant there, and thousands of workers lose their jobs.
The plant had a name as one of the worst in the country.
On a normal day, one worker in five didn't come in, and complaints ran into the thousands.
Cars left the line with parts missing, or fitted wrong.
Many said the problem was the workers.
For the people who bought those cars, it meant faults to fix. For the workers, it meant no job, and a name that followed them.
Blaming the workers hadn't fixed a single car.
In 1984, General Motors and Toyota reopen the plant together, as NUMMI.
More than eight in ten of its new workers are the same people, hired back.
Groups of thirty fly to a Toyota plant in Japan, and work beside the people there for two weeks.
Back in Fremont, they work in small teams, and a team leader steps in whenever something goes wrong.
Anyone can pull a cord above the line to call for help. If the problem isn't fixed, the line stops.
Within two years, its cars have about as few faults as those Toyota builds in Japan.
Absence and complaints fall steeply. One study found the old way would need half as many workers again to build the same car.
Managers had seen the absences. Workers had seen a line that never stopped, and nobody to help. Both were right about what they saw.
The same people, in a different system, did some of the best work in the country.
When someone's work falls behind, look first at what surrounds them.
What they were taught, what's in their way, and what they're asked to do.
At the university, a year from now, the data team moves its reports off the old warehouse.
Each report is now written as code on the platform, and reviewed before anyone reads it.
The team's days from a request to first use fall from 41 in February to 24 by June.
Tomás Ortega, the report developer, built most of the old reports. He knows every one, and who reads it.
His work speeds up too, but less, and unevenly: some weeks keep pace with the team, others go back for changes.
Helena Novak, the data manager, first read the team as a whole, as The team comes first showed.
Its shared work is going well. One person's is falling behind it.
Before she judges, she asks.
Two old books give her the questions.
Robert Mager and Peter Pipe asked: could they do it if they had to? If not, it's a skill. If they could, something is in the way.
Thomas Gilbert said: look at what surrounds the work, its information, its tools and its rewards, before you look at the person.
In his one-to-one on Wednesday 26 May, Helena asks Tomás what's getting in his way.
The first cause is training. The tools changed, and nobody taught them.
The others learned by doing, while Tomás kept the old reports running.
So he pairs with Jun twice a week, and his Thursday learning time is protected. He'd been giving it up to clear his list.
The second is fit for the role. His strength is the people who read the reports, more than the code behind them.
So the readers' release notes and their training become his, while he keeps building.
In June, he tells Helena he's having a hard time at home. Nobody needs to know more.
That's a good reason too, and it asks for patience. For two months his load is lighter, and nobody asks for more.
