At NUMMI, pulling the cord brought help, not blame. Helena's part is the same: clear what's in the way.
Amy Edmondson calls it psychological safety: people say what's wrong when it's safe to.
How far behind is he? Not behind Helena's expectations: behind the team.
In February, before the move, Tomás took 40 days from a request to first use. The team took 41.
By June, the new tools had brought the team to 24. Tomás was at 35.
He had improved. The team had improved faster, because the tools lifted everyone.
So his gap is read against the team's own change, never against a colleague, and it stays between him and Helena.
Tomás writes his own plan: what he'll learn, by when, and what he needs. Helena agrees it.
They read it together on the first Wednesday of each month.
The gains come unevenly. September goes well. In October, a report goes back twice.
By December, the team is at 14 days, and Tomás at 20. The gap has closed by about half.
On Wednesday 15 December, Helena says it plainly: the plan goes on into 2028.
And if building reports stops being where he's strongest, they'll talk about a role that fits him better. He hears it now, not later.
Lifting someone's work can take months, or even years. Patience is part of the plan.
Through all of it, his measures are his own, and his reasons stay private.
At NUMMI, the people didn't change first. What surrounded them did, and then their work did.
Helena did the same: she found the causes, cleared what she could, and gave it time.
On Monday, read the team's shared work before anyone's own.
Ask before you judge, and look for the cause: training, fit, or a hard time.
Clear the blockers first, and measure against the team's change, not your expectations.
Let them write the plan, read it each month, and say honestly where it's going.
Growing people, the next film, follows the everyday case: goals, feedback, and a next step.
Find the cause, clear the way, and give it time.

films.x: How people grow at work. In 2027 Ivy Reyes joins the university's data team, in her first job. Helena Novak asks her to write her own goals, gives her feedback every Tuesday about the work and what it changed, asks for feedback on herself, and looks forward with her to a next step with more to own.
c: Japan, in 1872. The new government sets out to give every child a school.
Teaching is new work, with new subjects and new methods, and few teachers are trained for it.
By 1877, four schools in ten have a single teacher, and nearly one in three has a single classroom.
A teacher alone with a class can't see what each child has understood, and nobody sees the lesson to help.
When a lesson loses the children, they fall behind, and the teacher may never learn why.
Teachers needed other eyes on their lessons.
Teachers opened their classrooms to each other.
From the first year, new teachers learned by watching lessons, and teachers formed groups to learn together.
A visitor watched the children, not the teacher: how they answered, whether they were interested, and whether the questions suited them.
Afterwards, in a reflection session, they talked about what the children had learned, and where they got stuck.
In the 1880s, the groups began lesson study: jugyō kenkyū, in Japanese.
Teachers choose a goal, and plan a lesson together.
One teaches it, while the others watch the children. Then they improve it, for next time.
Lesson study spread to schools across Japan. Today, 99 in 100 primary teachers there say they took part in the past year.
After 1999, a book about it carried it to many countries.
In a trial in the United States, 39 teams of teachers were split at random.
Some used it for about three months, with research on how children learn fractions.
Their students understood fractions better than those of teams who trained another way.
At work, a new analyst can be alone too: nobody sees her work until it's done, and she hears how she's doing once a year, as a grade.
People grow as those teachers did: with goals they help set, feedback every week about the work and its effect, and a next step.
At the university, a year from now, Ivy Reyes joins the data team on Monday 1 March. It's her first job, after a degree in statistics.
Helena Novak, the data manager, doesn't hand her a list of goals.
She asks Ivy to write three of her own, in her first week. On Friday 5 March, they agree them.
One: to know the whole route of one question's data, by Easter.
Two: to have a pull request merged, by May.
Three: to own a data product, by the middle of the year.
Helena's part is real work to grow on: a question from Graham Ellis, the Director of Facilities, about the teaching rooms.
Her goals are her own. The team's measures stay the team's, and never become her targets.
Like the teachers choosing their goal, she chose what to grow in.
On Thursday 25 March, the first goal is met: the whole route of Graham's question, from his decision back to the sensors, on one page.
Every Tuesday, Ivy and Helena meet for thirty minutes. It's Ivy's time, about her, and never a status report.
In 1996, Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi brought together more than six hundred results on feedback.
On average, feedback helped. But more than a third of the time, it made the work worse.
It helped least when it turned attention from the task to the person.
So Helena's feedback has three parts. The Center for Creative Leadership calls them situation, behaviour and impact.
Tuesday 13 April. Last Wednesday, reviewing the agent's draft, you checked it against Graham's own word for “used”.
So his answer counts people in rooms, not bookings.
Not “you're brilliant”, which is about who she is: what she did, and what it changed.
Hard feedback works the same way. Kim Scott's Radical Candor, in 2017, puts it as: care personally, and challenge directly.
Tuesday 25 May. Last week, you kept your change to yourself for four days, to make it perfect.
Jun had one afternoon to review it, so the review was rushed.
Ask for a review when it works, not when it's perfect.
Small and often, while the work is fresh. Nothing waits for a review once a year.
Helena asks for feedback on herself too: what should I do differently?
In June, Ivy tells her: when I bring you a question, you answer it at once, and I stop looking.
Helena thanks her. From then on, she first asks what Ivy has tried.
In lesson study, the group planned the lesson together, so the talk afterwards is about the lesson and the children's learning.
On Thursday 24 June, the University Council puts off the new teaching building, and Graham writes to thank Helena.
At the next review, she reads his note to the team.
She says who did each part: Ivy's route, Jun's models, Sam's sensors, and Mei's bookings.
The credit is the team's, in public.
From Thursday 1 July, Ivy owns her first data product: Teaching space use, the counts per room per hour, refreshed every Monday by seven.
On Tuesday 20 July, they look back at her half year, and forward. All three goals are met.
What went well: Graham's page for the University Council. What she'd do differently: ask for review earlier.
And what she wants next: to make her Monday refresh better, and to teach what she learns.
A growth conversation looks forward: where she wants to go, and what she needs to get there.
On Tuesday 14 December, she has owned Teaching space use for nearly six months.
Her next goal is one she chose: to coach the next graduate, in 2028.
Analyst, then owner, then coach: each step with more to own.
In Japan's schools, teachers have grown this way for a century and a half.
A goal they chose, eyes on the children's learning, and a better lesson next time.
Helena did the same for Ivy: goals of her own, feedback every week about the work, and the next step.
On Monday, let people write their own goals, then agree them.
Give feedback every week: the situation, what they did, and its effect.
Ask for feedback on yourself, and act on it.
Look forward in growth conversations, and give the team the credit, in public.
Data work needs new skills. Leading the people who do it is a skill too.
Their goals, weekly feedback about the work, the next step.

films.x: A first ninety days. On her first day, in February 2027, Helena Novak finds 46 open requests. She places them on DAMA-DMBOK's wheel of data management, finds who on her team is deep in each area, and by Friday has her first ninety days on one page, in three lanes: people, strategy and operations.
c: Chile, the Atacama desert, 5 August 2010.
Thirty-three miners are at work deep in the San José mine, a copper and gold mine near Copiapó.
That afternoon the rock gives way: a block of about seven hundred thousand tonnes closes the ramp, their road out.
They are trapped about seven hundred metres down, with a small shelter and emergency food for two or three days.
Above, nobody knows if they are alive. Their families come to the mine's gate, and wait.
Without help, the men will starve down there, and their families may never know what happened.
They have to be found, and brought up, before it's too late.
That takes drilling, medicine, food, engineering and the families' trust, all at once, and any one plan could fail.
The government puts a mining engineer, André Sougarret, in charge of the rescue.
Each part has someone who knows it: engineers on the drills, doctors on the men's health, ministers with the families.
The families wait at a camp by the gate, which they call Esperanza, hope.
Underground, the shift foreman, Luis Urzúa, holds the thirty-three together.
Food meant for two or three days is shared out to last two weeks.
Decisions are put to a vote, and each man has a job: one cares for the sick, one leads prayers, one keeps a diary.
On day seventeen, a narrow drill comes back up with a note tied to it: "We are well in the shelter, the 33."
Through that hole go food, water, medicine and letters, in tubes they call palomas, doves.
Meanwhile, three big drills work at once, each a different way, so the rescue never hangs on one.
On 9 October, one of them breaks through.
On 13 October, after sixty-nine days, all thirty-three come up, one by one, in a narrow capsule.
Their families, at the camp since August, have them back.
No one person drilled, doctored and fed them. Each part had someone who knew it, and every part ran at once.
A data manager's work is calmer, but it's shaped the same way.
Helena Novak starts at a university with forty-six requests, from every area of data, and someone waiting on each.
By Friday she has one plan for her first ninety days, in three lanes, run side by side.
And everyone waiting hears where their request stands.
These films follow one data manager's first year: every area of data at once, and the management work around it.
Monday 1 February 2027, a year from now, at the university.
Helena Novak starts as its data manager. She has been an architect, a data lead and a product owner.
Forty-six requests are open, in the tracker and in the team's inboxes.
The oldest has waited since 14 August 2026.
A report for Planning, a fix to the staff list, access for a researcher: each has someone waiting.
It's tempting to start with the oldest, or the loudest, or to change everything at once.
Helena does none of that yet. First, she sorts them, to see the whole job.
Data managers share a map of the job: the wheel in DAMA-DMBOK, the Data Management Association's body of knowledge.
Data governance sits at its centre, with ten areas around it, from architecture and modelling to quality and security.
Helena puts each request on the wheel, where most of its work is.
Data warehousing and business intelligence: ten. Data quality: seven. Data security: five.
Then governance and integration, four each, and three or fewer in each of the rest: forty-four in all.
Two sit beside the wheel: an agent for timetable questions, and a forecast model, which this site doesn't teach yet.
Most requests touch three or four areas: a new report needs its data modelled, checked for quality, and kept safe.
So no request is someone else's. The areas are one system, and the job holds all of them.
The site's other films go deep in each area.
From words to data in modelling, Fit for use in quality, The same one, everywhere in master data, and more.
Nobody is expert in all eleven areas, Helena included.
And her job holds the work every manager does: strategy, money, risk, people, stakeholders and delivery.
So she finds who is deep in each.
Noor, the data architect, in architecture and modelling. Sam, in the platform, storage and integration.
Jun, in the warehouse and its reports. Yusuf, in governance, metadata and quality.
Where no one on the team is deep, she writes that down too.
Her part is to see the areas as one system, know who is deep in each, and decide where to start.
The generalist's skill, seeing the whole, has its own film: Many hats, one picture.
For her first three months, she borrows a shape from Michael Watkins's book, The First 90 Days: learn fast, and secure early wins.
Her plan has three lanes, run side by side: people, strategy and operations.
People, all twelve weeks: the team, the data's owners, and the people who use it.
Strategy, in three steps: discover what is, define what should be, and plan how to get there.
Each step ends on a date she can be held to: 15 March, 5 April and 26 April.
Operations keeps today's work going while she learns.
The first two weeks, the urgent problems. From 15 February, delivery in two-week sprints, with the team's procedures as they are.
Only in week six does she propose better ways, and she tests them in weeks nine to twelve.
Don't change everything on day one, and don't wait ninety days to help.
At the mine, the big drills took weeks, but food went down the narrow hole the whole time.
On Friday, the plan fits on one page.
She shows it to David Mensah, the deputy vice-chancellor, and then to her team.
It promises no fix before she has listened, and dates she can be held to.
Everyone waiting on a request hears where it stands, and by the end of the ninety days, each has an answer.
In the Atacama, every part of the rescue had someone who knew it, and all thirty-three came up.
Helena's ninety days work the same way: every area is one job, and no one waits without an answer.
On Monday, keep today's work running while you learn.
Put your plan on one page, in three lanes, with dates you can be held to.
Learn each area's words, and who on your team is deep in each.
What Helena does first is listen. That's the next film.
See every area as one job; plan ninety days in three lanes.

films.x: Discovery, before design. In February 2027 Helena Novak becomes the university's data manager. Before designing anything, she spends six weeks listening: 31 people asked the same three questions, the strategy read, the systems counted. By 15 March the current state is in five layers, and sent back to everyone she heard.
c: Accra, in the early 1930s, on the Gold Coast, then a British colony, now Ghana.
Cicely Williams, a doctor from Jamaica, cares for the Ga people's children, with their mothers.
Children of one to four were falling sick: their hands and feet swelled, their skin peeled, and they wasted away.
Unless it was treated early, it nearly always killed them.
Many doctors took it for pellagra, a disease of a missing vitamin; treated that way, children kept dying.
Williams couldn't find it in any medical book.
The answer would have to come from outside the books.
So she listened: to mothers and grandmothers, to nurses and healers.
For three years, nobody said its name in front of her: the word was feared.
Then the mothers told her: kwashiorkor.
In Ga, the disease of the displaced child: the one moved from the breast when the next baby comes.
It came when that child ate little but maize.
Williams described it in 1933, and two years later gave it the mothers' word.
Three children she saw early were given milk, eggs and fruit, and each went home apparently cured.
Doctors everywhere still call it by the mothers' name.
They once blamed too little protein; today they know it's more than that.
But the mothers had seen when it comes.
Data is the same: the people who live with a problem often know it best.
A year from now, at a university, a request for data takes 41 working days, on average, to be used, and nobody sees the whole picture.
Its new data manager listens first: 31 people, three questions, and what the systems count.
Six weeks on, everyone can see where things stand, in their own words, with seven ways to do better.
February 2027. Helena Novak is the university's new data manager.
Her plan for ninety days starts with six weeks of listening.
Thirty-one conversations, from the deputy vice-chancellor to each of her own team.
She asks everyone the same three questions.
What do you decide?
What data do you trust?
What slows you down?
Asked of everyone, the same questions give answers she can lay side by side.
She goes to where people work: the registrar's counter, Finance, Facilities.
Lean thinking calls it go and see, genchi genbutsu: the real place, and the real thing.
She writes down what she hears in people's own words, as Williams kept the mothers' word.
Clara, in Planning: “I ask for one number, and I get three.”
Ingrid, in HR: “Our staff list is right. It's the copies.”
Anil, in the Faculty of Health: “I keep my own spreadsheet. I can't wait.”
Mei, at the registrar's office: “Our Thursday fifteen minutes works. Keep it.”
Graham Ellis, in Facilities, emails for a dashboard of room use by Easter: it waits its turn with the rest.
The leading data people module follows that one request, in The question behind the request.
Before proposing anything, she reads what's already written.
The university's strategy to 2030 has four goals:
students who succeed, research that reaches people, a campus used well, and finances that last.
The digital strategy serves it, and measures data quality, integration and satisfaction.
An earlier assessment found twelve decisions the university makes with data every year.
The budget, casual staff, the timetable and rooms, which courses to offer, research reporting, and seven more.
Every answer she hears can now be tied to a decision, and every decision to a goal.
People show where it hurts; the systems show how much.
The tracker: for the requests closed in February, 41 working days, on average, from the ask to first use.
The old warehouse's own logs: 38 reports, on the university's own servers since 2012.
Seventeen haven't been opened in a year.
The other 21 are used, by about 260 people.
It costs 310,000 Australian dollars a year, and its licence ends on 31 December.
Laid beside what people said, three findings stand out.
Requests arrive in eleven ways, from two inboxes to the agents' queue.
The staff list lives in three copies: HR's, the warehouse's, and a faculty's spreadsheet.
And about 40 people in faculties and offices do data work part of their week, mostly in spreadsheets.
One thing already works: since January 2026, the graduation list's team has met for fifteen minutes every Thursday.
Reprinted certificates fell from 41 to 3.
The data quality module tells how.
Write down what works too, so nobody breaks it.
Then she writes down what is: the current state, or, as TOGAF's method calls it, the baseline.
She writes it in the five layers architects use, each a page, with its picture beside it.
Strategy: the four goals, and what the university must be able to do. Governing data works; delivering it is slow.
Business: the twelve decisions, the services people can ask for, the processes, and who does what.
Its ways of working too: eleven ways to ask, and 41 working days to first use.
Information: what the data is about, and where each piece is born.
Staff are born in HR's system, then copied twice.
Application: the systems and reports, the old warehouse's 38 beside the platform's.
Technology: where they run, the university's own servers and the cloud.
ArchiMate, the architects' notation, has no information layer:
it keeps what the data is about in its business layer, and the data itself in its application layer.
Helena gives information a layer of its own, because data is her job.
Noor puts each page on her map, ready for the target.
The map before the data shows that map, in Today, and where it's going.
Any finding could read as someone's fault.
So she writes each one as an opportunity.
Not “requests get lost”, but one way to ask.
Not “faculties keep their own copies”, but data partners in faculties and offices.
Seven opportunities in all: one way to ask; retire the old warehouse; an owner for every report and product;
data partners; measure delivery; write down the critical procedures; and agents with mandates.
Monday, 15 March: the discovery milestone.
The current state in five layers, and seven opportunities.
She sends a summary back to everyone she spoke to: this is what I heard; tell me what I got wrong.
A few write back, and the pages change.
In Accra, the mothers knew their children's sickness, and when it came; Williams asked, and wrote it in their word.
At the university, the people who live with data knew too: in their words, the current state is one they recognise.
Next, she designs the target with them.
Ask people, count from the systems, and write down what is.

films.x: Define the target state. In March 2027 Helena Novak and her team design the target state: five principles, each with what it rules out; the target in five layers; a small team in the middle with seven data partners around it; six procedures of a page each, tried by one partner first; and one front door.
c: Korea, in the 1440s: the kingdom of Joseon, under King Sejong.
Its people wrote in Chinese characters: a sign for each word, thousands of them, made for another language.
Learning them took years, so most people couldn't write down what they wanted to say.
In a court, a person's words were written down in characters they couldn't read.
One wrong character could punish someone innocent, and they had no way to check.
Writing couldn't stay a skill for the few.
King Sejong started from what people needed: to write the way they speak.
In 1443 he made 28 letters, the consonants drawn from the mouth and throat as they make each sound.
Five basic shapes, and a stroke added for a stronger sound.
The vowels come from three marks: a dot for heaven, a flat line for the earth, a standing line for a person.
Put together a syllable at a time, they write any word.
One of his own scholars, Choe Manri, objected: it would turn people away from learning in characters.
The king argued for it, and in 1446 published the letters, with a book eight of his scholars wrote to explain them.
Its closing words say a quick learner can know them before the morning is over, and anyone within ten days.
Today we call them Hangul, and both Koreas write with them; in the South, about 98 adults in 100 can read and write.
Data is the same: a design people can learn in a morning is a design they use.
A year from now, at a university, there are eleven ways to ask for data, three copies of the staff list, and 41 working days to wait.
Its new data manager and team design the target simply: five principles, a small team with partners, six procedures, one front door.
Simple enough that anyone there can learn it in a morning.
March 2027. Helena Novak, the university's data manager, has the current state on the wall, in five layers.
Next in her ninety days: define the target, the state to reach, by Monday 5 April.
Before drawing anything, she and the team write the rules they'll design by: five principles.
One: start from the decision. Nothing is built without a decision behind it.
Two: one copy, governed once. No private copies of the things everyone shares.
Three: owners in the business, builders beside them. The data team doesn't decide what other people's data means.
Four: simple before clever. No new tool where one they have will do.
Five: measure what people use, not how busy the team is.
Each says what it rules out: a principle nothing could fail can't settle a choice.
The map before the data tests principles like these, in Why it moves.
Anyone can check a choice against them, without asking Helena.
A tool of their own for the faculties? The platform the team already runs will do.
A copy of the staff list for each faculty? One list, governed once, read by everyone allowed to.
Five shapes made every letter; five principles can shape every choice.
Then Helena and Noor, the data architect, draw the target on Noor's map, in the same five layers.
Strategy: the same four goals; delivering data becomes quick, and reporting happens in one place.
Business: the same twelve decisions, served by a small team in the middle, data partners around it, six procedures and one front door.
Information: one governed copy of each thing, with an owner in the business. One staff list, not three.
Application: one platform for data and reports, its catalog, and agents, each with a written mandate. The old warehouse is gone.
Technology: the platform, in the cloud; the old warehouse's servers, switched off.
Each page has its picture, drawn with it, never after.
Drawn together, every system and every copy has a decision behind it.
How to keep one copy of the people and things everyone shares: The same one, everywhere.
How each product keeps its promise: A product with an owner.
Who builds what? Today the university has the worst of two designs.
At the centre, one queue: 41 working days.
At the edges, people who can't wait keep their own copies: three staff lists, and numbers that disagree.
Helena designs the way between, as data mesh and Piethein Strengholt describe it.
A small team in the middle keeps the platform, the standards, the shared products and the guardrails, and it helps.
Seven data partners, in four faculties and three offices, build their own area's products with the team's tools.
Each spends about a day a week on it, given by their dean or director.
The leading data people module tells how a leader lets people decide.
She sends the draft to everyone she spoke to. A head of school writes back: partners take people away from teaching.
It's a fair worry, and the design answers it.
About 40 people already do data work part of their week, in spreadsheets.
A partner's day is that same work, planned by the dean, and done with the team's tools and help.
A good design still has to be argued for, as the king argued for his letters.
How the work flows: six procedures, a page each. Ask, choose, build, release, fix, retire.
Each page names who asks, who decides, who builds and who checks, its steps, and what it leaves behind.
And each has its picture: the four roles, and how the work passes between them.
It all starts at one front door: one form, five questions.
What decision? By when? Who decides? What data do you use already? Who else needs it?
It opens on Monday 7 June.
Behind it are governance's services too, each with its promise, as in A capability, not a project.
Before everyone uses them, one partner tries them.
Anil, in the Faculty of Health, kept his own spreadsheet because he couldn't wait.
Now he builds Health's report of casual teaching hours by the build page, from the one staff list.
Step four said: the team checks it.
His change waited four working days: everyone thought someone else had it.
So step four now names one reviewer, from a rota, within two working days: never the person who built it.
Tried by one partner, fixed before everyone.
Monday 5 April: the define milestone.
The target in five layers, each with its picture; five principles; a small team and seven partners; six pages; one door.
Every part fits on a page: a design simple enough to explain is simple enough to run.
In April, Anil becomes the first data partner.
In 1446, the king's letters could be learned in a morning, so people used them, and wrote their own words.
At the university, a design anyone can learn in a morning is one people use: to ask, to build, and to check.
Next, the gaps between today and the target become a roadmap.
Start from the decision; design the fewest parts that serve it.

films.x: Planning, in stages. In April 2027 Helena and the team set today's state beside the target and find nine gaps. They turn them into six work packages, each with an owner and a date, and three stages that each work on their own. On 27 April the data council approves a data strategy on one page.
c: Switzerland, in the 1970s: a country of valleys and small towns, joined by its railways.
More people drove, on new motorways: in ten years, the railways' share of travel fell from over a quarter to a sixth.
Trains left at different times every hour, and a change of trains could mean a long wait on the platform.
For people without a car, students, workers and older people, every trip meant looking up times, and waiting.
Fewer people rode, and the railways ran at a loss.
In 1972, three young railway engineers wrote that the trains no longer fit what people wanted, and the timetable was the heart of it.
The railways' own plan, new fast lines across the country, would cost billions, and in the early 1980s it was dropped.
With no money for new lines, the trains had to win people back another way.
From 23 May 1982, the trains ran by the clock: every line, every hour, at the same minutes past.
Then the railways turned planning around: Rail 2000 started from the timetable people wanted.
In the big stations, the hubs, trains from every direction would arrive just before the hour and leave just after, so everyone could change.
Where the trains between two hubs were too slow to arrive in time, that stretch was a gap.
Only the gaps would be built.
Its slogan: as fast as necessary, not as fast as possible.
Voters approved it on 6 December 1987.
When the costs rose, it was built in stages, and the first kept one new line of four: the one the timetable needed most.
On 12 December 2004, the first stage opened: about 130 projects, with the new line between Bern and Olten at its heart.
Bern to Zürich now took under an hour, so the two hubs connected.
In Bern, every half hour, trains from every direction fill the platforms, and people change in minutes.
By 2019, the Swiss travelled further by train than anyone else in Europe: about 2,500 kilometres each, in a year.
Data is the same: start from what people need, find the gaps, and build in stages that each work on their own.
A year from now, at a university, the target is drawn, and nine gaps lie between it and today.
Built all at once, it would take years, and if the money stopped half way, nobody would have anything to use.
Its data manager and team turn the gaps into three stages, each useful on its own, and get the plan approved.
Monday 5 April 2027. Helena Novak, the university's data manager, has the target drawn, and three weeks to plan.
By Monday 26 April: a roadmap and a data strategy, ready for the data council.
Noor, the data architect, sets the current state beside the target on her map, layer by layer.
Wherever the two differ, there's a gap.
TOGAF's method and ArchiMate name the steps: gaps, work packages, and plateaus, the steady states along the way.
The map before the data draws them, in Today, and where it's going.
Strategy: delivering data is slow, 41 working days, and nobody measures it.
Business: eleven ways to ask; requests in eleven places, in no order; and about 40 people doing data work alone, in spreadsheets.
Information: three copies of the staff list, and reports and products with no owner.
Application: reports in two places, the old warehouse's 38 beside the platform's; and agents at work without a written mandate.
Technology: the old warehouse's servers, still running.
Nine gaps: too many to close at once, and some can't start until others are closed.
Helena and the team group them into work packages: pieces a team can finish, each with an owner and a date.
Gaps that close together share one: the old warehouse's reports and its servers go together.
One front door and one list, by 30 June: Helena's.
Retire the old warehouse, by 17 December: Sam's.
Data partners: three by September, all seven by March 2028: Jun's.
An owner and a promise for every product, by March 2028: Yusuf's.
The measures, on one page, from July: Noor's.
And agents, each with a written mandate, by December: Yusuf's too.
Each ends in something people can see: a door that opens, a server switched off.
Then the order: not by who asks loudest, but by what each unlocks, and what it's worth.
The front door comes first: once every request comes in one way, there can be one list, and the days can be counted.
The old warehouse is worth the most to retire: it costs 310,000 Australian dollars a year, and its licence ends on 31 December.
Helena's first draft starts moving the reports in June.
Sam, who runs the platform, sees the catch: a report nobody owns can't be moved, because nobody can say it's still right.
So the 21 reports people use get their owners first, then move.
The packages wait on each other: the list on the door, the move on its owners.
As the timetable decided what Switzerland would build, the target decides what comes first.
Then Helena sets the packages in plateaus: here, simply, stages.
Each must pass one test: if the money stopped after it, would people still have something they use?
Her first draft has half the old reports moved by September.
Half a move is no use on its own: reports in two places, and the licence still paid.
So the whole move goes into stage two, and stage one keeps what people can use at once.
Stage one, by Thursday 30 September: one front door, one list, the measures page, and the first three data partners.
Stage two, by the end of March 2028: one platform, with the old warehouse gone; every product owned; agents with mandates.
Stage three, by the end of 2028: all seven partners building their own products.
The near stage is dated to the day; the far ones only to a month or a year, because they will change.
As fast as necessary, not as fast as possible: the old warehouse goes before its licence ends.
The partners grow as fast as the faculties can spare a day a week.
Like Rail 2000's first stage, each works on its own.
Then the data strategy, on one page.
Where the university is going: its four goals, from students who succeed to finances that last.
What data must do for them: reach the people who decide, quickly, from one trusted copy.
The five principles it's designed by.
The target, in one picture.
The roadmap: three stages, six packages, each with an owner and a date.
And the measures: days from ask to first use, products with an owner, and the people using them.
One page, so the people who fund it and the people who use it read the same plan.
Monday 26 April: the plan milestone. The strategy and its roadmap are ready.
Tuesday 27 April: the data council meets, with Professor David Mensah, the deputy vice-chancellor, there.
Around the table are the people who'll fund it and use it: the faculties, the offices and the data owners.
The dean of Arts asks why Arts waits until 2028 for a partner.
Because the far dates are loose: when Arts can spare a day a week, its partner starts.
The council approves the strategy and the roadmap.
One package needs money first: moving the old warehouse's reports. Its case comes to the council next month.
Helena's ninety days end with a plan anyone at the university can read.
In Switzerland, the first stage built only the gaps the timetable needed, and the hubs connected.
At the university, stage one gives people one door, one list and a measure they can see, even if the money stopped there.
A roadmap ends; keeping data well doesn't, as A capability, not a project shows.
Turn the gaps into stages that each work on their own.

films.x: Funding data work. The old warehouse costs A$310,000 a year, and its licence renews unless someone decides. Helena Novak, with Rohan Desai from Finance, asks the data council to retire it: three options, one carrying on as now; costs once and every year; benefits with owners and dates; one clear ask, on one page.
c: New York State, in 1816.
Farms and towns were spreading west, around the Great Lakes, with grain to sell on the coast.
But the only way east was by wagon, on rough roads.
Moving a ton from Buffalo, on Lake Erie, to New York City cost about a hundred dollars, and took weeks.
A family out west could grow plenty, and still not sell it at a price that paid.
A canal could carry it, but it would run 363 miles, through forest and swamp.
The federal government wouldn't pay; President Jefferson had called the idea little short of madness. Critics called it Clinton's Ditch.
If Washington wouldn't pay, the canal needed someone who would.
DeWitt Clinton and the state's canal commissioners made the case to New York's legislature.
Where it would run, from the Hudson to Lake Erie; what it would cost, about seven million dollars; and how taxes and tolls would repay it.
On 15 April 1817, the legislature said yes.
Thousands dug it with picks and shovels, many just arrived from Ireland and Wales, led by engineers who learned on the job.
It crossed the homelands of the Haudenosaunee nations, much of it taken from them in the years before.
It opened on 26 October 1825, two years ahead of plan.
Moving a ton now cost under nine dollars, not a hundred, and took days, not weeks.
Within ten years, the tolls had paid back the seven million.
Within fifteen years, New York was the busiest port in the country.
A data team asks for money too: to build something new, or to stop paying for something old.
Its case needs the same parts: the choices, what each costs once and every year, what it saves, and who will see the benefit.
May 2027, at the university.
The old warehouse has run on the university's own servers since 2012.
Its licence, servers and support cost A$310,000 a year.
The licence ends on 31 December; if nobody decides, it renews for three more years.
Helena Novak, the data manager, will ask the data council to retire it, on Tuesday 25 May.
She starts from the decision she needs, in one line: retire the old warehouse this year, or pay for three more.
Governance gets a budget line every year, as A capability, not a project showed. This ask is money once, to stop paying every year.
A good case answers five questions; the UK Treasury's Five Case Model names them.
Is it needed? Is it the best value? Can it be bought? Can it be afforded? Can it be delivered?
Helena uses them as a checklist, not a form.
Then the options, and one always carries on as now: doing nothing has a price too.
Option A: renew the licence for three years. A$930,000, for an old version on old servers.
Option B: move all 38 reports as they are. A$520,000, once.
But the warehouse's own logs show who opens what.
17 of the 38 reports haven't been opened in a year. The other 21 are used by about 260 people.
Option C: move those 21, rebuilt on the platform from governed products, and retire the 17 nobody opens. A$380,000, once.
C is the one Helena recommends. A and B stay on the page, so the council can see why.
Then the costs, once and every year: the canal's case counted its tolls, not only the digging.
Running the 21 rebuilt reports will cost about A$40,000 a year, from the platform's own cost records.
So A$310,000 a year stops, and A$40,000 starts: a saving of A$270,000 a year, from January 2028.
The A$380,000 is paid back in about 17 months: the case's payback, the time until the saving covers the cost.
Over five years, it saves A$970,000.
Rohan Desai, Finance's management accountant, checks every figure before it goes to the council.
Then the council can argue about the choice, not the numbers.
Then the benefits, each with an owner and a date.
The saving, from January 2028, belongs to the director of digital services, whose budget pays for the licence today.
Some benefits aren't money.
Every report reads one staff list, not the warehouse's old copy: Ingrid Holm in HR owns that, from December.
And every report has an owner, named in the catalog by March 2028: that benefit is Helena's.
Benefits management, as John Ward and Elizabeth Daniel describe it, adds one more step: track the benefits after the decision.
Each quarter, the council will see each benefit against its date. Without that, the case was only a pitch.
Tuesday 25 May. The data council meets.
Helena has ten minutes and one page, with Rohan beside her.
The page leads with the decision; the leading data people module shows how to write one.
Then the ask, said plainly: A$380,000 and two of the team for six months, and a decision today.
Mei, from the registrar's office, asks what waiting a year would cost.
The answer is on the page: waiting is option A, three more years of the old licence, A$930,000.
The council says yes, that day.
The Erie Canal's case put one decision plainly: the route, the cost, and how it would be paid back.
Its tolls repaid it within ten years. Helena's case should repay itself in 17 months, and the council will see it every quarter.
On Monday, start from the decision you need.
Always show the option of carrying on as now.
Count running costs, not only building.
Give each benefit an owner and a date, and track it after.
Have Finance check the money. One page, ten minutes, and ask for a decision, with a date.
Options, costs, benefits with owners, and one clear ask.

films.x: A risk register that lives. In 2027, Helena's team is moving 21 reports off the old warehouse. The data council says how much risk it will take; the team writes eight risks, each one sentence with an owner and an early sign. A pre-mortem finds one risk's cause, and on 16 June its early sign shows in time.
c: Antarctica, February 1911.
Later that year, Roald Amundsen and four of his team will go to the South Pole and back on skis: about three thousand kilometres.
First, they leave food on the ice along the way, in three stores called depots.
But the ice is flat and white for hundreds of kilometres. In fog, you could pass a depot a kilometre away, and never see it.
Miss one on the way home, and they run out of food, far from any help.
Marks set along the route are easily missed, and once you drift off the line, you may not find it again.
They needed depots they couldn't miss, even in fog.
So they talked it through, and marked each depot across the route instead, nine kilometres out on each side.
At the first, twenty black flags, each numbered to tell which side the depot lay, and how far.
Even off course, they would cross the line, and a flag would point them in.
Ninety-nine days after setting out, on 25 January 1912, all five were home, well, with food to spare.
“Victory awaits him who has everything in order,” Amundsen wrote. “Luck, people call it.”
Helena's team is about to move 21 reports off the university's old data warehouse.
Its risks are hard to see too, until one is missed: a report that stops, or personal data where it shouldn't be.
Said out loud, each with an owner and an early sign, they can be found in time.
April 2027. Before a single risk is written down, Helena asks the data council a question.
How much risk will you take, and on what?
The answer is the council's appetite for risk.
Low for personal data and security.
Medium for delays.
And high for trying new ways to deliver, such as a prototype.
So a risk to personal data must be avoided, not just watched.
The team names the risks. The people who decide say how much is too much.
In May, the team writes the move's risks in a register, each in one sentence: a cause, what could happen, and what it would do.
The licence ends on 31 December, so a report not moved by then would stop, and its readers would lose it.
Each risk has one owner, a person, not a team, and a date to look at it again.
How likely is it, and how bad would it be? Low, medium or high.
Then a response: avoid it, reduce it, share it, or accept it. R1 is reduced: the busiest reports move first.
And an early sign: what you would see first. For R1, a report two weeks behind its date.
ISO 31000, the international standard for managing risk, uses words like these.
R8, payroll's export kept by one person, was reduced long before, as Scripts became software showed.
On 25 May, the case goes to the council with eight risks, and it says yes.
But one of them, R3, is still only a worry: personal data could be exposed in the move.
Tuesday 1 June: the move begins. Helena asks the team of eight to imagine it's over.
It's January 2028, and the move has failed. Why?
It's a pre-mortem, as the psychologist Gary Klein described it in 2007.
Once failure is a given, people find its reasons more easily, and say them more freely.
Each writes their reasons alone for five minutes, then reads one out, in turn.
Every old report reads an extract: a copy taken from another system, such as HR's staff list.
Ivy, the newest, reads hers: the old extracts take whole tables, personal fields and all.
Now R3 has a cause, and an early sign: an extract carrying personal fields its report never shows.
Yusuf, its owner, writes the response that afternoon: before an extract moves, it's checked against the protection rules.
Whatever no report needs stays behind.
Wednesday 16 June, the move's third week. Next is Facilities' report of who holds an access card.
Its old extract brings 42 columns of the staff list. The report shows five.
The check reads the catalog's tags: home address and date of birth are personal, and no report uses them.
So the extract stays behind, and the report is rebuilt from the one governed staff list.
Had those fields moved, R3 would have become an issue: no longer something that might happen, but something that had.
Tags like these, and the locks behind them, are taught in Locks before the data.
Tuesday 29 June. The data council's one page for the month has room for three risks.
R1, the licence. R4, a team stretched between the move and new requests. And R3: its sign has shown, so it's now likely.
R8 is closed: payroll's export has run from the project every pay day for over a year.
R7, an agent with more rights than its job, stays watched, as How it goes wrong explains.
Said early, a risk builds trust. Hidden, it spends it.
Amundsen's flags were early signs too, set where they'd be crossed in time.
On Monday, take your three biggest risks, and write each in one sentence, with an owner and an early sign.
Name each risk, give it an owner, watch its early sign.

films.x: Every stakeholder, one story. Fourteen people and groups want different things from retiring the old warehouse. Helena Novak maps them by power and interest, asks each what they want from data, in their words, and sends everyone the same page every month. When HR shows a real constraint, the plan moves, and everyone hears why.
c: London, in 1850: a great exhibition of the work of every nation is planned for the next May, in Hyde Park.
A royal commission, with Prince Albert at its head, must put up a building to hold it.
Its building committee had turned down all 245 designs sent in, and drawn its own: a vast hall of brick, under a dome.
When the papers printed it, it was mocked.
Everyone with a stake in it, something to lose or gain, was against it, each for their own reason.
People who loved the park feared for its old elms, which would be cut down to make room.
The Times and some members of parliament wanted no building in Hyde Park at all.
And millions of bricks would be hard to take away again, though the building was only for the exhibition.
With less than a year to go, the exhibition itself was in doubt.
They needed a building that could go up in months, and come down again.
Joseph Paxton, a gardener who built glasshouses, saw a way to answer every worry.
On 11 June 1850, at a railway meeting in Derby, he sketched a hall of iron and glass on a sheet of blotting paper.
Made of the same few parts again and again, it could go up fast, and come down again after.
And he showed it to everyone at once: on 6 July, the Illustrated London News printed it for the whole country.
On 15 July it was accepted, on one condition: three old elms must stay, inside the building.
So the middle of the hall rose into an arched roof, high enough to stand over them.
It went up in months, and opened on 1 May 1851, as planned.
The elms stood inside, under the glass, and by October there were about six million visits.
Its surplus, over £186,000, bought land in South Kensington, where museums stand today.
Each worry had an answer, and everyone had seen the same picture.
Data work has stakeholders too: everyone a plan touches, or who can shape it.
A year from now, a university's data council says yes to retiring an old system; fourteen stakeholders want different things from the move.
Listen only to the loudest, and the move could land HR's reports in payroll's busiest weeks.
So its data manager asks each one what they need, in their own words, and tells everyone the same story, every month.
When HR shows her that constraint, the plan moves round it, and everyone hears why.
Tuesday 25 May 2027. The data council says yes to the case: the old warehouse will be retired by December.
The 21 reports people use move to the platform; the 17 nobody opens are retired.
The next morning, Helena Novak, the data manager, starts a list: everyone the plan touches.
The first names come at once: the people who ask most often, and most loudly.
She keeps going: who uses the data, who makes it, who pays for it, who decides, and whose data it is.
Fourteen people and groups.
She places each one by two questions: how much can they shape the plan, and how much does it touch them?
Planners call it a power and interest grid, after Aubrey Mendelow's work.
High on both: the deputy vice-chancellor, who sponsors the plan, and the director of digital services, whose budget gets the saving.
Finance and HR too: their reports are moving.
The four deans and IT can shape it a lot, but feel it less.
Close to it every day: the registrar's office, Planning, Facilities, the data partners, and about 260 people who use the reports.
And the team that makes the data is on the map too: the move is their work, on top of everything else.
Two groups sit low, because they rarely ask: staff and students, whose data it is.
Low on the grid isn't off the list: the quiet ones are asked too, through their representatives.
Then she asks each one the same question: what do you want from data?
She writes each answer down in their words, not hers.
The deputy vice-chancellor: “One set of numbers I can take to the University Council.”
Rohan, in Finance: “Month-end reports right on the first working day.”
Ingrid, in HR: “Every report built from our staff list, not from a copy.”
Staff, through their representatives: “Who sees our records, and why?”
And her own team: “Time to do the move well, not squeezed in between requests.”
Each answer is what that person will judge the plan by, so it goes on the map beside their name.
Then she decides how often each one hears from the team, and who speaks to them.
She speaks to the deputy vice-chancellor herself; each data partner speaks to their dean; Noor, the data architect, speaks to IT.
Yusuf, who leads data governance, meets the staff and student representatives every semester.
One person speaks for the team to each stakeholder, so nobody hears two versions.
Getting people to take part comes first in governance too, as Teachers of data showed.
Everyone gets the same page, on the first Monday of every month.
Where the plan is, the measures, the top three risks, and the decisions needed.
Below, a short line for each of the fourteen: what this month means for them.
Everyone reads the same story, so nobody hears their news second-hand.
The first goes out on Monday 7 June, the day the one front door for requests opens.
From July, it links to the measures page on the platform, so anyone can check a number.
And bad news goes on it too, as soon as it's known.
Wednesday 2 June. Ingrid goes through the move's dates with Jun, who speaks to HR for the team.
HR's reports are due to move in July.
She shows him payroll's year: the financial year ends on 30 June, and payroll's last returns go out by mid-July.
July is the month payroll can least afford a surprise.
That's a real constraint: a fact about the work, not a preference.
So the plan changes: HR's reports move in August, once payroll's year is done.
Helena puts it on the June page, under the decisions needed, with the reason.
On Tuesday 29 June, the data council agrees, and the July page tells everyone.
In Hyde Park, three elms had to stay, and the roof rose over them; here, payroll's weeks had to stay clear, and the plan moved round them.
Not everyone at the table hears yes.
In July, Clara's forecast will wait its turn on the one list, with a reason and a date.
On the July page, the staff representatives read that an old extract, with personal fields nobody needed, was left behind.
People stay at the table because they're heard, and because every month they see the plan move.
How to explain so people can decide, and how to say no, and what instead, the leading data people module tells.
In 1850, Paxton answered each one's worry, and showed everyone the same picture, in the open.
At the university, fourteen stakeholders say what they need from data, and every month they read the same page.
On Monday: list everyone your plan touches, and ask each what they want from data, in their words.
Decide who speaks to each, and how often; send everyone the same page every month.
And when someone shows a real constraint, change the plan, and say why.
Next: one front door, and one list for all the data work.
Know what each person needs from data; tell everyone the same story.

films.x: One list for all the work. Requests reach Helena's team in eleven places, and whoever reaches it first is answered first. From 7 June 2027, one front door and one list: 61 requests become 45, ordered in the open by value, urgency, risk and effort, six at most in progress, and every not now with a reason and a date.
c: The Rhine, in 1792. France is at war, and Dominique-Jean Larrey is a young surgeon in its army.
The army's rules keep its field hospital, called the ambulance, a league behind the fighting: about four kilometres.
The wounded lie where they fall until the battle ends. Then the ambulance sets out to reach them, stuck behind the army's wagons.
It never takes less than a day, or a day and a half. Most of the wounded die waiting for help.
At Speyer, that autumn, many die this way. Help has to reach them while the battle is still on.
Larrey builds what he calls a flying ambulance: a light carriage on springs that follows the front line.
From 1793, his surgeons bandage the wounded where they fall, and carry them back while the battle goes on.
It works. At Aboukir, in Egypt, in 1799, the army has eight hundred wounded.
By his own account, none waits more than a quarter of an hour to have his wounds bandaged.
A data team has its own field: requests lie in many places, and wait weeks before anyone picks them up.
Bring them in through one door, onto one list, ordered in the open, and the most needed work comes first.
The university, in 2027. Requests for data reach Helena Novak's team in eleven places.
Two inboxes, the tracker, three spreadsheets, two chat channels,
the old warehouse's own form, the agents' queue, and the data council's actions.
Nobody can see them all, so people ask twice, in two places, to be sure they're heard.
And the team answers whoever reaches it first, while bigger needs wait, unseen.
Larrey heard of the same at Jena, in 1806.
Soldiers who could walk reached the surgeons first, and took up their whole first day, while the worst wounds waited.
So the roadmap's first work package is one front door, and one list, by the end of June.
On Monday 7 June, the front door opens: one form, with five questions.
What decision is it for? By when? Who decides? What data do you use now? And who else needs it?
They ask what the work is for, not what to build.
Each old door is closed, kindly, with a note pointing to the new one.
A request for access, or for what a word means, goes on to data governance's own services, from A capability, not a project.
That day, sixty-one requests come onto one list, from all eleven places.
Nine are duplicates: each joins its twin, and whoever asked is told.
Seven are no longer needed, and are closed, with thanks.
Forty-five are left, on one list, in the tracker the team already uses.
After Jena, Larrey wrote down one order: the most dangerously wounded first, without regard to rank or distinction.
Those hurt less could wait. Their lives weren't in danger.
Helena's team orders its list the same way, in the open: each request is weighed for its value, its urgency, and the risk while it waits.
Together, they say what waiting costs: what Donald Reinertsen calls the cost of delay.
Divided by the effort, it puts small, urgent, valuable work first.
Anil's request is small, and while it waits, his own spreadsheet keeps a copy of staff records. It goes near the top.
A dashboard asked for three times names no decision yet. It waits, with a note saying why, and when it's looked at again.
Never by who asks, or how loudly.
The list is a board in the tracker that anyone at the university can see, and the data council reads it every month.
Next, the team's time, split on purpose: half for the roadmap, a third for requests, and the rest for running and improving what it has.
Without the split, requests would take it all, and nothing on the roadmap would move.
And at most six pieces of work are in progress at once: three for the roadmap, two for requests, one for running and improving.
Kanban, as David J. Anderson set it out, calls this a limit on work in progress.
With fewer things started, each finishes sooner, and people get their answers sooner.
When one is done, the top of the list moves in. Finish, then start.
On Thursday 24 June, the University Council asks for the timetable to change from 2028.
The registrar's office needs the rooms' data for it by the end of August. That date can't move, so it goes near the top.
On Monday 12 July, Clara, in Planning, asks for a new student forecast model, by the end of August too.
It goes on the same list, weighed the same way, and it hears not now, with a reason and a date.
The reason: the timetable's date can't move. The date: the current model refreshed by the end of August, and the new one in October.
Saying it well, face to face, is a skill of its own, shown in the leading data people module.
Emergency departments still do this, and call it triage: in Australia, five categories, each with a longest wait, from at once to two hours.
Not now always comes with a when.
Larrey brought the wounded in from wherever they fell, and treated the worst first.
Helena's team does the same with data: every request through one door, on one list, the most needed first.
On Monday, close every side door, kindly, and ask what each request is for.
Order the list in the open, by value, urgency, risk and effort.
Protect time for the roadmap and for running what you have, and limit what's in progress.
Give every request that waits a reason and a date, and show the list to everyone.

films.x: Services and customers. In May 2027, Helena writes her team's four services on one page, then its suppliers and its customers in four groups, with what hurts and what drives each. She and Noor walk one service down five layers. When the front door opens, 42 of 45 requests land on a service.
c: Madurai, in the south of India, in 1976.
Dr Govindappa Venkataswamy has just retired as a government eye surgeon, at 58.
He opens a hospital of his own, with eleven beds.
Around him, millions of people are blind from a cataract: the lens inside the eye turns cloudy, until it lets no light through.
A blind farmer can't work his field. A blind grandmother needs a child to lead her, and the child stops going to school.
A short operation can give their sight back.
But most of them are too poor to pay for it, and live far from any surgeon.
Surgery as hospitals did it then would never reach them all.
He starts by saying what his hospital is for: sight given back, to everyone who needs it.
Then who it's for, in groups: those who can pay, those who can pay a little, and those who can pay nothing.
Six of the eleven beds are for those who pay nothing.
Those who can't come are reached in their villages, at eye camps, and brought in by bus.
Then he designs everything below for them: how each operating room flows, who does each step, and what it costs.
When bought lenses cost too much, the hospital makes its own, from 1992, for a few dollars each.
Today Aravind's hospitals do over four hundred thousand operations a year, more than half of them free or for very little.
Those who pay cover those who can't, and the outcomes hold: in 2007, complications in under two operations in a hundred.
A data team serves people too, and it can lose sight of who.
Say what each service is, and who it's for, and every system below can be designed for someone.
These films take the product owner's side of a data manager's job, and borrow from architecture to do it.
May 2027, at the university. The data council approved Helena Novak's strategy in April.
Now she runs her team's work as a business of its own, with suppliers and customers.
First, the services, on one page, in words a customer would use.
One: governed data products, each with an owner and a promise.
Two: the platform, where data partners in the faculties build their own.
Three: analysis that answers a decision.
Four: advice and training.
A list like this is a service catalogue; governance's own services have one, in A capability, not a project.
Then the suppliers: the owners of payroll, the timetable, the rooms' sensors and HR, and digital services, who run the machines.
Then the customers, in four groups, each with what hurts and what drives them.
Their words come from the 31 conversations Helena held in her first weeks, in Listen first.
People who decide, like Graham Ellis in Facilities: two numbers for the same thing; they want answers they can defend, in time.
The data partners: weeks of waiting for access; they want to build their faculty's products themselves.
Analysts and report readers: they can't tell which table to trust; they want to find it, trust it and use it.
And staff and students, whose data it is: who can see it? They want it used fairly, and kept safe.
Pains and drivers in a customer's own words: the value proposition canvas asks for the same.
Noor Rahman, the data architect, puts the services and their customers on her map, beside everything else.
Then Helena and Noor walk one service, governed data products, down every layer, with a picture for each.
Five layers: strategy, business, information, application and technology.
They're ArchiMate's layers, with TOGAF's data called information; The map before the data draws them in full.
Strategy: the capability it serves, deciding from trusted data.
Business: the service and its promise, checked by seven each morning, and who builds, reviews and owns each product.
Information: what it's about, such as rooms, bookings and the people counted in them.
Application: the platform, the catalog, and the project where the products are built.
Technology: where it all runs.
Each picture names the customer it serves, at the top.
In the old warehouse, the same walk finds 17 of 38 reports that no one has opened in a year.
A system that serves no customer's need raises one question: why is it there?
On Monday 7 June, the team's one front door opens.
Of the 45 requests put in order, 42 land on one of the four services.
Graham's question about his rooms lands on analysis that answers a decision.
Three land on none, and Helena says so openly.
Two are for a new booking system, and go to digital services, with a note.
One, help with a staff survey, shows a gap the team can fill, and joins advice and training.
A request that lands on no service isn't a failure. It shows where the page needs to change.
In Madurai, the eleven beds came after one sentence: sight, for everyone who needs it.
Helena's team did the same with data: every request now finds its service, and every system its customer.
On Monday, write your services on one page, in a customer's words.
Name your suppliers and your customers, in groups, with what hurts and what drives each.
Walk each service down every layer, with a picture for each.
And if a system serves no one, ask why it's there.
Know your services and who they're for; then design every layer for them.

films.x: One source of truth. In spring 2027, Helena's target picture exists three times, and the council's slide is out of date. In June the map's source moves into the team's repository. Every change is reviewed like code, an agent drafts and a person decides, and the wiki and the slides are made from it.
c: Great Britain, in the late 1990s.
Ordnance Survey, the national mapping agency, keeps the most detailed maps of the country.
Its paper maps have been turned into digital ones, and cut into tiles, square by square.
But on a tile, a building is only lines on a picture. It has no name, no number, nothing to point to.
Councils, water companies and the emergency services each keep their own records of the same buildings and roads.
Each matches its records to the lines in its own way.
So one school can be one thing in a council's records, and another in a water company's.
Nobody can be sure that two records mean the same place.
And when a new road is built, each of them must find it, and change it, on its own.
Each keeping its own copy of the same streets can't go on.
In 2001, Ordnance Survey launches OS MasterMap: one seamless database of the whole country, instead of tiles.
Every feature in it, about 440 million at first, gets its own identifier, a TOID, with a version and a date.
Surveyors, on the ground and from the air, keep it up to date, and users receive only what has changed.
Now a council and a water company can point to the same building by its identifier, with no doubt which one they mean.
Each change carries its version and its date, so anyone can see what changed, and when.
By 2016, it holds over 500 million features.
A data team's architecture has the same problem: one picture of its platform, kept in copies that drift apart.
Keep one source, date every change, and make every copy from it.
These films are the product owner's side of a data manager's job, borrowed from architecture.
A university, in the spring of 2027. Helena Novak, the data manager, has a target picture for the data platform.
It exists three times: Noor's map in the architecture tool, a page on the wiki, and the slides for the data council.
Each was right the day it was made. Each has been changed by hand, on its own, since.
On Tuesday 25 May, Helena asks the council to retire the old warehouse.
The council's slide still shows the old warehouse in the target.
Which picture is true? Nobody in the room can say for sure.
Project managers have the same trouble: who does what, when and how, sits in a deck from March.
Noor, the data architect, says what Ordnance Survey found: copies drift. Keep one source.
In June, the map's source moves into the data team's repository, as files, beside the platform's code.
Noor writes it in ArchiMate's exchange format, a standard language for architecture, from The Open Group.
She adds only what is the team's own, such as each product's owner. Standards first; then what's relevant to you.
The diagrams are kept as text too, in Mermaid, or as draw.io files, so a change to a picture is a change you can read.
Each night, everything else is made from it: the architecture tool's views, the wiki, and the picture on the monthly page.
And the project managers' page of who does what, when and how.
Of the team's seven places for its work, from Where each piece lives, the map's source now lives in one: the repository.
The wiki and the slides can't disagree with the map any more. They're made from it.
Every change to the map is a pull request, with its reason, reviewed by someone other than its author.
Noor, Helena and the principal engineers, Sam and Jun, review. Data partners in the faculties propose.
In July, Sam's team adds the rooms' sensor feed to the platform.
The same pull request adds the feed to the map's current state. The code and the map change together.
And a check fails if a new source has no place on the map.
Nobody waits for a funded project to update the current state and the target.
Wait for that, and the team ends up building tomorrow's legacy.
A big choice gets a short decision record beside it, as Michael Nygard proposed in 2011: what was decided, and why.
In August, Helena asks the team's agent to draft the change that retires the old warehouse, from her notes.
In minutes, it writes the new target state, and draws its diagram, as text.
Noor reviews it, line by line.
One relationship is wrong: payroll's reports still read from the old warehouse, after it's gone.
She asks for the fix, checks it, and approves.
The agent films have the same rule: an agent proposes, and a person decides.
The map isn't one person's job. It starts with Helena: she opened its first pull request herself.
The principal engineers keep it with her, and anyone on the team can propose a change.
By Friday 17 December, the old warehouse is retired, and 63 changes of the year are in the map's history, each with its reason.
At its reviews, the council reads that history, not a slide made the night before.
Ordnance Survey stopped keeping its map in pieces: one database, every feature with its identifier, every change with its date.
Helena's team did the same with its architecture: one map, and every other picture made from it.
On Monday, put your architecture in a repository, as files, in a standard language.
Review every change like code, and update the current and target state in the change that moves them.
Make the wiki, the slides and the who-does-what pages from it.
Let agents draft the structure and the diagrams, and review what they draft.
And make architecture everyone's job, starting with yours.
One map in the repository; every change updates it; everything else comes from it.

films.x: Data from every provider. In June 2027, Helena and Noor write the team's preferred way to receive data on one page, then a decision tree for providers who can't meet it. A new timetable never says what was deleted, so the team compares its full list each night, and Graham's room counts stay true.
c: Port Newark, New Jersey, in April 1956.
A trucking man, Malcom McLean, sends an old tanker, the Ideal X, to Houston with 58 metal boxes on its deck.
Each box is lifted on and off whole, by crane, instead of sack by sack and crate by crate.
By McLean's own figures, loading costs under 16 cents a ton, against $5.83 by hand.
But a box needs a crane strong enough to lift it, at both ends of the trip.
Few ports have one, and building one takes years, and money most of them don't have.
For those ports, the box changes nothing: ships still sit at the quay for days, unloaded by hand, and their goods cost more.
Unless it can reach ports without cranes, the box will stop wherever the cranes do.
In October 1957, McLean's company sends out a rebuilt ship, the Gateway City, with two cranes of its own.
They run on rails along its deck, and reach out over the quay.
Now a port with a quay can take boxes, crane or not.
Over the years, ports build cranes of their own, and the ships' cranes are no longer needed there.
Ships with their own cranes still call at ports that have none.
The box's savings reached each port before it could meet the standard, and each port joined the standard when it could.
Data has its standard ways too, and providers who can't meet them yet.
A path for each of them lets their data arrive now, not after every one of them catches up.
These films borrow from architecture to run a data team's services. This one is about the data coming in.
June 2027, at a university, a year from now.
Helena Novak, the data manager, and Noor Rahman, the data architect, write the team's preferred way to receive data, on one page.
The source publishes its data as a governed product, with an owner and a contract.
It sends each change as an event, the moment it happens.
And it says what was deleted, so a deletion reaches every copy.
Contracts and deletions have films of their own: Moving is easy, agreeing is the work, and Deleted means deleted.
Sam Okafor, who runs the data platform, lists the systems the team takes data from.
The rooms' sensors can do all of it.
Payroll, on a system from 2004, sends one file a night.
The new timetable, bought as a service in 2026, can give its changes, but can't say what was deleted.
And the Faculty of Health books its nine clinical labs in a spreadsheet.
Old systems fall short of the preferred way, and so do new ones.
So the page gets a second half: a decision tree, for the providers who can't meet it.
First: can it send each change as an event? Then use the events.
If not, can it give its changes since a given time? Then fetch them every hour.
Can it say what was deleted? If not, compare its full list with ours every night. What's gone from its list was deleted.
Only a file? Take the whole file each night, and compare it the same way.
A spreadsheet? A data partner moves it into a governed table, with an owner.
The first paths have names: event-driven integration, and change data capture.
Every branch ends in a recommendation, and every path still keeps a contract with an owner.
The tree is kept as text in the team's repository, and its picture is drawn from it.
Monday 14 June: Sam tests the new timetable.
Mei Tanaka, in the registrar's office, cancels a class. The hourly changes never mention it.
So on the platform, the class stays booked.
Graham Ellis, the Director of Facilities, would see a booked room with nobody in it: a room that looks wasted, when it was free all along.
The vendor can add deletions to its changes, but not before its renewal, in 2028.
The tree has the answer: the changes every hour, and the full list of bookings every night.
Each night, a booking on the platform that's missing from the full list is marked deleted.
The new timetable goes live on Monday 19 July.
By Friday 30 July, the first week of teaching, the nightly comparison has found 212 deleted bookings the changes never mentioned.
212 hours that would have looked booked and empty on Graham's page stay off it.
The rooms' sensors take the preferred way: each hour's count arrives as an event.
Payroll's file is taken whole each night and compared, for Finance's casual staff costs.
A weaker path is checked more often.
If a night's file is much smaller than the night before, the comparison stops, and asks a person.
On Tuesday 24 August, payroll's file arrives cut short, and the check stops it before 2,400 staff are marked as gone.
Anil Kurian, the Faculty of Health's data partner, moves the labs' spreadsheet into a governed table, and owns it.
And each provider is asked for its next step up, in writing.
The timetable: its deletions, in the 2028 renewal. Payroll: a file of its changes, at its next upgrade. The labs: into the timetable.
The team lifts its providers towards the preferred way, a step at a time.
But it never holds the data back, waiting for the ideal.
On Thursday 30 September, Graham's page shows every teaching room and every lab, from four sources, by four paths.
Graham doesn't see the paths. He sees counts he can trust.
And Helena's page is still one page: the preferred way, the tree, and each provider's next step.
The Gateway City took its own cranes to ports that had none, and the box reached them years before their cranes did.
Helena's team did the same: a path for every provider, and Graham's counts true from the first week.
On Monday, write your preferred way on one page.
Draw the tree for the providers who can't meet it, each branch with its recommendation.
Ask each provider for its next step up, in its contract or its renewal.
Check the weaker paths more often, and don't hold value back.
One preferred way, a path for every provider, and value first.

films.x: Prototype and iterate. Graham Ellis asks for a dashboard of room use by Easter. Behind it is whether to ask for a new building, and requests wait 41 working days. Helena's team puts something real in front of him within two weeks, with governed data, and improves it a round at a time until his decision is served.
c: Curitiba, in the south of Brazil. Friday the 19th of May, 1972, six in the evening.
City crews arrive by truck in the old centre's main street, Rua XV de Novembro, and close it to cars.
For years, cars and buses had filled it, and people on foot were squeezed to its edges.
One plan was to widen the streets, knocking down buildings from the turn of the century.
The young mayor, Jaime Lerner, an architect, wanted the street given back to people on foot.
The shopkeepers feared the opposite: without cars, their customers would stay away, and their sales would fall.
Arguing over plans on paper couldn't show anyone what the street would be like.
So the mayor's team built the real thing, fast.
On Saturday morning, grey and damp, the street was handed to the people, without ceremony.
Over the weekend, crews took up the road, laid stones, and put in streetlights and kiosks.
They planted tens of thousands of flowers.
The next weekend, drivers came to take the street back.
They found long strips of paper on it, and dozens of children painting.
Within days, the shopkeepers told the newspapers their sales were up a little.
Soon they were asking for more of the street.
Other streets followed, and fifty years on, it is still a street for people on foot.
The city didn't win the argument on paper. It put the real thing in front of the people who had to decide.
A data team can work the same way.
Put something real in front of the person who decides, learn from what they do with it, and do it again.
February 2027. Graham Ellis, the university's new director of Facilities, has a request.
Could Helena Novak's team make him a dashboard of room use, by Easter?
The question behind it is bigger: whether to ask the University Council for a new teaching building.
It would cost about A$140 million.
Then the request waits, as every request did: on average, 41 working days from asking to first use.
On Tuesday the 30th of March, the team takes it up the new way, as Helena's ninety-day plan set out.
Ivy Reyes, the team's new analyst, has already drawn its whole route on one page.
All 186 rooms are on it, the 14 named two ways included.
So the prototype starts from real data: thirteen weeks of bookings, and head counts from the rooms' sensors.
Governed from the first day: counts per room, per hour, never a person.
In 2001, the Agile Manifesto put it plainly: working software over comprehensive documentation.
The first round asks one thing: when are the rooms booked, and when are they used, hour by hour?
On Wednesday the 7th of April, the team's agent drafts a first model, in a minute.
It counts booked hours as used ones.
Ivy catches it herself: she reads the agent's notes to the end, and checks the draft against the sensors.
Room use, as Graham means it, goes into the glossary: people in the room. The model is built from it.
Then Jun reviews Ivy's change, the same day.
Fast isn't careless. The agent proposes, people check, and no one approves their own work.
On Friday the 9th of April, ten days after the start, Graham sees the prototype.
A heat map of the week, on a dashboard in Databricks.
Helena asks him one question, and will ask it every round: what would change your mind?
