His answer: if the rooms are full all week, he'll ask for the building. If they aren't, he won't.
The work runs in rounds of a week, each ending on a Friday, with the person who decides and the real thing.
Scrum calls it a sprint review. Here, it's half an hour with Graham, at one screen.
On Wednesday the 14th of April, Graham uses it himself, with his team: eleven working days from the start.
It had waited about seven weeks before anyone began, like every request.
Then the new way took eleven working days, against forty-one.
As in Curitiba, the talk changes once people can use the real thing.
And the real thing surprises everyone.
Rooms are booked 38% of the week, but 93% from ten to two, Tuesday to Thursday.
In one booked hour in five, nobody comes. When people do come, about half the seats are filled.
Everyone was right about what they saw. The average hid both the crowded peak and the empty rooms.
At the second review, his answer moves: show me it works in 2030, when Planning expects 6% more students.
Friday the 23rd of April, the third round. The answer is plain: the rooms are short only at the peak.
Move about one peak class in six to other hours, and release the bookings nobody uses.
That meets the forecast to 2030 without a new building.
The decision is served, so the rounds stop. A fourth would only polish it.
What the prototype taught stays in the product: the definition, and the reviewed model.
And the dashboard becomes a product of its own, which Ivy owns from July.
In June, Graham takes one page to the University Council.
It puts the building off for two years, and asks for the timetable to change.
In Curitiba, a street built in a weekend settled what plans on paper couldn't.
Helena's team did it in three weeks: real data in front of the person who decides, a round at a time.
On Monday, put something real in front of the person who decides, within two weeks.
Use real data from the start, and govern it.
Ask, every round: what would change your mind?
Keep the rounds short and fixed, stop when the decision is served, and keep what you learned in the product.
Something real in front of them in two weeks; learn; repeat.

films.x: Measuring what people get. In July 2027, Helena's team is busy, but no one can say whether people get what they need. She puts eight measures on one page, in three groups, each with a baseline, one definition, a reader and a decision. By December, days from ask to first use are 14, not 41.
c: New York, 1952: a delivery room at the Sloane Hospital for Women.
Dr Virginia Apgar is there for the mothers: she's an anaesthetist, the doctor who keeps them out of pain.
In America, about one baby in fifty dies in its first four weeks, and deaths in the first day have hardly fallen in twenty years.
At least half of those deaths come from a lack of oxygen: a baby who can't breathe well, and needs help in its first minutes.
But in the room, everyone looks after the mother, and the newborn is left to the most junior doctor.
Is the baby well? Each doctor judges by eye, in words like mild or severe, and each means something different.
So a baby in trouble can be missed until it's too late, and no hospital can tell whether what it does helps.
Doctors need words for a newborn that mean the same to everyone.
In 1952, Apgar proposes a score that anyone in the room can take, the same way every time.
One minute after birth, five signs: the heartbeat, breathing, how firmly the baby moves, how it reacts when touched, and its colour.
Each gets zero, one or two. Ten is a baby doing well.
She tries it on over a thousand babies, and publishes it in 1953.
Now a baby in trouble shows at once, as a low score, to everyone in the room.
And doctors can compare what they do.
After a caesarean, babies whose mothers were put to sleep scored five on average; with a spinal anaesthetic, eight.
By the early 1960s many hospitals used it; today most score every baby at one minute, and again at five.
Newborn deaths fell, for many reasons, from about twenty in a thousand in 1950 to under four by 2016.
A data team can be busy every day, and still not know whether people get what they need.
A few measures, taken the same way every month, can show it.
July 2027, at the university. Helena Novak's data strategy promised the team's measures on one page.
The easy things to count are what keeps a team busy: requests closed, hours worked, reports built.
Each of them can rise while the people who asked are still waiting.
So Helena starts from what people get, and from the decisions the measures will serve.
For every measure, one question: when it moves, what will we do differently, and who decides?
Data governance already measures itself this way, from the work, as Teachers of data showed.
In 1992, Robert Kaplan and David Norton called it a balanced scorecard:
a few measures, in groups, so a gain in one place can't hide a loss in another.
Helena's page has three groups.
Delivery: days from ask to first use, what's sent back for changes, and how much work is open at once.
Data management: products with an owner, and their promise met.
And value: benefits against each case, decisions informed, people using the products each month,
and two questions, twice a year, to the people the team serves.
Eight measures on one page. Apgar needed five signs.
Anything else can still be counted; it just stays off the page.
Each measure gets four things: a baseline, one definition, a reader, and the decision it serves.
Take days from ask to first use. Its baseline came first, from February, before anything changed: 41 working days.
Its one definition lives in the catalog's glossary:
working days from a request reaching the one list to its first use by the person who asked.
Its readers: the team, every second Thursday, and the data council, every month.
And its decision: where to take the waiting out of the work.
Beside it sits a quality measure, sent back: the share of finished work that people send back for changes. In July, one piece in eight.
Without it, speed could hide rework: half-done work sent out, and back again.
The page itself is a small governed product, and Helena owns it.
By June, days from ask to first use had fallen to 24.
On the page, each measure is a line across the months, its baseline drawn beneath it, never one number lit red or green.
On Thursday 12 August, products' promises met stood at 82 percent, up from 58 in March.
Alone, that looked fine. Beside it, nine pieces of work were open against a limit of six: new work was starting before old work finished.
So the team finished before it started, and by mid-September the load was six again.
Value has its lines too. A decision informed: on 24 June, the University Council deferred a new building, using the rooms' data.
And a benefit against its case: retiring the old warehouse should save 270,000 Australian dollars a year from January,
owned by the director of digital services.
Every measure carries a risk. Goodhart's law, from 1975, as it's often put: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
Apgar saw it in the delivery room: doctors scored their own babies several points higher than others did, so someone else took the score.
Helena's measures are counted the same way: from the tracker and the platform's own logs.
And first use is confirmed by the person who asked, never by the person who built it.
And every measure is the team's: never one person's number, and never a target for anyone.
How the team reads its measures together is told in the leading data people module.
In New York, five signs, taken the same way, by someone else, made every baby seen in its first minute.
By December, Helena's page showed what people got: 14 days from ask to first use, not 41, and half as much sent back.
Promises met: 86 percent. People using the products each month: 910.
And the old warehouse was retired on 17 December, its saving starting in January.
On Monday, list the decisions your measures will serve.
Keep them few, in groups.
Take a baseline before you change anything, and write one definition for each.
Put a quality measure beside every speed measure, and show the trend.
And keep every measure for the team, never a target for one person.

films.x: Improving how the team works. In September 2027, a request to Helena's team waits six working days for its first question back, and nobody stops to look. She keeps half an hour every Friday: one measure, one small change, tried for a week, then kept or dropped out loud. By December, fourteen changes are kept.
c: The United States, 1940. Factories must suddenly make far more, with millions of new workers, many in a factory for the first time.
There are too few experienced supervisors: the people who lead a group of workers on the floor, and show them how.
So work is done the long way. Picture one job: riveting two metal sheets into a part for a radio.
For every twelve parts, the worker walks back and forth to the boxes, stamps each part, and carries each full box to a scale.
Every extra step costs time the factory doesn't have, and the carrying is heavy work that wears people out.
And nobody has time to stop and rethink the job.
Someone had to help them find the time, and the better way.
A government service, Training Within Industry, trains the supervisors themselves, ten at a table.
From 1942, its course Job Methods teaches them to make small improvements in the jobs they know best.
Break the job down into its details; question every one: why, what for, where, when, who, how.
Then drop, combine, rearrange or simplify, and write the new way down.
The four steps fit on a pocket card. The last one says: use it until a better way is developed.
In the course's own example, the sheets move to the bench, both hands work, and the stamp and the scale go: neither was needed.
Not a speed-up: thirty details become fourteen, and much of the tiring, heavy work is gone.
By 1945, of the plants that reported a rise in output, 86 in every 100 said it was a quarter or more.
After the war it was taught in Japan, and became one root of kaizen: improving a little at a time.
A data team works the long way too, when nobody stops to look.
Helena Novak's team took half an hour every Friday, and by December had kept fourteen small changes.
Whoever asked for data now heard back within a day, not six.
September 2027, at the university. Since July, the team has read its measures together every second Thursday.
Those readings have fixed two waits already: the leading data people module tells how.
From Friday 3 September, Helena protects half an hour a week for how the team works: Fridays, half past three to four.
One measure. One small change, tried for a week, then kept or dropped, out loud: plan, do, check, act.
The data quality module keeps the same rhythm for one list, fifteen minutes on Thursdays; here, it's for how the team works.
On the first Friday, Noor looks in the tracker for where the work waits longest.
It's at the very start: a request through the front door waits six working days for its first question back.
So they start where the pocket card does: break the job down, detail by detail.
It lands on the one list. It waits for Monday's planning. It goes to someone, who reads it, and asks.
Then they question every detail. Why wait for Monday? The form's five answers are enough to ask the first question that day.
Ivy proposes one change: the next free person reads each new request the day it lands, and asks within a working day.
Monday's planning still sets the order of the work. Only the first question moves.
They try it for a week.
Friday 10 September: every request that came in that week had its first question back within a working day.
One day, not six. The team keeps it, and says so.
Then they try a second change: ten minutes every morning, the whole team looking at the whole list.
A week later they drop it, out loud: it took ten minutes a day from the whole team, and found nothing new.
Dropped is a result too: nobody goes on doing it out of habit.
Every Friday, the same half-hour. By 17 December: fifteen changes tried, fourteen kept, one dropped.
Each kept change is written into the procedure it changed, one of the six, that same day.
The ask procedure's second step now says it, with the date it changed, and why.
So it lasts: someone new learns it from the page, and it holds while the person who thought of it is away.
Days from ask to first use are down to 14, from 24 in June: the Friday changes are part of that, with July's fixes.
And work sent back for changes is down to 6 in 100: faster hasn't meant worse.
At each fortnightly review, the people who asked hear what changed, and why: the small wins, shown.
In the 1940s, the pocket card's last step said: use it until a better way is developed.
Each procedure's page works the same way: the best way so far, until a Friday finds a better one.
On Monday, protect half an hour, at the same time every week.
Pick one measure, and look for where the work waits.
Change one thing for a week; then keep it or drop it, out loud.
Write what you keep into the procedure, and show the small wins.
How a leader makes it everyone's habit, the leading data people module shows.
One measure, one small change, every week.

films.x: Reviewing the strategy. Helena's data strategy is approved in April 2027, and she puts its reviews in the calendar. In October the university decides to offer short online courses, and the plan must move: one part moves up, one waits, and everyone it touches hears why. In January, promised sits beside delivered.
c: In the 1970s, fridges, spray cans and foam all over the world use gases called CFCs: cheap, safe to handle, and slow to break down.
In 1974, in California, two chemists, Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland, ask where those gases end up.
Their answer: they drift up, over years, to the ozone layer, high above the clouds, and break it down.
That thin layer of gas stops most of the sun's harmful ultraviolet light.
Without it, more people get skin cancer, more eyes are damaged, and crops grow less.
In 1985, British scientists in Antarctica, Joe Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jonathan Shanklin, publish what they've measured there since 1957.
Each spring, the layer above them is now only about two thirds as thick as it once was.
Much is still unsure, but waiting until everyone is sure could be too late. The world has to act before it knows everything.
On 16 September 1987, in Montreal, countries sign a treaty: the Montreal Protocol.
Its first step is modest: cut the main CFCs by half, by 1998.
But it builds in a habit: from 1990, and at least every four years, look at the science again, and decide whether to go further.
In London, in 1990, with stronger evidence, they go further.
No more CFCs by 2000 in richer countries, and a fund to help poorer ones follow.
In Copenhagen, in 1992, they bring that forward to 1996.
Each time, the plan moves out loud, with the science behind it.
By 2023, nearly 99 per cent of the banned gases are no longer made or used.
The ozone layer is healing: back to its 1980 thickness around 2040 over most of the world, and around 2066 over Antarctica.
By 2030, UN scientists expect it to prevent up to two million cases of skin cancer a year.
A data strategy is written with what's known on the day, too, and the world won't wait for it.
Look at it again on a rhythm, move it out loud, and it stays the plan everyone works to.
A university, a year from now. On Tuesday 27 April 2027, the data council approves Helena Novak's data strategy.
On one page: where the university is going, what data must do for it, five principles, the target, six packages of work, and the measures.
Richard Rumelt says a good strategy has a core: a diagnosis, a guiding policy, and actions that fit together.
Helena's has all three: what slows data down, five principles to decide by, and six packages of work.
Before anyone leaves the room, she puts the year's reviews in the calendar.
The last Tuesday of July, October and January, when the deputy vice-chancellor chairs the council as the strategy's steering group.
No new committee.
And one more, for the whole year: Monday 31 January 2028.
Each review asks the same three questions: what do the measures say, what do the risks say, and what has changed around us?
Tuesday 27 July: the first review.
The measures page has its first readings: 24 days from ask to first use, down from 41.
The eight risks are read in turn, each with the early sign that would warn of it.
And the council reads the map's history in the repository: what changed in the current and target state since June, and why.
Nothing needs to move, and the minutes say so: reviewed, no change.
A review that changes nothing still counts: now everyone knows the plan still holds.
Thursday 14 October. The University Council decides to offer short online courses for working adults, from 2028.
A new kind of student: someone with a job, studying online, a few weeks at a time.
To choose which courses to offer, the faculties need data they can trust on who asks about what, by December.
Twelve days later, on Tuesday 26 October, the steering group reviews the strategy.
The diagnosis has grown. The guiding policy holds. The actions move.
Up: an owner and a promise for the products that choice needs, by December, not March.
Waits: the agents' written mandates, to March, not December.
The team gives half its time to the plan, and it can't do both by December.
Until then, no new agent starts, and the risk of an agent with more rights than its job is read at every review.
It's written on the one page, and everyone it touches hears why, and the new date, that week.
The same day, Noor adds the online courses' platform to the target on her map, with its reason.
When strategy moves, in The map before the data, walks a change like this down every layer of the map.
TOGAF calls this change management: some changes fit the plan, some move it, and some need a new one.
Monday 31 January 2028: the first year's review.
On one side, what the strategy promised; on the other, what was delivered.
Days from ask to first use: from 41 to 14.
Products whose promise is met: from 58 per cent to 86.
People using products each month: from 340 to 910.
The old warehouse, retired on Friday 17 December, saves A$270,000 a year from January.
Three data partners, named by September, as promised.
And what didn't work, said as plainly: four more partners are due by March, and two faculties haven't named one.
Helena will see both deans in February, and that risk goes to the top of the register.
The next year starts from here: the same three questions, asked again of the people she spoke to a year ago.
In Montreal, the first step was small. The habit of looking again made it enough.
Helena's strategy kept the same habit: read every quarter, moved out loud when the university moved, and set beside what it delivered.
On Monday, put the year's reviews in the calendar.
At each one, read the measures, the risks, and what's changed around you.
When the world moves, move the plan out loud: what moves up, what waits, and why.
Keep the one page current, and the map with it.
End the year with what you promised beside what you delivered, and start the next from there.
That's the whole job: every area at once, a plan in stages, each proved with something real, and everyone at the table.
Discover, define, plan. Deliver, measure, improve. And again.
Review the plan every quarter; move it out loud when the world moves.

Seven films on data modelling, from how minds turn the world into words to how AI can help keep meaning true.

For anyone who builds pipelines, owns a source system or a data product, or depends on data being right. What good enough means for data, what goes wrong, and what catches it: changes, contracts, checks, and errors fixed where they start.
Two bad mornings at the university: a change only half of it saw, and a number too good to be true. Each ends with what catches it next time.
A list can pass every check and still be wrong. Ask what it's for, measure it, and check it against the truth and the clock.
Fixing data by hand hides the cause. Count the hidden work, fix it where errors are born, and improve a little every week.
For architects, and anyone new to an organisation. How an organisation works, in layers, before you ask what its data should answer.
A new enterprise architect maps a public energy utility, layer by layer, before asking what its data should answer.
What the business owns about its data: its concepts, their owners, the processes they're born in, and the rules on them.
Between the business and the systems: where each fact is born, how it travels, who owns it, and one language for it.
Why a data platform is a platform, not an application: its parts, its seams, its security, and one solution on it.
Agents and AI on the map, a first draft instead of a blank page, every change checked, and the map kept alive.
For data stewards and architects, and anyone whose data lives in many systems. The people and things a business is about, kept once and shared across its systems, and the lists that sort them.
One person, four systems, five records. A series on master and reference data, from the person behind the role to a hub at work.
For governance teams and data owners, and anyone asked to make the rules work. Who decides what, and how each decision reaches the work: policies that run as checks, owners and tests, not on a shelf.
Thirty-four policies on a shelf, and two numbers that disagree. A series on data governance that runs where the work happens.
The project that paid for governance ends in June. A series that puts governance on the university's architecture map.
Every decision and every flow on the map, built in dbt and on Databricks, so governance runs in the work.

For platform teams, data owners and anyone who gives or gets access to data. Who and what may reach the data, what each person may see, and how long personal data is kept: each lock built from a role, a boundary or a rule already decided.
Who and what may reach the platform, from where, with which proof, and who can switch on more power.
Classify once, protect by class everywhere the data goes, and prove it held.
Keep personal data for a reason and a time, then let it go, and answer when a person asks.

For everyone who works with data, and will work beside an AI agent. Agentic data engineering from the ground up: what an AI agent is and how we got here, what agents are like to work with, and why that means governing them.
An agent now works beside the data team. Ten films on what it is, what it's like to work with, and why we govern it.
Jun's agent goes to work on the census count: what it reads, its skills, its hands, its memory, and the rules it runs under.
Planning's agent goes from a helper on Jun's sign-in to a colleague with a place on the map, and rights from its role.

For anyone who works in data, and anyone who leads the people who do. The skills data work needs now, and leading the people who do it: seeing the whole, working beside agents, listening, explaining, saying no well, leading a team, owning an outcome, and growing people.
See the hats your team wears and grow people who see the whole, frame and check an agent's draft, and keep learning on the real work.
Find the question behind the request, explain so people can decide, and never give a bare no.
Four ideas to lead by: do less on purpose, improve in small steps, put the team first, and let people decide.
Own the outcome, measure the work together, help whoever falls behind, and grow people with goals and feedback.

For data managers, and anyone who leads data work across an organisation. A data manager's whole job: every area in one picture, a plan in stages, a case and its risks, everyone at the table, and small steps, measured.
46 requests on day one, touching every area. Listen, design it simple, and plan in stages that each work on their own.
A case on one page, risks said out loud, everyone at the table, and one list for all the work.
Services with customers, one map in the repository kept current, and a path for every provider.
A prototype in two weeks, a few measures that matter, one change a week, and a strategy reviewed every quarter.
